reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario concerns identity, permission, disclosure or valid values.
reviews.explanation: Inference control targets learning protected individual facts from aggregate answers. For example, subtracting a sum excluding one person from a sum including that person can reveal their value even when their row is hidden. Ordinary access control grants or denies actions, integrity validates data and encryption protects encoded content. The specified indirect-disclosure threat identifies inference control specifically.

evidence.quote: Authentication establishes identity; authorization/access control determines permitted actions. Encryption protects stored or transmitted content; integrity constraints restrict valid data; auditing records actions. A user who can view but cannot change a record has restricted access privileges. A view can restrict visible rows/columns, but its privilege and execution rules must support that restriction.
Inference control concerns learning protected individual facts indirectly from allowed aggregate answers.
Releasing SUM for a group and SUM for the same group excluding one known person may disclose that person's value by subtraction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This directly prevents disclosure of individual facts inferred from allowed aggregates.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Authorization alone does not prevent inference from otherwise allowed answers.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Integrity constrains valid data rather than indirect disclosure.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encryption does not stop an authorized user combining decrypted aggregate answers.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Inference control directly matches the threat.

reviews.answer_text: The rows-and-tables claim is false for the object-oriented model.
reviews.hint: Distinguish an object instance from its class, attribute values and persistent identity.
reviews.explanation: ADB01 distinguishes an OODBMS from relational rows and tables: its primary model is persistent objects with identity, state and behavior. ADB02 supports communication through methods and object references, and ADB03 supports reuse through inheritance. Relational presentation as tables is the contrasting model. Therefore A is the false statement; the source image is not needed to establish that conceptual distinction.

evidence.quote: An object combines identity, state and behavior. A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance. The object identifier (OID) distinguishes objects independently of their attribute values and remains stable over that object's lifetime. Two objects can have equal values and different identities; changing a name does not create a new identity.
It does not primarily present objects as rows and tables.
An object-relational DBMS extends a relational system with richer types; ORM maps programming objects into relational tables.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is false: an OODBMS primarily models persistent objects rather than relational rows and tables.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Presenting relations as tables describes the relational contrast correctly.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Object identity and method-based collaboration are supported object-model concepts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inheritance and reusable object behavior support reuse, so this is not the false statement.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: A is false, so none of the above cannot answer this negative question.

reviews.answer_text: Relation is not the defining concept of an OODBMS.
reviews.hint: Distinguish an object instance from its class, attribute values and persistent identity.
reviews.explanation: The defining unit of an object database is an object with identity, state and behavior. ADB01 explains both persistence beyond program execution and identifier stability throughout an object lifetime. Relation is instead the characteristic abstraction of the relational model. Thus C is the one statement that fails to describe an OODBMS.

evidence.quote: An object combines identity, state and behavior. A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance. The object identifier (OID) distinguishes objects independently of their attribute values and remains stable over that object's lifetime. Two objects can have equal values and different identities; changing a name does not create a new identity.
Persistence lets an object survive beyond the program execution that created it.
Complex CAD or multimedia structures can suit an object model, but many-to-many relationships alone do not require abandoning relational design.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

reviews.answer_text: Array is not an atom constructor.
reviews.hint: Classify the shape of a value separately from an operation that creates an instance.
reviews.explanation: ADB04 lists integer, real, Boolean and string as examples of basic atomic values. An array instead supplies indexed positions and is a collection constructor, even when a programming variable holds it as one value. Consequently integers, reals and strings fit the atom category while an array is the requested exception.

evidence.quote: In a common object model, an object is described by (OID,type constructor,state). An atom is one basic value, such as an integer, real, Boolean or string. A tuple constructor groups named component values into one structured record, such as (Street:'A',City:'B'). It is not a collection of records.
An array is not an atomic constructor merely because stored as one programming variable.
A set is an unordered collection without duplicates; a bag allows duplicates; a list has order; an array provides indexed positions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An integer is explicitly listed as a basic atomic value.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A real number is explicitly included among atomic values.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A string is a basic atomic value under the object-model convention used here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An array contains indexed positions and is a collection constructor rather than an atomic one.

reviews.answer_text: At transaction end, on commit or abort.
reviews.hint: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.
reviews.explanation: Rigorous 2PL retains both shared and exclusive locks until commit or abort, unlike basic 2PL, which permits release in its shrinking phase. FDB-style early release would allow interference before completion and would not meet rigorous locking. The locks are eventually released at the transaction boundary, so never is also false.

evidence.quote: Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until commit/abort. Rigorous 2PL retains both shared and exclusive locks until that point. Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock. It requires knowing the lock set and can reduce concurrency. Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Releasing locks at the beginning would not protect the transaction's later accesses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rigorous 2PL does not permit early release during ongoing transaction execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both shared and exclusive locks remain held until commit or abort ends the transaction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Locks are released at completion; the protocol does not hold them forever.

reviews.hint: Distinguish coordinated transaction outcome from concurrent access and local storage.
reviews.explanation: ADB39 explicitly links Oracle COMMIT_POINT_STRENGTH to choosing the commit point site in distributed transactions. This is a role in two-phase commit, which coordinates an atomic outcome among participants. It is not a setting for acquiring or releasing locks, nor for checkpoints that bound recovery work. Higher eligible strength is preferred for the commit point.

evidence.quote: Two-phase commit (2PC) first asks participants to prepare and durably promise they can commit. If all vote yes, the coordinator records commit durably and tells participants; otherwise it decides abort. A prepared participant must retain enough state to obey the final decision. Coordinator/communication failure can leave it in doubt and block progress until the decision is learned. Timeout after preparation is not permission to invent a commit or abort.
Oracle's COMMIT_POINT_STRENGTH helps choose the commit point site in its distributed transaction mechanism, with higher eligible strength preferred.
Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Commit-point strength selects an Oracle distributed-commit role within the two-phase commit mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Transaction locking controls concurrent access rather than choosing the distributed commit point site.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two-phase locking governs lock acquisition and release, not the distributed commit decision.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Checkpoints record recovery state and do not choose an Oracle commit point site.

A tuple constructor groups named component values into one structured record, such as (Street:'A',City:'B'). It is not a collection of records.

reviews.explanation: An inverse declaration connects two navigation directions of the same association, such as Department.employees and Employee.department. reviews.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
reviews.explanation: No-wait aborts immediately when a lock request conflicts, so transactions cannot form a lock-wait cycle and no age comparison is needed. Wait–die and wound–wait use relative transaction ages to decide who waits or aborts. Under the explicitly defined wait-wait alternative, every conflicting request may wait without a cycle-prevention restriction, so a transaction can hold one item while waiting for another in a cycle. That alternative therefore fails the deadlock-prevention requirement.

evidence.quote: Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles. A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp. A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock. Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle. Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.

A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Incorrect: unrestricted waiting permits a hold-and-wait cycle, so this defined policy does not prevent deadlock.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct: immediate abort on a conflicting request prevents lock waits without comparing ages.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incorrect: wound–wait compares requester and holder ages to choose waiting or aborting a younger holder.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect: wait–die compares ages to choose whether the requester waits or aborts.

assumptions: The interpretation of wait-wait is an explicit practice definition, not a claimed named protocol from the module.
Use the usual wait–die, wound–wait and no-wait rules.

reviews.hint: Distinguish operational transactions, analytical workloads and physical storage layout.
reviews.explanation: ADB41 defines columnar storage as grouping values by column, which avoids reading irrelevant columns and can improve compression for scans. Row-oriented storage instead groups each record's fields. Hierarchical and network models are logical representation alternatives rather than the physical column-oriented layout requested by the stem. Columnar layout alone does not determine the logical data model.

evidence.quote: OLTP handles frequent operational transactions, such as account updates; OLAP scans and summarizes large datasets for analysis. A warehouse integrates data for historical analysis, often through extraction, transformation and loading. These are workload tendencies: OLTP can retain history and warehouses can be updated.
Columnar storage groups values by column, reducing unnecessary column reads and aiding compression in scans; row-oriented storage groups each record's fields.
Neither physical layout alone determines whether the logical model is relational.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Row-wise grouping is row-oriented storage, the contrasting physical layout.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A hierarchy describes parent-child organization, not the columnar physical storage arrangement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Columnar storage groups the values of each column together.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A network model concerns linked records rather than this column-oriented physical layout.

reviews.hint: Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost.
reviews.explanation: Replication creates additional copies of selected data and can improve read locality by placing them near users. That directly satisfies the specified regional read-copy requirement. Distribution is the broader arrangement across sites, partitioning divides data into fragments, and NoSQL names a family of data models. Neither the broader architecture nor a model label specifically says that extra copies are created.

evidence.quote: Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once. Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups.
Partitioning improves locality and parallelism but alone creates no spare copy.
Flexible schema does not mean no schema rules, and NoSQL does not imply no transactions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Replication creates the required regional read copies.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NoSQL selects a model family and does not itself create copies.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Distribution is broader than the requested copy-creation policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Partitioning divides data; by itself it creates no spare copy.

reviews.hint: Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required.
reviews.explanation: Recovery is the specialized responsibility for restoring valid database state after failure or loss. Backups supply a separate stored copy, and available logs can restore later recoverable changes. The recovery-manager role therefore matches the question's generic component model. Buffer management caches working pages; transaction management is the broader parent responsibility, while the query engine processes requests. This makes no claim about MySQL's internal module names.

evidence.quote: Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts. Enforcing concurrency can deliberately abort work; it does not prevent every transaction failure. A system crash loses volatile memory while disks may survive. Media failure damages persistent storage and normally requires restoring a backup, then replaying available archived logs. Human mistakes may require point-in-time restoration before the bad committed operation.
Generic recovery-manager terminology should not be mistaken for an exact MySQL component specification.
A full backup copies the database to separate storage; scheduled backups plus archived logs support restoration to a chosen recoverable point.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Buffers cache working data and are not durable backup copies.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Transaction management is broader than the specialized restoration role requested.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A query engine processes queries rather than coordinating restoration.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The generic recovery role coordinates restoration using durable recovery resources.

reviews.answer_text: Association-rule mining: shoes ⇒ socks has confidence 0.75.
reviews.hint: Classify the actual content or pattern being analyzed rather than the storage product.
reviews.explanation: The observation is a conditional co-purchase pattern: among shoe purchases, socks also appear with probability 0.75. ADB43 defines this as the confidence of an association rule and explicitly distinguishes co-occurrence mining from clustering, classification and numeric regression. The store-layout decision uses that rule; it does not change the underlying technique or prove causation.

evidence.quote: An association rule X⇒Y describes co-occurrence. Support=count(X and Y)/N; confidence=count(X and Y)/count(X)=P(Y|X). If 75 of 100 shoe purchases include socks, confidence(shoes⇒socks)=0.75. This does not prove causation or specify support without total transaction count. Clustering groups similar cases without target labels; classification predicts categories and regression predicts numeric outcomes. Purchasing co-occurrence is association mining even when its result informs store layout.

choices.label: C

reviews.explanation: ADB02 describes encapsulation as grouping state with operations and controlling access to implementation details. A withdrawal method can enforce rules while hiding storage. B states the relevant information-hiding aspect. Combining classes, associating objects and defining subtype hierarchies are distinct activities; none describes the encapsulation boundary around an object's state and operations.

evidence.quote: Encapsulation groups state with operations and controls access to implementation details. Account.withdraw(amount) can enforce a balance rule while hiding its storage. Abstraction presents the relevant contract—what withdrawal does—without exposing how it is implemented. These ideas overlap in information hiding, but combining state and methods specifically describes encapsulation.
A class defines structure and behavior; an attribute describes state; a method implements an operation.
It is different from inheritance, which means an is-a relationship between types.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encapsulation groups an object's state and operations, not multiple classes into one entity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Encapsulation controls access to the internal representation behind the object's operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Links between objects are associations rather than encapsulation itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Superclass/subclass structure concerns inheritance rather than information-hiding boundaries.

reviews.answer_text: Inherit applicable attributes and behavior from a superclass.
reviews.hint: Distinguish the subtype relationship from use through a common interface.
reviews.explanation: ADB03 defines inheritance as deriving a subtype from a superclass and reusing its applicable attributes and behavior. B captures that idea. It does not inherently require multiple parents, dynamically create objects, or merely link unrelated objects. Those alternatives concern particular inheritance forms, instantiation or association rather than the general meaning of inheritance.

evidence.quote: Inheritance derives a subtype from a superclass, reusing applicable attributes and behavior. GraduateStudent is a Student; association instead says Student belongs to Department. EER teaches inherited attributes and relationships, while a programming object model also specifies behavior.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multiple parents are not a general requirement or guarantee of inheritance.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A subtype inherits applicable superclass attributes and behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dynamic object creation is instantiation, not the capability defined by inheritance.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Relationships between separate objects are associations rather than the is-a subtype relationship.

reviews.hint: Distinguish the subtype relationship from use through a common interface.
reviews.explanation: ADB03 illustrates Shape.area dispatching to Circle.area or Rectangle.area according to the actual object. The common operation name has different compatible implementations, which is polymorphism. Inheritance can provide the subtype structure used by that mechanism, but is not itself the runtime dispatch behavior. Abstraction and encapsulation concern contracts and implementation access instead.

evidence.quote: Subtype polymorphism lets a superclass/interface reference denote objects of different compatible subclasses. The same operation can dispatch to different implementations: Shape.area() calls Circle.area() or Rectangle.area() according to the actual object. This is not arbitrary conversion of an object into an unrelated class, nor dynamic class mutation. Inheritance establishes a subtype relationship; polymorphism uses that relationship through a common interface. If a question asks whether treating subclasses as a superclass is inheritance or polymorphism, clarify whether it asks about the structural prerequisite or the runtime use.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Polymorphism lets the same interface operation invoke different implementations for compatible object types.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Abstraction exposes a relevant contract rather than selecting among differing method implementations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Encapsulation controls internal access rather than providing type-dependent method dispatch.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inheritance supplies a structural subtype relation; polymorphism describes the differing implementations through a common interface.

reviews.hint: Separate the object boundary, the exposed contract and links between objects.
reviews.explanation: The question specifically asks about placing data and methods inside one entity. ADB02 identifies that grouping as encapsulation, along with controlled access to implementation details. Abstraction concerns what the contract exposes; inheritance derives compatible subtypes; polymorphism invokes different implementations through a common interface. None of those replaces the state-and-method grouping named in the stem.

evidence.quote: Encapsulation groups state with operations and controls access to implementation details. Account.withdraw(amount) can enforce a balance rule while hiding its storage. Abstraction presents the relevant contract—what withdrawal does—without exposing how it is implemented. These ideas overlap in information hiding, but combining state and methods specifically describes encapsulation.
It is different from inheritance, which means an is-a relationship between types.
A class defines structure and behavior; an attribute describes state; a method implements an operation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Inheritance derives a subtype and reuses superclass features rather than naming state/method grouping.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Polymorphism varies implementations behind a compatible common interface rather than grouping data and methods.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Abstraction presents a relevant contract; the specific grouping asked for is encapsulation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encapsulation packages state and operations together within the object boundary.

reviews.hint: Separate the object boundary, the exposed contract and links between objects.
reviews.explanation: ADB02 defines association as links between objects, commonly implemented with references, and describes methods invoking operations on other objects. C is the closest description of that collaboration. An association is not an is-a inheritance hierarchy, shared attribute definitions or duplication. For example, Student belonging to Department links objects without making either a subtype of the other.

evidence.quote: An association links objects, often through references; Department.employees can reference Employee objects. It is different from inheritance, which means an is-a relationship between types. Methods can invoke operations on other objects, supporting collaboration. A class defines structure and behavior; an attribute describes state; a method implements an operation. Do not treat each of these as an interchangeable name for the whole object.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Inheritance is an is-a relationship between types, distinct from association links between objects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Having similar attributes does not itself define an association between particular objects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Associations link objects and support their interactions or collaboration through references.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Association represents relationships rather than duplicated copies of the same database facts.

reviews.hint: Distinguish the subtype relationship from use through a common interface.
reviews.explanation: Subtype polymorphism allows a common superclass or interface reference to denote different compatible subclass objects. Dispatching area() according to whether the actual object is a Circle or Rectangle is that runtime use. Inheritance establishes the subtype relationship already given in the stem. Abstraction exposes a contract and encapsulation controls representation, but neither names this particular substitutable runtime dispatch.

evidence.quote: Subtype polymorphism lets a superclass/interface reference denote objects of different compatible subclasses. The same operation can dispatch to different implementations: Shape.area() calls Circle.area() or Rectangle.area() according to the actual object. This is not arbitrary conversion of an object into an unrelated class, nor dynamic class mutation. Inheritance establishes a subtype relationship; polymorphism uses that relationship through a common interface. If a question asks whether treating subclasses as a superclass is inheritance or polymorphism, clarify whether it asks about the structural prerequisite or the runtime use.
Encapsulation groups state with operations and controls access to implementation details.
These ideas overlap in information hiding, but combining state and methods specifically describes encapsulation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Using one superclass interface with subclass-specific dispatch is subtype polymorphism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Inheritance is the established structural prerequisite, not the runtime use requested.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Abstraction describes a contract rather than the dispatch behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encapsulation controls internal representation and access.

question_revision.original_stem:
Which concept in the object-oriented model ensures that objects of different classes can be
treated as objects of the same superclass?
question_revision.stem: Circle and Rectangle already inherit from Shape. A Shape reference can hold either object and dispatch area() to its actual implementation at runtime. Which concept names this common-interface use, rather than the structural subtype relationship?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Distinguish runtime use from the prerequisite inheritance relation.
assumptions: The subclasses are compatible subtypes; dynamic dispatch is supported.

reviews.answer_text: Hide implementation details while exposing a relevant contract.
reviews.hint: Separate the object boundary, the exposed contract and links between objects.
reviews.explanation: ADB02 explains abstraction through an operation's relevant contract: what withdrawal does is exposed without showing how storage implements it. B captures hiding those irrelevant internal details. This overlaps encapsulation, but abstraction emphasizes the view or contract. Combining classes, creating associations or listing class members is not its defining purpose.

evidence.quote: Encapsulation groups state with operations and controls access to implementation details. Account.withdraw(amount) can enforce a balance rule while hiding its storage. Abstraction presents the relevant contract—what withdrawal does—without exposing how it is implemented. These ideas overlap in information hiding, but combining state and methods specifically describes encapsulation.
EER teaches inherited attributes and relationships, while a programming object model also specifies behavior.
An association links objects, often through references; Department.employees can reference Employee objects.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Abstraction does not mean merging several classes into one entity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Abstraction exposes relevant behavior while hiding implementation details from the client view.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Establishing links between objects is association rather than abstraction's defining purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A class specifies attributes and behavior; abstraction chooses the relevant contract exposed to users.

reviews.answer_text: Use an object through a compatible superclass or interface type.
reviews.hint: Distinguish the subtype relationship from use through a common interface.
reviews.explanation: ADB03 allows a superclass or interface reference to denote compatible subclass objects. D is correct in that sense: the same object can be treated through its actual type and a compatible supertype. This does not permit arbitrary conversion to unrelated classes. Multiple inheritance, runtime class mutation and access to another object's private methods are different concepts and are not granted by polymorphism.

evidence.quote: Subtype polymorphism lets a superclass/interface reference denote objects of different compatible subclasses. The same operation can dispatch to different implementations: Shape.area() calls Circle.area() or Rectangle.area() according to the actual object. This is not arbitrary conversion of an object into an unrelated class, nor dynamic class mutation. Inheritance establishes a subtype relationship; polymorphism uses that relationship through a common interface. If a question asks whether treating subclasses as a superclass is inheritance or polymorphism, clarify whether it asks about the structural prerequisite or the runtime use.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Inheriting from multiple classes is multiple inheritance, not the operation described by polymorphism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Polymorphism does not change the actual class of an object dynamically.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Polymorphism does not bypass private-access restrictions on other objects.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An object can be used through compatible superclass/interface types; this does not mean arbitrary unrelated classes.

reviews.hint: Distinguish an object instance from its class, attribute values and persistent identity.
reviews.explanation: A class is the specification that defines attributes and operations for its instances, as ADB01 states. An object is an instance conforming to that specification. An attribute accounts for part of state and a method for one operation, but neither individually defines the whole structure and behavior of the object type.

evidence.quote: An object combines identity, state and behavior. A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance. The object identifier (OID) distinguishes objects independently of their attribute values and remains stable over that object's lifetime. Two objects can have equal values and different identities; changing a name does not create a new identity.
Complex CAD or multimedia structures can suit an object model, but many-to-many relationships alone do not require abandoning relational design.
An object-relational DBMS extends a relational system with richer types; ORM maps programming objects into relational tables.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A class specifies the structure and available operations for its object instances.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An object is one instance of the specification rather than the specification itself.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An attribute represents part of an object's state rather than its whole structure and behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A method implements an operation but does not alone define the complete object type.

reviews.answer_text: A. Eager replication; B. Lazy replication; C. Snapshot replication; D. Incremental replication
reviews.hint: Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost.
reviews.explanation: Eager and lazy replication differ in when propagation occurs relative to the acknowledgment or commit point. Snapshot and incremental replication differ in whether a copy or changes are transferred. These are legitimate replication dimensions and can coexist, so all four qualify. The question asks for recognized approaches rather than claiming that one policy is most prevalent or universally preferable.

evidence.quote: Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once. Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups.
Eager/synchronous replication coordinates propagation before the specified commit/acknowledgment point, increasing update latency.
Snapshot replication transfers a copy at intervals; incremental replication transfers changes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Eager replication coordinates propagation before the specified acknowledgment or commit point.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Lazy replication propagates changes later and can expose stale reads or require conflict handling.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Snapshot replication distributes a copy at intervals rather than necessarily sending each individual update.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incremental replication transfers changes and can coexist with a propagation-timing policy.

question_revision.original_stem: Which approach is commonly used for data replication in a distributed database system?
question_revision.stem: Which listed approaches are replication policies or transfer methods in distributed databases, allowing dimensions to coexist? Select all that apply.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Remove unsupported prevalence ranking and allow all stated approaches.
assumptions: Timing policies and transfer methods are not treated as mutually exclusive.

reviews.answer_text: A. B-tree index; B. Hash index; C. Bitmap index; D. Clustered index
reviews.hint: Match the predicate and workload to the access structure or reasons to choose a plan again.
reviews.explanation: B-tree indexes support ordered and range access, hash indexes target equality, and bitmap indexes can support analytic selections. Clustered storage places related rows close together and can reduce access work for suitable queries. Each approach can therefore help an appropriate workload. Space, maintenance and selectivity still matter, so accepting all four does not claim that every query benefits or that one design is universally best.

evidence.quote: B/B+ tree indexes support ordered and range predicates; hash indexes target equality; bitmap indexes can help some analytic selections. Clustered storage keeps related rows close. An index may reduce reads but adds space and update work; scanning can be faster when most rows qualify. Commonly useful is not a unique property of one index type.
Avoid universal rules that joins always beat subqueries, functions can never use indexes or more indexes always improve performance.
Updating statistics does not itself execute the query.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: B-tree indexes support selective ordered and range access for suitable queries.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hash indexes can accelerate equality lookups on the indexed key.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Bitmap indexes can accelerate suitable analytic selection workloads.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Clustered storage keeps related rows close and can reduce reads for appropriate access patterns.

question_revision.stem: Which listed index or clustered-storage approaches can speed a suitable query workload, without a claim that any always wins? Select all that apply.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Ask about workload-dependent usefulness rather than unsupported prevalence.
assumptions: Clustered index is interpreted as the clustered-storage access approach described in the note.

reviews.answer_text: Reconsider the plan using updated cost information or statistics.
reviews.hint: Match the predicate and workload to the access structure or reasons to choose a plan again.
reviews.explanation: ADB23 defines re-optimization as choosing a plan again when statistics, parameters or observed cardinalities suggest that the existing plan is unsuitable. B is the listed description of this cost reconsideration. Merely executing again with other values does not necessarily re-optimize, and changing the query language or redesigning the schema is not the definition.

evidence.quote: B/B+ tree indexes support ordered and range predicates; hash indexes target equality; bitmap indexes can help some analytic selections. Clustered storage keeps related rows close. An index may reduce reads but adds space and update work; scanning can be faster when most rows qualify. Commonly useful is not a unique property of one index type.
Re-optimization chooses a plan again when statistics, parameters or observed cardinalities suggest the old plan is unsuitable.
Updating statistics does not itself execute the query.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Re-execution with new parameters can reuse the same plan and is not inherently re-optimization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Updated statistics can change cost estimates and lead to choosing a new execution plan.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Changing query language is not required to reconsider an execution strategy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Schema reorganization is a design change rather than the definition of query re-optimization.

reviews.answer_text: A. Storing query results for future reuse
reviews.hint: Distinguish overlapping dependent operators, independent workers and reused cached objects.
reviews.explanation: Result caching stores a query's returned rows or answer for future reuse. It needs suitable invalidation when underlying data changes. Plan caching instead stores the execution strategy without its returned rows. Intermediate rows retained during one execution are materialization, while database metadata supports optimization. Naming the cached object makes result caching distinct from these other useful storage mechanisms.

evidence.quote: Parallel execution uses multiple workers, for example partitioned scans/joins, independent subplans or operator pipelines. Interleaving on one CPU is concurrency; simultaneous cores provide parallelism. Result caching reuses answers and needs invalidation when underlying data changes. Plan caching reuses an execution strategy, not the rows returned. Buffer caching keeps data pages; materialization retains intermediate rows. A vague query caching question must specify which of these it means.
Materialization stores an intermediate result before the next operator consumes it.
Catalog statistics include row/page counts, distinct values and distributions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This stores final query answers for future reuse.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Intermediate-row storage is materialization rather than final-answer caching.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Metadata supports optimization but is not the query's returned answer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Plan caching stores strategy rather than returned rows.

reviews.answer_text: C. Durable compensation records and pageLSNs preserve recovery progress, so already-installed actions can be skipped or safely redone as required.
reviews.hint: Trace durable recovery metadata and what progress survives a second crash.
reviews.explanation: ARIES records recovery progress in durable metadata. PageLSNs help determine whether a redo action is already installed, and compensation records preserve undo progress and its continuation. A second restart can therefore recover safely without assuming that the same undo and redo work lists recur. Lack of checkpoints may increase scanning work, but it does not erase this progress or make further recovery impossible.

evidence.quote: ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table. Analysis reconstructs active/loser transactions and dirty-page information. Redo repeats history, starting from the relevant earliest dirty-page update; pageLSNs help skip already-installed actions. Undo reverses loser transactions.
This makes recovery restartable: after a second crash, durable undo progress need not be undone again as if no progress occurred.
Compensation log records (CLRs) describe undo actions and their continuation information.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Durable progress can change the required work, so identical lists are not guaranteed.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Restartable recovery does not make inconsistency inevitable.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: PageLSNs and durable CLRs support safe continuation after repeated crashes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: ARIES can restart using surviving durable recovery metadata.

original_options.label: C

question_revision.stem: A system crashes again during ARIES recovery. Durable WAL, pageLSNs and compensation log records survive; storage is intact. No checkpoints were taken. Which statement correctly describes the second restart?

options.label: A
options.text: The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again

options.label: C
options.text: Durable compensation records and pageLSNs preserve recovery progress, so already-installed actions can be skipped or safely redone as required.

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: State ARIES and durable progress metadata; refine the progress claim.
assumptions: Stable log and pages survive both crashes.
Use ARIES analysis, redo and undo with durable CLRs.

reviews.answer_text: A. Abort all deadlocked transaction; D. Aborting one transaction at a time until the deadlock cycle is eliminated
reviews.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
reviews.explanation: Aborting all deadlocked transactions removes every participating wait, although it wastes work. A more selective complete method aborts a suitable victim, releases its locks and repeats until no cycles remain. An arbitrary half of the participants can leave a cycle intact, and one arbitrary victim may resolve only one of several independent cycles. The guarantee therefore applies to A and D.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp.
Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Removing all deadlocked participants eliminates all their cycles.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An arbitrary half may miss an entire remaining cycle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One victim need not break other independent cycles.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Repeated victim selection and graph checking continues until every cycle is gone.

transaction termination to eliminate deadlock. Which of the following transaction termination method
will clearly break the deadlock cycle

original_options.label: B

original_options.label: D

question_revision.stem: A lock wait-for graph may contain several independent deadlock cycles. Which termination methods guarantee eliminating all deadlock cycles? Assume each aborted transaction is undone and releases its locks. Select all that apply. 'Half' and 'single' mean arbitrary selections without a repeated cycle check.

options.label: B
options.text: Abort half of the deadlocked transaction

options.label: D
options.text: Aborting one transaction at a time until the deadlock cycle is eliminated

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specify multiple cycles and the guarantee being tested.
assumptions: The graph is rechecked after each victim in D.
No new transactions introduce cycles during the procedure.

reviews.answer_text: B. ARIES Recovery Algorithm; D. Deferred Database Modification
reviews.hint: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.
reviews.explanation: ARIES uses write-ahead logging and log-driven recovery metadata. Conventional logged deferred modification also uses recorded updates to redo committed effects that have not reached persistent pages. Both are log-based techniques under the stated model. Shadow paging instead preserves committed page mappings and installs a new map at commit. Recovery in multidatabase systems names an environment rather than one particular algorithm.

evidence.quote: Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.
ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table.
Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multidatabase recovery names an environment rather than identifying a particular log-based technique.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ARIES explicitly relies on WAL and logged recovery metadata.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shadow paging preserves page maps as an alternative to conventional log-based recovery.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Deferred modification can use a log to redo committed changes without undo.

question_revision.original_stem:
Which one of the following is categorized under Log based Recovery Techniques in
database?
question_revision.stem: Which listed techniques use transaction logs for recovery in the course model? Interpret deferred modification as the conventional logged, no-force deferred-update method. Select all that apply.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: State the deferred-update model and allow both logged techniques.
assumptions: Shadow paging means the page-map alternative to conventional log-based recovery.

reviews.answer_text: A. Immediate Update; C. ARIES Algorithm
reviews.hint: Determine whether uncommitted changes or unflushed committed changes may exist on persistent pages.
reviews.explanation: Steal allows uncommitted changes to reach persistent pages, creating a possible need for undo. No-force allows committed changes to remain buffered, creating a possible need for redo. Immediate update under the specified combined policy therefore needs both. ARIES also performs redo and then undoes losers. The specified deferred no-steal/no-force model needs redo but no undo, so it does not qualify.

evidence.quote: Steal permits a page with uncommitted changes to be written to disk; hence recovery may need undo. No-steal prevents those uncommitted effects reaching the persistent database. Force writes a transaction's updated data pages at commit; no-force permits committed dirty pages to remain buffered, hence recovery may need redo.

For the conventional page/log model: steal/no-force needs undo and redo; steal/force needs undo but no redo; no-steal/no-force needs redo but no undo; no-steal/force needs neither data-page undo nor redo after a system crash.
Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The stated steal/no-force policy requires undo and redo.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The specified deferred policy prevents persistent uncommitted effects and needs redo only.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: ARIES repeats history with redo and reverses losers with undo.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Two listed approaches use both actions.

question_revision.original_stem: Which recovery technique uses the undo/redo approach?
question_revision.stem: Which listed approaches use both undo and redo? Interpret Immediate Update as the conventional steal/no-force logged model and Deferred Update as no-steal/no-force; use the course's ARIES definition. Select all that apply.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specify buffer policies for the update methods.
assumptions: Use the conventional page/log recovery requirements.
ARIES repeats history before undoing losers.

reviews.answer_text: D. Recovery management component of DBMS
reviews.hint: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.
reviews.explanation: Atomicity requires all transaction effects or none. After failure, recovery can undo incomplete persistent changes to enforce that outcome. Transaction management is the broader subsystem containing these responsibilities, but the question asks for the specialized component. Concurrency control primarily addresses isolation, and application code alone cannot provide the DBMS's crash-recovery undo of partially persisted work.

evidence.quote: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.
Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward.
Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the parent subsystem, not the specialized failure-undo component requested.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Application logic alone does not provide durable crash undo.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrency control primarily enforces isolation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Recovery directly supports atomicity by undoing incomplete effects.

question_revision.stem: Which specific DBMS component directly handles undo of incomplete persistent changes after failure to support transaction atomicity? Choose the specialized component rather than its broader parent subsystem.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Ask for the specialized failure-undo responsibility.
assumptions: Transaction management is the broader subsystem; recovery is the specialized role.

reviews.answer_text:
C. Both improve the performance of the database by efficiently executing a

Relation sizes affect scans and intermediate work, network bandwidth affects data-transfer time, and replica placement changes which copies are available near the computation. All these inputs can alter a distributed strategy's cost. They are complementary considerations rather than competing names for one exclusively important factor.

evidence.quote: A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. Catalog statistics include row/page counts, distinct values and distributions. Selection with fraction s predicts s×N rows. For non-NULL equijoin keys, a common estimate is |R|×|S|/max(V(R,k),V(S,k)), assuming uniform values and containment of the smaller distinct-value domain within the larger. Adjust counts for NULLs; if either non-NULL input is empty, the result is zero. Skew, correlations or incomplete domain overlap can invalidate this estimate; known disjoint domains give zero matches.
Distributed processing decomposes a logical query, localizes referenced relations to fragments/replicas, chooses global placement/order and optimizes local subplans.
Include bytes moved, message latency, bandwidth and local work.

reviews.answer_text: Homogeneous systems use compatible DBMS technology; heterogeneous systems integrate differing DBMSs, models, schemas or interfaces.

Homogeneous sites need not have identical schemas or automatic replication. Heterogeneous integration requires explicit mappings for names, types and semantics, rather than assuming that common connectivity alone reconciles their meanings.

evidence.quote: A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system. A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites; a heterogeneous system integrates differing DBMSs, data models, schemas or interfaces. Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction. Same DBMS does not imply identical local schemas, automatic replication or immediate synchronization.
ODBC and JDBC provide connectivity interfaces; they do not automatically solve semantic differences or create one distributed transaction.
Heterogeneous design must reconcile naming, types, units, identifiers, query capabilities and transaction semantics.

reviews.answer_text: Fragmentation improves locality, manageable placement and parallelism by splitting data across useful site boundaries.
reviews.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 splits rows with predicates and columns with projections while preserving reconstruction through unions or key joins. This can place frequently used data near its consumers and allow independent work on pieces. Correct fragments must preserve completeness and required disjointness. Fragmentation alone creates no spare copy, so losing the only site containing a fragment still makes it unavailable.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Partitioning improves locality and parallelism but alone creates no spare copy.
Losing the only site containing a fragment makes that fragment unavailable, even while other sites continue.

reviews.answer_text: 2PL guarantees conflict serializability by separating lock acquisition from release.
reviews.hint: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.
reviews.explanation: During the growing phase a transaction acquires or upgrades locks; after it releases any lock, the shrinking phase forbids acquiring new ones. For well-formed transactions this guarantees conflict serializability. Basic 2PL can still deadlock and permit cascading aborts, so strict or conservative variants add different protections. It is distinct from distributed two-phase commit.

evidence.quote: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.
Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.
Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until commit/abort.

reviews.answer_text: WAL makes recovery information durable before its changed data pages, enabling safe undo/redo after crashes.
reviews.hint: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 requires needed update logs to reach stable storage before corresponding changed pages. A durable commit also forces required log records, including commit. Recovery can then use before-images for undo and after-images for redo if buffered data was lost. WAL orders durable writes; modifying an in-memory buffer before the log flush does not itself violate it.

evidence.quote: Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk. To acknowledge a durable commit, force the transaction's required log records, including its commit record, to stable storage. A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment.
Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.
Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward.

reviews.answer_text: A warehouse integrates historical data for analysis; an operational database serves frequent business transactions.
reviews.hint: Distinguish operational transactions, analytical workloads and physical storage layout.
reviews.explanation: ADB41 contrasts OLTP account updates and other frequent operational transactions with OLAP scans and summaries over large datasets. A warehouse commonly integrates sources through extraction, transformation and loading for historical analysis. choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The older requester causes the younger resource holder to abort and release its lock.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The protocol aborts the younger holder, not both transactions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is a prevention action based on ages, not a requirement to run cycle detection first.

reviews.answer_text: Conflicts between transactions are rare (read-heavy workloads)
reviews.hint: Consider conflicts, private work and validation costs, or lock-management overhead.
reviews.explanation: Optimistic concurrency control lets transactions read and compute privately, then validates overlapping read/write activity before publishing changes. When conflicts are rare, most work can commit without being discarded. Frequent competing writes or persistent read/write conflicts instead lead to costly retries. Strict timestamp completion describes a separate ordering constraint; it does not supply the low-conflict condition that makes optimistic execution suitable. Read-heavy activity is useful here only insofar as actual conflicts remain uncommon.

evidence.quote: Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries. It works well when conflicts are uncommon, but high contention wastes work on aborts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Incorrect: frequent competing writes cause validation failures and discarded work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Incorrect: persistent read/write conflicts increase retry costs rather than favoring optimistic execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Correct: rare conflicts allow most private work to validate and commit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect: a required completion order does not imply low contention; optimistic suitability depends on conflicts and retry cost.

reviews.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 explicitly names S→X an upgrade and X→S a downgrade. The stronger exclusive lock permits writing and can be granted only after conflicting other holders leave. Acquiring a new shared lock is initial acquisition rather than conversion, while releasing an exclusive lock is unlocking. Thus B alone names a lock upgrade.

evidence.quote: A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks. S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave. X→S is a downgrade. The lock manager decides requests; the lock table stores granted locks and waiting requests. One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy. No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Exclusive-to-shared weakens permissions and is a downgrade.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared-to-exclusive strengthens the held lock to permit writing, subject to compatibility.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No-lock-to-shared is initial acquisition, not conversion of an already held lock.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Exclusive-to-no-lock is release rather than upgrade.

reviews.answer_text: B. Initially A=B=100. During T2's transfer of 10 from A to B, T1 sums old A=100 and new B=110, returning 210 although the total-balance invariant is 200.
reviews.hint: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.
reviews.explanation: The transfer preserves the total balance at 200, but T1 combines the pre-transfer debit balance with the post-transfer credit balance. Its computed 100+110=210 is not a valid summary of a consistent state. This is an incorrect-summary anomaly. Dirty reading is defined by an uncommitted dependency, and lock failure or simultaneous deletion alone does not establish this mixed aggregate.

evidence.quote: Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.
Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions: a transfer moves 10 from A=100 to B=100; a sum reading old A=100 and new B=110 gets 210 instead of the invariant 200.
A single committed update from B=20 to B=50 does not alone prove an invalid summary of 90.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Concurrent deletion alone does not specify an inconsistent aggregate.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The mixed old/new balances yield 210 instead of the invariant 200.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Reading another transaction's uncommitted value defines a dirty read.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Failure to acquire locks concerns scheduling rather than this aggregate result.

options.text: Two transactions both delete the same record simultaneously

options.label: B
options.text: Initially A=B=100. During T2's transfer of 10 from A to B, T1 sums old A=100 and new B=110, returning 210 although the total-balance invariant is 200.

options.label: C
