reviews.answer_text: Compatible readers, with no writing under a shared lock.
reviews.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 permits multiple shared locks on one item, each for reading. Writing requires a suitable exclusive lock, which conflicts with other shared holders. Thus B describes shared-lock behavior in the basic lock-based model. Exclusive read/write ownership and multiple simultaneous writers are not shared locking; multiversion snapshot rules are a separate model.

evidence.quote: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.
One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.
No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: More than one transaction may hold compatible shared read locks on the same item.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared locks permit multiple readers but do not authorize writes under that lock mode.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Sole read/write ownership describes an exclusive lock.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shared locks do not allow multiple transactions to write simultaneously.

reviews.answer_text: The exclusive holder may read and write; conflicting access to that item is blocked.
reviews.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 permits an exclusive lock holder to read and write and makes that item’s X lock conflict with another S or X. C is correct in this basic model. Blocking all other access means conflicting access to the same item, not the entire database; locks on other items remain independent and multiversion systems can have additional snapshot-reader behavior.

evidence.quote: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.
One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.
S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Other transactions' shared reads conflict with an exclusive lock on the same item in this model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Two exclusive writers cannot hold compatible locks on the same item.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One holder can read/write the locked item while incompatible same-item accesses wait or abort.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Concurrent same-item shared readers conflict with this exclusive writer under the basic rules.

reviews.answer_text: Acquire or upgrade locks without releasing them.
reviews.hint: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.
reviews.explanation: ADB12 defines growing as the acquisition/upgrade phase and shrinking as the release/downgrade phase. Once any lock is released, no further acquisition is allowed. B therefore matches growing. Freely mixing acquisition and release would abandon the two-phase discipline that guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions.

evidence.quote: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.
Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.
Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Releasing locks belongs to shrinking rather than growing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Growing acquires or upgrades locks before any release occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Freely acquiring after release violates the defining 2PL phase restriction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Growing is precisely the phase in which lock requests may be made.

reviews.hint: Compare the transaction timestamp with the item's recorded read and write timestamps.
reviews.explanation: ADB15 assigns each transaction a timestamp and checks reads and writes against item read/write timestamps. These checks preserve timestamp order and can abort stale operations. Locking instead uses ownership compatibility, optimistic control validates private work and shadow paging concerns recovery page maps. Only C names the start-time ordering technique described.

evidence.quote: Assign each transaction TS(T). For item X track read_TS(X), the largest timestamp of a successful reader, and write_TS(X), that of its latest successful writer. A read by T aborts if TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and updates read_TS. A write aborts if TS(T)<read_TS(X) or TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and sets write_TS. These tests preserve timestamp order.
Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries.
Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Locking uses lock compatibility and protocols rather than being defined by transaction start-time ordering.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optimistic control validates private read/write sets rather than applying these timestamp-order tests.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Timestamp-based control orders valid conflicting operations using transaction timestamps.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shadow paging preserves committed page maps for recovery rather than ordering concurrent operations.

reviews.hint: Consider conflicts, private work and validation costs, or lock-management overhead.
reviews.explanation: ADB16 computes privately, validates and publishes, retrying failed validation. Low-conflict workloads let most work succeed; high write contention wastes computation on aborts. B states that criterion explicitly. Single-user systems do not need intertransaction conflict control, and OCC is not restricted to distributed transactions. Actual conflict frequency matters more than the read-heavy label alone.

evidence.quote: Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries. It works well when conflicts are uncommon, but high contention wastes work on aborts. Multiversion control keeps versions so a reader can use an appropriate snapshot. Snapshot isolation is not automatically serializable: concurrent writes to different rows can violate a shared invariant.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: High conflicts cause validation failures and repeated wasted work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rare conflicts allow optimistic private work to validate successfully with few retries.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A single-user setting lacks the concurrent conflict problem motivating this choice.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Optimistic control is not limited to distributed transaction environments.

reviews.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 requires a waiting cycle: participants hold resources needed by others and cannot make progress without a victim release or another intervention. Waiting for an unheld resource does not state such a cycle. Slow commit and simultaneous reads can occur without deadlock; compatible shared readers in particular need not block one another.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.
No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A resource held by no one does not create the stated circular hold-and-wait dependency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Each participant waits for another holder in a cycle, preventing independent progress.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A slow commit may still progress and need not form a waiting cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Compatible shared reads of the same data do not inherently deadlock.

reviews.hint: Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.
reviews.explanation: The requester is younger and the holder older. ADB14 makes that requester die in wait–die; only an older requester may wait for a younger holder. On retry the aborted transaction retains its original timestamp. Wounding a holder belongs to a different protocol, and both participants need not be aborted.

evidence.quote: A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.
Retain the original timestamp when restarting an aborted transaction so it gains relative priority as new transactions arrive.
The new guides reverse wait–die in several explanations; younger waits and older dies is incorrect for wait–die.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Wait–die aborts the younger requester when the needed resource is held by an older transaction.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The older holder keeps its resource; this protocol does not kill it for a younger requester.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Waiting is allowed for an older requester facing a younger holder, not this case.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The policy aborts the younger requester, not both participants.

reviews.answer_text: Abort the younger holder so the older requester can proceed.
reviews.hint: Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.
reviews.explanation: ADB14 says an older requester wounds a younger holder, while a younger requester waits. B is therefore the rule for the given ages. The protocol uses priority to prevent cycles rather than arbitrarily aborting both or handing the work to a new transaction. Any retry should preserve the original timestamp to reduce starvation.

evidence.quote: A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.
Retain the original timestamp when restarting an aborted transaction so it gains relative priority as new transactions arrive.
The new guides reverse wait–die in several explanations; younger waits and older dies is incorrect for wait–die.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An older requester wounds the younger holder rather than waiting under this policy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The younger holder is aborted, releasing the resource for the older requester.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Aborting both is unnecessary and is not the wound–wait rule.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No replacement transaction takes over; the older requester continues after the conflicting holder releases.

reviews.answer_text: Abort a transaction whose wait exceeds the configured limit.
reviews.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 defines timeout by excessive wait duration and warns it can mistake slow progress for deadlock. B matches that mechanism. Wait-for graphs detect cycles, conservative locking obtains all locks before execution and age priorities define wait–die/wound–wait decisions. Those are distinct policies rather than implementations of a time limit.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.
Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Graph analysis detects cycles rather than deciding from elapsed lock-wait time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Timeout aborts a waiting transaction after its configured wait limit is exceeded.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Preacquiring all locks is conservative locking rather than timeout handling.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Age-based priorities define other prevention policies, not an elapsed-wait threshold.

reviews.answer_text: Equivalent behavior to some serial execution, even if interleaved.
reviews.hint: Distinguish transaction ordering, conflict conditions and full execution equivalence.
reviews.explanation: ADB09 defines a serializable schedule as equivalent to a serial order while permitting interleaving. B matches when same result means the required full transaction equivalence, not an accidental equality of one final value. A describes a serial schedule, which is a special case but not the general definition. Commit simultaneity and disjoint tables are not required.

evidence.quote: A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively. A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial order; it may interleave transactions. Equality of one final value is insufficient evidence because different executions can accidentally coincide. Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes. Read/read pairs do not conflict.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This defines serial execution, a stricter special case that omits permitted serializable interleavings.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Serializable behavior is equivalent to some serial ordering; coincidental equality of one value alone is insufficient.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Simultaneous commits do not establish the required transaction-execution equivalence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Serializable transactions may access the same tables if their operations are correctly ordered.

reviews.hint: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 identifies S→X as an upgrade, possible only after incompatible other holders leave. It strengthens an existing read lock to permit writing. X→S is a downgrade, releasing all locks is transaction cleanup and granting compatible readers is shared acquisition. Only B names the requested conversion of a held lock.

evidence.quote: A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks. S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave. X→S is a downgrade. The lock manager decides requests; the lock table stores granted locks and waiting requests. One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy. No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Exclusive-to-shared is a downgrade rather than an upgrade.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared-to-exclusive strengthens the lock to permit writing when compatibility allows.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Removing locks is release rather than conversion to a stronger mode.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Granting compatible shared readers is not the upgrade of one existing lock.

reviews.answer_text: Indefinite postponement caused by repeated priority to other work.
reviews.hint: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 defines starvation as indefinite postponement while other transactions progress, without requiring a deadlock cycle. B states that repeated bypass precisely. Holding many locks can create contention but does not itself prove starvation. Storage exhaustion and premature commit are different failures, so neither supplies the scheduling-fairness definition.

evidence.quote: Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles. A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp. A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock. Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle. Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Holding many locks describes resource use rather than being perpetually denied execution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Repeated priority to others can indefinitely postpone the transaction while other work continues.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Running out of storage is a capacity failure rather than the defined scheduling starvation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Premature commit concerns transaction correctness rather than indefinite postponement.

reviews.hint: Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.
reviews.explanation: ADB17 first checks syntax and semantics and constructs a logical query representation, before optimization and evaluation. C groups those initial activities. Result delivery follows execution, while optimization needs an understood query to compare valid plans. The phase grouping is conventional, but the ordering dependency is explicit in the complete note.

evidence.quote: Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.
Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization.
DDL is not a mandatory stage before each SELECT, so authentication→DDL→DML permutations do not describe the processing sequence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Optimization follows understanding and representing the query rather than preceding it.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Evaluation executes a selected plan and is not the first processing activity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Parsing/translation establishes query meaning and logical representation before optimization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Results can be delivered only after the required evaluation produces them.

reviews.hint: Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.
reviews.explanation: ADB17 translates a query into relational algebra or a logical query tree for equivalent rewrites and plan selection. B names that logical representation. A particular engine may later compile execution code, but machine code, Python scripts and XML documents are not the general logical translation target taught here. Logical meaning precedes implementation-specific execution choices.

evidence.quote: Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.
A physical execution plan adds scan/index choices and algorithms.
A query tree has base relations at leaves and operators at internal nodes; a query graph emphasizes relations and predicates.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Machine code may be an implementation detail but is not the stated logical translation target.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Relational algebra represents the logical operations used for rewriting and planning.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Python scripts are not the general internal representation specified by the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: XML documents are not the defined general relational query representation.

reviews.answer_text: Overall execution cost under the chosen resource model.
reviews.hint: Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.
reviews.explanation: ADB19 measures candidate plans using I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. The aim is a suitable low-cost equivalent plan, not syntactic brevity or indiscriminate removal of joins and tables. Required tables and semantics must be preserved; even fewer operations do not necessarily imply lower runtime or resource cost.

evidence.quote: A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. Catalog statistics include row/page counts, distinct values and distributions. Selection with fraction s predicts s×N rows. For non-NULL equijoin keys, a common estimate is |R|×|S|/max(V(R,k),V(S,k)), assuming uniform values and containment of the smaller distinct-value domain within the larger. Adjust counts for NULLs; if either non-NULL input is empty, the result is zero. Skew, correlations or incomplete domain overlap can invalidate this estimate; known disjoint domains give zero matches.
Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans.
For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Required tables cannot be discarded merely to reduce the table count.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optimization compares equivalent plans using estimated time and resource costs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Join count alone ignores access paths, cardinalities and the cost of each join.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Short SQL text does not necessarily produce a cheaper execution plan.

reviews.answer_text: Disk I/O in the conventional local-disk query-cost model.
reviews.hint: Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.
reviews.explanation: ADB19 says disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples, matching the question’s typical teaching model. C includes both seek and transfer work. This is a contextual tendency, not a universal claim: CPU can dominate in-memory work and communication can dominate distributed plans. The answer should retain that local-disk qualification rather than extend it to every system.

evidence.quote: For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time. Five seeks at 5 ms plus ten blocks at 1 ms cost 35 ms. Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans. State the assumed cost objective before ranking strategies.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU can dominate in-memory work but is not the typical local-disk-model answer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Network cost can dominate distributed plans rather than the conventional local-disk model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Seek and transfer I/O often dominate the conventional disk-based cost model.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory allocation is not the dominant term specified for the textbook local-disk model.

reviews.hint: Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.
reviews.explanation: ADB19 adds seeks times seek duration to blocks times per-block transfer duration. Five seeks cost 5×5=25 ms and ten block transfers cost 10×1=10 ms. Their sum is 35 ms. The terms must be added, not multiplied together or considered separately; this is the supplied simple disk model rather than a measured universal query runtime.

evidence.quote: For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time. Five seeks at 5 ms plus ten blocks at 1 ms cost 35 ms. Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans. State the assumed cost objective before ranking strategies.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fifty does not equal the sum of 25 ms seeking and 10 ms transfer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Five times five plus ten times one gives 35 ms.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fifteen omits the correct five-seek multiplication.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Twenty-five counts only seek time and omits ten milliseconds of transfer.

reviews.answer_text: A valid recovered state preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects.
reviews.hint: Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required.
reviews.explanation: ADB26 defines restart recovery by preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects after failure. B matches the simple undo/redo teaching model. The detailed work depends on buffer policy and algorithm; not every committed update needs physical redo if already installed. Recovery does not reset the database to creation, last login or an empty replacement state.

evidence.quote: Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts. Enforcing concurrency can deliberately abort work; it does not prevent every transaction failure. A system crash loses volatile memory while disks may survive. Media failure damages persistent storage and normally requires restoring a backup, then replaying available archived logs. Human mistakes may require point-in-time restoration before the bad committed operation.
Restart recovery restores a valid database after a crash while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects.
In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Returning to creation would discard legitimate later durable commits.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Recovery preserves committed work and removes incomplete effects to restore valid state.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: User login time is not the transaction recovery boundary.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Emptying the database would destroy committed data rather than recover it.

reviews.hint: Classify the stated cause rather than inferring it from the observed symptom.
reviews.explanation: The stem directly identifies DBMS software bugs as the cause. That is a software error rather than failed hardware, a natural event or broken communication. ADB26 separates transaction/system/media failure concerns so the recovery resource can be chosen appropriately; an observed crash alone would not identify its cause, but this question explicitly supplies it.

evidence.quote: A software failure originates in erroneous program behavior, such as a logical programming defect, invalid operation or operating-system fault. A hardware failure originates in malfunctioning physical equipment; loss of disk contents is media failure. An accidental user deletion is human error even if the software executes the requested command correctly. Physical catastrophes such as fire can also cause failure. The observed symptom of a crash does not alone identify which cause occurred.
Generic recovery-manager terminology should not be mistaken for an exact MySQL component specification.
Enforcing concurrency can deliberately abort work; it does not prevent every transaction failure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The stated cause is faulty software behavior rather than a malfunctioning hardware component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No natural event is described; the prompt names a software bug.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Unexpected behavior caused by DBMS bugs is a software error.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No failed network connection is given as the cause of the behavior.

reviews.answer_text: B. Log records written to stable storage BEFORE corresponding data changes
reviews.hint: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.
reviews.explanation: The update log needed for recovery must be stable before the changed data page becomes persistent. B states that order under the question's explicit durable-write meaning. The buffer can be modified earlier. Data-before-log reverses the rule, waiting until after commit is not the required logging policy and checkpointing before every write is not a WAL requirement.

evidence.quote: Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk. To acknowledge a durable commit, force the transaction's required log records, including its commit record, to stable storage. A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment.
Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not.
Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The durable log must precede the changed page, not follow it.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: With the stated scope, stable logs precede corresponding durable page output.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Update logging is not deferred until after commit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: WAL does not require a checkpoint for every write.

question_revision.original_stem: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) requires:

original_options.label: A
original_options.text: Data written to disk before the log record

original_options.label: B
original_options.text: Log records written to stable storage BEFORE corresponding data changes

original_options.label: C
original_options.text: Logs written only after transaction commits

question_revision.stem: What does WAL require? In B, 'corresponding data changes' specifically means durable output of the changed data page; volatile buffer changes may occur earlier.

options.label: A
options.text: Data written to disk before the log record

options.label: B
options.text: Log records written to stable storage BEFORE corresponding data changes

options.label: C
options.text: Logs written only after transaction commits

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specify durable page-write scope.
assumptions: The question concerns stable log-before-data ordering, not all memory assignments.

reviews.answer_text: Reapply missing logged committed effects in the simple undo/redo model.
reviews.hint: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 uses redo to install logged after-images when necessary. B describes preserving committed work missing from disk pages in the simple teaching model. It does not mean re-running application side effects or blindly adding an amount twice. ARIES has a broader repeat-history phase before undo, but that does not make reversal, checkpoint creation or lock acquisition the definition of redo.

evidence.quote: Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not. In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.
In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo.
Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reversing incomplete changes is undo rather than redo.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Redo installs required logged effects missing from data pages, preserving committed work in the simple model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Checkpoint creation records recovery state rather than reapplying update after-images.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Locking may coordinate access but is not the operation of logged redo.

reviews.answer_text: Restore before-images of incomplete or aborted work.
reviews.hint: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 restores before-images when undoing incomplete effects, normally following that transaction’s updates backward. B states both the affected work and the supporting log information. Applying committed after-images is redo, forcing logs is a WAL durability action, and copying pages is part of a different update/recovery approach. None is the reversal operation itself.

evidence.quote: Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not. In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.
It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.
Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reapplying committed effects is the redo purpose in the simple model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Undo restores logged old values to remove incomplete or aborted transaction effects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Forcing the log supports durable ordering but does not itself reverse data changes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shadow-page copies preserve versions instead of defining logged before-image undo.

reviews.answer_text: Copy changed pages and atomically install the new durable map on commit.
reviews.hint: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.
reviews.explanation: ADB29 keeps the committed page map unchanged while modifications use new locations and a modified map. Commit durably installs the new root/map pointer after required pages are durable. B captures that preservation-and-switch mechanism. Timestamp ordering, mandatory per-transaction checkpoints and universal log-based rollback are not the defining shadow-paging steps.

evidence.quote: In-place update overwrites the original location. Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version. Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable. Before commit, a crash uses the old map. It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.
Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.
A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Timestamp ordering controls concurrent operations rather than defining shadow page-map replacement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Copy-on-write preserves originals and commit safely installs the new page map.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shadow paging is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, not mandatory logged rollback for all changes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A checkpoint every transaction is not the mechanism that preserves the old page map.

reviews.answer_text: A checkpoint supplies recovery state that avoids scanning all historical logs from the beginning.
reviews.hint: Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it.
reviews.explanation: ADB30 uses durable checkpoint state to avoid processing all old history. B describes that benefit if start means entering recovery analysis, not assuming every earlier update is irrelevant. Active transactions can span a checkpoint and fuzzy-checkpoint redo may require earlier log positions. A checkpoint is not a full backup, universal stop or lock grant.

evidence.quote: A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history. In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo. Active transactions can span the checkpoint, so their relevant earlier updates can still need undo. Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.
Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position.
A checkpoint is neither a full backup nor an automatic commit of active transactions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fuzzy checkpoints permit ongoing transactions, so stopping all work is not required.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Recorded recovery state provides a bounded starting point, while earlier necessary undo/redo must still be considered.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A checkpoint stores recovery metadata and is not a full separate database backup.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Checkpointing does not grant every active transaction exclusive locks.

reviews.answer_text: C. REDO only; D. NO UNDO / REDO
reviews.hint: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.
reviews.explanation: Because uncommitted changes have not reached the persistent database, crash recovery does not need to undo them there. No-force permits committed changes to remain uninstalled, so redo may be required. REDO only and NO UNDO / REDO express the same classification under the stated notation. Undo-only and undo/redo both assert an undo requirement that this deferred model avoids.

evidence.quote: Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.
Force writes a transaction's updated data pages at commit; no-force permits committed dirty pages to remain buffered, hence recovery may need redo.
Steal permits a page with uncommitted changes to be written to disk; hence recovery may need undo.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Usual deferred update does not require undo of uncommitted persistent database changes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Undo only gives the opposite recovery requirement from the usual deferred no-force model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: REDO only is the usual deferred-update recovery classification.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NO UNDO/REDO is another spelling of the same redo-only requirement.

question_revision.original_stem: Deferred Update strategy is classified as:
question_revision.stem: Under conventional deferred update with no-force, which recovery classifications describe the policy? Select all that apply. Interpret NO UNDO / REDO as 'no undo, redo required'.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: State no-force and the equivalent classification notation.
assumptions: Use the conventional persistent-page recovery model.
NO UNDO / REDO is not read as 'neither undo nor redo'.

reviews.hint: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.
reviews.explanation: ADB29 distinguishes where an update is written from when it may become persistent. Shadow/copy-on-write uses a new location while retaining the committed version, matching C. Immediate and deferred classify commit timing, not necessarily a separate location. In-place update overwrites the original location, which directly contradicts the preservation condition in the stem.

evidence.quote: In-place update overwrites the original location. Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version. Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable. Before commit, a crash uses the old map. It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.
Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.
Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Immediate update concerns allowing persistent changes before commit rather than requiring new locations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Deferred update concerns withholding uncommitted persistent effects rather than necessarily copying pages.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shadow/copy-on-write preserves the original and writes the changed value at a separate location.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: In-place update overwrites the original location rather than preserving it intact.

reviews.answer_text: C. Both old (before-image) AND new (after-image) values
reviews.hint: Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event.
reviews.explanation: The given UPDATE record contains both the old and new values. The old value supplies a before-image for undo, while the new value supplies an after-image for redo. Therefore the record stores both kinds of image. Real systems can use other physical or logical formats, but that variation does not alter the explicit conceptual record being examined here.

evidence.quote: A conceptual log can contain START, UPDATE(T,X,old,new), COMMIT, ABORT and END records. Before-images support undo; after-images support redo. Real systems may use physical or logical records, and need not log every read. COMMIT records successful completion; an ABORT record can mark the start of rollback rather than prove every undo step is complete.
Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward.
In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The given format includes old as well as new, so after-images alone are incomplete.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The format includes new as well as old, so before-images alone are incomplete.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both before-image and after-image fields are present.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Transaction identifiers alone omit the explicitly supplied value fields.

question_revision.original_stem: The transaction log stores which values for write operations?
question_revision.stem: In the course's conceptual transaction-log model supporting undo of incomplete changes and redo of committed changes, what value information does a write-operation record store?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specify the conceptual before/after-image log format.
assumptions: Use the explicit teaching format rather than a universal claim about real implementations.

reviews.answer_text: Logically related data across networked sites under coordinated database management.
reviews.hint: Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration.
reviews.explanation: ADB33 defines logically related data across networked sites managed as a coordinated system. B matches that architecture and its logical abstraction. Full replication is only one placement choice, not a defining requirement. A single powerful server is centralized, and generic web file storage does not establish coordinated database semantics across related distributed data.

evidence.quote: A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system. A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites; a heterogeneous system integrates differing DBMSs, data models, schemas or interfaces. Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction. Same DBMS does not imply identical local schemas, automatic replication or immediate synchronization.
Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.
Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A database confined to one server is centralized rather than distributed across networked sites.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Networked, logically related data with coordinated management fits the distributed database definition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A distributed database need not replicate every row at every network location.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Generic web file storage does not by itself establish coordinated distributed database management.

reviews.answer_text: The same compatible DBMS technology at the sites.
reviews.hint: Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration.
reviews.explanation: ADB33 defines homogeneity through compatible DBMS technology across sites. B is the listed form of that condition. It does not imply identical local schemas, replication or immediate synchronization. Different DBMSs describe heterogeneity, while removing the network or demanding full independence contradicts coordinated distributed management rather than defining homogeneity.

evidence.quote: A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system. A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites; a heterogeneous system integrates differing DBMSs, data models, schemas or interfaces. Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction. Same DBMS does not imply identical local schemas, automatic replication or immediate synchronization.
These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.
State how much schema, transaction and administrative autonomy local sites retain.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Different DBMS technologies characterize heterogeneous integration rather than homogeneity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The same DBMS software supplies the compatible database technology described by homogeneous systems.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Distributed sites need network communication for coordinated management.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Full local independence is an autonomy choice rather than a homogeneity requirement.

reviews.hint: Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration.
reviews.explanation: ADB33 explicitly names ODBC and JDBC as connectivity interfaces for differing systems. C therefore identifies the offered communication interfaces. They do not automatically reconcile schemas, units or transaction semantics and do not create a distributed transaction by themselves. Identical DBMS software is not heterogeneity, and generic LAN protocols do not replace database-level connectivity interfaces.

evidence.quote: Heterogeneous design must reconcile naming, types, units, identifiers, query capabilities and transaction semantics. ODBC and JDBC provide connectivity interfaces; they do not automatically solve semantic differences or create one distributed transaction. Locality, expansion and replicated availability are potential benefits. Distribution adds communication, coordination and security costs; a site outage can still make needed data unavailable if no usable replica exists.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Requiring the same DBMS removes the differing-engine situation rather than identifying its connectivity interfaces.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Direct SQL alone does not identify the generic cross-system connectivity standards named in the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: ODBC and JDBC provide generic database connectivity while semantic mappings remain necessary.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: LAN protocols alone do not supply the database API/interface compatibility described.

reviews.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 defines horizontal fragmentation by selecting row subsets with predicates. B directly states that operation. Column division is vertical fragmentation, and combining both dimensions is hybrid fragmentation. Schema names and geographic placement can influence a design, but are not the definition of what is split by horizontal fragmentation.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.
Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Splitting attributes is vertical rather than horizontal fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Horizontal fragmentation partitions rows according to stated predicates or criteria.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Splitting both dimensions combines horizontal and vertical operations in hybrid fragmentation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Schemas are not the row units divided by the defined horizontal operation.

reviews.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
reviews.explanation: Horizontal fragments contain selected subsets of the original relation’s rows. ADB36 reconstructs the relation by their union, assuming completeness and the intended overlap rules. Joining is used to align vertical column pieces by a key; intersection would keep only shared rows and difference would remove rows, so neither reconstructs all horizontal fragments.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces.
A relation is represented by a table of tuples.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Key joins reconstruct matching vertical column pieces, not ordinary horizontal row partitions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Union collects the rows from every complete horizontal fragment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Intersection keeps only common rows and would discard rows unique to individual fragments.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Difference removes rows instead of recombining all fragment members.

reviews.answer_text: Column subsets with a repeated key or row identifier.
reviews.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 splits a relation by columns and repeats a key or row identifier so the pieces can be joined without spurious matches. B describes that usual primary-key form. Rows are split horizontally; transaction counts and geography concern workload or placement rather than the attribute-level split defining vertical fragmentation. The shared identifier can be an appropriate equivalent key.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.
Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Row subsets define horizontal rather than vertical fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Vertical fragments contain column subsets plus a repeated identifier for reconstruction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrent transaction count is a workload property rather than the dimension being split.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Geographic placement does not define the column projection used for vertical fragments.

reviews.answer_text: Propagating each update across all copies adds maintenance overhead.
reviews.hint: Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost.
reviews.explanation: ADB37 says copies improve locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. B names that maintenance burden for full replication. Propagation timing may be synchronous or asynchronous, so the answer does not imply every copy is updated simultaneously. Fast reads are a possible benefit, and concurrency control becomes more involved rather than inherently simple.

evidence.quote: Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once. Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups.
Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.
Lazy/asynchronous replication propagates later and may expose stale reads or need conflict resolution.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Usable replicas can improve availability rather than inherently making it low.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: All copies must eventually reflect relevant updates, creating propagation and coordination overhead.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fast reads are a potential benefit rather than the listed disadvantage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Maintaining consistent copies does not inherently simplify concurrency control.

reviews.answer_text: Users query the logical relation without knowing its fragments.
reviews.hint: Identify exactly which detail is hidden from the user.
reviews.explanation: ADB35 defines fragmentation transparency as hiding the existence and reconstruction of fragments. B states that user-facing abstraction directly. It does not require literally only DBAs to know the implementation; developers and administrators may also need that knowledge. Exposing fragment tables or all fragmentation details to users would make fragmentation visible instead of transparent.

evidence.quote: Location transparency hides which site holds a named object. Fragmentation transparency hides the existence and reconstruction of fragments: users query the whole logical relation. Replication transparency hides which copy is used and how copies are maintained. The broad single-logical-database experience may involve all three.
If users explicitly name a fragment but need not specify its site, fragmentation is visible while location can remain transparent.
Hiding this column split from queries is fragmentation transparency; the split itself is a data-design operation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Showing all fragmentation details is the opposite of hiding them from ordinary queries.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Users operate on the whole logical relation without managing its fragment reconstruction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transparency describes the user abstraction, not exclusive knowledge restricted to DBAs alone.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Naming fragments separately exposes fragmentation rather than concealing it from the querying user.

reviews.answer_text: Middleware mediates between clients and independent database servers.
reviews.hint: Identify which tier submits, mediates or executes a request.
reviews.explanation: ADB34 lets middleware translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. C describes that mediating tier. The logical responsibility does not require exactly one physical machine in every implementation. Direct connections omit this mediator, universal server collaboration is a different arrangement, and one centralized server is not the stated distributed middleware design.

evidence.quote: In client/server architecture, clients submit requests while servers manage shared data, execute operations and enforce supported integrity/transaction rules. In collaborating-server designs, servers cooperate on subqueries and transactions. Middleware can translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Direct client-server links alone omit the middleware mediation that defines the requested architecture.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Every server need not participate in every query; relevant sources depend on the request.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A middleware tier mediates client requests across multiple independent database servers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: One centralized database server does not describe mediation across independent distributed servers.

reviews.hint: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 explicitly defines hybrid fragmentation as combining row and column splits in an appropriate order. B names those two operations. Replication changes copy placement, locking and timestamps control concurrent access, and client-server/middleware describe architecture responsibilities. They can coexist with hybrid fragmentation but are not its two component fragmentation techniques.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.
These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Full/no replication concerns copies rather than the row and column splits of hybrid fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hybrid fragmentation combines horizontal row subsets with vertical column subsets.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Locking and timestamps are concurrency-control mechanisms, not fragmentation types.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: These are architecture forms rather than the two data-fragmentation operations.

reviews.answer_text: Manage shared data, process requests and enforce supported transaction/integrity guarantees.
reviews.hint: Identify which tier submits, mediates or executes a request.
reviews.explanation: ADB34 assigns clients request submission and servers shared-data management, operation execution and supported integrity/transaction enforcement. C matches those responsibilities. User interfaces usually belong to clients, while initiating all connections, polling every client or caching all sessions for offline use are not the server role defined by this architecture. Guarantees still depend on supported mechanisms and correct application use.

evidence.quote: In client/server architecture, clients submit requests while servers manage shared data, execute operations and enforce supported integrity/transaction rules. In collaborating-server designs, servers cooperate on subqueries and transactions. Middleware can translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.
Calling a system heterogeneous does not require all sites to surrender autonomy or to copy every row everywhere.
A tightly integrated distributed system can present one global schema and shared control.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The user-facing GUI is normally a client responsibility rather than the database server's primary role.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The server need not initiate every connection or poll clients for every update.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shared-data management, query execution and supported integrity/transaction enforcement are server duties.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Caching every session for offline access is not the defined database-server responsibility.

reviews.hint: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.
reviews.explanation: ADB12 allows acquiring or upgrading locks during growing and releasing or downgrading them during shrinking. Once any lock is released, a transaction may not acquire another. A is therefore the phase described. Commit is a transaction event, validation belongs to optimistic control and shrinking has the opposite lock-release role.

evidence.quote: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.
Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.
Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Growing permits acquisitions and upgrades before any release starts.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Commit is not the general 2PL phase for new lock acquisition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Validation is an optimistic-control stage rather than the 2PL growing phase.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shrinking releases or downgrades locks and forbids acquiring new ones.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario concerns identity, permission, disclosure or valid values.
reviews.explanation: ADB24 explicitly describes a user allowed to view but not change a record as having restricted access privileges. That is authorization/access control. Integrity concerns valid values, availability concerns readiness for use and non-repudiation concerns attributable actions rather than whether a particular read or write is permitted. A matches the actual permission distinction.

evidence.quote: Authentication establishes identity; authorization/access control determines permitted actions. Encryption protects stored or transmitted content; integrity constraints restrict valid data; auditing records actions. A user who can view but cannot change a record has restricted access privileges. A view can restrict visible rows/columns, but its privilege and execution rules must support that restriction.
Neither property specifies which particular user has permission to change a database row; that is the separate authorization decision.
Availability concerns keeping services and resources accessible to their authorized users.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Access control grants reading while denying modification for the specified user.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Availability concerns service readiness rather than the read-versus-write privilege distinction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Non-repudiation does not define whether this user is authorized to modify a record.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Integrity restricts valid data states rather than assigning user-specific read/update permissions.

reviews.answer_text: Long-running log scans can make recovery expensive.
reviews.hint: Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it.
reviews.explanation: ADB30 warns that without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, a long-running system may scan expensive amounts of log history. Deferred update removes uncommitted persistent effects but does not remove that search problem. Page copying belongs to shadow approaches, while shared locks and serializability are independent concurrency concerns rather than consequences of omitting checkpoints.

evidence.quote: A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history. In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo. Active transactions can span the checkpoint, so their relevant earlier updates can still need undo. Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.
Without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, long-running systems may need expensive log scans; deferred update does not avoid that problem.
Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: High transaction volume and long uptime can produce costly recovery log scans without a valid boundary.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Frequent copy-on-write pages characterize shadow updating rather than the absence of checkpoints in deferred update.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Omitting checkpoints does not inherently prohibit shared locks.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: View serializability is a concurrency-order property, not inherently lost by this checkpoint omission.

reviews.answer_text: B. ARIES Recovery Algorithm; D. Deferred Database Modification
reviews.hint: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.
reviews.explanation: ARIES relies on WAL and log-driven analysis, redo and undo. Conventional logged deferred update also uses recorded updates for redo of committed work, with no undo of uncommitted persistent changes. Both therefore belong to the requested category. Shadow paging preserves old page mappings instead, while recovery in multidatabase systems names an environment rather than a particular log-based technique.

evidence.quote: Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.
ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table.
It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multidatabase recovery describes an environment rather than one specific recovery technique.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ARIES explicitly uses WAL and log-driven analysis, redo and undo.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shadow paging preserves committed page maps rather than being the conventional log-based technique.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Deferred modification can use logged changes for redo after commitment.

Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
Hiding this column split from queries is fragmentation transparency; the split itself is a data-design operation.

reviews.explanation: Language concatenation preserves order: each word of L₂ is followed by a word of L₁. The four products are ec, ed, fghc and fghd. evidence.quote: CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, star, reversal and intersection with a regular language. reviews.explanation: The clarified language contains equal numbers of a, b and c in that order. AUT26 identifies this family as context-sensitive but not context-free. evidence.quote: A context-sensitive rule αAβ→αγβ replaces A in context, with γ nonempty. Equivalently, noncontracting grammar presentations preserve/increase total length, with the isolated ε exception. The condition is on the complete sides, not an unrelated comparison |β|≥|α|.

A linear bounded automaton (LBA) is a TM with O(n) tape cells on length-n input; the standard CSL characterization uses nondeterministic LBAs. For aⁿbⁿcⁿ first verify a*b*c* order, repeatedly mark one unmarked a, b and c, and reject missing/excess symbols.
Thus every CSL is decidable.

If L is context-free, some p ensures each sufficiently long s∈L has s=uvxyz with |vxy|≤p, |vy|≥1 and uvⁱxyⁱz∈L for every i≥0. The two pieces v and y are pumped together; either may be empty, not both. A non-CFL proof must defeat every allowed decomposition.

For s=aᵖbᵖcᵖ, the window vxy cannot contain both an a and a c. Pumping affects at most two blocks and at least one count. Use i=0 or 2: the unaffected third block retains p while another count changes, or symbol order breaks. Hence aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not CFL.

choices.label: D

reviews.explanation: AUT03 defines Σⁿ as all words of length n, including Σ⁰={ε}; AUT01 identifies λ with ε. There is exactly one length-zero word, so its set is {λ}. evidence.quote: Σⁿ contains words of exactly n symbols; for |Σ|=k, |Σⁿ|=kⁿ, including Σ⁰={ε}. Σ*=⋃n≥0Σⁿ and Σ⁺=⋃n≥1Σⁿ. Over a nonempty alphabet, Σ⁺ excludes ε and Σ*=Σ⁺∪{ε}. Σ² over {a,b} is {aa,ab,ba,bb}.

For an arbitrary language L, L*=⋃n≥0Lⁿ and L⁺=LL*. Unlike alphabet positive closure, L⁺ can contain ε when ε∈L. ∅*={ε}, ∅⁺=∅, and {ε}*={ε}. Union means membership in either set; intersection requires the same word in both, not concatenation. Complement is Σ*−L and needs a fixed alphabet.

An alphabet Σ is a finite set of symbols. A word/string is a finite ordered sequence of symbols from Σ; a language is a set of words, L⊆Σ*. An empty word ε, also written λ, has length zero. The empty language ∅ contains no words; {ε} contains one.
Length counts occurrences, not distinct symbols: |caddba|=6, so |caddba|²=36.

A reverses the first strict inclusion: every regular language is context-free, but not every context-free language is regular. Therefore the three recursive-containment statements are all true.

SAT, coloring and tour-decision formulations illustrate meaningful problems, so the blanket denial of applications is also false.

evidence.quote: X is NP-hard if every A∈NP satisfies A≤pX. It need not belong to NP and can even be undecidable. X is NP-complete if X∈NP and X is NP-hard. Thus NP-complete languages lie inside NP and can be decided by finite exhaustive certificate search in exponential time; both statements can be true options. They are not known to require exponential time.

reviews.answer_text: The general halting problem is undecidable.
reviews.hint: Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances.
reviews.explanation: AUT30 constructs a machine that contradicts a hypothetical universal halting decider when run on its own description. Hence no decider answers halting correctly for all machine/input pairs. HALT is recognizable by simulation, but that process need not terminate on nonhalting instances; recognizing some yes-instances is not solving the general decision problem.

evidence.quote: HALT={⟨M,w⟩:M halts on w} is recognizable: simulate and accept upon any halt. Suppose a decider H determines halting. Construct D(x) that loops if H(x,x) says halt, otherwise halts. Running D on its own description contradicts H in both cases. Thus HALT is undecidable and witnesses RE beyond DECIDABLE. Its complement is not RE, or both recognizers would yield a decider.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Simulation recognizes halting yes-instances but no TM decides the general halting problem on every input.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The diagonal argument rules out a decider correct for all programs and inputs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Undecidability is the exact result proved by the halting diagonalization argument in AUT30.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: HALT concerns arbitrary computations and is not confined to regular languages or finite automata.

reviews.answer_text: Determining whether an arbitrary TM halts on its given input.
reviews.hint: Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances.
reviews.explanation: AUT30 proves HALT undecidable, directly matching D. The other choices describe ordinary finite mathematical computation: primality can test finitely many candidate divisors, a finite list can be sorted, and an exact finite linear system can be processed by elimination. Their cost can vary, but no general undecidability follows from those ordinary formulations.

evidence.quote: Thus HALT is undecidable and witnesses RE beyond DECIDABLE.
It is nevertheless context-sensitive: count the input in bounded workspace and test divisors.

Sorting a finite numeric list is a terminating computation. Quicksort, for example, chooses a pivot, partitions the other entries and recursively sorts the smaller sublists. Each recursive subproblem has fewer entries. A large running time does not make the task undecidable.

A finite linear system with exactly represented rational coefficients can be processed by Gaussian elimination and back substitution. Row exchanges handle unsuitable pivots; row reduction detects inconsistency or leaves free variables describing multiple solutions. These finite algebraic procedures differ from a general halting decider, which does not exist.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: For an integer, testing finitely many candidate divisors decides primality; AUT26 uses bounded divisor testing.

reviews.explanation: Renaming the symbols in aⁿbⁿcⁿ gives 0ⁿ1ⁿ2ⁿ without changing its classification. The three matched blocks form a context-sensitive language but not a context-free one. For s=aᵖbᵖcᵖ, the window vxy cannot contain both an a and a c. Pumping affects at most two blocks and at least one count. Use i=0 or 2: the unaffected third block retains p while another count changes, or symbol order breaks. Hence aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not CFL.

reviews.hint: Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations.
reviews.explanation: PSPACE consists of decision languages decidable with deterministic workspace bounded by a polynomial in input length. P and NP use polynomial-time definitions, whereas EXPTIME uses an exponential-time definition and contains PSPACE. Those containments do not change which class the workspace condition defines. Nor is it necessary to assume unresolved strict separations among the classes to identify the definition.

evidence.quote: PSPACE is ⋃kSPACE(nᵏ), using deterministic polynomial workspace. NP⊆PSPACE because candidate polynomial witnesses can be enumerated and checked one at a time, reusing memory; exponentially many candidates do not require retaining them all.

Complexity classes here contain decision languages. P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decidable languages; NP consists of nondeterministic polynomial-time decidable languages, equivalently polynomially verifiable yes-instances with polynomial-size certificates. A verifier must accept some certificate exactly for yes-inputs; no certificate may falsely establish a no-instance. NP means nondeterministic polynomial, not non-polynomial.
P⊆NP because a verifier can ignore its certificate and run the P algorithm. P=NP remains open; NP does not mean definitely hard or definitely outside P.

Use L⊆NL⊆P⊆NP⊆PSPACE⊆EXPTIME⊆EXPSPACE. Here L/NL use logarithmic workspace; EXPTIME is ⋃kTIME(2^(nᵏ)), an upper-bound class that also contains P, not a statement that every member requires exponential time.
P versus NP, NP versus PSPACE and PSPACE versus EXPTIME remain unresolved. coNP contains complements of NP languages; P⊆NP∩coNP, and NP=coNP is open.
