choices.explanation: P has a deterministic polynomial-time definition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NP has a nondeterministic polynomial-time or certificate-verification definition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: PSPACE has exactly the stated deterministic polynomial-workspace definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: EXPTIME contains PSPACE but is defined by a time bound.

reviews.explanation: AUT35 defines a polynomial reduction as a computable transformation preserving yes/no membership and explains how reducing a known hard problem to a new target proves target hardness. Thus reductions name the proof concept itself, while hierarchy, completeness and classes describe relationships or resulting properties rather than the transformation method.

evidence.quote: A≤pB means f is computable in polynomial time and x∈A iff f(x)∈B. Solving B then solves A, so B is at least as hard under this reduction. If B∈P then A∈P; if A is NP-hard then B is NP-hard. A∈P does not force B∈P, and the reduction alone does not place both problems in the same class. Polynomial reductions compose.

Reading the binary stars in A as the displayed concatenation separators, A is the third-power definition; C and D are the unions defining star and positive closure in AUT03.

evidence.quote: Σⁿ contains words of exactly n symbols; for |Σ|=k, |Σⁿ|=kⁿ, including Σ⁰={ε}. Σ*=⋃n≥0Σⁿ and Σ⁺=⋃n≥1Σⁿ. Over a nonempty alphabet, Σ⁺ excludes ε and Σ*=Σ⁺∪{ε}. Σ² over {a,b} is {aa,ab,ba,bb}.

For an arbitrary language L, L*=⋃n≥0Lⁿ and L⁺=LL*. Unlike alphabet positive closure, L⁺ can contain ε when ε∈L. ∅*={ε}, ∅⁺=∅, and {ε}*={ε}. Union means membership in either set; intersection requires the same word in both, not concatenation. Complement is Σ*−L and needs a fixed alphabet.

Concatenation xy writes x followed by y: cddc·ababb=cddcababb; order generally matters. εx=xε=x. Define x⁰=ε and xⁿ as n copies for n≥1. Reverse xᴿ reads symbols backward: caddba reverses to abddac; (xy)ᴿ=yᴿxᴿ and (xᴿ)ᴿ=x.
For languages, LM={xy:x∈L,y∈M}, L⁰={ε}, and Lⁿ⁺¹=LⁿL. Thus {e,fgh}{c,d}={ec,ed,fghc,fghd}; fghe is absent.

An alphabet Σ is a finite set of symbols. A word/string is a finite ordered sequence of symbols from Σ; a language is a set of words, L⊆Σ*. An empty word ε, also written λ, has length zero. The empty language ∅ contains no words; {ε} contains one.
Length counts occurrences, not distinct symbols: |caddba|=6, so |caddba|²=36.

reviews.explanation: A derivation is a sequence of production applications beginning at S and ending at a terminal word. Under the specified graph model, each application is one directed edge, so the root-to-terminal-vertex path records the complete sequence. A root alone gives only the start; degree and an immediate parent give local information. This graph is not being treated as a parse tree.

evidence.quote: In a context-free grammar (CFG) each production has one variable on the left, A→α with α∈(V∪Σ)*. The left side therefore also belongs to V∪Σ and its string closure; alternatives stating these weaker memberships can all be true. A sentential form is any string derived from S, including terminal-only sentences and S itself.

A leftmost derivation always replaces the leftmost variable; a rightmost one replaces the rightmost variable. This is not scanning the completed input in opposite directions. A complete parse tree has root S, internal variable nodes expanded by productions and terminal leaves, with ε leaves when that convention is used. Read the leaves left-to-right for the yielded word. The whole tree represents derivation structure; a path in a derivation graph is a different object.

reviews.explanation: Unary prime length is context-sensitive because bounded-workspace counting and divisor testing decide it. It is not regular by the prime-length pumping argument, and every unary CFL is regular; consequently it is not context-free. In contrast, aⁿbⁿ is context-free, while independently chosen a/b counts and any number of a followed by one b are regular. These weaker examples are excluded by the explicit non-CFL condition.

evidence.quote: a*b* and {aⁿb:n≥0} are regular. aⁿbⁿ is CFL but not regular. Over a two-symbol alphabet, wwᴿ is CFL, ww is not CFL; both are decidable. aⁿbⁿcⁿ is CSL but not CFL, and therefore decidable. Every finite language is regular. A stronger grammar or TM can still recognize any of these lower-family languages.

Unary prime length {aᵖ:p prime} is nonregular: choose prime q above pumping length p; if pump piece has length k≥1, using exponent q+1 gives length q(k+1), composite. Every unary CFL is regular, so this language is not CFL either. It is nevertheless context-sensitive: count the input in bounded workspace and test divisors. Therefore none of the bank's balanced-three-count, prime-length, palindrome or aⁿb examples is nonrecursive.

reviews.hint: Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations.
reviews.explanation: P is defined by deterministic polynomial-time decidability. NP, PSPACE and EXPTIME all contain P, so broad containment would not distinguish the choices. They have different defining bounds: nondeterministic polynomial time, deterministic polynomial workspace and deterministic exponential time, respectively. The explicit deterministic-time definition uniquely identifies P without assuming any unresolved separation among neighboring classes.

evidence.quote: Complexity classes here contain decision languages. P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decidable languages; NP consists of nondeterministic polynomial-time decidable languages, equivalently polynomially verifiable yes-instances with polynomial-size certificates. A verifier must accept some certificate exactly for yes-inputs; no certificate may falsely establish a no-instance. NP means nondeterministic polynomial, not non-polynomial.
P⊆NP because a verifier can ignore its certificate and run the P algorithm. P=NP remains open; NP does not mean definitely hard or definitely outside P.

Use L⊆NL⊆P⊆NP⊆PSPACE⊆EXPTIME⊆EXPSPACE. Here L/NL use logarithmic workspace; EXPTIME is ⋃kTIME(2^(nᵏ)), an upper-bound class that also contains P, not a statement that every member requires exponential time.
P versus NP, NP versus PSPACE and PSPACE versus EXPTIME remain unresolved. coNP contains complements of NP languages; P⊆NP∩coNP, and NP=coNP is open.

reviews.explanation: NP-completeness combines two conditions: the target problem belongs to NP, and every NP language reduces to it in polynomial time. That gives a precise meaning to hardest within NP under the chosen reductions. P, PSPACE and EXPTIME instead name resource-bounded language classes and do not by themselves assert that each member is hard for NP or belongs to NP.

evidence.quote: X is NP-hard if every A∈NP satisfies A≤pX. It need not belong to NP and can even be undecidable. X is NP-complete if X∈NP and X is NP-hard. Thus NP-complete languages lie inside NP and can be decided by finite exhaustive certificate search in exponential time; both statements can be true options. They are not known to require exponential time.

evidence.quote: An alphabet Σ is a finite set of symbols. A word/string is a finite ordered sequence of symbols from Σ; a language is a set of words, L⊆Σ*. An empty word ε, also written λ, has length zero. The empty language ∅ contains no words; {ε} contains one.
Length counts occurrences, not distinct symbols: |caddba|=6, so |caddba|²=36.

Concatenation xy writes x followed by y: cddc·ababb=cddcababb; order generally matters. εx=xε=x. Define x⁰=ε and xⁿ as n copies for n≥1. Reverse xᴿ reads symbols backward: caddba reverses to abddac; (xy)ᴿ=yᴿxᴿ and (xᴿ)ᴿ=x.
For languages, LM={xy:x∈L,y∈M}, L⁰={ε}, and Lⁿ⁺¹=LⁿL. Thus {e,fgh}{c,d}={ec,ed,fghc,fghd}; fghe is absent.
Σⁿ contains words of exactly n symbols; for |Σ|=k, |Σⁿ|=kⁿ, including Σ⁰={ε}. Σ*=⋃n≥0Σⁿ and Σ⁺=⋃n≥1Σⁿ. Over a nonempty alphabet, Σ⁺ excludes ε and Σ*=Σ⁺∪{ε}. Σ² over {a,b} is {aa,ab,ba,bb}.

For an arbitrary language L, L*=⋃n≥0Lⁿ and L⁺=LL*. Unlike alphabet positive closure, L⁺ can contain ε when ε∈L. ∅*={ε}, ∅⁺=∅, and {ε}*={ε}. Union means membership in either set; intersection requires the same word in both, not concatenation. Complement is Σ*−L and needs a fixed alphabet.

reviews.answer_text: DFA has one successor per state/symbol; NFA permits sets. They recognize the same languages.
reviews.hint: Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine.
reviews.explanation: AUT09 permits an NFA to have zero, one or several next states and states that DFA and NFA recognize exactly REG. Subset construction simulates the simultaneous NFA possibilities by DFA states.

evidence.quote: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is M=(Q,Σ,δ,q₀,F), with finite nonempty Q, start q₀∈Q, accepting set F⊆Q and total δ:Q×Σ→Q. Exactly one next state is specified per state/symbol pair; this does not mean the whole machine has one transition.
A nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) permits zero, one or many successors: δ:Q×Σ→𝒫(Q).
An NFA is not more expressive than a DFA: both recognize exactly REG. Nondeterminism can make a description smaller.

ε-closure(T) contains T and every state reachable through ε moves. Start the DFA at ε-closure({q₀}); for each current subset T and symbol a compute ε-closure(⋃q∈Tδ(q,a)). A subset accepts iff it intersects F.

reviews.answer_text: A proposed halting decider yields a program contradicting its own prediction.
reviews.hint: Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances.
reviews.explanation: AUT30 constructs D(x) to loop when H(x,x) predicts halting and to halt otherwise. On D’s own description, either prediction is contradicted. Therefore no general halting decider exists, although simulation recognizes halting instances.

evidence.quote: HALT={⟨M,w⟩:M halts on w} is recognizable: simulate and accept upon any halt. Suppose a decider H determines halting. Construct D(x) that loops if H(x,x) says halt, otherwise halts. Running D on its own description contradicts H in both cases. Thus HALT is undecidable and witnesses RE beyond DECIDABLE. Its complement is not RE, or both recognizers would yield a decider.

reviews.answer_text: REG⊊CFL⊊CSL⊊RE by increasing generative power; separating examples witness proper inclusions.

Separate precedence levels: E→E+T|T, T→T*F|F, F→id|(E). Multiplication binds inside T before addition at E, and left recursion encodes left association. Ambiguous grammar and inherently ambiguous language differ: another grammar may remove ambiguity.

choices.explanation: Infinite languages can have unambiguous grammars, so infinitude does not define ambiguity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Multiple parse trees for one generated word are the precise ambiguity criterion.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Left recursion can encode unambiguous left associativity; it does not alone prove ambiguity.

reviews.explanation: AUT21 defines a PDA by adding a stack to finite control, with its own alphabet and initial symbol. Finite automata already have states, accepting states and transition rules and process input. The distinguishing unbounded LIFO storage is what supports matched-count recognition beyond finite-state memory.

evidence.quote: A nondeterministic pushdown automaton (PDA) adds a stack to finite control: (Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q₀,Z₀,F). Its transition relation maps (state,input symbol or ε,stack top) to possible (new state,replacement stack string) pairs.

A stack is last-in, first-out: push adds an item at the top and pop removes the top item, so the most recently pushed item is removed first. A PDA accesses this top rather than an arbitrary interior position.

A queue is first-in, first-out: insertion at the rear and removal at the front returns the oldest waiting item. A linked list can implement a storage discipline, but the implementation container is different from the abstract push/pop or enqueue/dequeue access rule.

evidence.quote: A context-sensitive rule αAβ→αγβ replaces A in context, with γ nonempty. Equivalently, noncontracting grammar presentations preserve/increase total length, with the isolated ε exception. The condition is on the complete sides, not an unrelated comparison |β|≥|α|.

A linear bounded automaton (LBA) is a TM with O(n) tape cells on length-n input; the standard CSL characterization uses nondeterministic LBAs. For aⁿbⁿcⁿ first verify a*b*c* order, repeatedly mark one unmarked a, b and c, and reject missing/excess symbols.
Thus every CSL is decidable.

If L is context-free, some p ensures each sufficiently long s∈L has s=uvxyz with |vxy|≤p, |vy|≥1 and uvⁱxyⁱz∈L for every i≥0. The two pieces v and y are pumped together; either may be empty, not both. A non-CFL proof must defeat every allowed decomposition.

For s=aᵖbᵖcᵖ, the window vxy cannot contain both an a and a c. Pumping affects at most two blocks and at least one count. Use i=0 or 2: the unaffected third block retains p while another count changes, or symbol order breaks. Hence aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not CFL.

reviews.explanation: The Cook–Levin theorem made SAT the first problem proved NP-complete: its proof encodes an arbitrary nondeterministic polynomial-time computation as a Boolean formula. Hence every NP decision problem has a polynomial-time reduction to SAT. This starts the chain of later hardness reductions. A satisfying assignment can be checked in polynomial time. Whether SAT itself has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is unresolved, so neither membership in P nor such an algorithm is an established reason.

This starting point matters: once one NP-complete problem is available, later hardness proofs can reduce that known problem to a new target. Membership in NP remains a separate obligation. Checking a satisfying assignment is efficient; whether finding one is always polynomial-time remains unresolved.

reviews.explanation: COMP10 defines ambiguity by the existence of one terminal string with two different parse trees. This is exactly the property asked for. An unambiguous grammar excludes it. evidence.quote: A grammar is ambiguous if at least one terminal string has two different parse trees, equivalently two leftmost derivations. Merely changing derivation order on the same tree does not establish ambiguity. E→E+E|E*E|id allows different trees for id+id*id.

The dangling-else grammar permits else to attach to either nested if; a nearest-unmatched-if rule or grammar rewrite resolves it. Taking a leftmost derivation by itself does not resolve ambiguous interpretation.

reviews.explanation: A postfix evaluator reads operands before the operator that combines them. evidence.quote: A syntax-directed translation scheme embeds executable actions in productions; the actions run while translating a source program, not while generating the compiler. Attributes may compute types, values, AST pointers or generated code. The scheme defines an input-to-output translation, not merely an input language.

Create an identifier leaf with mkleaf(id,entry), a number with mkleaf(num,value), and an operator node with mknode(op,left,right). For a−4+c, construct +(−(a,4),c). Postorder traversal prints postfix: a 4 − c +. A stack evaluator pushes operands and pops right then left operands for an operator. Infix-to-postfix is useful for stack machines but not mandatory for all compilers.

choices.explanation: Infix-to-postfix supplies the required target order.

evidence.quote: A symbol table maps names or symbol identities to attributes: type, scope, width, storage offset, parameter signature, constant information or linkage. A hash table gives expected O(1) insertion/lookup with suitable hashing; a stack of scope tables supports lexical nesting. Search the nearest scope first, insert declarations in the current scope, and remove visibility when leaving it.

Scanning may intern a spelling first; semantic analysis determines the declaration and type. Implementations differ, so first interaction is conventional rather than universal. Not every punctuation token needs a symbol-table entry; literals may use a separate literal table. A hash table is an implementation, not the information’s semantic role.
Grouping characters into token classes is lexical analysis; grouping tokens into expressions and statements is syntax analysis.
Trees store hierarchical constructs, while a symbol table stores declaration metadata.

reviews.explanation: Three-address code is intermediate in the specified pipeline: analysis and optimization transform it before code generation lowers it further. Assembly, absolute machine code and VM bytecode can each be final target forms for an appropriate compiler. This pipeline-specific distinction does not assert that TAC could never be another translator’s target; it identifies the expressly stated intermediate role here.

evidence.quote: Code generation lowers checked IR to a target form. Instruction selection chooses target operations; register allocation chooses where values reside; scheduling orders instructions while respecting dependencies; storage layout assigns offsets and follows ABI requirements. Register assignment names actual physical registers after allocation decisions.

For t=a+b, a simple target could emit LOAD R1,a; LOAD R2,b; ADD R3,R1,R2; STORE t,R3. Other targets may combine loads with arithmetic or keep t in a register. Machine idioms, register availability and instruction order affect execution time.
IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused. It should be easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower.

Ordinary TAC arithmetic has at most one operation, two sources and one destination: t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=t2. Quadruples store (op,arg1,arg2,result); triples omit an explicit result field and refer to instruction positions. Indirect triples reference a separate ordering list, easing rearrangement. Trees describe expressions; DAGs share common subexpressions, while quadruples/triples are instruction-record structures.

reviews.explanation: COMP11 defines predictive parsing by choosing productions with lookahead without backtracking. evidence.quote: Top-down parsing starts with S and expands productions toward the input, usually constructing a leftmost derivation. Recursive descent typically has one procedure per nonterminal. A general recursive-descent implementation can backtrack; a predictive parser chooses a production using lookahead without backtracking. Bottom-up parsing starts from input and reduces toward S, constructing a rightmost derivation in reverse.

Operator-precedence parsing is a restricted bottom-up expression-parsing method using a stack and precedence relations. With a suitable expression grammar, the stack retains unfinished surrounding expressions while nested parentheses are processed.

evidence.quote: A basic block is a maximal straight-line instruction sequence entered at its beginning and exited at its end. Leaders are the first instruction, every jump target, and each instruction after a branch. Start a block at each leader and continue until the next leader.

A control-flow graph has blocks as vertices and possible next-block transfers as edges, including fall-through. A node D dominates N when every entry-to-N path passes through D. For an edge N→H where H dominates N, H is a loop header of a natural loop. This structure supports loop analysis. An expression DAG records value dependencies, not arbitrary control flow.

reviews.explanation: COMP26 explains that IR separates source analysis from target implementation, making optimizers and backends reusable. This directly supports reusing a machine-independent optimizer in different compilers. An IR can support allocation and analysis, but none of the other proposed improvements is its defining architectural function, nor does merely introducing IR guarantee them.

evidence.quote: IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused. It should be easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower.

Ordinary TAC arithmetic has at most one operation, two sources and one destination: t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=t2. Quadruples store (op,arg1,arg2,result); triples omit an explicit result field and refer to instruction positions. Indirect triples reference a separate ordering list, easing rearrangement. Trees describe expressions; DAGs share common subexpressions, while quadruples/triples are instruction-record structures.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Error reporting and recovery are shared compiler services, not the defining purpose of introducing IR.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Semantic analysis normally establishes source correctness before lowering; IR is not introduced chiefly to simplify it.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Separating source and target through IR enables reuse of machine-independent optimization passes.

reviews.explanation: The stated criterion divides optimizations into machine-dependent and machine-independent categories, giving two categories. Naming the criterion fixes the count without claiming a universal number of optimization types across all classifications.

evidence.quote: A loop-invariant expression has unchanged inputs during a loop. Hoist it to a preheader only when evaluation is safe on the paths where it will newly run. Induction variables change by a loop-invariant increment, such as i=i+1. For repeated t=4*i, maintain a running t increased by 4 when equivalent, reducing repeated multiplication.

Loop fusion or jamming combines loops with compatible bounds and safe dependence order. Unrolling replicates a body to reduce branch overhead and expose parallelism; handle remaining iterations and increased code size. Loop-invariant code motion, fusion, unrolling and strength reduction are different transformations. A finite taxonomy needs a criterion: machine dependent/independent versus local/global/loop are different classifications.

reviews.explanation: COMP12 writes immediate left recursion as A→Aα: the production’s left-hand nonterminal occurs first on its right-hand side. This is precisely the pattern in the question. Leftmost derivation chooses which nonterminal to expand; left factoring extracts a shared prefix. Neither is the repeated-leftmost-self-reference property.

evidence.quote:
Immediate left recursion has A→Aα. For A→Aα|β, where β does not start with A, introduce a new nonterminal A′ and use:
A→βA′
A′→αA′|ε
This preserves the generated language; tree shape changes, so semantic actions must preserve intended associativity. Indirect left recursion follows a cycle through other nonterminals and also needs removal for ordinary predictive descent.

Left factoring rewrites A→αβ|αγ using:
A→αA′
A′→β|γ
It postpones a choice until after the common prefix. It does not by itself remove ambiguity or guarantee LL(1). LR parsers can handle suitable left-recursive grammars; ordinary unmodified recursive descent can recurse forever before consuming input.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Leftmost derivation chooses the leftmost remaining nonterminal to rewrite, regardless of self-reference.

choices.label: B

evidence.quote: Panic-mode recovery skips input until a synchronizing token such as ; or } permits parsing to resume. Phrase-level recovery makes a local insertion/deletion. Report the location and cause while avoiding cascades of misleading diagnostics. Lexical, syntax and semantic phases each detect their own errors; error handling is a shared service.

Lex/flex generates scanners from patterns and actions. Yacc means Yet Another Compiler Compiler; Yacc/Bison generates parsers from grammar rules and semantic actions. reviews.explanation: COMP17 distinguishes a shift/reduce conflict, where shifting competes with reduction, from reduce/reduce, where two reductions compete. Both can arise in shift-reduce table construction. The combined option therefore answers the question completely; either individual conflict is a valid example but omits the other named kind.

evidence.quote: SLR(1) uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW(A) for reduction by a completed A production. Canonical LR(1) attaches context-specific lookahead to items. LALR(1) merges canonical states with the same LR(0) core, combining lookaheads; merging can introduce reduce/reduce conflicts. The standard grammar-class hierarchy is LR(0)⊆SLR(1)⊆LALR(1)⊆LR(1), with increasing capability and often table size.

A shift/reduce conflict offers both consuming a token and reducing; reduce/reduce offers two reductions. An SLR or LALR conflict does not by itself prove the grammar ambiguous. Canonical LR(1) handles LR(1) grammars, not every unambiguous CFG. Precedence and associativity can resolve suitable expression conflicts; changing parser names alone does not repair all ambiguity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Two competing reductions form a reduce/reduce conflict, one of the listed possible types.

choices.explanation: This aggregate includes both conflict types explicitly defined in COMP17.

reviews.explanation: COMP35 directly associates getReg with a simple code-generation algorithm. It selects operand/result registers for a TAC instruction before loads and the target operation are emitted and descriptors are updated. Code motion and general optimization serve other transformation purposes; intermediate code is the input representation here rather than the algorithm making the register choice.

evidence.quote: A register descriptor records which current values are held in a register. An address descriptor for a name records all current locations containing its value, possibly memory and multiple registers. A memory copy can become stale after a register-only assignment. These are code-generator bookkeeping structures, not source-language types.

A simple code-generation algorithm calls getReg for a TAC instruction to select operand/result registers, emits necessary loads, emits the operation, then updates descriptors. Prefer an already suitable register or a reusable dead operand; otherwise choose a spill victim and store any live value lacking another current copy. At a block exit, preserve values needed by successors.

Better register use can reduce loads/spills; target idioms affect instruction cost, and legal scheduling changes execution efficiency. evidence.quote: Code generation lowers checked IR to a target form. Instruction selection chooses target operations; register allocation chooses where values reside; scheduling orders instructions while respecting dependencies; storage layout assigns offsets and follows ABI requirements. Register assignment names actual physical registers after allocation decisions.

For t=a+b, a simple target could emit LOAD R1,a; LOAD R2,b; ADD R3,R1,R2; STORE t,R3. Other targets may combine loads with arithmetic or keep t in a register. Machine idioms, register availability and instruction order affect execution time.

evidence.quote: A syntax-directed translation scheme embeds executable actions in productions; the actions run while translating a source program, not while generating the compiler. Attributes may compute types, values, AST pointers or generated code. The scheme defines an input-to-output translation, not merely an input language.

Create an identifier leaf with mkleaf(id,entry), a number with mkleaf(num,value), and an operator node with mknode(op,left,right). For a−4+c, construct +(−(a,4),c). Postorder traversal prints postfix: a 4 − c +. A stack evaluator pushes operands and pops right then left operands for an operator. Infix-to-postfix is useful for stack machines but not mandatory for all compilers.

evidence.quote: Augment the grammar with S′→S. An LR(0) item A→α·β records progress through a production. CLOSURE(I) repeatedly adds B→·γ whenever an item has its dot before nonterminal B and B→γ is a production.

GOTO(I,X) moves the dot past X in every eligible item and takes closure. Start with CLOSURE({S′→·S}); repeatedly compute nonempty GOTO sets for all grammar symbols until no new state appears. The resulting set of item sets is the canonical collection, not GOTO itself.

evidence.quote: Bottom-up parsing starts from input and reduces toward S, constructing a rightmost derivation in reverse. A handle is a production RHS occurrence whose reduction is the next step of that reverse derivation. Not every substring matching a RHS is a handle in the current context.

Shift pushes the next input token and a state; reduce replaces a recognized RHS by its LHS and consults GOTO; accept recognizes completion; error reports an invalid situation. For A→XYZ, pop three grammar symbols and their states, expose state q, then push A and GOTO[q,A]. “Go” is not a separate standard shift-reduce ACTION, although GOTO is essential table machinery.

evidence.quote: LL, LR and recursive-descent parsers can all handle nested parentheses for suitable grammars. An explicit or implicit stack, not the LR label alone, supports unbounded nesting. Both LL and LR can use parsing tables. Deterministic LL/LR grammars must be unambiguous; a general ambiguous grammar requires rewriting, disambiguation policy or a generalized method such as GLR.

An operator grammar conventionally forbids adjacent nonterminals on a RHS and usually ε productions. Operator-precedence parsing additionally requires conflict-free precedence relations. Ordinary right-linear regular grammars also lack adjacent nonterminals, so that property alone does not uniquely identify the operator-grammar category. Regular patterns are chiefly lexical specifications; CFGs chiefly describe nested syntax.

A break is valid only in constructs allowed by the language; in C/C++ it can exit a loop or switch. A compiler may annotate an AST or create typed IR; there is no mandatory uniquely named output tree.

Dynamic checks depend on runtime values, such as some bounds and null checks. Static analysis can prove some accesses safe or faulty; “all memory errors cannot be statically checked” is too strong. Unreachable code is not universally a semantic error: some languages reject it in specified cases, others merely warn or optimize it away.

reviews.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.
reviews.explanation: The grammar permits multiple groupings of expressions such as id+id*id. An explicit precedence and associativity policy selects multiplication before addition and left association within each level. A parser may enforce this through declarations or a grammar rewrite. Lexical analysis and generic semantic checking do not themselves establish that policy, and taking a leftmost derivation does not remove the competing parse trees.

evidence.quote: A grammar is ambiguous if at least one terminal string has two different parse trees, equivalently two leftmost derivations. Merely changing derivation order on the same tree does not establish ambiguity. E→E+E|E*E|id allows different trees for id+id*id.

Use E→E+T|T, T→T*F|F, F→(E)|id to give * higher precedence and both operators left associativity. For subtraction, a−b−c then groups (a−b)−c. The dangling-else grammar permits else to attach to either nested if; a nearest-unmatched-if rule or grammar rewrite resolves it. Taking a leftmost derivation by itself does not resolve ambiguous interpretation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The stated policy selects the intended grouping.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Token recognition does not determine operator grouping.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Generic semantic checking supplies no stated grouping policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An ambiguous grammar can have multiple leftmost derivations.

question_revision.stem: For E→E+E|E*E|id, which technique resolves the ambiguity by requiring * to bind more tightly than + and both operators to associate left?

options.label: A

reviews.answer_text: Represent program meaning in a reusable, substantially platform-independent intermediate form.
reviews.hint: Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task.
reviews.explanation: COMP26 identifies separation of source analysis and target implementation as IR’s architectural purpose, allowing reuse across targets. C expresses that purpose best. Optimization and assembly generation are operations enabled by the representation, while a control-flow graph is one possible representation aspect. Platform independence is a design benefit here, not a claim that every IR has no target details.

evidence.quote: IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused. It should be easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower.

Ordinary TAC arithmetic has at most one operation, two sources and one destination: t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=t2. Quadruples store (op,arg1,arg2,result); triples omit an explicit result field and refer to instruction positions. Indirect triples reference a separate ordering list, easing rearrangement. Trees describe expressions; DAGs share common subexpressions, while quadruples/triples are instruction-record structures.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Optimization is enabled by IR, but it is not the general representational purpose distinguishing this choice.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Assembly is one possible later output; an IR need not be tied to assembly generation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A reusable representation of program semantics separates front-end meaning from target-specific implementation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Control-flow visualization is one possible use and does not exhaust the purpose of IR.

reviews.hint: Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases.
reviews.explanation: COMP06 describes converting regular expressions to an NFA and then a DFA. This is the automaton construction used for ordinary generated token recognizers. CFGs and pushdown machinery address nested syntax rather than the regular token-pattern mechanism; a Turing machine is not the specific scanner model in the supplied construction.

evidence.quote: A common generator pipeline is regular expressions → NFA using Thompson construction → DFA using subset construction; minimization is optional. For concatenation rs, connect r’s final state to s’s start by ε. Alternation introduces branching ε paths; star adds a way to skip and repeat the fragment.

The ε-closure of states includes those reachable by zero or more ε edges. A DFA state is a set of NFA states; its a-transition is ε-closure(move(set,a)). Start with the NFA start closure, repeatedly add unseen subsets, and mark subsets containing an NFA final state as accepting. Token identity and rule priority annotate accepting states; the empty subset acts as a dead state.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: NFA/DFA finite automata implement recognition of regular token patterns in the stated generator pipeline.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: CFGs describe nested syntactic structure rather than the regular scanner-automaton construction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Pushdown machinery adds a stack for context-free structure and is not the ordinary token-recognizer construction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A Turing machine is more general but is not the specific model used in this scanner-generation pipeline.

reviews.hint: Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases.
reviews.explanation: Classical regular expressions combine alternation, concatenation and repetition to specify ordinary token patterns. CFGs and BNF are production-based grammar descriptions and can also describe regular languages, so mere expressive capability would not distinguish them. An AST represents the analyzed structure of a particular program. The revised comparison asks for the direct pattern notation characterized by its operators, making regular expressions the specific answer.

evidence.quote:
Regular expressions use concatenation, alternation r|s, Kleene star r* for zero or more, and r+ for one or more. In a simplified alphabet, identifier = Letter(Letter|Digit)*; it permits a single letter and forbids a leading digit. A C-like ASCII rule commonly also allows underscore:
[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*
State the convention instead of claiming this covers every language’s identifiers.

Backus–Naur form, or BNF, is a notation for context-free grammar production rules. It describes how syntactic constructs are formed; it is different from an abstract syntax tree representing one particular program.
An AST omits grammar scaffolding and punctuation; expression operands are leaves and operators internal nodes. The parser can build either representation, depending on implementation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Regular expressions directly use the stated pattern-combination operators.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A CFG is a general production grammar, not the direct expression notation described.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: BNF is a notation for context-free productions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An AST represents one analyzed program structure rather than the permitted token patterns.

question_revision.original_stem: Which of the following is used to specify the lexical structure of a programming language?
question_revision.stem: Which listed notation directly specifies ordinary token patterns using alternation, concatenation and repetition, rather than a general production notation or a tree of one program?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: the specification notation or language model is explicit.
assumptions: Use the explicit scope and standard definitions stated in the clarified prompt.

reviews.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.
reviews.explanation: Operator-precedence parsing applies precedence relations to a suitable operator grammar to choose expression parsing actions. The question specifies that concrete method rather than asking for a universal cure for shift/reduce conflicts. Precedence parsing is a broader label, while LR and LL name larger parser families without supplying these particular relations. Therefore B is the most specific match to the described technique.

evidence.quote: An operator grammar conventionally forbids adjacent nonterminals on a RHS and usually ε productions. Operator-precedence parsing additionally requires conflict-free precedence relations.

Operator-precedence parsing is a restricted bottom-up expression-parsing method using a stack and precedence relations. With a suitable expression grammar, the stack retains unfinished surrounding expressions while nested parentheses are processed.

Top-down parsing starts with S and expands productions toward the input, usually constructing a leftmost derivation. Recursive descent typically has one procedure per nonterminal. A general recursive-descent implementation can backtrack; a predictive parser chooses a production using lookahead without backtracking. LL(1) scans Left to right, produces a Leftmost derivation and uses one lookahead token.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Precedence parsing is broader than the specific method requested.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Operator-precedence parsing directly names this method.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: LR alone does not specify the operator-precedence method.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: LL alone does not specify the operator-precedence method.

question_revision.original_stem: Which technique is used to resolve shift-reduce conflicts in parsing?
question_revision.stem: Which is the most specific listed name for a stack-based expression parsing method using pairwise operator-precedence relations in a suitable conflict-free operator grammar?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: terminology and the pipeline or parsing assumptions are made explicit.
assumptions: Ask for the specific operator-grammar method, not a generic precedence policy or all conflict resolution.

reviews.answer_text: LL Parsing; LR Parsing; Top-Down Parsing
reviews.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.
reviews.explanation: A nonrecursive LL parser consults a nonterminal/lookahead table to select productions. LR parsers use ACTION and GOTO tables for shifts, reductions and state changes. Table-driven predictive parsing is also a top-down implementation, so the broader D category applies. The stipulated ordinary recursive-descent alternative encodes decisions directly in procedures instead of consulting an explicit parsing table. Thus A, B and D are selected.

evidence.quote: Both LL and LR can use parsing tables.
A nonrecursive predictive parser stores grammar symbols on an explicit stack and consults a table.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Table-driven LL selects productions from lookahead entries.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: LR uses ACTION/GOTO tables.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The stipulated implementation encodes decisions in procedures rather than an explicit table.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Nonrecursive predictive parsing is a table-driven top-down method.

question_revision.original_stem: Which parsing technique uses a parsing table to determine the next action?
question_revision.stem: Which listed parsing categories have a standard table-driven implementation that uses lookahead to select the next parsing action? Select all that apply. For C, mean ordinary procedure-based recursive descent with choices encoded directly in code.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: terminology and the pipeline or parsing assumptions are made explicit.
assumptions: Ask about standard table-driven implementations, allowing overlapping broad categories.
C excludes an added explicit parsing-table mechanism.

reviews.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.
reviews.explanation: COMP12 states that suitable left-recursive grammars are handled by LR parsers, while ordinary unmodified recursive descent can recurse forever without consuming input. LL/top-down prediction generally needs left recursion removed first. This directly supports LR as the suitable choice, without claiming LR accepts every possible left-recursive grammar.

evidence.quote:
Immediate left recursion has A→Aα. For A→Aα|β, where β does not start with A, introduce a new nonterminal A′ and use:
A→βA′
A′→αA′|ε
This preserves the generated language; tree shape changes, so semantic actions must preserve intended associativity. Indirect left recursion follows a cycle through other nonterminals and also needs removal for ordinary predictive descent.

Left factoring rewrites A→αβ|αγ using:
A→αA′
A′→β|γ
It postpones a choice until after the common prefix. It does not by itself remove ambiguity or guarantee LL(1). LR parsers can handle suitable left-recursive grammars; ordinary unmodified recursive descent can recurse forever before consuming input.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary LL prediction requires eliminating left recursion rather than directly exploiting it.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: LR can directly handle suitable left-recursive grammar rules using bottom-up recognition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Unmodified recursive descent can recurse indefinitely before consuming input on a left-recursive rule.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ordinary top-down prediction needs recursion removal; it is not the suitable direct handling choice.

reviews.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.
reviews.explanation: A general ambiguous grammar has multiple parse trees for at least one input. Generalized LR parsing can handle those possibilities, whereas ordinary deterministic LL/LR grammars must be unambiguous. A separate disambiguation policy may still be needed to select intended meaning. Recursive descent and top-down labels alone do not provide a generalized multi-parse method, so the repaired GLR alternative uniquely answers the question.

evidence.quote: LL, LR and recursive-descent parsers can all handle nested parentheses for suitable grammars. An explicit or implicit stack, not the LR label alone, supports unbounded nesting. Both LL and LR can use parsing tables. Deterministic LL/LR grammars must be unambiguous; a general ambiguous grammar requires rewriting, disambiguation policy or a generalized method such as GLR.

An operator grammar conventionally forbids adjacent nonterminals on a RHS and usually ε productions. Operator-precedence parsing additionally requires conflict-free precedence relations. Ordinary right-linear regular grammars also lack adjacent nonterminals, so that property alone does not uniquely identify the operator-grammar category. Regular patterns are chiefly lexical specifications; CFGs chiefly describe nested syntax.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary deterministic LL requires an unambiguous predictive grammar.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: GLR is the generalized method identified for ambiguous grammars.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary recursive descent alone does not specify a generalized multi-parse algorithm.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Top-down direction alone does not handle general ambiguity.

question_revision.original_stem: Which parsing technique is more suitable for handling ambiguous grammars?
question_revision.stem: Which listed method can retain multiple parse possibilities for a general ambiguous CFG rather than requiring an ordinary deterministic LL/LR grammar?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: terminology and the pipeline or parsing assumptions are made explicit.
assumptions: Refine LR to its generalized GLR form.
Ask about handling multiple parses, not selecting one intended interpretation automatically.

reviews.hint: Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens.
reviews.explanation: COMP19 explicitly says a hash table offers expected constant-time insertion and lookup with suitable hashing. That makes it the conventional structure for the name-to-attribute mapping. A stack can organize nested scope tables, and lists are possible implementation choices, but the common keyed lookup structure asked for here is the hash table.

evidence.quote: A symbol table maps names or symbol identities to attributes: type, scope, width, storage offset, parameter signature, constant information or linkage. A hash table gives expected O(1) insertion/lookup with suitable hashing; a stack of scope tables supports lexical nesting. Search the nearest scope first, insert declarations in the current scope, and remove visibility when leaving it.

Scanning may intern a spelling first; semantic analysis determines the declaration and type. Implementations differ, so first interaction is conventional rather than universal. Not every punctuation token needs a symbol-table entry; literals may use a separate literal table. A hash table is an implementation, not the information’s semantic role.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A stack manages nested scope order, while the keyed mapping within a scope commonly uses hashing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FIFO queue order does not directly provide the keyed lookup role of a symbol table.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hashing commonly implements efficient name-to-attribute insertion and lookup.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A linked list is possible but does not provide the expected constant-time keyed lookup highlighted in COMP19.

reviews.hint: Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task.
reviews.explanation: COMP26 explains that IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused. This supports retargeting and portability across platforms. Introducing IR does not inherently promise faster compilation, better error detection or lower memory use; it can add processing stages and data structures while improving architecture.

evidence.quote: IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused. It should be easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower.

Ordinary TAC arithmetic has at most one operation, two sources and one destination: t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=t2. Quadruples store (op,arg1,arg2,result); triples omit an explicit result field and refer to instruction positions. Indirect triples reference a separate ordering list, easing rearrangement. Trees describe expressions; DAGs share common subexpressions, while quadruples/triples are instruction-record structures.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An extra representation and processing stage do not inherently guarantee faster compilation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Error detection depends on analyses and language rules; it is not the stated architectural advantage.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Separating source meaning from target lowering enables reuse across different platforms.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: IR introduces storage and does not guarantee reduced compiler memory consumption.

reviews.answer_text: It can generate intermediate code using parse-tree structure and semantic actions.
reviews.hint: Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information.
reviews.explanation: COMP25 says syntax-directed actions may compute types, values, AST pointers or generated code. Generating IR from grammatical structure is therefore a supported use of syntax-directed translation. B describes that standard use without limiting it to lexical analysis or a single final phase. Optimization may use other analyses, and syntax-directed translation is not defined solely by optimization.

evidence.quote: A syntax-directed translation scheme embeds executable actions in productions; the actions run while translating a source program, not while generating the compiler. Attributes may compute types, values, AST pointers or generated code. The scheme defines an input-to-output translation, not merely an input language.

Create an identifier leaf with mkleaf(id,entry), a number with mkleaf(num,value), and an operator node with mknode(op,left,right). For a−4+c, construct +(−(a,4),c). Postorder traversal prints postfix: a 4 − c +. A stack evaluator pushes operands and pops right then left operands for an operator. Infix-to-postfix is useful for stack machines but not mandatory for all compilers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Syntax-directed translation is tied to grammatical productions and semantic actions, not solely tokenization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Semantic actions associated with parsed structure can compute and emit an intermediate representation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Optimization is not the defining task; translation actions can construct many forms of semantic output.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It is not restricted to final target-code generation; actions can run while parsing and constructing IR.

reviews.hint: Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning.
reviews.explanation: COMP22 defines type inference as deriving types from constraints and explicitly calls it static even without explicit type annotations. Dynamic typing and runtime checks concern execution-time behavior. Operator overloading defines several meanings for an operation, but is not a replacement for the checking technique itself. Thus only type inference is the named static technique.

evidence.quote: A type checker verifies that operations are defined for their operands. In a simple strict language, integer mod requires two integers; array indexing requires an array and integer index; an if condition requires Boolean; assignment requires equal or convertible types. Function calls check parameter count and compatibility, and returns match result types.

Type inference derives types from constraints: if x is integer and + expects numeric operands, infer the expression type from numeric promotion rules. It is a static technique even without explicit annotations. Operator overloading supplies multiple operation meanings, not a substitute for type checking. int x="hello" is a type mismatch in ordinary C++/Java; division by zero and bounds violations are not automatically operand-type mismatches.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Type inference derives expression types from constraints before execution and is explicitly a static technique.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Dynamic typing does not name the requested before-execution type-inference technique.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Runtime type checking occurs during execution, so it is not static checking.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Overloading supplies operation meanings; COMP22 distinguishes it from type checking itself.

reviews.answer_text: Converting a floating-point value when assigning to an integer variable, where the language permits it.
reviews.hint: Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning.
reviews.explanation: COMP23 gives C++ int x=3.14 as an ordinary conversion yielding 3 when representable. That is the listed example of conversion, with the language caveat that Java needs a permitted cast and C++ brace initialization rejects narrowing. The remaining choices concern initialization, inference or undeclared names rather than converting one value type to another.

evidence.quote: Coercion is an implicit conversion permitted by the language; a cast requests an explicit conversion. Widening often increases representable range, but can still lose precision: Java int→float is widening although large integers round. Java int→long is exact. Narrowing can lose range or fractional information.

In C++ ordinary int x=3.14 converts to 3 when representable; it is not inherently a type error. int x{3.14} is rejected as narrowing. C++ floating-to-integer conversion discards the fraction and has undefined behavior if the truncated value is unrepresentable. Java ordinary double→int assignment needs a permitted explicit cast. Mixing char and int is ordinarily valid after promotion in C++/Java; do not import a fictitious universal ban.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Floating-to-integer assignment performs conversion where permitted; exact legality and precision loss depend on the language.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: First assigning to a variable is initialization or assignment, not inherently a change of value type.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Omitting an explicit declaration type may invoke inference; it does not itself convert a value.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An undeclared name is a name-resolution problem rather than an example of value conversion.

reviews.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.
reviews.explanation: COMP02 defines incremental compilation as recompiling affected fragments or dependent units after edits. This is the compiler category intended by updating code after source changes. The question’s only changed lines wording is simplified: real dependency tracking can require recompiling more than literal edited lines. Retargeting and one-pass organization describe different properties.

evidence.quote: A preprocessor handles directives such as file inclusion and macros. An assembler translates assembly to object code. A linker combines object files and libraries, resolves external symbols and performs relocation. A loader maps an executable into memory and starts it. Compilation alone does not necessarily produce a ready executable.

A cross-compiler runs on a host platform and generates code for a different target. Multiple targets require appropriate backends, not a special definition of cross-compilation. A retargetable compiler supports changing target descriptions. Incremental compilation recompiles affected fragments or dependent units after edits; it is more than literally replacing changed lines. One-pass versus multipass counts traversals, not supported targets.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Retargetable compilers support changing target descriptions rather than selecting edited source fragments.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One pass counts traversals of the program, not whether edits trigger selective recompilation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incremental compilation updates affected fragments after edits, accounting for dependencies beyond literal changed lines.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Parallelizing compilation is not the category defined by selective recompilation after source changes.

reviews.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.
reviews.explanation: Lexical analysis groups the source character sequence into lexemes and emits token categories with attributes. Syntax analysis instead combines already recognized tokens into larger grammatical structures such as expressions and statements. Specifying characters and token categories resolves the original mixture of lexical classification and parsing terminology. The generic interpretation and syntax labels do not describe the requested character-to-token phase.

evidence.quote: Grouping characters into token classes is lexical analysis; grouping tokens into expressions and statements is syntax analysis.
Trees store hierarchical constructs, while a symbol table stores declaration metadata.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Interpretation executes a representation rather than classifying lexemes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Lexical analysis turns character sequences into tokens.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Syntax analysis groups tokens into grammatical structures.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This syntax label concerns parsing rather than lexical classification.

question_revision.original_stem: What is the action of parsing the source program into proper syntactic classes?
question_revision.stem: Which compiler phase groups source characters into lexemes and classifies them as identifier, keyword, literal or operator tokens?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: terminology and the pipeline or parsing assumptions are made explicit.
assumptions: Classes means token classes formed from characters.

reviews.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.
reviews.explanation: A lexeme is the actual character sequence occurring in source text. A token is the category and optional attribute emitted for that occurrence, while a pattern defines which spellings are members of the category. For example, total is a lexeme classified as an identifier token. These are related but distinct objects, so the aggregate choice cannot name the concrete occurrence.

evidence.quote: A token is a category with optional attribute, such as (ID, symbol-entry) or (INT_LITERAL,42). A lexeme is the actual character sequence, such as total or 42. A pattern specifies which lexemes belong to a token class. The scanner emits an ordered token stream, not an unordered mathematical set.

Keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuation are token classes. Whitespace and comments are usually skipped while line/column positions are retained. In indentation-sensitive or newline-sensitive languages, layout can carry tokens. Parse-tree construction is a parser task; scanning can intern identifier spellings, but declaration scope and types need later analysis.
Grouping characters into token classes is lexical analysis; grouping tokens into expressions and statements is syntax analysis.
Trees store hierarchical constructs, while a symbol table stores declaration metadata.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A pattern describes possible spellings.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Lexeme names the actual matched source sequence.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Token names the category and optional attribute.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The three concepts are distinct, not synonymous.

reviews.hint: Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases.
reviews.explanation: The tokens are for, (, int, i, =, 0, ;, i, <=, 10, ;, i, ++, ). There are fourteen occurrences. Whitespace contributes nothing, but both semicolons and both parentheses count. Longest match makes <= and ++ one token each; it does not merge neighboring identifiers or discard repeated tokens. The repaired numerical option therefore gives the unique count.

evidence.quote: At each input position, choose the longest matching lexeme; if equal lengths match multiple flex rules, choose the earliest rule. Thus ifx is an identifier rather than if followed by x; <= and ++ are each one operator token.
There are 14 tokens, irrespective of spacing. The increment operator is one token.

reviews.hint: Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning.
reviews.explanation: A symbol table supplies the identities and attributes needed to resolve names and check types during semantic analysis. Type checking is an important activity using that information, but is not itself the requested data structure. Yacc and Lex generate parsers and scanners respectively. This narrower role makes the symbol table unique without denying that several components contribute to semantic processing.

evidence.quote: A symbol table maps names or symbol identities to attributes: type, scope, width, storage offset, parameter signature, constant information or linkage.
Lex/flex generates scanners from patterns and actions. Yacc means Yet Another Compiler Compiler; Yacc/Bison generates parsers from grammar rules and semantic actions.
A type checker verifies that operations are defined for their operands.

choices.explanation: Yacc is a parser generator.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Lex is a scanner generator.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The symbol table stores declaration and type metadata.

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: terminology and the pipeline or parsing assumptions are made explicit.
assumptions: Ask for a data structure rather than an activity or generator.

reviews.answer_text: AST annotated with resolved declarations and checked types
reviews.hint: Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens.
reviews.explanation: The stated implementation resolves names and checks types on an existing abstract syntax tree, so its result is that AST with semantic annotations. An unannotated syntax tree omits the newly checked information; language constructs is too generic to identify the representation. Tokens are the scanner’s earlier output. Other compilers may produce typed IR, but the question specifies the retained-tree implementation.

evidence.quote: Static checks occur before execution: type compatibility, duplicate declarations within a restricted scope, valid names, argument counts, return compatibility and control-flow placement. evidence.quote: A syntax-directed definition is a CFG with attributes on grammar symbols and semantic rules on productions. A compiler preserves language semantics, not the programmer’s unstated intention.

AOT compilation happens before execution; JIT compilation happens during execution and may use runtime profiles. Neither is universally faster; startup cost, optimization and workload matter.

reviews.answer_text: Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens; syntax analysis groups tokens into structures.
reviews.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.
reviews.explanation: COMP41 separates character-to-token classification from token-to-expression or statement structure. The scanner recognizes lexemes such as identifiers and operators and emits an ordered token stream. The parser checks how those tokens form grammatical constructs and can build a parse tree or AST; legal tokens can still appear in an illegal syntactic arrangement.

evidence.quote: A token is a category with optional attribute, such as (ID, symbol-entry) or (INT_LITERAL,42). A lexeme is the actual character sequence, such as total or 42. A pattern specifies which lexemes belong to a token class.
Keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuation are token classes. Whitespace and comments are usually skipped while line/column positions are retained.

reviews.answer_text: A symbol table associates names with declaration attributes.

evidence.quote: A symbol table maps names or symbol identities to attributes: type, scope, width, storage offset, parameter signature, constant information or linkage. A hash table gives expected O(1) insertion/lookup with suitable hashing; a stack of scope tables supports lexical nesting. Search the nearest scope first, insert declarations in the current scope, and remove visibility when leaving it.

Scanning may intern a spelling first; semantic analysis determines the declaration and type. Implementations differ, so first interaction is conventional rather than universal. Not every punctuation token needs a symbol-table entry; literals may use a separate literal table. A hash table is an implementation, not the information’s semantic role.

reviews.answer_text: Top-down expands from the start symbol; bottom-up reduces input toward it.
reviews.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.
reviews.explanation: COMP15 describes bottom-up recognition as input reductions toward S, reversing a rightmost derivation. COMP11 describes top-down expansion from S toward the input, normally a leftmost derivation.

evidence.quote: Top-down parsing starts with S and expands productions toward the input, usually constructing a leftmost derivation. Recursive descent typically has one procedure per nonterminal. A general recursive-descent implementation can backtrack; a predictive parser chooses a production using lookahead without backtracking. Bottom-up parsing starts from input and reduces toward S, constructing a rightmost derivation in reverse. A handle is a production RHS occurrence whose reduction is the next step of that reverse derivation. Not every substring matching a RHS is a handle in the current context.

reviews.answer_text: IR separates source analysis from target lowering and enables reuse.
reviews.hint: Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task.
reviews.explanation: COMP26 defines IR’s role in separating source meaning from target implementation so analysis, optimization and backends can be reused. ASTs, graphs, TAC and bytecode are possible forms. A useful IR is easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower; portability does not require every IR to exclude all target-specific details.

evidence.quote: IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused. It should be easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower.

Ordinary TAC arithmetic has at most one operation, two sources and one destination: t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=t2. Quadruples store (op,arg1,arg2,result); triples omit an explicit result field and refer to instruction positions. Indirect triples reference a separate ordering list, easing rearrangement. Trees describe expressions; DAGs share common subexpressions, while quadruples/triples are instruction-record structures.
