reviews.hint: Separate symbol replacement from position changes and apply the alphabet and modular direction.
reviews.explanation: SEC13 distinguishes symbol replacement from transposition and stresses that fixed mappings leak patterns. Increasing the nominal number of possible substitution alphabets does not erase language statistics. Classical substitution therefore serves teaching purposes rather than providing modern data protection, even if exhaustive enumeration of every alphabet is impractical.

evidence.quote: Substitution replaces symbols; transposition changes their positions. A monoalphabetic substitution preserves one mapping throughout the message and leaks frequency patterns despite a large nominal key space. Classical ciphers are teaching devices, not modern data protection.

reviews.answer_text: Vigenère applies position-dependent shifts from a key, so the same plaintext letter can encrypt differently at different positions. That reduces the single fixed-substitution frequency pattern, but repeating a short key still leaks periodic structure.
reviews.hint: Identify the cipher's unit, key structure and assumptions before judging its strength.
reviews.explanation: SEC14 gives C_i=(P_i+K_i) mod26 and explains the position dependence. The improvement is multiple mappings rather than a guarantee of modern security. A periodic key allows related positions to share the same shift, preserving exploitable regularities instead of eliminating statistical structure altogether.

evidence.quote: Vigenère repeats or otherwise supplies shifts K_i and computes C_i=(P_i+K_i) mod26. The same plaintext letter may encrypt differently by position; repeated short keys still leak periodic structure. An autokey scheme extends its initial key using message material.

reviews.answer_text: Steganography conceals the existence of a message by hiding it within other data. Encryption conceals its meaning by transforming plaintext into ciphertext. Cryptography also includes integrity/authenticity mechanisms; it is broader than just encryption.
reviews.hint: Trace message transformations and separate data, keys, algorithms and codebreaking.
reviews.explanation: SEC12 states the existence-versus-meaning distinction. Discovering a hidden carrier can defeat concealment of existence without necessarily revealing separately encrypted content. SEC20’s MAC/signature roles further explain why cryptography cannot be reduced to steganography or to secrecy of the communication’s existence.

evidence.quote: Plaintext is the original message, ciphertext its encrypted representation, a key is input to an algorithm, encryption computes C=E_k(P), and decryption recovers P=D_k(C). The five conventional symmetric ingredients are plaintext, encryption algorithm, secret key, ciphertext and decryption algorithm. Cryptanalysis seeks recovery or other breaks without the authorized secret; cryptology includes cryptography and cryptanalysis. Steganography hides that a message exists; encryption hides its meaning.
Verification checks origin/integrity under key-identity and key-custody assumptions; it does not conceal content.
A keyed MAC provides integrity and shared-secret authentication; both holders can create it, limiting third-party non-repudiation.

reviews.answer_text: For the conventional symmetric-encryption model, the five ingredients are plaintext, encryption algorithm, secret key, ciphertext and decryption algorithm. This is not a universal inventory of every cryptographic construction.
reviews.hint: Trace message transformations and separate data, keys, algorithms and codebreaking.
reviews.explanation: SEC12 supplies this five-part teaching model. Plaintext enters encryption with a secret key, producing ciphertext; decryption recovers the plaintext with the appropriate secret. The qualifier symmetric matters because signature, hash and public-key constructions have different interfaces and cannot all be reduced to this particular five-item list.

evidence.quote: Plaintext is the original message, ciphertext its encrypted representation, a key is input to an algorithm, encryption computes C=E_k(P), and decryption recovers P=D_k(C). The five conventional symmetric ingredients are plaintext, encryption algorithm, secret key, ciphertext and decryption algorithm. Cryptanalysis seeks recovery or other breaks without the authorized secret; cryptology includes cryptography and cryptanalysis. Steganography hides that a message exists; encryption hides its meaning.
Symmetric cryptography is not inherently less secure than public-key cryptography, and speed ratios are not fixed constants.
Security depends on algorithm, key size, randomness, mode and implementation.

reviews.answer_text: DES uses 64-bit data blocks and 56 effective key bits. A commonly stored 64-bit key representation includes eight parity bits, which do not increase the effective key space. DES has 16 Feistel rounds and is a legacy algorithm.
reviews.hint: Track block width, effective key bits and the transformations within a round.
reviews.explanation: SEC17 distinguishes block width from effective key entropy and parity representation. Calling DES a 64-bit-key security level would count nonsecret parity bits as independent choices. The note also warns that DES/triple DES are legacy mechanisms rather than recommendations for new protection.

evidence.quote: DES has a 64-bit block, 56 effective key bits (eight other bits serve parity), and 16 Feistel rounds. After initial permutation, each round computes L_i=R_(i-1), R_i=L_(i-1) XOR f(R_(i-1),K_i). Its right-half expansion makes 48 bits, XOR mixes a 48-bit subkey, eight S-boxes each map six bits to four, and permutation rearranges the 32 output bits. The outer S-box input bits select a row and the inner four select a column.
DES and triple DES are legacy algorithms, not choices for new protection.
Triple DES repeats DES operations but does not provide 168-bit effective security merely because three 56-bit keys are supplied.

reviews.answer_text: DES splits its 64-bit block into two 32-bit halves for Feistel rounds: L_i=R_(i-1) and R_i=L_(i-1) XOR f(R_(i-1),K_i). This permits inversion using the same overall structure with reversed round keys, without requiring f to be invertible.
reviews.hint: Track block width, effective key bits and the transformations within a round.
reviews.explanation: SEC17 gives the round equations and inversion property. The old right half becomes the new left half; the old left is mixed with a keyed transformation of the old right. Keeping those relationships allows recovery by reversing the key order rather than independently inverting every S-box/transformation.

evidence.quote: DES has a 64-bit block, 56 effective key bits (eight other bits serve parity), and 16 Feistel rounds. After initial permutation, each round computes L_i=R_(i-1), R_i=L_(i-1) XOR f(R_(i-1),K_i). Its right-half expansion makes 48 bits, XOR mixes a 48-bit subkey, eight S-boxes each map six bits to four, and permutation rearranges the 32 output bits. The outer S-box input bits select a row and the inner four select a column.
Feistel inversion uses the same overall structure with reversed round keys; f need not itself be invertible.
Triple DES repeats DES operations but does not provide 168-bit effective security merely because three 56-bit keys are supplied.

reviews.answer_text: DES S-boxes provide nonlinear substitution: each of eight boxes maps six input bits to four output bits. The outer two bits select the row and the inner four select the column, giving 32 output bits altogether.
reviews.hint: Track block width, effective key bits and the transformations within a round.
reviews.explanation: SEC17 identifies the S-boxes as the nonlinear component that resists simple linear descriptions. Their six-to-four mapping follows expansion and key mixing, then a permutation rearranges the outputs. They are not merely a reversible bit permutation; Feistel structure supplies overall invertibility without requiring each S-box itself to be invertible.

evidence.quote: DES has a 64-bit block, 56 effective key bits (eight other bits serve parity), and 16 Feistel rounds. After initial permutation, each round computes L_i=R_(i-1), R_i=L_(i-1) XOR f(R_(i-1),K_i). Its right-half expansion makes 48 bits, XOR mixes a 48-bit subkey, eight S-boxes each map six bits to four, and permutation rearranges the 32 output bits. The outer S-box input bits select a row and the inner four select a column.
The nonlinear S-boxes resist simple linear descriptions.
Feistel inversion uses the same overall structure with reversed round keys; f need not itself be invertible.

reviews.answer_text: Textbook RSA encrypts c=m^e mod n and decrypts m=c^d mod n, for 0≤m<n. Here n=pq, e is coprime to φ=(p−1)(q−1), and d=e^−1 mod φ. Real RSA additionally requires appropriate standardized padding.
reviews.hint: Check key-generation conditions as well as modular arithmetic.
reviews.explanation: SEC19 supplies the formulas and their key-generation preconditions. The modular-inverse condition is necessary for a valid key pair, so arbitrary e values are not acceptable. These arithmetic expressions teach RSA operations; raw unpadded modular exponentiation is not a complete secure deployment recipe.

evidence.quote: For textbook RSA choose distinct primes p,q; n=pq and φ=(p-1)(q-1). Choose 1<e<φ with gcd(e,φ)=1, then compute d=e^-1 modφ. Public key is (n,e), private includes d. Encrypt 0≤m<n by c=m^e modn; decrypt by m=c^d modn. Use modular repeated squaring for large exponents. Real RSA requires appropriate standardized padding; raw arithmetic is not a secure deployment recipe.
With p=3,q=13,e=3,m=5, 5^3 mod39=8 arithmetically, but gcd(3,24)=3, so e has no inverse and this is not a valid RSA key.
State the defect rather than endorsing a working encryption/decryption pair.

reviews.hint: Check key-generation conditions as well as modular arithmetic.
reviews.explanation: The exponent must be greater than one, below 108 and coprime to 108. Testing candidates in increasing order, 2 shares factor 2, 3 shares factor 3 and 4 shares factor 2 with 108. Five shares neither prime factor of 108, so gcd(5,108)=1. It is therefore the smallest admissible exponent. Other values can also be admissible, but the explicit smallest-value rule makes this open-ended answer unique.

evidence.quote: For textbook RSA choose distinct primes p,q; n=pq and φ=(p-1)(q-1). Choose 1<e<φ with gcd(e,φ)=1, then compute d=e^-1 modφ. Public key is (n,e), private includes d. Encrypt 0≤m<n by c=m^e modn; decrypt by m=c^d modn. Use modular repeated squaring for large exponents. Real RSA requires appropriate standardized padding; raw arithmetic is not a secure deployment recipe.
With p=7,q=19, n=133 and φ=108, e=5 is the smallest admissible e>1, but 7 and other coprime choices also work.
With p=3,q=13,e=3,m=5, 5^3 mod39=8 arithmetically, but gcd(3,24)=3, so e has no inverse and this is not a valid RSA key.

question_revision.original_stem: In RSA key generation with p=7, q=19, and Φ=108, which value of 'e' is chosen?
question_revision.stem: In textbook RSA key generation with p=7, q=19 and φ=108, choose the smallest integer e greater than 1 satisfying 1<e<φ and gcd(e,φ)=1. What is e?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Added the exponent-selection policy while retaining the open-ended format.
assumptions: Use textbook RSA and choose the smallest admissible integer exponent greater than one.

reviews.answer_text: Playfair is a digraph substitution cipher using a keyed 5×5 letter grid, commonly combining I and J into one cell. It encrypts pairs by same-row, same-column or rectangle rules; fillers and padding must be specified.
reviews.hint: Identify the cipher's unit, key structure and assumptions before judging its strength.
reviews.explanation: SEC14 explains the 25-cell grid and letter-pair operations. Combining I/J is the conventional element that fits the alphabet into the grid, not a claim about numeric cells. Repeated-letter fillers and final padding affect actual ciphertext, so computations require those conventions rather than guessing them.

evidence.quote: Playfair uses a keyed 5×5 grid, commonly combining I/J, and encrypts letter pairs. Specify duplicate-letter fillers and padding. Same row moves right, same column moves down, and rectangle pairs take the other column in their original row; decryption reverses shifts.

reviews.answer_text: ARP spoofing supplies false local IPv4-to-MAC associations, directing traffic toward an unintended link endpoint. It targets local link-address resolution at the network/data-link boundary and is commonly treated as a data-link-layer attack.
reviews.hint: Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused.
reviews.explanation: SEC05 identifies the poisoned association rather than DNS names or transport state. Its scope is local IPv4-to-MAC resolution, so describing it simply as arbitrary IP routing would miss the mechanism. The layer answer refers to manipulating the local link mapping, while ARP connects network and link addressing.

evidence.quote: Masquerade claims another identity. ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address. An intermediary attack intercepts and can alter exchanges. A replay reuses a valid old message; nonces, timestamps and sequence checks can reject it. Session hijacking steals or predicts a valid session token. Protect transport, regenerate session IDs after login, restrict cookies and check authorization server-side on every sensitive request.

reviews.answer_text: The principal IPsec services are confidentiality, integrity and origin authentication for IP traffic. They depend on the chosen protocol/association: AH supplies integrity/authentication without encryption, while ESP can supply confidentiality and integrity; IKE negotiates associations and keys.
reviews.hint: Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing.
reviews.explanation: SEC22 places IPsec at network layer and separates AH, ESP and IKE roles. Listing the service set must not imply every IPsec packet is encrypted or that IKE itself carries protected application content. Transport/tunnel mode describes coverage/encapsulation rather than replacing the service-selection and key assumptions.

evidence.quote: SSH protects remote login, commands and file transfer such as SFTP; it supports host keys and several client-authentication methods. IPsec protects IP traffic at network layer. AH provides integrity/origin authentication, not encryption; ESP can provide confidentiality and integrity; IKE negotiates security associations and keys. Transport mode protects upper-layer payload; tunnel mode encapsulates an inner IP packet inside an outer header. A VPN is a logical private connection; its actual security depends on the chosen authenticated tunnel.

reviews.answer_text: A TCP SYN flood creates many incomplete connection handshakes, occupying server state and exhausting resources needed for legitimate connections. Rate limits, SYN cookies, filtering or upstream controls address different parts of that resource bottleneck.
reviews.hint: Match the resource bottleneck or wireless mechanism to the relevant protection layer.
reviews.explanation: SEC06 defines the attack by incomplete-handshake state consumption. The goal is denial of usable service, not necessarily gaining control of the target. Defenses must match the constrained resource and traffic path; no single listed measure guarantees resistance to every distributed load or bandwidth bottleneck.

evidence.quote: DoS exhausts or disables a resource; distributed DoS uses multiple sources, often bots or reflected/amplified responses. A SYN flood leaves many incomplete TCP handshakes occupying state. DNS flooding targets query capacity; NXDOMAIN attacks generate queries for nonexistent names to stress resolvers. Fragment floods abuse reassembly or packet-processing resources. Rate limits, SYN cookies, filtering and upstream capacity controls address different bottlenecks.
Passive attacks observe without changing the target exchange: sniffing and traffic analysis.
Rogue access points imitate or bypass approved wireless service.

reviews.answer_text: TLS is the successor to obsolete SSL and provides an authenticated protected channel. Handshakes negotiate parameters, authenticate peers as required and establish keys; symmetric authenticated record protection carries data. Exact handshake messages depend on TLS version.
reviews.hint: Distinguish peer identity, channel protection and risks outside that channel.
reviews.explanation: SEC21 warns against treating an old SSL/ChangeCipherSpec narrative as the universal TLS1.3 sequence. The useful distinction is protocol succession and version-specific behavior, not a claim that the names are interchangeable or that every deployment of either is automatically secure.

evidence.quote: A certificate binds a public key to a named subject through an issuer signature. Validate the chain to a trusted root, intended hostname, time validity and applicable key usage/revocation policy. A genuine certificate is not proof that a business is honest.
Exact messages depend on TLS version: the old ChangeCipherSpec narrative is not a universal TLS1.3 sequence.
TLS succeeds obsolete SSL and supplies an authenticated protected channel.

reviews.answer_text: HTTPS is secure HTTP: HTTP over TLS. It adds authenticated channel protection for HTTP paths, headers and content. It does not conceal all metadata, such as endpoint IPs/timing, or protect plaintext after a compromised endpoint decrypts it.
reviews.hint: Distinguish peer identity, channel protection and risks outside that channel.
reviews.explanation: SEC21 identifies the composition and coverage. Protection depends on authentication and certificate validation rather than the mere appearance of the URL scheme. It concerns the communication channel; endpoint compromise and visible traffic metadata remain outside that confidentiality boundary.

evidence.quote: A certificate binds a public key to a named subject through an issuer signature. Validate the chain to a trusted root, intended hostname, time validity and applicable key usage/revocation policy. A genuine certificate is not proof that a business is honest.
It protects HTTP paths, headers and content on the channel, but does not hide all metadata such as IP endpoints and traffic timing, nor protect data after a compromised endpoint decrypts it.
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.

reviews.answer_text: DNS spoofing provides false name-resolution data, potentially redirecting a requested domain to an attacker-chosen destination. Cache poisoning is a form that places false answers in a resolver cache. DNSSEC authenticates DNS data when appropriately deployed and validated.
reviews.hint: Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused.
reviews.explanation: SEC05 distinguishes false DNS mapping from ARP/IP spoofing. SEC06 separates DNS flooding, which consumes query capacity, from answer authenticity. A successful-looking name lookup can still be maliciously wrong; checking that a response exists is different from establishing its trusted origin and integrity.

evidence.quote: Masquerade claims another identity. ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address. An intermediary attack intercepts and can alter exchanges. A replay reuses a valid old message; nonces, timestamps and sequence checks can reject it. Session hijacking steals or predicts a valid session token. Protect transport, regenerate session IDs after login, restrict cookies and check authorization server-side on every sensitive request.
DNS flooding targets query capacity; NXDOMAIN attacks generate queries for nonexistent names to stress resolvers.

Match a defense to its layer: authenticated IPsec can resist IP impersonation, DNSSEC authenticates DNS data, TLS authenticates/protects application transport, and bounds-safe code prevents overflows.

reviews.answer_text: SSH (Secure Shell) protects remote login, command execution and file transfer such as SFTP. It uses host keys and supports several client-authentication methods. Correct host-key validation and restricted management access remain important.
reviews.hint: Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing.
reviews.explanation: SEC22 states the protected remote-administration functions. SSH is not merely encryption of a password; it protects the session and requires authentic peer identity. File transfer through SFTP is related to SSH rather than being ordinary FTP with a new name.

evidence.quote: SSH protects remote login, commands and file transfer such as SFTP; it supports host keys and several client-authentication methods. IPsec protects IP traffic at network layer. AH provides integrity/origin authentication, not encryption; ESP can provide confidentiality and integrity; IKE negotiates security associations and keys. Transport mode protects upper-layer payload; tunnel mode encapsulates an inner IP packet inside an outer header. A VPN is a logical private connection; its actual security depends on the chosen authenticated tunnel.
SSH expands to Secure Shell and provides secure remote login and related network services.
AAA names authentication, authorization and accounting functions, rather than a particular remote-shell channel.

reviews.answer_text: A man-in-the-middle attack places an attacker between communicating parties to intercept and potentially alter their exchange. Authentication of the intended peer and a protected channel are needed; encryption without authentic key binding can still allow intermediary substitution.
reviews.hint: Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused.
reviews.explanation: SEC05 gives the interception/alteration mechanism, while SEC18’s unauthenticated Diffie–Hellman example explains why secrecy mechanisms alone are insufficient. The attacker may relay messages so both victims believe they communicate directly, making peer authentication and correct certificate/key checks essential.

evidence.quote: Masquerade claims another identity. ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address. An intermediary attack intercepts and can alter exchanges. A replay reuses a valid old message; nonces, timestamps and sequence checks can reject it. Session hijacking steals or predicts a valid session token. Protect transport, regenerate session IDs after login, restrict cookies and check authorization server-side on every sensitive request.
Diffie–Hellman agrees on a secret but unauthenticated DH permits intermediary substitution.
Hybrid systems establish or encapsulate a symmetric secret with public-key mechanisms, then protect bulk data symmetrically.

reviews.answer_text: SET means Secure Electronic Transaction. It was a Visa/Mastercard-led specification for protecting payment-card transactions with certificates and signatures. It is distinct from an ordinary HTTPS connection or a general payment-processing system.
reviews.hint: Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing.
reviews.explanation: SEC22 supplies the expansion, origin and protection role. Certificates/signatures support authenticated transaction relationships rather than defining the entire financial settlement infrastructure. Calling every TLS-protected checkout SET would conflate separate protocols with different scope and structure.

evidence.quote: PGP/OpenPGP combines symmetric content protection with public-key key handling and signatures. S/MIME uses certificates for signed and/or enveloped MIME content. Signatures can be sent separately/clear-signed without confidentiality; enveloped data encrypts content and wraps content keys for recipients. SET, Secure Electronic Transaction, was a Visa/Mastercard-led specification for protecting card transactions using certificates and signatures; it is distinct from a payment-processing system or ordinary HTTPS.
TLS succeeds obsolete SSL and supplies an authenticated protected channel.
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.

reviews.answer_text: Session hijacking is taking over an existing authenticated session by stealing or predicting a valid session token. Defenses include protected transport, regenerating IDs after login, restrictive cookie handling and server-side authorization on sensitive requests.
reviews.hint: Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused.
reviews.explanation: SEC05 identifies token possession/prediction as the takeover path. Establishing a secure initial login does not alone protect the later bearer token, and checking authorization on every sensitive action remains necessary. The mechanism differs from replaying an old message, although stolen session material can enable reused requests.

evidence.quote: Masquerade claims another identity. ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address. An intermediary attack intercepts and can alter exchanges. A replay reuses a valid old message; nonces, timestamps and sequence checks can reject it. Session hijacking steals or predicts a valid session token. Protect transport, regenerate session IDs after login, restrict cookies and check authorization server-side on every sensitive request.

reviews.answer_text: A firewall enforces traffic policy on flows it mediates. As a reference-monitor design, enforcement must cover every relevant access, resist tampering and be small/simple enough to analyze. For a firewall this is its traffic boundary, not every host-memory operation.
reviews.hint: Separate security-policy enforcement and assurance from ordinary OS features.
reviews.explanation: SEC28 defines the three reference-monitor requirements and explicitly limits a firewall to traversing traffic. SEC23 describes policy enforcement and bypass limits. Thus complete mediation requires preventing alternate paths within the claimed boundary; deploying a firewall does not make it a universal host security kernel.

evidence.quote: A reference monitor is an abstract access-checking mechanism: it must mediate every relevant access, resist tampering and be sufficiently small/simple to analyze. A security kernel implements core enforcement. A firewall can mediate its traversing traffic but cannot enforce every host-memory access. Assurance is justified confidence that controls implement the claims; functionality is what controls claim to do. A GUI or multitasking support alone does not establish trust.
A firewall enforces traffic policy.
Bypass paths, insiders, encrypted uninspected content and infected removable media limit firewall protection.

reviews.answer_text: A stateless packet-filtering firewall matches each packet’s header fields such as addresses, protocol and ports. Stateful inspection also tracks permitted connection context, allowing decisions based on whether traffic belongs to an allowed exchange.
reviews.hint: Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions.
reviews.explanation: SEC23 distinguishes header matching from connection-aware inspection. Both can filter ports, so the difference is not port-filtering capability alone. State tracking does not imply unlimited application-content understanding or automatic encryption; those are additional, separate functions.

evidence.quote: A firewall enforces traffic policy. Stateless packet filtering matches headers such as source/destination, protocol and ports. Stateful inspection tracks permitted connection context; application proxies terminate and relay application exchanges and can inspect their content. A circuit gateway relays connections, commonly SOCKS, without full application-content interpretation; textbooks associate it with session/transport functions. Such a gateway need not encrypt and is not automatically a VPN.

reviews.answer_text: An application-level gateway/proxy terminates and relays application exchanges on behalf of clients/services and can inspect application content. It differs from a simple header packet filter or circuit relay that lacks full application-content interpretation.
reviews.hint: Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions.
reviews.explanation: SEC23 defines the proxy by its application mediation boundary. It can enforce application-specific policy because it participates in the exchanges rather than merely routing packets. That role does not inherently mean encryption or protection against traffic that bypasses the proxy.

evidence.quote: A firewall enforces traffic policy. Stateless packet filtering matches headers such as source/destination, protocol and ports. Stateful inspection tracks permitted connection context; application proxies terminate and relay application exchanges and can inspect their content. A circuit gateway relays connections, commonly SOCKS, without full application-content interpretation; textbooks associate it with session/transport functions. Such a gateway need not encrypt and is not automatically a VPN.

reviews.answer_text: An IDS detects suspicious activity and alerts. An IPS can enforce prevention/blocking, usually on the traffic path. Both need contextual analysis because false positives and missed attacks remain possible.
reviews.hint: Separate observation from blocking and sensor placement from detection method.
reviews.explanation: SEC24 makes action the distinction, independently of host/network sensor location or signature/anomaly detection method. Observing a suspected attack does not itself prevent it. Inline blocking can affect legitimate service when an alert is false, so evidence and policy determine the appropriate response.

evidence.quote: An IDS observes and alerts; an IPS can enforce blocking, usually inline. Host-based sensors examine host events, network-based sensors inspect traffic. Signature detection recognizes known patterns; anomaly detection compares with a baseline and may detect novel behavior. Neither guarantees every attack is detected; anomaly detection can raise many false positives, and signatures can sometimes match variants.
A true positive is a real attack detected, false negative is a missed attack, false positive is innocent activity flagged, and true negative is innocent activity accepted.
Obfuscation makes code harder to understand and can hamper analysis, but does not reliably protect embedded secrets or remove vulnerabilities.

reviews.answer_text: The two main detection methods are signature-based and anomaly-based. Signatures recognize known patterns; anomaly methods compare behavior with a baseline and may find novel deviations. Both can miss attacks or produce false positives.
reviews.hint: Separate observation from blocking and sensor placement from detection method.
reviews.explanation: SEC24 explicitly gives these methods and their limitations. A deviation is not automatically malicious, and a matching signature does not prove every attack variant is captured. Host-based versus network-based describes sensor placement, a different classification from how the detection decision is made.

evidence.quote: An IDS observes and alerts; an IPS can enforce blocking, usually inline. Host-based sensors examine host events, network-based sensors inspect traffic. Signature detection recognizes known patterns; anomaly detection compares with a baseline and may detect novel behavior. Neither guarantees every attack is detected; anomaly detection can raise many false positives, and signatures can sometimes match variants.
Detecting 90 of 100 spam messages with five innocent messages flagged gives recall90%, precision90/95≈94.7%.
A true positive is a real attack detected, false negative is a missed attack, false positive is innocent activity flagged, and true negative is innocent activity accepted.

reviews.answer_text: A firewall cannot enforce policy on data or attack paths that bypass it. Insiders, removable media and uninspected encrypted content can evade its protection, so outside/perimeter-bypassing data needs endpoint, access and other controls.
reviews.hint: Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions.
reviews.explanation: SEC23 confines firewall protection to traffic actually mediated and inspectable under its design. A boundary rule does not sanitize every file after it arrives through another path. This is a scope limitation rather than proof that firewalls are useless or that all encrypted traffic is malicious.

evidence.quote: Host firewalls protect individual machines; network firewalls segment networks and can create a DMZ for public-facing services. Rules should be explicit, ordered as implemented, least-privilege and logged appropriately. Stateful and next-generation devices also filter ports, so a stem asking merely which device “can filter ports” is nonexclusive. Bypass paths, insiders, encrypted uninspected content and infected removable media limit firewall protection. Hardware firewall does not imply any fixed number of ports.

reviews.answer_text: PGP (Pretty Good Privacy)/OpenPGP combines symmetric encryption for content, public-key handling of content keys and digital signatures. It can provide confidentiality and integrity/origin-authentication evidence according to which operations are used and how keys are validated.
reviews.hint: Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing.
reviews.explanation: SEC22 gives the hybrid composition and SEC20 explains signature scope. A signature alone does not conceal content; encryption alone is not the same as a validated signature. Recipient/signer key authenticity and custody therefore matter to the protection actually obtained.

evidence.quote: PGP/OpenPGP combines symmetric content protection with public-key key handling and signatures. S/MIME uses certificates for signed and/or enveloped MIME content. Signatures can be sent separately/clear-signed without confidentiality; enveloped data encrypts content and wraps content keys for recipients. SET, Secure Electronic Transaction, was a Visa/Mastercard-led specification for protecting card transactions using certificates and signatures; it is distinct from a payment-processing system or ordinary HTTPS.
PGP expands to Pretty Good Privacy; its message-protection design combines conventional and public-key encryption with digital signatures.
Verification checks origin/integrity under key-identity and key-custody assumptions; it does not conceal content.

reviews.answer_text: S/MIME protects MIME messages using certificates for signatures and/or enveloped encryption. In sign-then-encrypt, sign the MIME entity, package its content/signature, encrypt it with a fresh symmetric content key and protect that key for each recipient. The recipient recovers the key, decrypts, then verifies with the validated signer certificate.
reviews.hint: Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing.
reviews.explanation: SEC22 specifies this construction while allowing other nesting orders with different coverage. Signed data supplies origin/integrity evidence without inherently concealing content; enveloped data encrypts content and wraps keys. Signing is not generic private-key encryption of the whole message, and certificate/key validation is essential to interpreting verification.

evidence.quote: PGP/OpenPGP combines symmetric content protection with public-key key handling and signatures. S/MIME uses certificates for signed and/or enveloped MIME content. Signatures can be sent separately/clear-signed without confidentiality; enveloped data encrypts content and wraps content keys for recipients. SET, Secure Electronic Transaction, was a Visa/Mastercard-led specification for protecting card transactions using certificates and signatures; it is distinct from a payment-processing system or ordinary HTTPS.
A recipient recovers the key, decrypts the signed entity and verifies its signature using the validated signer certificate/public key.
One signed-and-encrypted S/MIME construction first signs the MIME entity, packages its content and signature, then encrypts that signed entity with a fresh symmetric content key.

reviews.answer_text: A circuit-level gateway relays connections, commonly using SOCKS, without full application-content interpretation. Textbook OSI mappings associate it with session/transport functions rather than a universally fixed physical OSI device layer. It need not encrypt traffic or constitute a VPN.
reviews.hint: Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions.
reviews.explanation: SEC23 describes its scope by connection relay, in contrast with application proxies inspecting content and packet filters matching headers. The session/transport layer label is a teaching mapping; the relay function is the stable distinction. Unspecified circuit gateways must not be assumed to supply authenticated encrypted tunnels.

evidence.quote: A firewall enforces traffic policy. Stateless packet filtering matches headers such as source/destination, protocol and ports. Stateful inspection tracks permitted connection context; application proxies terminate and relay application exchanges and can inspect their content. A circuit gateway relays connections, commonly SOCKS, without full application-content interpretation; textbooks associate it with session/transport functions. Such a gateway need not encrypt and is not automatically a VPN.

reviews.answer_text: The modular exponentiation gives c=5^3 mod(3×13)=125 mod39=8. However φ=(3−1)(13−1)=24 and gcd(3,24)=3, so e=3 has no modular inverse. This is an arithmetic result, not a valid RSA encryption/decryption key pair.
reviews.hint: Check key-generation conditions as well as modular arithmetic.
reviews.explanation: SEC19 explicitly identifies the defective source example. Showing ciphertext 8 must not endorse the key setup: RSA requires e coprime to φ so a private exponent can invert it. The calculation and the validity check answer different parts of the example, and both must be preserved.

evidence.quote: For textbook RSA choose distinct primes p,q; n=pq and φ=(p-1)(q-1). Choose 1<e<φ with gcd(e,φ)=1, then compute d=e^-1 modφ. Public key is (n,e), private includes d. Encrypt 0≤m<n by c=m^e modn; decrypt by m=c^d modn. Use modular repeated squaring for large exponents. Real RSA requires appropriate standardized padding; raw arithmetic is not a secure deployment recipe.
With p=3,q=13,e=3,m=5, 5^3 mod39=8 arithmetically, but gcd(3,24)=3, so e has no inverse and this is not a valid RSA key.
State the defect rather than endorsing a working encryption/decryption pair.

reviews.answer_text: Hill is a polygraphic matrix substitution cipher, C=KP mod26. Its key must be invertible modulo 26, with determinant coprime to 26. It is not strong by modern standards: enough independent known plaintext/ciphertext blocks reveal the key through its linear structure.
reviews.hint: Identify the cipher's unit, key structure and assumptions before judging its strength.
reviews.explanation: SEC14 rejects the supplied claim of known-plaintext resistance. Combining letters into vectors does not remove linear algebraic relationships, and a large-looking matrix key is not proof of modern security. The correct answer explains the construction while correcting the question’s implied blanket strength claim.

evidence.quote: Hill uses C=KP mod26 for letter vectors. K needs an inverse modulo26, equivalently determinant coprime to26. It is linear: enough independent known plaintext/ciphertext blocks reveal K=CP^-1 mod26. The supplied claim of resistance to known-plaintext attacks is false; polygraphic substitution alone is not modern strength.

reviews.hint: Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions.
reviews.explanation: NET30 defines a random walk by probabilistically choosing a neighbor, exactly the forwarding behavior in the stem. Flooding instead replicates packets. Adaptive and distributed describe broader properties of routing algorithms; neither alone specifies random single-neighbor selection.

evidence.quote: Flooding sends copies on eligible outgoing links with duplicate/lifetime controls; random walk picks a neighbor probabilistically. Unicast targets one destination, broadcast all in a scope, multicast a subscribed group and anycast one member sharing an address, normally nearest under routing metrics. Multi-destination packets can list multiple targets; this is not necessarily identical to broadcast. Group multicast trees use mechanisms such as reverse-path checks; Ethernet spanning tree is a different layer-2 mechanism.

Adaptive or dynamic routing changes routes in response to updated network information; nonadaptive or static routing uses configured choices. Distributed routing means routers perform computations using exchanged information instead of requiring one central route computation. These properties do not imply random next-hop selection: the path-selection rule is a separate classification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Adaptive routing responds to network conditions; adaptation alone does not mean choosing a random neighbor.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Flooding sends copies on multiple eligible links rather than selecting just one neighbor randomly.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Random walk selects the next neighbor probabilistically, matching the stated packet-forwarding procedure.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Distributed routing spreads computation among routers; it does not specify the random choice described.

reviews.hint: Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule.
reviews.explanation: The wording loosely calls translation “address resolution,” but its decisive qualifier is use of port numbers. NET29 identifies PAT/NAPT as translation of address-plus-port combinations, allowing shared public addresses. This is not hardware-address resolution by ARP, and ordinary static or pooled dynamic address mappings do not themselves describe port multiplexing.

evidence.quote: Static NAT gives a fixed address mapping; dynamic NAT allocates mappings from a pool. PAT/NAPT maps address-plus-port combinations so multiple private clients share a public address. It is translation, not ARP resolution and not encryption. Return traffic must match the translation state or a configured inbound mapping.

ARP resolves an on-link IPv4 next hop to a link address, using a broadcast request and normally unicast reply. For an off-subnet target, ARP resolves the gateway, not the remote target’s MAC. It bridges the network/link addressing boundary and is often classified at the link layer; a bank calling ARP simply a network protocol uses a loose textbook convention. RARP reverses hardware-to-IP lookup; BOOTP/DHCP support boot configuration. ICMP reports errors and diagnostics; IGMP manages IPv4 multicast membership. These are separate companion protocols, not four pieces whose combination is IP.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: NAT is the broad translation family; this option does not identify the port-based form specifically.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: PAT translates address-and-port combinations, distinguishing simultaneous clients that share an external address.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dynamic NAT allocates address mappings from a pool, without necessarily multiplexing transport ports.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Static NAT fixes an address mapping; port-based sharing is the separate PAT mechanism.

reviews.hint: Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule.
reviews.explanation: Moving from /16 to /19 borrows three subnet bits, producing 2^3 = 8 equal subnets. Each /19 leaves thirteen host bits, so it contains 8192 addresses. Reserving the network and directed-broadcast addresses leaves 8190 usable hosts. Subnet counts describe subdivision of the stated parent; they must not be confused with addresses or hosts within a child subnet.

evidence.quote: To split parent /a into equal /p blocks, borrow b=p-a bits and obtain 2^b subnets. Do not subtract two subnets under modern practice. For a Class B /16 parent split to /19, b=3 gives eight subnets, each with 8192 addresses and 8190 conventional hosts. A /19 alone does not state its parent.

For ordinary broadcast LANs let h=32-p. Total addresses=2^h; usable hosts=2^h-2, reserving network and directed broadcast. Find the changing octet’s increment as 256-mask octet, round the address down to a multiple, and extend through the next boundary minus one.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Eight subnets is correct, but each /19 has 8192 total addresses rather than 32.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Three borrowed bits yield eight subnets; thirteen host bits yield 8190 usable hosts per subnet.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Thirty usable hosts belongs to /27, not /19.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A /19 contains 8192 addresses, not 2046.

question_revision.original_stem: Given the network address of 172.16.0.0/19, which of the following is correct?

original_options.label: A

original_options.label: D

question_revision.stem: A 172.16.0.0/16 parent network is divided into equal /19 broadcast subnets. Counting all subnets, which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It provides 8 subnets, 32 IP addresses each

options.label: D
options.text: It provides 8 subnets, 2,046 IP addresses each

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Parent prefix is /16.; Count subnet zero and the all-ones subnet; reserve network and broadcast addresses within each child.
assumptions: Parent prefix is /16.
Count subnet zero and the all-ones subnet; reserve network and broadcast addresses within each child.

reviews.answer_text: The transport layer does not provide only unreliable transmission
reviews.hint: Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule.
reviews.explanation: The question asks for WRONG statements. TCP is a transport-layer protocol with reliable ordered delivery, disproving the absolute “only unreliable” in D. The other substantive statements fit the layer model: network routing and host delivery, physical signaling specifications, and administratively assigned MAC addresses. NET33 explicitly permits locally administered MAC addresses, so B must not be rejected.

evidence.quote: First identify the exact layer, protocol and scope. Flow/error control can exist at both link and transport layers; MAC addresses can be locally administered; bridges and switches both operate at layer 2. A LAN can use public or private unicast space. UDP and IP are both connectionless. Session dialogs and TCP connections are distinct senses of connection. These overlaps require multiple selections or a narrower stem.

TCP offers a reliable ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission and windows. Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects network capacity. UDP sends independent datagrams with ports and a checksum but no built-in setup, delivery guarantee, retransmission or ordering. Live interactive traffic may choose UDP when late data is less useful than lost data. Application protocols can add reliability over UDP.

A NIC supplies a computer’s network interface and commonly implements both physical and link functions. Calling a NIC a physical interface does not mean all its functions are layer 1. Physical specifications include connectors, signaling, voltage, timing and physical coding/modulation; the PHY interface to MAC handles hardware signaling.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This statement is true: routing is a network/Internet-layer responsibility, so it is not a wrong statement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NET33 permits locally administered MAC addresses; physical addresses need not always be factory assigned.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Physical signaling, transmission-medium characteristics and data rate belong to the physical layer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The word only is false: TCP supplies reliable transport, whereas UDP lacks built-in delivery guarantees.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Host-to-host packet delivery is a network-layer function, distinct from transport process delivery.

choices.label: F
choices.explanation: At least D is wrong, so none of the above cannot answer the requested negative test.

reviews.hint: Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions.
reviews.explanation: NET14 names CSMA/CA as the 802.11 Wi-Fi access procedure. It combines carrier sensing, waiting/backoff and acknowledgments rather than Ethernet-style collision detection or token turns. Generic CSMA describes its family, but B gives the specifically supported WLAN mechanism requested by the stem; E omits its collision-avoidance procedure.

evidence.quote: Random access allows contention: ALOHA sends opportunistically; CSMA senses before sending. In legacy half-duplex Ethernet, CSMA/CD detects collision, sends a jam indication, stops, and retries after random backoff. The jam signals a collision, not its clearance. Wi-Fi 802.11 uses CSMA/CA with waiting/backoff and acknowledgments; sensing does not eliminate hidden-terminal collisions.

Controlled access uses polling, reservations or a token to grant turns; correctly coordinated access avoids contention collisions. Channelization divides frequency, time or code resources. Stop-and-wait sends one frame and waits for ACK, retransmitting on timeout; sequence bits distinguish duplicates. Sliding windows permit multiple unacknowledged frames. Link reliability/flow control is hop-local; transport reliability/flow control is end-to-end. Ethernet detects corruption but does not itself guarantee reliable delivery.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: ALOHA sends opportunistically and is not the 802.11 contention mechanism identified in NET14.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: CSMA/CA is the specifically identified WLAN mechanism, using waiting/backoff and acknowledgments.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Token passing is controlled access, unlike the contention procedure used by ordinary 802.11 WLANs.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: FDMA divides frequency resources; it is not the stated WLAN medium-access protocol.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: CSMA names the broader carrier-sensing family but omits the specific collision-avoidance WLAN protocol offered in B.

reviews.answer_text: In message switching technique, it is not required to create a dedicated path.; In circuit switching techniques, resources are allocated on demand.; Packet switching can have nonuniform delay because packets share links and may queue.
reviews.hint: Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions.
reviews.explanation: Message switching stores and forwards whole messages without a dedicated end-to-end path. Circuit switching instead reserves resources when a call is established and retains them through the session. Packet switching shares links, so queueing can produce variable delay, although packet voice remains possible. Virtual-circuit forwarding state alone does not require resource reservation. These distinctions support the three selected statements without equating all connection-oriented methods.

evidence.quote: Circuit switching sets up a path with reserved resources, transfers data, then releases it. Predictable allocated bandwidth trades against setup/blocking and wasted reservation during silence. A traditional telephone call is the standard example. Packet switching divides data into packets that share links statistically; queueing can add variable delay and loss. This does not make modern voice-over-packet impossible: buffering, scheduling and capacity planning manage it.

Datagram packets are forwarded independently. Virtual circuits establish forwarding state, but resource reservation is optional, not a necessary property of every virtual circuit. Message switching stores a complete message before forwarding, without a dedicated end-to-end path. Packet store-and-forward waits for the full packet/frame; cut-through starts after enough header arrives; fragment-free historically waits through the initial collision-sensitive portion. No routing algorithm guarantees that every packet always takes the geometrically shortest route.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Circuit switching reserves resources, but virtual-circuit packet switching need not reserve them throughout a session.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Circuit switching uses an established reserved path; complete-message or packet buffering describes store-and-forward switching.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Message switching forwards stored messages without requiring a dedicated end-to-end circuit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circuit resources are allocated when a connection is requested and reserved for its session.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Shared links and queueing can give packets different delays.
