reviews.hint: Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery.
reviews.explanation: DNS is the name-resolution application protocol in NET20. A/AAAA records provide address data for names. SMTP submits/relays mail, FTP transfers files and HTTP serves web requests; none provides the requested general domain-name record service. Its lookup role is separate from DHCP address assignment.

evidence.quote: DNS resolves names to records, including IPv4 A and IPv6 AAAA addresses; it can use UDP or TCP port 53. DHCP dynamically leases IPv4 settings, commonly address, mask, gateway and DNS server. Its basic exchange is discover, offer, request, acknowledge. IP itself does not assign addresses.

HTTP defines web request/response semantics; it is stateless, and a message body may be absent. HTTPS adds TLS protection. FTP transfers files using control and separate data connections; it is not the same protocol as SFTP. SMTP submits and relays mail; POP3 retrieves messages and IMAP accesses/synchronizes server mailboxes. Saying SMTP handles both sending and end-user mailbox retrieval is inaccurate.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SMTP submits and relays mail rather than resolving hostnames to addresses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FTP transfers files and does not supply the name-resolution record service.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: HTTP defines web exchanges, not the general hostname-to-address service.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DNS resolves names into records such as A and AAAA address records.

reviews.answer_text: Leakage from an adjacent communication channel
reviews.hint: Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions.
reviews.explanation: Crosstalk is unwanted coupling from a neighboring communication channel, directly matching B. Strength loss is attenuation, random thermal motion creates thermal noise and differential frequency delay produces distortion. These impairments can coexist but their definitions are distinct, so the question’s mechanism identifies crosstalk specifically.

evidence.quote: Attenuation reduces signal strength. Distortion changes shape, often because frequencies have different delays. Noise adds unwanted energy: thermal noise comes from random thermal motion, crosstalk leaks from nearby channels, and impulse noise is a short disturbance. Amplifiers amplify noise too; digital repeaters regenerate decisions but cannot reconstruct every corrupted bit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Signal-strength loss is attenuation rather than coupling from a neighboring channel.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Signals leaking into an adjacent channel are crosstalk.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Random electron/thermal motion describes thermal noise.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Different component-frequency delays distort waveform shape rather than defining crosstalk.

reviews.hint: Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule.
reviews.explanation: A /26 leaves six host bits, so the block has 64 addresses. In the specified block, .64 is the network and .127 the broadcast; usable hosts span .65–.126 inclusive, totaling 62. The question asks usable hosts, not block size, and /31 point-to-point exceptions do not apply.

evidence.quote: For ordinary broadcast LANs let h=32-p. Total addresses=2^h; usable hosts=2^h-2, reserving network and directed broadcast. Find the changing octet’s increment as 256-mask octet, round the address down to a multiple, and extend through the next boundary minus one.

192.168.2.64/26 spans .64–.127; usable .65–.126 gives 62 hosts. 192.168.10.25/28 spans .16–.31, so its network is .16. 172.17.128.0/21 spans 172.17.128.0–172.17.135.255; .128.255 and .135.0 are valid interior hosts, but .135.255 is broadcast. /27 gives 32 total and 30 usable, not 32 usable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thirty-two is not the usable count of this /26 block; /26 has 64 total addresses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sixty-four is the total block size before network/broadcast reservations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Six host bits give 64 total addresses minus two reservations, leaving 62 usable hosts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Thirty usable hosts is the /27 result, not /26.

reviews.hint: Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery.
reviews.explanation: The stem explicitly specifies communication sessions, matching the OSI session role rather than merely a TCP connection. NET19 assigns dialog management and checkpoints to that layer. Transport serves process endpoints, application supplies services and presentation handles representations. B is therefore the specific reference-model lifecycle role.

evidence.quote: OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption. Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption. Compression reduces representation size; encryption hides content and need not shrink it. Application protocols provide services directly to applications. Practical implementations distribute these functions differently; TLS is not proof of a separate physical presentation-layer device.

TCP establishes state with SYN, SYN+ACK, then ACK. SYN consumes one sequence position even with no application bytes. An acknowledgment states the next expected sequence number. For client ISN=395 and server ISN=260: client sends SYN seq395; server sends SYN+ACK seq260 ack396; client sends ACK seq396 ack261. Later byte counts advance sequence numbers. FIN also consumes one sequence position.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transport connection state is distinct from the explicitly named OSI session/dialog lifecycle.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Session manages dialogs and their setup, maintenance and recovery/end lifecycle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Application supplies user/application network services rather than the distinct session-layer lifecycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Presentation translates/compresses/encrypts representations instead of managing dialogs.

reviews.answer_text: A main-backbone break can disrupt the whole basic bus segment
reviews.hint: Draw the links and identify shared components, alternate paths and the effect of the specified failure or growth requirement.
reviews.explanation: In the conventional single-backbone bus assumed by these options, a main-cable break disrupts the shared segment, affecting the network rather than just one endpoint. NET08 qualifies the physical mechanism as an unterminated break. Redundant segmentation or protected designs are not specified, so C expresses the standard basic-bus failure consequence.

evidence.quote: Bus uses a shared backbone; an unterminated break can disrupt the segment. Star connects endpoints through a central device: one edge failure isolates that endpoint, whereas central failure affects the star. Ring forms a loop; basic single rings are vulnerable to a break, while protected dual rings differ. Token passing is associated with Token Ring but is an access method, not a necessary property of every ring. Tree is hierarchical; hybrid combines arrangements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A main-backbone fault affects shared signaling, not merely the two closest nodes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A broken unterminated backbone does not preserve normal basic-bus operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The shared basic bus segment can fail as a whole when its main backbone is broken.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A backbone break differs from an isolated endpoint spur failure and need not be limited to one node.

reviews.answer_text: Ongoing synchronized clock recovery rather than per-character start/stop
reviews.hint: Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule.
reviews.explanation: NET06 contrasts character start/stop framing with ongoing clock recovery in synchronous transmission. B is the intended synchronized-transfer description; “same clock” should mean synchronized timing, not necessarily a single physical clock device. The note gives no universal speed ordering, and both methods can transmit digital/binary data.

evidence.quote: Simplex is one way, half duplex alternates directions, and full duplex permits simultaneous sending/receiving. A walkie-talkie is half duplex; a telephone conversation uses full duplex. Serial sends sequential bits; parallel uses multiple conductors and may suffer skew. Character-oriented asynchronous serial adds start/stop bits; synchronous framing uses ongoing clock recovery. Neither is synonymous with browser asynchronous requests.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Per-character start/stop bits describe character-oriented asynchronous serial transmission.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Synchronous transfer maintains coordinated timing through ongoing clock recovery rather than character start/stop framing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No universal slower-than-asynchronous rule follows from the timing method.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Synchronous framing can carry binary data; the timing convention does not prohibit it.

reviews.answer_text: Logical IP addressing and routing across networks
reviews.hint: Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery.
reviews.explanation: NET12 gives network-layer logical addressing and routing; NET11 explains forwarding IP packets among networks by destination prefixes. C directly states that responsibility. The other options assign physical signaling, link MAC/error detection and session-dialog management, which belong to different model layers.

evidence.quote: Routers forward IP packets between networks using destination prefixes and next hops. They separate broadcast domains and normally do not forward local link broadcasts. A default gateway is usually a router, while a protocol gateway can translate application formats; therefore a gateway is not inherently a device that implements every OSI layer.

Sending proceeds from application data to transport segment/datagram, network packet, link frame and physical bits/symbols; receiving reverses the order. Each layer serves the layer above. A router removes a received link frame, inspects IP, and creates a new link frame for the next hop. MAC addresses usually change across routed hops; end-to-end IP addresses ordinarily remain until translation.

OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption. Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption. Compression reduces representation size; encryption hides content and need not shrink it. Application protocols provide services directly to applications. Practical implementations distribute these functions differently; TLS is not proof of a separate physical presentation-layer device.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transporting raw physical bits/symbols is the physical-layer function.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: MAC addressing and hop frame error detection are data-link responsibilities.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Network-layer logical addressing and routing carry IP packets between networks.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Establishing application dialogs is a session-layer role rather than IP routing.

reviews.hint: Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention.
reviews.explanation: An IPv4 decimal octet must fit eight bits, from 0 through 255. D has 256 and is therefore syntactically invalid. A–C each meet that range condition. B’s .255 ending alone does not establish a broadcast without a prefix, so it cannot be rejected merely by its last octet.

evidence.quote: Write IPv4 as four decimal octets 0–255, or as 32 binary bits. Use weights 128,64,32,16,8,4,2,1 within each octet. Thus 11000001 10000011 00011011 11111111 is 193.131.27.255. A value such as 257 is impossible. Syntactic validity differs from assignability: an address ending .0 or .255 can be a host under some prefixes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: All four octets are within 0–255, so this notation is valid.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Every octet is valid; a .255 ending alone does not determine broadcast status without a prefix.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: All four values fit eight-bit octets and form valid dotted-decimal notation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The second octet 256 exceeds the maximum representable eight-bit value 255.

reviews.hint: Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention.
reviews.explanation: NET23 explicitly gives IPv6 addresses a 128-bit width. IPv4 uses 32 bits; 64 may describe a common subnet interface boundary but is not the whole IPv6 address length. Ninety-six bits is likewise not the full width. D therefore answers the requested address size.

evidence.quote: IPv6 has 128-bit hexadecimal addresses, flexible prefixes and no IPv4-style broadcast. Sources, not routers, fragment IPv6 packets. IPv6 does not automatically encrypt traffic or make authentication unnecessary. Several choices saying larger address space, 128 bits and encryption support can all be true; the requested comparison must be specific.

IP supplies connectionless best-effort packet delivery, not end-to-end ordering or retransmission. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits. Its minimum header is 20 bytes and can grow to 60 bytes; it is not a 32-bit header. IHL counts 32-bit words; total length includes header and payload. TTL limits lifetime across routers; the protocol field identifies TCP, UDP or another upper-layer protocol.

A common IPv6 unicast subnet uses a 64-bit subnet prefix and a 64-bit interface identifier. This split does not make the complete address 64 bits: it remains 128 bits. Special uses and explicitly different prefix lengths must be considered separately.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thirty-two bits is the IPv4 address width, not IPv6.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sixty-four bits is not the complete IPv6 address width.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ninety-six bits does not match the specified 128-bit IPv6 address length.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits as explicitly stated in NET23.

reviews.answer_text: Learn source MACs and forward according to destination MAC
reviews.hint: Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions.
reviews.explanation: A bridge learns which sources are reachable through each port and consults the destination MAC when forwarding/filtering a frame. C names the relevant link addresses. IP, transport ports and TTL belong to higher-layer packet/segment processing, not the ordinary bridge forwarding decision. Unknown destinations may be flooded, so learning does not imply always-one-port forwarding.

evidence.quote: A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2. It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings, looks up the destination, forwards a known unicast to its port, filters it if the destination is on the incoming segment, and floods an unknown unicast or broadcast within its VLAN. A switch does not always send only to one destination port. Wireless access points normally bridge wireless and wired link-layer traffic.

Ports identify transport endpoints; the application can choose a transport and request socket buffer sizes, subject to OS limits. A TCP connection is identified by source/destination IP and source/destination port, with TCP understood. IPv4 protocol numbers identify upper protocols; 80 is a usual HTTP port, not an IP protocol number. Clients often use ephemeral ports. SCTP is a reliable message-oriented transport with multiple streams.

IP supplies connectionless best-effort packet delivery, not end-to-end ordering or retransmission. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits. Its minimum header is 20 bytes and can grow to 60 bytes; it is not a 32-bit header. IHL counts 32-bit words; total length includes header and payload. TTL limits lifetime across routers; the protocol field identifies TCP, UDP or another upper-layer protocol.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Destination IP prefixes drive routing, not ordinary layer-2 bridge frame forwarding.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Transport ports identify process endpoints and are not the bridge MAC-table lookup key.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Source MAC informs learning and destination MAC informs forwarding/filtering to the appropriate segment.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: TTL is an IP header field used in routed packet lifetime, not ordinary bridging.

reviews.answer_text: Reserved bandwidth can be wasted during silence
reviews.hint: Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions.
reviews.explanation: Circuit switching holds resources for the call even while endpoints are silent, so unused reservation cannot be statistically shared as packet traffic would be. B gives that cost. The note does not identify inherent out-of-order packet delivery or inability to carry voice; traditional telephone calls are its standard circuit example.

evidence.quote: Circuit switching sets up a path with reserved resources, transfers data, then releases it. Predictable allocated bandwidth trades against setup/blocking and wasted reservation during silence. A traditional telephone call is the standard example. Packet switching divides data into packets that share links statistically; queueing can add variable delay and loss. This does not make modern voice-over-packet impossible: buffering, scheduling and capacity planning manage it.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reserved circuits can offer predictable transfer behavior; setup cost is distinct from universally high transfer latency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Capacity remains reserved during silence and can be wasted when no data is sent.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Independent out-of-order packet routing is not the defining reserved-circuit disadvantage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Traditional telephone calls are the note’s standard circuit-switching example, so voice is supported.

reviews.answer_text: Microwave and infrared under the conventional line-of-sight assumption
reviews.hint: Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions.
reviews.explanation: Conventional directional microwave links need suitable path visibility, and infrared generally does not penetrate walls. Obstacles can therefore interrupt the direct links specified here. Both individual technologies fit, so the combined option is the complete response. Radio waves is a broader physical category that includes microwave but also other propagation modes; the question does not assert that all radio links share the same line-of-sight restriction.

evidence.quote: Radio, microwave and infrared are unguided media. Ground waves follow Earth, sky waves can reflect from ionized layers, and line-of-sight paths require suitable visibility. Microwaves are radio waves in the broader physical classification. Infrared generally does not penetrate walls. Directionality depends on antennas: omnidirectional means broad azimuth coverage, not equal radiation in every 3-D direction. Legacy Ethernet straight-through cables join unlike MDI/MDI-X roles; crossover joins like roles, such as PC–PC or switch–switch. Auto-MDI-X can remove that requirement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The broad radio category includes propagation modes beyond the specified line-of-sight comparison.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Microwave fits the stated direct-link case, but this alone omits infrared.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Infrared fits the stated obstructed-direct-path case, but this alone omits microwave.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Both microwave and infrared fit the specified comparison, making this the complete set.

question_revision.original_stem: Which wireless technology requires line-of-sight and is blocked by buildings or mountains?
question_revision.stem: Under the textbook direct line-of-sight wireless-link convention, which option gives the most complete set of listed technologies whose direct path can be blocked by buildings or terrain? Treat radio waves as the broad category rather than assuming every radio propagation mode needs line of sight.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: distinguish the requested role and choose the complete combined response when specified.
assumptions: Use conventional direct links; neither reflected indoor paths nor a universal claim about all radio propagation is intended.

reviews.answer_text: Classless Inter-Domain Routing; flexible prefixes reduce rigid class allocation waste
reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: NET28 gives the exact expansion and says CIDR replaces rigid class allocation. Flexible prefixes allow blocks sized to requirements and aggregation of aligned blocks, addressing waste from fixed historical class sizes. The other expansions are incorrect and their proposed packet-loss, loop or latency cures are not the defined purpose.

evidence.quote: CIDR, Classless Inter-Domain Routing, replaces rigid class allocation and supports aggregation. Combine contiguous aligned blocks sharing leading bits; unrelated adjacent-looking labels may not aggregate cleanly. Four consecutive /26 blocks covering a /24 summarize to /24. More-specific routes must remain available where the aggregate would otherwise send traffic to the wrong next hop.

For H hosts, choose the smallest h satisfying 2^h-2≥H, then p=32-h. For 24 hosts use /27; 52 or 57 use /26; 100 use /25; 500 use /23. For at least six equal subnets choose b=3. A Class C /24 split to /27 yields eight subnets. Always check both the number of subnets and the host capacity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This gives the correct expansion and relates flexible prefix allocation to avoiding rigid class-size waste.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Classful Internet Domain Routing is the wrong expansion, and CIDR is not defined as a packet-loss cure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Centralized IP Domain Routing is not the acronym expansion or the stated mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Classless Internet Data Routing is incorrect; CIDR is not defined as a general WAN-latency cure.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: Borrowing five bits yields 2^5=32 equal subnets under modern counting. The parent Class B /16 would become /21, but the direct subnet count only needs the specified five borrowed bits. NET26 says not to subtract two subnets under modern practice.

evidence.quote: To split parent /a into equal /p blocks, borrow b=p-a bits and obtain 2^b subnets. Do not subtract two subnets under modern practice. For a Class B /16 parent split to /19, b=3 gives eight subnets, each with 8192 addresses and 8190 conventional hosts. A /19 alone does not state its parent.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Five is the number of borrowed bits, not the exponential number of resulting subnet combinations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sixteen subnets would use four borrowed bits rather than five.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Five borrowed bits have 32 distinct combinations and therefore produce 32 subnets.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixty-four subnets would require six borrowed bits.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: The bridge forwarding database records MAC-to-port associations learned from source addresses and used for destination lookups. MAC table is therefore the matching name. A routing table maps IP prefixes to next hops; ARP associates on-link IPv4 addresses with link addresses. Those are different tables even if one device maintains several of them.

evidence.quote: A bridge or switch’s MAC address table is its learned forwarding database: it associates MAC addresses with ports for frame forwarding. It differs from an ARP cache, which associates an IPv4 next hop with a link address, and from a routing table, which selects next hops for IP prefixes.

A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2. It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings, looks up the destination, forwards a known unicast to its port, filters it if the destination is on the incoming segment, and floods an unknown unicast or broadcast within its VLAN. A switch does not always send only to one destination port. Wireless access points normally bridge wireless and wired link-layer traffic.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Routing tables describe destination IP prefixes and next hops rather than bridge MAC-to-port mappings.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ARP caches associate IPv4 next hops with link addresses, not MAC addresses with bridge ports.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The bridge’s learned source-MAC-to-port forwarding database is its MAC table.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: IP table does not name the layer-2 learned MAC forwarding database described in NET10.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: Voltage, cable/interface characteristics and signal transport are the physical-layer scope in NET09. Data-link functions operate on frames and MAC access, network handles IP routing and transport handles process delivery. The wording explicitly asks how bits are physically represented and carried, so C is the corresponding layer.

evidence.quote: A NIC supplies a computer’s network interface and commonly implements both physical and link functions. Calling a NIC a physical interface does not mean all its functions are layer 1. Physical specifications include connectors, signaling, voltage, timing and physical coding/modulation; the PHY interface to MAC handles hardware signaling.

Sending proceeds from application data to transport segment/datagram, network packet, link frame and physical bits/symbols; receiving reverses the order. Each layer serves the layer above. A router removes a received link frame, inspects IP, and creates a new link frame for the next hop. MAC addresses usually change across routed hops; end-to-end IP addresses ordinarily remain until translation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Data link manages frames/access rather than defining the physical voltage and cable interface.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Network manages logical addressing/routing rather than electrical signal specifications.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Physical-layer specifications include connectors, signaling, voltage and timing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Transport supplies process delivery rather than cable and voltage definitions.

reviews.answer_text: The dependent star loses connectivity when its center fails
reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: In a basic star every endpoint depends on the central hub for communication with other endpoints. Failure of that common center therefore affects the whole star. No alternate center or automatic topology reconfiguration is specified; the network does not become a bus or ring merely because the hub stops functioning.

evidence.quote: Bus uses a shared backbone; an unterminated break can disrupt the segment. Star connects endpoints through a central device: one edge failure isolates that endpoint, whereas central failure affects the star. Ring forms a loop; basic single rings are vulnerable to a break, while protected dual rings differ. Token passing is associated with Token Ring but is an access method, not a necessary property of every ring. Tree is hierarchical; hybrid combines arrangements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The center serves all star endpoints, so its failure is not limited to the nearest neighbor.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: All endpoints depend on the central hub, so the basic star loses inter-endpoint connectivity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A hub failure does not physically or logically rewire the star into an operational bus.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No automatic ring reconnection mechanism follows from the basic star topology.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: The stated cause—random motion associated with temperature—is thermal noise in NET06. Crosstalk is neighboring-channel coupling and impulse noise is a short disturbance. D names a different noise phenomenon not defined by random thermal motion. The cause identifies C without requiring a claim that all other real noise can be perfectly eliminated.

evidence.quote: Attenuation reduces signal strength. Distortion changes shape, often because frequencies have different delays. Noise adds unwanted energy: thermal noise comes from random thermal motion, crosstalk leaks from nearby channels, and impulse noise is a short disturbance. Amplifiers amplify noise too; digital repeaters regenerate decisions but cannot reconstruct every corrupted bit.

Intermodulation distortion occurs when multiple signals interact through a nonlinear component and generate unwanted combination-frequency products. Its mechanism differs from random thermal motion, adjacent-channel leakage and an isolated impulse disturbance.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Crosstalk arises from coupling between nearby communication channels, not the stated thermal-motion cause.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Impulse noise is a short disturbance rather than persistent random thermal motion.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Thermal noise is explicitly caused by random thermal motion, matching the temperature-dependent clue.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This option does not match the random thermal-motion definition supplied in NET06.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: NET22 gives first-octet 128–191 for historical Class B, corresponding to leading bits 10. Ordinary Class A is 1–126, Class C is 192–223 and Class D uses leading 1110 for multicast. Since the question explicitly asks classes, the historical categorization is appropriate rather than inferring a current CIDR prefix.

evidence.quote: Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8, B 10 with /16, C 110 with /24; D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved. Ordinary class-A first octets are 1–126 because 0 and 127 have special uses. B spans 128–191 and C 192–223. Default usable counts are 2^24-2, 2^16-2 and 254. Modern CIDR requires the actual prefix and overrides class defaults.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary historical Class A uses first octets 1–126 rather than 128–191.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Historical Class B spans first octets 128–191, with leading bits 10.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Historical Class C spans 192–223, above the supplied interval.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Class D multicast begins with 1110, outside the Class B 128–191 interval.

reviews.answer_text: Checkpoint state supports resuming after interruption
reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: A checkpoint records recoverable progress/state so interrupted work can resume from an agreed point. NET19 assigns such coordination to the session role. Encryption, compression and encoding translation belong to representation handling and do not by themselves preserve resumable dialog progress. C matches the checkpoint recovery purpose.

evidence.quote: OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption. Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption. Compression reduces representation size; encryption hides content and need not shrink it. Application protocols provide services directly to applications. Practical implementations distribute these functions differently; TLS is not proof of a separate physical presentation-layer device.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encryption conceals content and does not define saving resumable session progress.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Compression reduces representation size rather than recording recovery checkpoints.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Saving agreed progress/state enables continuation after interruption rather than restarting from the beginning.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encoding translation changes representation format, not checkpoint recovery state.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: NET03 defines de jure by formal approval. B directly states official approval, while industry adoption without that approval is de facto. Corporate origin does not alone decide status, but C specifically lacks formal approval and D emphasizes informal use. Therefore B is the option establishing the defining approval condition.

evidence.quote: Protocol syntax defines message structure, semantics defines field meanings, and timing defines when/how fast exchanges occur. A standard supports interoperability. De facto means established through use; de jure means formally approved. ISO develops international standards; IEEE develops LAN standards such as 802.3 and 802.11; ITU-T develops telecommunications standards. ANSI coordinates US standards, EIA is associated with interface standards, and FCC is a regulator.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Widespread adoption alone demonstrates de facto use rather than formal de jure approval.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Official approval matches the defining de jure criterion in NET03.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A corporate format without the stated formal approval does not meet the offered de jure definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Widespread informal use without formal approval is de facto rather than de jure.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: Parallel transfer needs several conductors to carry simultaneous bits. Those paths can experience skew and neighboring-channel coupling, as NET06’s impairment definitions explain. C states the extra-line and interference burden. No universal slower-speed claim, inability to carry digital data or fiber-only restriction follows from parallel transmission.

evidence.quote: Simplex is one way, half duplex alternates directions, and full duplex permits simultaneous sending/receiving. A walkie-talkie is half duplex; a telephone conversation uses full duplex. Serial sends sequential bits; parallel uses multiple conductors and may suffer skew. Character-oriented asynchronous serial adds start/stop bits; synchronous framing uses ongoing clock recovery. Neither is synonymous with browser asynchronous requests.

Attenuation reduces signal strength. Distortion changes shape, often because frequencies have different delays. Noise adds unwanted energy: thermal noise comes from random thermal motion, crosstalk leaks from nearby channels, and impulse noise is a short disturbance. Amplifiers amplify noise too; digital repeaters regenerate decisions but cannot reconstruct every corrupted bit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Parallel is not universally slower; performance depends on implementation, distance and synchronization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Parallel transmission can carry digital bits simultaneously, exactly as the stem states.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple conductors add wiring and can suffer skew or coupled interference between adjacent lines.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Parallel transmission is not restricted to fiber and commonly concerns multiple electrical conductors.

reviews.answer_text: Variable delay and packet loss can disturb real-time audio
reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: Real-time audio is sensitive to late or missing data. Packet networks may introduce variable queueing delay and loss, so B gives a plausible suitability issue. NET31 explicitly says modern voice over packets remains possible with buffering, scheduling and capacity planning; it is not intrinsically prohibited or dependent on reserved circuits.

evidence.quote: Circuit switching sets up a path with reserved resources, transfers data, then releases it. Predictable allocated bandwidth trades against setup/blocking and wasted reservation during silence. A traditional telephone call is the standard example. Packet switching divides data into packets that share links statistically; queueing can add variable delay and loss. This does not make modern voice-over-packet impossible: buffering, scheduling and capacity planning manage it.

TCP offers a reliable ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission and windows. Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects network capacity. UDP sends independent datagrams with ports and a checksum but no built-in setup, delivery guarantee, retransmission or ordering. Live interactive traffic may choose UDP when late data is less useful than lost data. Application protocols can add reliability over UDP.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Datagram packet switching does not require a dedicated circuit before every communication.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Variable queueing latency and loss can make audio arrive late or incomplete.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NET31 explicitly allows voice over packets with suitable engineering.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Statistical link sharing differs from reserving all bandwidth for established circuits.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: A /27 leaves five host bits regardless of the historical class of its parent. Those bits provide 32 total addresses. On an ordinary broadcast subnet, network and broadcast reserve two, leaving 30 usable host addresses. Parent classification matters for subnet counting, not this explicit-prefix host calculation.

evidence.quote: For ordinary broadcast LANs let h=32-p. Total addresses=2^h; usable hosts=2^h-2, reserving network and directed broadcast. Find the changing octet’s increment as 256-mask octet, round the address down to a multiple, and extend through the next boundary minus one.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thirty-two is the total address count before reserving network and broadcast.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Five host bits give 32−2=30 ordinary usable hosts.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Twenty-eight does not follow from the stated five host bits and two standard reservations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixty-two usable hosts corresponds to /26 rather than the supplied /27.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: Anycast routes to one member of a set sharing the address, typically the nearest by routing metrics. That is not necessarily geographic distance. Multicast targets a subscribed group, broadcast all in scope and ordinary unicast a single designated destination. D uniquely matches the shared-address nearest-member rule.

evidence.quote: Flooding sends copies on eligible outgoing links with duplicate/lifetime controls; random walk picks a neighbor probabilistically. Unicast targets one destination, broadcast all in a scope, multicast a subscribed group and anycast one member sharing an address, normally nearest under routing metrics. Multi-destination packets can list multiple targets; this is not necessarily identical to broadcast. Group multicast trees use mechanisms such as reverse-path checks; Ethernet spanning tree is a different layer-2 mechanism.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multicast targets a subscribed group rather than selecting only one nearest shared-address member.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Broadcast targets all destinations within its scope, not the nearest member.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary unicast targets one designated destination without the shared-address nearest-member semantics.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Anycast selects one shared-address member, normally nearest according to routing metrics.

reviews.answer_text: The conductor and shield share an axis
reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: The name coaxial refers to a common geometric axis for the inner conductor and surrounding shield. NET07 states this directly. Neither identical material, opposite signal directions nor a particular insulation covering defines the term; those are separate construction or usage details rather than the shared-axis relationship.

evidence.quote: Twisted pairs reduce coupled interference; UTP has no added shield and STP adds shielding. Coax has an inner conductor and outer shield sharing an axis. Fiber guides light and resists electromagnetic interference; it supports high capacity and long reach, but requires suitable optics and installation. Exact speed, cost and reach depend on the specification, not the material alone. Fiber can still be tapped.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The definition concerns geometric arrangement, not whether both conductive parts use the same material.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The inner conductor and outer shield share a central axis, giving the coaxial name.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Opposite signal directions are not the defining common-axis geometry.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insulation details do not define coaxial; sharing an axis does.

reviews.answer_text: A device that connects two or more networks using different protocols, topologies, or architectures
reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: Gateway has several networking meanings. A default IP gateway is commonly a router, while a protocol gateway translates between unlike protocols or application formats. The clarified question asks for that translating role, so the option joining unlike systems fits. Signal regeneration belongs to repeaters, same-protocol routing does not require translation, and MAC-based filtering describes bridging or switching rather than protocol conversion.

evidence.quote: Routers forward IP packets between networks using destination prefixes and next hops. They separate broadcast domains and normally do not forward local link broadcasts. A default gateway is usually a router, while a protocol gateway can translate application formats; therefore a gateway is not inherently a device that implements every OSI layer.

A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2. It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings, looks up the destination, forwards a known unicast to its port, filters it if the destination is on the incoming segment, and floods an unknown unicast or broadcast within its VLAN. A switch does not always send only to one destination port. Wireless access points normally bridge wireless and wired link-layer traffic.

A repeater regenerates layer-1 signals without inspecting destination addresses. An active hub is a multiport repeater: it repeats incoming signals onto other ports, placing half-duplex endpoints in one collision domain. A passive hub is a connector. A hub neither learns MAC addresses nor eliminates collisions. An endpoint such as a network printer consumes services; routers, hubs and access points are intermediary devices.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Signal regeneration/strength extension is a repeater function rather than either gateway meaning defined here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Connecting networks using the same protocol describes routing without the required protocol translation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A protocol gateway joins unlike systems through the translation required by the clarified scope.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: MAC-address frame filtering describes bridging/switching rather than the gateway distinction in NET11.

assumptions: Gateway means protocol translator rather than a default IP router.

reviews.answer_text: 10.0.0.0 under the explicitly requested Class A default
reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: Because the question explicitly assigns Class A, its historical default /8 supplies the intended network/host boundary. Keep first octet 10 and zero the remaining 24 host bits to obtain 10.0.0.0. If a different CIDR prefix were supplied it would override the default, but none is given in this class-specific question.

evidence.quote: Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8, B 10 with /16, C 110 with /24; D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved. Ordinary class-A first octets are 1–126 because 0 and 127 have special uses. B spans 128–191 and C 192–223. Default usable counts are 2^24-2, 2^16-2 and 254. Modern CIDR requires the actual prefix and overrides class defaults.

Compute network=address AND mask. Host bits zero identify the block start; host bits one give broadcast. With 172.16.28.252/20, the third octet is grouped in blocks of 16, so the network is 172.16.16.0 and broadcast 172.16.31.255. A written host/prefix such as 172.105.180.0/21 need not be an aligned block label: masking yields 172.105.176.0/21.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The Class A /8 default keeps first octet 10 and clears the remaining three octets.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This assumes a /16 boundary instead of the explicitly invoked Class A /8 default.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This assumes /24, retaining host bits that the Class A default would clear.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Clearing the network octet too loses the assigned Class A network identifier 10.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: UTP is unshielded copper: twisting reduces coupled interference but does not remove all electromagnetic coupling. NET06 identifies crosstalk as leakage from nearby channels. B names the relevant ordinary interference types, whereas thermal-only excludes other sources and infrared/gamma are not the note’s cabling-susceptibility mechanism.

evidence.quote: Twisted pairs reduce coupled interference; UTP has no added shield and STP adds shielding. Coax has an inner conductor and outer shield sharing an axis. Fiber guides light and resists electromagnetic interference; it supports high capacity and long reach, but requires suitable optics and installation. Exact speed, cost and reach depend on the specification, not the material alone. Fiber can still be tapped.

Attenuation reduces signal strength. Distortion changes shape, often because frequencies have different delays. Noise adds unwanted energy: thermal noise comes from random thermal motion, crosstalk leaks from nearby channels, and impulse noise is a short disturbance. Amplifiers amplify noise too; digital repeaters regenerate decisions but cannot reconstruct every corrupted bit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thermal noise is not the only impairment; unshielded pairs can experience coupled electromagnetic interference.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: EMI and adjacent-pair/channel crosstalk are relevant to unshielded copper, though twisting reduces coupling.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Infrared is an optical/unguided signaling category rather than the stated ordinary copper-coupling issue.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Gamma radiation is not the interference mechanism identified for UTP in the supplied note.

reviews.answer_text: Hubs send data to all connected devices; switches send data only to the intended device
reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: An active hub repeats incoming signals onto its other ports without examining addresses. A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and, for the specified known unicast on another port, forwards the frame only to that destination port. Unknown unicasts and broadcasts are different cases and can be flooded. The scope restriction makes the intended contrast accurate without treating selective forwarding as a universal rule for all switch traffic.

evidence.quote: A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2. It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings, looks up the destination, forwards a known unicast to its port, filters it if the destination is on the incoming segment, and floods an unknown unicast or broadcast within its VLAN. A switch does not always send only to one destination port. Wireless access points normally bridge wireless and wired link-layer traffic.

A repeater regenerates layer-1 signals without inspecting destination addresses. An active hub is a multiport repeater: it repeats incoming signals onto other ports, placing half-duplex endpoints in one collision domain. A passive hub is a connector. A hub neither learns MAC addresses nor eliminates collisions. An endpoint such as a network printer consumes services; routers, hubs and access points are intermediary devices.

Ethernet switches can have fiber-optic interfaces with suitable optical transceivers. A forwarding role therefore does not impose a copper-only restriction: distinguish what the device does with frames from the physical medium used by its ports.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Hubs are layer-1 repeaters, not layer-3 routers; ordinary switches are layer 2.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: In this known-unicast case the hub repeats to other ports, while the switch sends only to the learned destination port.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hubs do not use IP addresses to decide forwarding; they repeat signals without address inspection.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Hub versus switch is a signal-repetition versus frame-forwarding distinction; it does not impose the claimed prohibition on optical switch links.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: NET30 distinguishes multicast group delivery from unicast, broadcast and anycast. Receivers express membership/interest in a group, rather than every network device receiving by definition or only one nearest destination being selected. D matches that destination-set meaning. Delivery still depends on the deployed network’s forwarding and membership mechanisms.

evidence.quote: Flooding sends copies on eligible outgoing links with duplicate/lifetime controls; random walk picks a neighbor probabilistically. Unicast targets one destination, broadcast all in a scope, multicast a subscribed group and anycast one member sharing an address, normally nearest under routing metrics. Multi-destination packets can list multiple targets; this is not necessarily identical to broadcast. Group multicast trees use mechanisms such as reverse-path checks; Ethernet spanning tree is a different layer-2 mechanism.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: All devices regardless of interest describes broadcast scope rather than multicast group selection.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One specific destination is ordinary unicast rather than a receiver group.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One nearest shared-address member is anycast.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Multicast targets a subscribed group of receivers that expressed interest.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: Historical IPv4 Class D begins with bits 1110 and is designated for multicast. Classes A, B and C describe historical unicast network allocations, with differing default prefixes. The question explicitly asks that historical class designation, so D is supported independently of how modern unicast prefixes are allocated.

evidence.quote: Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8, B 10 with /16, C 110 with /24; D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved. Ordinary class-A first octets are 1–126 because 0 and 127 have special uses. B spans 128–191 and C 192–223. Default usable counts are 2^24-2, 2^16-2 and 254. Modern CIDR requires the actual prefix and overrides class defaults.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Class A is historical unicast network space rather than the multicast class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Class B is historical unicast space with a /16 default, not multicast.

choices.label: C

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: TCP uses sequence numbers, acknowledgments and windows to provide reliable ordered delivery between transport endpoints. Reliable link protocols can use similar mechanisms, but their scope is a single hop. The explicit end-to-end process requirement therefore selects transport. IP supplies best-effort network delivery, while session coordinates dialogs and checkpoints rather than defining TCP’s ordered-byte-stream reliability and receiver flow control.

evidence.quote: TCP offers a reliable ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission and windows. Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects network capacity. UDP sends independent datagrams with ports and a checksum but no built-in setup, delivery guarantee, retransmission or ordering. Live interactive traffic may choose UDP when late data is less useful than lost data. Application protocols can add reliability over UDP.

Controlled access uses polling, reservations or a token to grant turns; correctly coordinated access avoids contention collisions. Channelization divides frequency, time or code resources. Stop-and-wait sends one frame and waits for ACK, retransmitting on timeout; sequence bits distinguish duplicates. Sliding windows permit multiple unacknowledged frames. Link reliability/flow control is hop-local; transport reliability/flow control is end-to-end. Ethernet detects corruption but does not itself guarantee reliable delivery.

OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption. Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption. Compression reduces representation size; encryption hides content and need not shrink it. Application protocols provide services directly to applications. Practical implementations distribute these functions differently; TLS is not proof of a separate physical presentation-layer device.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: IP is best effort and does not supply the listed reliable acknowledgment/retransmission service.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Data-link reliability is hop-local rather than the required end-to-end process service.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transport supplies TCP’s end-to-end sequencing, acknowledgments and receiver flow control.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Session manages dialogs/checkpoints rather than the specifically listed link/TCP reliability machinery.

question_revision.original_stem: Which OSI layer adds sequencing, acknowledgement, and flow control to ensure reliable data delivery?

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: A /26 has blocks of 64 addresses. Starting at .64, this block runs through .127; the final address has all six host bits one and is broadcast. .65 and .126 are ordinary first/last hosts. .255 belongs to another /26 block, so it is not this subnet’s broadcast.

evidence.quote: 192.168.2.64/26 spans .64–.127; usable .65–.126 gives 62 hosts. 192.168.10.25/28 spans .16–.31, so its network is .16. 172.17.128.0/21 spans 172.17.128.0–172.17.135.255; .128.255 and .135.0 are valid interior hosts, but .135.255 is broadcast. /27 gives 32 total and 30 usable, not 32 usable.

Compute network=address AND mask. Host bits zero identify the block start; host bits one give broadcast. With 172.16.28.252/20, the third octet is grouped in blocks of 16, so the network is 172.16.16.0 and broadcast 172.16.31.255. A written host/prefix such as 172.105.180.0/21 need not be an aligned block label: masking yields 172.105.176.0/21.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 192.168.2.65 is the first usable host, not the all-host-bits-one address.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 192.168.2.126 is the last usable host, one address below broadcast.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The .64–.127 /26 block ends at .127, its directed broadcast.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The .255 address is outside this .64–.127 subnet block.

reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: NET21 assigns SMTP mail submission and relay. A client sending a message to a mail server is therefore a correct SMTP role. DNS resolves names, HTTP serves web requests and FTP transfers files. This does not assign end-user mailbox retrieval to SMTP; POP3/IMAP serve that separate task.

evidence.quote: HTTP defines web request/response semantics; it is stateless, and a message body may be absent. HTTPS adds TLS protection. FTP transfers files using control and separate data connections; it is not the same protocol as SFTP. SMTP submits and relays mail; POP3 retrieves messages and IMAP accesses/synchronizes server mailboxes. Saying SMTP handles both sending and end-user mailbox retrieval is inaccurate.

DNS resolves names to records, including IPv4 A and IPv6 AAAA addresses; it can use UDP or TCP port 53. DHCP dynamically leases IPv4 settings, commonly address, mask, gateway and DNS server. Its basic exchange is discover, offer, request, acknowledge. IP itself does not assign addresses.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DNS resolves domain names to address records rather than SMTP.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: HTTP governs web requests/responses, not SMTP.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SMTP submits mail from a client to a server and relays messages between mail servers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: File transfer is the FTP service role in this comparison, not SMTP’s defining mail role.

reviews.answer_text: 360-degree azimuth coverage, with a nonuniform vertical pattern
reviews.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
reviews.explanation: NET07 defines omnidirectional as broad azimuth coverage. C is correct when its 360 degrees refers to the horizontal plane, not equal power in every three-dimensional direction. Directional beams or upward-only radiation do not describe this pattern. Antenna elevation patterns can still have lobes/nulls, so the answer retains that scope qualification.

evidence.quote: Radio, microwave and infrared are unguided media. Ground waves follow Earth, sky waves can reflect from ionized layers, and line-of-sight paths require suitable visibility. Microwaves are radio waves in the broader physical classification. Infrared generally does not penetrate walls. Directionality depends on antennas: omnidirectional means broad azimuth coverage, not equal radiation in every 3-D direction. Legacy Ethernet straight-through cables join unlike MDI/MDI-X roles; crossover joins like roles, such as PC–PC or switch–switch. Auto-MDI-X can remove that requirement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A narrow targeted beam is directional rather than omnidirectional azimuth coverage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Upward-only radiation does not provide the broad around-the-antenna azimuth pattern.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 360-degree azimuth coverage is the intended meaning, without asserting equal power in all three-dimensional directions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A single focused path describes a directional antenna pattern.

reviews.hint: Trace the initial state and each executed operation in order, preserving the requested output layout.
reviews.explanation: DSA25 defines uniformity as spreading expected keys evenly among addresses. That directly matches the question’s wording. Determinism is a different obligation: repeated equal keys receive the same address for the chosen function. Continuity and data normalization do not name this distribution property, so only Uniformity answers the literal stem.

evidence.quote: Determinism means repeated equal keys get the same address for the chosen function. Uniformity means expected keys spread evenly. Universal hashing chooses one function randomly from a suitable family for the table, independently of a fixed key set; it does not choose a fresh unrelated function for each lookup. Random choice controls collision probability, not a promise of zero collisions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Uniformity describes spreading expected input keys evenly across the output address range, exactly as the stem requires.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Determinism requires repeated equal keys to map identically; it does not require an even address distribution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Continuity is not the key-distribution property defined for hash functions in DSA25.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Data normalization does not name the even-distribution requirement of a hash function.

reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: DSA41 repeatedly dequeues a vertex and enqueues its undiscovered neighbors. FIFO ordering ensures earlier distance layers are processed before later ones. Arrays or linked nodes can store this frontier, but Queue names its required access discipline. A stack instead serves latest pending work. The saved source image confirms the literal options without adding another algorithm.

evidence.quote: Mark the source when enqueuing it. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it. Store predecessor[v] when discovering v if a path must be reconstructed. FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A stack serves the latest pending vertex first and does not preserve BFS distance-layer order.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An array can store a queue, but an array alone specifies no FIFO frontier discipline.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linked nodes can represent a queue, but Linked List alone does not specify breadth-first processing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A FIFO queue processes discovered vertices by distance layer, the standard BFS frontier rule.

reviews.hint: Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage.
reviews.explanation: The loop visits about N/2 even indices, but LinkedList.get(i) walks from the nearer endpoint. A linear number of those indices lie near the middle, each requiring linear traversal. DSA07 analyzes exactly this access pattern and obtains Θ(N²) total work. Incrementing by two changes a constant factor, not the quadratic order.

evidence.quote: Indexed access is not constant for every List implementation. Java LinkedList.get(i) walks from the nearer endpoint. Summing get(0), get(2), get(4), … over a length-N list still gives Theta(N²), because a linear number of middle indices each require linear traversal. An iterator scans once in linear time. A damaged return statement or missing cost convention cannot justify an exact executable runtime.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: O(N) would require constant-cost indexed access; LinkedList.get(i) instead traverses nodes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A growing number of accesses and additions prevents a constant bound on total work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A linear number of middle-index accesses each traverse a linear number of nodes, yielding quadratic time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Neither the iteration count nor the accumulated linked-node traversal has logarithmic growth.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Quadratic traversal grows faster than N log N, so this is not a valid upper bound.

reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: This asks about constructing an optimal BST, rather than searching a tree after construction. The standard dynamic program considers quadratically many key intervals. For each interval it tries up to a linear number of candidate roots, combining the relevant subproblem costs. Multiplying those counts gives cubic construction time. The repaired cubic option states that bound; the linear, logarithmic and factorial alternatives do not give the tight construction order.

evidence.quote: Standard optimal-BST dynamic programming tries each possible root for each key interval: O(n²) intervals times O(n) roots gives O(n³) construction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear time does not cover all intervals and root candidates.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quadratic intervals times linear root trials give cubic time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Logarithmic time concerns balanced search paths, not this construction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Factorial is a loose upper bound rather than the tight listed order.

reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: Pending operators must be retrieved in reverse order when grouping or precedence requires them to be emitted. A stack provides that last-in, first-out discipline. An expression tree is another possible representation for conversion, but it is not the requested pending-operator ADT in this specified algorithm. A queue retrieves the oldest entry first, while a linked list alone describes storage links without prescribing the needed access policy.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].

To evaluate postfix, push operands. At a binary operator, pop right operand first, then left, and push left op right. Build an expression tree for either prefix (preorder) or postfix (postorder); a stack is useful but is not the only possible conversion representation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A stack retrieves the latest pending operator first.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A queue uses first-in, first-out access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An expression tree can support another conversion method but is not this pending-operator ADT.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A linked list can implement storage but alone does not specify LIFO behavior.

reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: DSA05 names best, average, and worst as the ordinary cases for comparing costs on inputs of equal size. Average additionally needs an input distribution. Counting these cases gives three. This is a classification of input cases, rather than a count of resources, data structures, or asymptotic bound notations.

evidence.quote: Fix the input size before comparing cases. Best-case cost is the minimum resource use over legal inputs of that size; worst-case cost is the maximum. Average-case cost averages costs using a stated input distribution. These three input-case functions can each be described using upper, lower or tight asymptotic bounds; the case name does not select the bound notation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two omits one of the three named categories: best, average, and worst case.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note lists three ordinary fixed-size input cases: best, average, and worst.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Four does not match the three ordinary input-case categories listed in DSA05.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Five adds categories outside the stated best, average, and worst input-case classification.

reviews.hint: Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage.
reviews.explanation: DSA05 distinguishes best, average, and worst over inputs of the same size. Worst selects the largest runtime; best selects the smallest, while average takes an expectation under a distribution. Therefore Worst Case directly matches maximum time. This input-case distinction is independent of whether the resulting cost function is described with O, Ω, or Θ notation.

evidence.quote: Fix the input size before comparing cases. Best-case cost is the minimum resource use over legal inputs of that size; worst-case cost is the maximum. Average-case cost averages costs using a stated input distribution. These three input-case functions can each be described using upper, lower or tight asymptotic bounds; the case name does not select the bound notation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Worst case takes the maximum operation cost over valid inputs of the same size.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Average case computes an expected cost under a distribution instead of selecting the maximum.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Best case selects the minimum cost, the opposite extremum from the question.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Worst Case is offered and directly identifies the requested maximum-time input case.

reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: Correctness asks whether operations produce their specified results. Time and space complexity measure operation counts and memory use under a resource model. Completeness, under the explicit meaning supplied here, instead describes how a binary tree’s levels are filled: earlier levels are full and the last fills from the left. It is a particular shape condition, rather than a universal assessment criterion for every data structure.

evidence.quote: Binary means at most two children. Full means each node has zero or two children. Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left. Perfect means all leaves share a level and every internal node has two children. Balanced means height stays logarithmic under a stated rule; it does not require a perfect shape.

Finiteness means termination after finitely many steps for every valid input. Definiteness means each instruction has one interpretation; effectiveness means each step is executable. Correctness means meeting the stated result for every valid input. A finite program can still return the wrong answer.
Time counts chosen operations; space counts memory, including live recursive frames.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Completeness describes a particular binary-tree shape.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correctness assesses whether an operation meets its specification.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Time complexity assesses operation cost.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Space complexity assesses memory cost.

reviews.hint: Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage.
reviews.explanation: With digit count d and radix r fixed, the radix cost O(d(n+r)) reduces to linear growth in n. Its counting-based stable passes use auxiliary storage for output and digit counts. The key assumptions make this an eligible radix-sorting workload rather than an unspecified large-list claim. Bubble, selection and insertion use constant extra element storage in their ordinary forms and can require quadratic work.

evidence.quote: With d digits and radix r, counting-based passes take O(d(n+r)) time and O(n+r) auxiliary storage.
For ascending order, compare each adjacent pair and swap only when left>right.
For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap.
At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i].

choices.explanation: Bubble uses adjacent comparisons and can require quadratic work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selection uses quadratic comparisons and constant extra element storage.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Radix uses the stated digit passes and auxiliary storage.

choices.label: D
