question_revision.original_stem: Which sorting algorithm is efficient for large lists but requires additional memory?
question_revision.stem: For a large array of nonnegative integer keys with fixed digit count and fixed radix, which listed ordinary algorithm can achieve linear time using counting-based digit passes and O(n+r) auxiliary storage?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the intended scope, terminology and comparison conditions.
assumptions: Supply fixed-width nonnegative keys, a fixed radix and the counting-based pass model.

reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: Strings can be compared lexicographically, but the clarified question asks for a digit-based mechanism rather than whole-key comparisons. LSD radix sorting treats each character position as a digit, stably sorting from the last position toward the first. Stability retains the ordering established by earlier passes. Bubble, selection and merge use comparisons between keys in their ordinary forms, so they do not implement this specified character-pass mechanism.

evidence.quote: LSD radix sorting handles fixed-width digit keys by stably sorting least-significant digit first, then moving left. Stable intermediate passes preserve the ordering already established by less-significant digits. With d digits and radix r, counting-based passes take O(d(n+r)) time and O(n+r) auxiliary storage.
For ascending order, compare each adjacent pair and swap only when left>right.
At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i].
Split into halves, sort them, then merge by advancing the smaller current front.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary bubble sort compares adjacent whole keys.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary selection chooses a minimum through key comparisons.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary merge compares the fronts of sorted key runs.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: LSD radix uses stable character-position passes from least significant to most significant.

question_revision.original_stem: Which sorting algorithm can be used to sort elements with non-comparable keys, such as strings?
question_revision.stem: Which listed sorting algorithm orders fixed-length strings by stably processing individual character positions, without using whole-string comparison operations? Assume an ordered finite character alphabet and LSD passes.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the intended scope, terminology and comparison conditions.
assumptions: Replace the false non-comparable-string premise with a specified character-digit access model.

reviews.answer_text: Sorting using external storage such as disk or tape.
reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 defines external sorting through datasets beyond main memory and buffered disk runs. Option A captures this distinguishing external-storage use. Main memory may still hold buffers, but using it alone does not define external sorting. Swapping and being in place are separate implementation properties and do not identify whether the working dataset resides externally.

evidence.quote: Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively. In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant. Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory. External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Tape or disk stores external runs when the working dataset does not fit wholly in main memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Main-memory use alone does not distinguish external sorting; external algorithms also use memory for buffers.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Swapping is an operation used by many sorts and does not define external storage use.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: In-place concerns auxiliary element storage, independently of whether sorting accesses an external dataset.

reviews.answer_text: O(n²) under the usual average-case model.
reviews.hint: Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage.
reviews.explanation: DSA32 identifies quadratic average and worst work from repeated adjacent comparisons. Under the usual random-permutation average model, bubble sort therefore takes Θ(n²), which implies O(n²). Early stopping makes an already sorted input linear, but that is the optimized best case rather than the ordinary average over input arrangements.

evidence.quote: For ascending order, compare each adjacent pair and swap only when left>right. The largest remaining value moves to the final unsorted position after one left-to-right pass. Shrink the next pass by one position. Quadratic worst/average work comes from up to n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons.

Fix the input size before comparing cases. Best-case cost is the minimum resource use over legal inputs of that size; worst-case cost is the maximum. Average-case cost averages costs using a stated input distribution. These three input-case functions can each be described using upper, lower or tight asymptotic bounds; the case name does not select the bound notation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Quadratic average work grows faster than n log n, so this bound is too small.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Repeated adjacent passes do not have logarithmic average growth under the usual input model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linear work is the optimized sorted-input best case, not ordinary average-case bubble sorting.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Quadratic average work is bounded by O(n²), matching the adjacent-pass analysis in DSA32.

reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: Top-down mergesort recursively divides the sequence, while bottom-up mergesort iteratively combines runs of increasing widths. In-place variants change the storage tradeoff used while merging. Under the note’s stated terminology, linear merge names the combining operation itself rather than a separate standardized sort variant. This is a distinction within the supplied naming convention, not a claim that no author could ever use that phrase differently.

evidence.quote: Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively. In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant. Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory. External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: In-place merging is a recognized storage variant.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Bottom-up mergesort is the iterative run-merging organization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Top-down mergesort is the recursive organization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Linear merge names the combining operation under the stated terminology.

question_revision.original_stem: Which of the following is not a variant of merge sort?
question_revision.stem: Using the terminology of the course note, which listed phrase names the combining operation rather than a recognized organization or storage variant of mergesort?

reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: The DSA31 sorting table identifies quicksort as unstable. Cocktail and bubble sorts preserve equal-key order when swapping only strict adjacent inversions. Ordinary merge sort preserves equal-key order when ties are taken from the left run first. Under these usual implementations, quicksort is the single listed algorithm that does not guarantee stability.

evidence.quote: Early stopping makes a sorted input linear: one no-swap pass finishes. A fixed pass schedule stays quadratic. Strict swaps preserve equal-key order. Cocktail sort runs bubble passes in both directions and is stable with strict swaps.
With left-first tie handling, equal keys retain order.
stack usually log n average, n worst; unstable

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Standard quicksort partition exchanges can move equal keys past one another and do not guarantee stability.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Cocktail sort is stable with strict adjacent swaps, as described in DSA32.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Bubble sort preserves equal-key order when it swaps only strict adjacent inversions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Merge sort preserves equal-key order by taking equal elements from the left run first.

reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: On a strictly increasing array, the first key is the minimum and the last key is the maximum, so those deterministic endpoint rules choose extremes. The median of the first, middle and last keys is the middle-position value, which is neither extreme for the stated size. A random element is not a deterministic rule and can choose an endpoint. This criterion selects C without claiming a universally best practical pivot strategy.

evidence.quote: Choose a pivot, partition, then recursively sort the pieces. Balanced partitions give n log n work; repeated extreme pivots sum n+(n-1)+… to quadratic work. Expected n log n needs an input/random-pivot model. Random and median-of-three choices have different tradeoffs; neither is universally best.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The first key is the minimum on this input.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The last key is the maximum on this input.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The sample median is the middle-position value and is not extreme.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Random selection is not deterministic and may choose an extreme.

question_revision.stem: For a strictly increasing array of at least five distinct keys, which listed pivot rule is deterministic and avoids choosing an extreme key on the first partition? Interpret median-of-three as the median of the first, middle and last keys.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the intended scope, terminology and comparison conditions.
assumptions: Specify strictly increasing distinct input, a deterministic nonextreme first-pivot criterion, and the sampled positions.

reviews.answer_text: D. Directly searching an unordered list without sorting or an ordered index
reviews.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
reviews.explanation: Binary search needs ordering that justifies rejecting one half of its candidate interval. Lower and upper bounds in an ordered sequence have that property. Searching sorted interval endpoints during an interval-union task also supplies an ordered subproblem, and a monotone debugging boundary permits the same halving logic. Direct searching in an unordered list supplies no such invariant, so a midpoint comparison cannot safely discard a half.

evidence.quote: On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Linear search may scan all items; adverse hash collisions may require linear work; DFS can inspect all vertices and edges. Their ordinary worst cases do not share binary search’s logarithmic bound.

evidence.quote: Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.

Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted. Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too. A first-element match costs Theta(1). An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time. Uniformly likely successful positions average (n+1)/2 comparisons, still linear.

Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search can inspect every item when the target is absent or last, giving linear worst-case time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Each comparison discards about half the ordered interval, giving logarithmic worst-case probes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary hash lookup can degrade to linear time under adverse collisions, despite expected constant-time performance.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS may visit all graph vertices and edges, rather than guarantee logarithmic worst-case work.

reviews.answer_text: Linear search directly searches an unsorted sequence.
reviews.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA28 explicitly allows unsorted data for linear search: compare successive elements until the target is found or the sequence ends. Binary search requires sortedness. Hash lookup can be useful after building a table, but it does not directly search the supplied ordinary list without that preprocessing. DFS presumes graph or tree adjacency rather than a simple sequence query.

evidence.quote: Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted. Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too. A first-element match costs Theta(1). An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time. Uniformly likely successful positions average (n+1)/2 comparisons, still linear.

On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.

Direct addressing reserves a position for every possible key in a finite universe U, costing Theta(|U|) slots. A hash table uses h(key) in 0..m-1 and stores only actual entries plus bucket capacity. With h(k)=k mod 6, key 36 has home address 0; collisions may move its final storage position.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search can inspect an unsorted array or list directly without sorting or building another structure.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search needs ordering to safely eliminate half the remaining candidate positions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash search needs a constructed hash table; the stem supplies an ordinary unsorted array or list.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS explores graph or tree adjacency and is not the direct unsorted-sequence scan described here.

reviews.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA42 describes marking a vertex and recursively visiting each unmarked neighbor before resuming later neighbors. That procedure is standard depth-first traversal and applies to graphs and trees. Linear search scans a sequence, binary search uses an ordered interval, and hash search queries table addresses. None of those alternatives names the adjacency-following traversal in this option set.

evidence.quote: Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours. An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline. Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search scans sequence elements and is not the named adjacency-following graph/tree traversal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search reduces an ordered interval rather than visiting arbitrary graph or tree connections.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash search probes key-derived table addresses rather than traversing graph or tree edges.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS follows unvisited neighbors recursively or through an explicit stack, providing a standard traversal.

reviews.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA30 explicitly describes sorted-array ternary search as comparing two split points and retaining the relevant third. The three candidate regions give the technique its name. Binary search uses one midpoint and two regions, linear search scans successively, and DFS explores graph branches. Thus Ternary search uniquely matches the described three-part split.

evidence.quote: Sorted-array ternary search compares two split points and keeps the relevant third, still logarithmic. Jump search probes block boundaries then scans within a block. Regular intervals could mean unit-step scanning or larger jumps. Interpolation also needs sortedness, so prerequisite questions can overlap binary search.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search advances through successive items and does not divide the remaining interval into thirds.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search uses one midpoint and retains one of two halves, not one of three regions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ternary search uses two split points to divide the ordered search interval into three candidate parts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS explores graph or tree branches rather than repeatedly trisecting an ordered search interval.

reviews.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 compares the middle value with the target and continues only in the half that can contain it. This solves a smaller instance of the same ordered-search problem and is the divide-and-conquer reduction intended here. Linear scanning removes one candidate at a time, hashing computes addresses, and DFS follows adjacency without this ordered half-elimination rule.

evidence.quote: Divide and conquer reduces a problem to smaller instances of the same kind, solves the required smaller instances and obtains the original result from them. Mergesort recursively sorts two halves and merges; quicksort partitions and recursively sorts the resulting ranges. This course also classifies binary search as divide and conquer: an ordered comparison selects the only half that can contain the target. This is different from simply repeating adjacent swaps, choosing successive minima, or making stable LSD digit passes.

On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search scans successive candidates rather than repeatedly solving a half-size ordered-search instance.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search divides the ordered interval and continues in the only half that can contain the target.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash search derives an address and resolves collisions rather than recursively dividing an ordered problem.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS follows adjacency branches and does not inherently apply the ordered half-elimination strategy described here.

reviews.answer_text: Merge sort using buffered external runs.
reviews.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 describes external sorting by building sorted runs and merging buffered disk streams to reduce I/O. Merge sort naturally supports that strategy even when the whole dataset does not fit RAM. Bubble and insertion sorting repeatedly move local data, while ordinary quicksort assumes partition access rather than the external sequential-run pattern specified by the note.

evidence.quote: Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively. In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant. Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory. External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sort’s repeated adjacent passes do not provide the buffered sorted-run strategy used for efficient external sorting.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary quicksort partitioning is not the sequential buffered-run merging strategy identified for external data here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sorting combines buffered sorted runs sequentially and is directly suited to disk-backed external sorting.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion sort’s repeated local insertion work does not provide the note’s efficient external-run merging mechanism.

reviews.answer_text: Hash table for expected fast dictionary lookup and insertion.
reviews.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA27 explicitly names hashing as a dictionary implementation with expected constant lookup. DSA26 qualifies this by a suitable distribution and controlled load; insertion is likewise expected fast under those conditions. Arrays and linked lists lack the same ordinary key-lookup performance, while a stack specifies LIFO access. This is an expected-performance recommendation, not a universal worst-case guarantee.

evidence.quote: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.

A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering. A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list. Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full. No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An ordinary array lacks key-derived lookup and may require scanning or maintaining a sorted order with costly insertions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ordinary linked list needs traversal to locate an arbitrary dictionary key, giving linear worst-case lookup.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A well-sized hash table offers expected fast key lookup and insertion under suitable hashing and load assumptions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A stack exposes LIFO top operations and does not directly provide efficient arbitrary-key dictionary lookup.

reviews.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
reviews.explanation: Standard Dijkstra repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges. Nonnegative edge weights justify this shortest-path procedure even when different edges have different costs. BFS minimizes edge count and is sufficient when edge costs are equal, which is weaker than the stated guarantee. DFS supplies reachability paths, while Prim minimizes total spanning-tree cost rather than source-to-vertex route lengths.

evidence.quote: For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)). A min-priority queue supports the next choice. BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.
BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A DFS path need not have minimum total weight.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: BFS minimizes edge count and does not guarantee minimum weight for arbitrary differing costs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dijkstra guarantees source shortest paths under nonnegative weights.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Prim solves the spanning-tree objective rather than source shortest paths.

reviews.answer_text: B. Doubly linked list with head and tail
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: The hash index handles locating an entry, while the recency component must unlink a known entry and reconnect it at the recent end. A doubly linked list supplies both neighboring links for that constant-time removal and maintains endpoints for movement and eviction. An array would generally shift entries, a bare hash table does not supply recency order, and an ordinary FIFO queue cannot remove an arbitrary known interior entry.

evidence.quote: A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering. A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list. Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full. No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements.

Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends. Singly linked tail deletion still needs its predecessor. A circular tail links back to head; stop traversal on returning to the start, handling empty separately.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Maintaining array recency order generally requires shifts.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A doubly linked recency list supports unlinking a known node and endpoint updates.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The existing hash index handles lookup but does not itself maintain LRU order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An ordinary queue lacks arbitrary known-interior-node removal.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA44 directly identifies Kadane as the contiguous maximum-sum-subarray algorithm. It updates the best sum ending at the current item and the best sum seen overall, using linear time and constant working storage. Binary search does not optimize contiguous sums, and quicksort or merge sort reorder values rather than preserve the original adjacency needed by this problem.

evidence.quote: Kadane’s algorithm finds a contiguous maximum-sum subarray. For a required nonempty answer, initialize ending=best=A[0]; update ending=max(x,ending+x), then best=max(best,ending). It is linear time with constant working storage. Initializing best=0 instead silently allows an empty answer and fails the nonempty all-negative case.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Binary search locates targets or ordered boundaries; it does not compute a contiguous maximum-sum subarray.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort reorders values and does not preserve the original adjacency required for maximum subarray sum.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort orders values; the named sorting algorithm is not the maximum-subarray recurrence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Kadane maintains the best sum ending here and the best anywhere, directly solving the stated problem.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA40 describes adjacency lists as storing each vertex’s neighbors in Θ(V+E) space. This names a complete graph representation among the choices. Arrays, linked lists, or maps may store parts of a representation, but those container names alone do not specify how vertices and their edges are encoded. The answer identifies the graph-specific organization.

evidence.quote: A matrix uses Theta(V²) space and constant edge lookup. Adjacency lists use Theta(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours. Dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts. Examining every edge costs more on denser graphs; vertex-only operations need not inspect every edge.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An array can store a matrix or adjacency containers, but its name alone does not specify a graph representation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A linked list can hold neighbor records, but alone does not describe the vertex-to-neighbor organization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash tables may index vertices or neighbors, but do not by themselves name the graph representation supplied here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An adjacency list explicitly associates vertices with their neighbors and is a standard graph representation.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA43 defines an MST as a minimum-total-cost connection of all vertices in a connected undirected weighted graph. Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Dijkstra minimizes source-path distances instead, while BFS and DFS are traversals without a general minimum-weight spanning-tree guarantee. Thus Prim is the listed MST algorithm.

evidence.quote: An MST minimizes the total cost of connecting all vertices of a connected undirected weighted graph. Prim adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Kruskal processes edges by increasing weight and rejects those joining vertices already connected. An MST need not give shortest source-to-vertex routes, and equal weights can permit several MSTs.

For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)). A min-priority queue supports the next choice. BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DFS can produce a spanning tree but does not generally minimize total edge weight.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: BFS produces minimum-edge source layers in unweighted graphs, not a general minimum-weight spanning tree.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dijkstra minimizes source-to-vertex distances, a different objective from total spanning-tree connection cost.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Prim grows a spanning tree by repeatedly choosing a cheapest edge crossing to an outside vertex.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: A binary heap exposes the extreme key at its root, so peek is constant, and insertion or extraction restores order along a logarithmic-height path. Ordinary unordered arrays or lists need a linear search for an extreme, while ordered versions pay linear insertion in the general case. An unmodified FIFO queue follows arrival order rather than priority. The stated operation bounds make the heap the unique matching standard representation.

evidence.quote: A priority queue returns the smallest or largest priority key under its convention. Urgent patients may precede earlier arrivals. Insertions and extractions can interleave. Binary heaps support constant peek and logarithmic insert/extract.

Arrays and lists can also implement priority queues: an unordered sequence gives cheap insertion but linear extremum removal; an ordered sequence reverses that tradeoff. Equal priorities have no inherent FIFO guarantee. If stable service is required, compare (priority, arrival_counter). Choose the priority direction and tie rule before tracing.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary ordered/unsorted arrays trade linear insertion against linear extremum selection.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary lists likewise have a linear cost in one required operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A binary heap provides constant peek and logarithmic insertion/extraction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An unmodified queue serves FIFO rather than priority order.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA44 explicitly defines KMP as finding a pattern inside text. It preprocesses longest proper prefix/suffix lengths and uses them to avoid restarting comparisons after mismatch, giving linear combined pattern-and-text work. DFS, BFS, and Dijkstra concern graph exploration or paths, rather than this specialized substring-matching mechanism. KMP uniquely matches the question among these choices.

evidence.quote: Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) finds a pattern inside text. Preprocess the pattern’s longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. After mismatch, fall back using those prefix lengths rather than restarting comparisons from the beginning; the text pointer need not move backward. Pattern preprocessing plus scanning takes O(pattern length+text length).

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DFS explores graph or tree branches; it is not the substring-pattern algorithm identified in DSA44.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: BFS explores graph distance layers rather than applying prefix/suffix reuse for text matching.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dijkstra computes nonnegative weighted shortest paths, not substring pattern occurrences.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: KMP is the pattern-matching algorithm using preprocessed prefix/suffix lengths to avoid repeated text comparisons.

reviews.answer_text: C. Hash table allocates one separate memory slot for each key in the universe U
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: Direct addressing reserves a distinct slot for every possible key in the universe, whether present or absent, so its storage is proportional to |U|. The specified hash table stores the actual entries plus capacity proportional to n. For this sparse-universe storage comparison, hashing uses less space. C incorrectly attributes the direct-address allocation rule to hashing, while direct key-to-slot mapping and separate universe slots accurately describe direct addressing.

evidence.quote: Direct addressing reserves a position for every possible key in a finite universe U, costing Theta(|U|) slots. A hash table uses h(key) in 0..m-1 and stores only actual entries plus bucket capacity. With h(k)=k mod 6, key 36 has home address 0; collisions may move its final storage position.

choices.explanation: Under the sparse-universe storage assumptions, the hash table uses fewer allocated slots.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Direct addressing maps directly to a key’s universe slot without compressive hashing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One slot for every possible key describes direct addressing, not the specified hash table.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Each universe key has a separate direct-address slot.

The question stops before collision resolution, so occupied slots cannot change this computed address. evidence.quote: Direct addressing reserves a position for every possible key in a finite universe U, costing Theta(|U|) slots. reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA26 defines open addressing as keeping entries within the array and probing until an available slot is found. Checking successive positions is its linear-probing form. Multiple hashing changes probe steps, chaining stores collisions in bucket lists, and cluster indexing is not this insertion procedure. Therefore Open addressing is the matching general method among the options.

evidence.quote: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.

Linear probing tries (h(k)+j)%m. For size 7 and keys 10,17,24, all home addresses are 3 and occupied positions become 3,4,5. Quadratic probing changes the step; double hashing uses h1(k)+j h2(k), modulo m, with a step relatively prime to m to cover all slots. Neither method guarantees no collisions. Deletion needs tombstones or reinsertion so searches do not stop prematurely.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Open addressing searches alternative table positions; checking successive positions is its linear-probing form.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Multiple or double hashing derives another probe step rather than the stated simple successive-slot scan.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Chaining puts colliding entries in a bucket list instead of searching successive array slots.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cluster indexing does not name the collision insertion strategy described by the successive-position probing rule.

reviews.answer_text: D. New records are inserted at the beginning of the file
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: A heap file does not maintain record order by a chosen field. With no ordered index or sorted copy, ordered output therefore requires sorting; an ordinary scan can locate a record, and insertion can place a record in available storage. Nothing requires new records to be inserted at the beginning of the file. D is the incorrect claim, while the explicit no-index scope makes A’s ordering requirement appropriate.

evidence.quote: Specify whether a question asks which structure can implement something or which is best under stated costs. ADTs do not force one representation, and serial-access memory is not inherently LIFO. A heap file is an unordered database record file, unrelated to a binary heap: insertion uses available space, scanning can find records, and ordered output requires sorting or an index. It need not insert at the beginning.

choices.explanation: Under the specified no-index/no-sorted-copy scope, field-ordered output requires ordering the records.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A linear scan can search unordered records.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Using available storage avoids maintaining a sorted record sequence during insertion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Heap-file insertion is not required to place every new record at the beginning.

evidence.quote: Divide and conquer reduces a problem to smaller instances of the same kind, solves the required smaller instances and obtains the original result from them. reviews.explanation: DSA01 explicitly defines an abstract data type through values and operations, leaving representation to the implementation. The same LIFO stack can therefore use arrays or linked nodes without changing its contract.

evidence.quote: An abstract data type (ADT) defines values and operations; representation supplies implementation. Arrays or linked nodes can implement the same LIFO stack. Abstraction keeps relevant details: patient urgency and arrival order matter for service; hair colour does not.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA01 directly identifies a record grouping integer, character, and floating fields as heterogeneous. The different field types distinguish it from an ordinary same-element-type array. Linear describes relationships, and static describes storage behavior, neither of which follows merely from the field types. Thus Non-homogeneous is the requested classification.

evidence.quote: Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues are linear. Trees model hierarchies; graphs model general connections. A record grouping integer, character and floating fields is heterogeneous; an ordinary array has one element type.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Homogeneous would mean a uniform element type, contrary to the mixed int, char, and float fields.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The record combines different field types and is therefore heterogeneous or non-homogeneous.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linear concerns relationships or order, not the mixed-type classification asked here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Static concerns allocation or lifetime and is not established merely by these field types.

reviews.answer_text: Abstraction preserves relevant behavior and hides irrelevant implementation detail.
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA01 illustrates abstraction using patient urgency and arrival order while ignoring hair colour. Programmers retain the data and operations needed for the task and separate that contract from representation details. This supports the substantive answer without additional facts.

evidence.quote: An abstract data type (ADT) defines values and operations; representation supplies implementation. Arrays or linked nodes can implement the same LIFO stack. Abstraction keeps relevant details: patient urgency and arrival order matter for service; hair colour does not.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA03 calls combining sequences merging and works through sorted inputs by repeatedly emitting the smaller current front. Advancing only the selected sequence preserves sorted output until the remaining suffix is appended. For mathematical sets, duplicate handling additionally follows the set contract.

evidence.quote: Traversal processes every item; searching locates a target; insertion and deletion change membership; updating changes a stored value. Sorting reorders items, while merging combines sequences. To merge sorted [1,4] and [2,3], repeatedly emit the smaller front, producing [1,2,3,4]. Destroying a structure releases owned storage.
A set forbids duplicate elements.

reviews.answer_text: Destruction or deallocation of owned storage.
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA03 says destroying a structure releases owned storage. In a linked chain, DSA09 visits and releases each owned node; C++ allocation forms must be matched to their deletion forms, and freed nodes must not be dereferenced.

evidence.quote: A C struct groups named fields, including arrays and pointers. A singly linked node needs payload plus a same-type link. C fields cannot have initializers inside the type declaration; modern C++ permits default member initializers. In C++, match new with delete and new[] with delete[]. Repair links before freeing a node; never dereference it afterwards.

Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known. Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null. To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation. Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.
