reviews.explanation: For n≥1, 6n+4≤10n, while 6n+4≥6n. These constant upper and lower multiples establish linear growth by DSA06. O(n) is the natural tightest-order response, though larger upper bounds also exist.

evidence.quote: For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. Little-o means f/g tends to zero; little-omega means it grows without bound. These relations can describe best-case, average-case, worst-case or space functions.

reviews.answer_text: One valid witness pair is c=8, k=1.
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: For every n≥1, 4n≤4n² and 1≤n², so 3n²+4n+1≤8n². DSA06 supplies the same inequality, proving the required eventual upper bound with c=8 and k=1. Other larger constants may also work.

evidence.quote: For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. Little-o means f/g tends to zero; little-omega means it grows without bound. These relations can describe best-case, average-case, worst-case or space functions.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA04 defines finiteness as terminating after finitely many steps for every valid input. It is distinct from definiteness, executable instructions, or correctness: a terminating procedure can still return a wrong answer. The required concept is directly covered.

evidence.quote: Finiteness means termination after finitely many steps for every valid input. Definiteness means each instruction has one interpretation; effectiveness means each step is executable. Correctness means meeting the stated result for every valid input. A finite program can still return the wrong answer.

reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: For each of the n outer iterations, the inner loop executes n times, so the constant-cost body runs n×n=n² times. Outer-loop overhead is linear and inner-loop control is also bounded by a constant per body execution. Those contributions do not change the dominant quadratic growth. Under the stated independence, fixed loop count and body-cost assumptions, the tight time complexity is Theta(n²).

evidence.quote: A loop i=1; i<n; i*=2 takes about log₂n iterations. Two independent n-iteration loops nested around constant work take Theta(n²). An n-level ordinary recursion with constant live storage per level needs Theta(n) stack space.

Time counts chosen operations; space counts memory, including live recursive frames. Distributed algorithms may also measure communication volume. A single assignment is one unit in the elementary model, not literally one second. Sequential blocks add costs; independent nested loops multiply their iteration counts. Conditional worst-case cost includes the test and the more expensive branch.

question_revision.original_stem: An algorithm has nested loops each running n times. What is its time complexity?
question_revision.stem: An algorithm has exactly two independent nested loops. Each executes n iterations, and the innermost body performs constant work. Loop-control operations are constant time, with no early exits or hidden nonconstant operations. What is the tight time complexity as n grows?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the missing execution or service model.
assumptions: Specify exactly two independent n-iteration levels, constant body/control cost and no early exits.

reviews.answer_text: Both upper and lower asymptotic bounds.
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA06 defines Big-O as an eventual upper bound, Omega as the reverse bound, and Theta as requiring both. Thus Theta expresses a tight growth class up to positive constants. It is independent of choosing best, average, or worst input cases; Average case only confuses the bound relation with an input-distribution choice.

evidence.quote: For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. Little-o means f/g tends to zero; little-omega means it grows without bound. These relations can describe best-case, average-case, worst-case or space functions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An upper bound alone is Big-O and does not supply Theta’s lower requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A lower bound alone is Omega and does not supply Theta’s upper requirement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Theta requires simultaneous eventual upper and lower constant-factor bounds.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Theta can describe any case or resource function, not only an average case.

reviews.answer_text: Representative n log n grows faster than n; Big-O classes themselves overlap.
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA06 orders representative rates with n before n log n. Their ratio is log n, which grows without bound, so the representative n log n rate grows faster. However an O(n) function is also O(n log n), so membership alone does not compare actual runtimes.

evidence.quote: For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. Little-o means f/g tends to zero; little-omega means it grows without bound. These relations can describe best-case, average-case, worst-case or space functions.
Increasing representative rates: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2^n, 3^n, n!, n^n. Logarithm bases differ only by a constant factor.

reviews.answer_text: One constant time unit in the elementary-operation model.
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA05 explicitly treats a single assignment as one unit in an elementary model, not one physical second. The convention abstracts hardware and requires that evaluating the assigned expression itself be constant cost; complicated expressions need their own accounting.

evidence.quote: Time counts chosen operations; space counts memory, including live recursive frames. Distributed algorithms may also measure communication volume. A single assignment is one unit in the elementary model, not literally one second. Sequential blocks add costs; independent nested loops multiply their iteration counts. Conditional worst-case cost includes the test and the more expensive branch.

reviews.answer_text: If f∈O(g) and g∈O(h), then f∈O(h); this composes upper bounds.
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA06 composes the eventual inequalities f≤c g and g≤d h to obtain f≤cd h beyond both thresholds. Choose the larger threshold and multiply the positive witness constants. This lets a complicated bound pass through a simpler intermediate function.

evidence.quote: For n≥1, 3n²+4n+1≤8n²: c=8,k=1 witness O(n²). Constants and lower-order terms disappear from tight polynomial growth. Transitivity multiplies witnesses: f≤c g≤cd h beyond both thresholds.

reviews.answer_text: Increasing representative growth: 1, log n, n, n², 2^n.
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA06 gives the standard growth ordering, with constants below logarithms, then linear and quadratic functions, then exponential. The ranking compares representative rates, not disjoint Big-O classes, since loose upper bounds overlap.

evidence.quote: Increasing representative rates: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2^n, 3^n, n!, n^n. Logarithm bases differ only by a constant factor.

reviews.answer_text: Time, memory space, and—in distributed settings—communication volume.
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA05 measures operation counts and live memory, and adds communication volume for distributed algorithms. Thus the third resource is context-dependent rather than a universal resource needed by every local algorithm. These are the three supported categories in the note.

evidence.quote: Time counts chosen operations; space counts memory, including live recursive frames. Distributed algorithms may also measure communication volume. A single assignment is one unit in the elementary model, not literally one second. Sequential blocks add costs; independent nested loops multiply their iteration counts. Conditional worst-case cost includes the test and the more expensive branch.

reviews.answer_text: Θ(n) worst time, when absent or at the last position.
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA28 scans until equality or exhaustion. An absent target or one in the final position requires all n comparisons, giving linear worst time; a first-position match instead takes constant time. The operation and cases are directly supported.

evidence.quote: Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted. Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too. A first-element match costs Theta(1). An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time. Uniformly likely successful positions average (n+1)/2 comparisons, still linear.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 eliminates half an ordered interval according to the midpoint comparison. That elimination is valid only when comparable values follow a consistent order; descending input works with reversed comparisons. Circularity and links are representation properties, not substitutes for sortedness. An unsorted sequence gives no safe smaller-half decision. Therefore Sorted is the required prerequisite.

evidence.quote: On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Without order, a midpoint comparison cannot safely eliminate either half.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistent sorted order supports the midpoint half-elimination invariant.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Circular storage does not establish the value ordering needed by binary search.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Linked storage does not imply sortedness and also changes midpoint-access costs.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 gives floor(log₂n)+1 probes for n>0. Since 2^19=524288 and 2^20=1048576, one million lies between them, so the worst probe count is twenty under the ordinary interval algorithm. A root/midpoint hit can finish earlier.

evidence.quote: Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.

reviews.answer_text: Worst and usual average Θ(n²); early-stop best Θ(n).
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA32 sums repeated adjacent passes to at most n(n−1)/2 comparisons, yielding quadratic worst and ordinary average work. A no-swap early-stop pass makes sorted input linear, while a fixed pass schedule remains quadratic. The answer needs these implementation and case distinctions.

evidence.quote: For ascending order, compare each adjacent pair and swap only when left>right. The largest remaining value moves to the final unsorted position after one left-to-right pass. Shrink the next pass by one position. Quadratic worst/average work comes from up to n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons.

reviews.answer_text: Select the remaining minimum and put it at the next prefix position.
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA33 scans the unsorted suffix for its minimum and exchanges it with A[i]. After each meaningful pass, the sorted prefix grows by one and contains the smallest keys placed so far. This differs from inserting the next encountered item into a prefix.

evidence.quote: At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i]. There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order. At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed. A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.

reviews.answer_text: Selection finds a suffix minimum; insertion places the next item into a sorted prefix.
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA33 chooses the globally smallest remaining key for each next output position. DSA34 instead takes the next input item, shifts larger prefix values, and inserts it into their gap. Both grow sorted prefixes, but choose their next item differently.

evidence.quote: At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i]. There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order. At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed. A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.

Begin with the first element already sorted. For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap. That gives n-1 insertion passes. On sorted input each pass needs one ordering check and no shifts: linear time. Reverse order causes 1+2+…+(n-1) shifts: quadratic time.

reviews.answer_text: Already sorted input; Θ(n) with no-swap early stopping.
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA32 performs one pass over an already sorted array, makes no swaps, and stops when early-exit detection is enabled. That is linear best work. A fixed-pass implementation still executes its quadratic comparison schedule even on the same input.

evidence.quote: Early stopping makes a sorted input linear: one no-swap pass finishes. A fixed pass schedule stays quadratic. Strict swaps preserve equal-key order. Cocktail sort runs bubble passes in both directions and is stable with strict swaps.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA08 defines a singly linked node as data plus next. The head reference points to the first node, and a null next terminates an ordinary noncircular chain. Head is a list-level reference rather than a second payload field inside every node.

evidence.quote: A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain. Empty means head==null. Nodes allocated as needed grow dynamically, with pointer overhead and no direct index arithmetic.

reviews.answer_text: A circular tail links back to head instead of ending at null.
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA10 defines circularity by the tail-to-head link and stops traversal after returning to the start. This is independent of singly versus doubly linked: a singly linked list can itself be circular. Compared with the ordinary noncircular singly linked chain, termination changes from null to return-to-start.

evidence.quote: Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends. Singly linked tail deletion still needs its predecessor. A circular tail links back to head; stop traversal on returning to the start, handling empty separately.

A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain. Empty means head==null. Nodes allocated as needed grow dynamically, with pointer overhead and no direct index arithmetic.

reviews.answer_text: Advance head to the old head’s next link, then reclaim the old node.
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA09 saves old=head, sets head=head.next, and releases old in an owned C++ chain. The essential link update is advancing head; check empty before dereferencing, and clear tail too if the only node was removed. This answers the operation without hiding ownership work.

evidence.quote: Prepend with new.next=head; head=new. To insert after a known predecessor p, set new.next=p.next before p.next=new. Appending with only head requires a tail traversal; maintaining tail avoids it. Delete the head by saving old=head, advancing head=head.next and releasing old in C++.

Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known. Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null. To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation. Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.

reviews.answer_text: A prev link to the predecessor.
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA10 says doubly linked nodes add prev alongside next. That extra link permits backward traversal and supports endpoint updates when head and tail are maintained. It does not automatically give constant arbitrary positional access, which may still need traversal.

evidence.quote: Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends. Singly linked tail deletion still needs its predecessor. A circular tail links back to head; stop traversal on returning to the start, handling empty separately.

reviews.answer_text: Arrays compute addresses directly; linked positional access follows a chain.
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA02 computes an element address from base, index, and element size in constant time. DSA08’s chain lacks direct index arithmetic, so reaching an arbitrary position may traverse linearly many links. This comparison concerns positional access rather than every operation: a known-head update can be constant.

evidence.quote: For equal-size elements, address(A[i]) = base + i × element_size under zero-based indexing. This arithmetic gives constant-time positional access in the usual RAM cost model. A row-major rectangular matrix uses base + (row × columns + column) × element_size.

A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain. Empty means head==null. Nodes allocated as needed grow dynamically, with pointer overhead and no direct index arithmetic.

reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA13 works the exact expression. Multiplication groups B*C and division groups D/E before addition and subtraction. Emit A, then B C *, then +, then D E /, then −, producing ABC*+DE/-.

evidence.quote: Infix places an operator between operands and uses precedence and parentheses. Prefix places it first; postfix places it last. Their fixed operator arity determines grouping. To convert infix to postfix, output operands immediately and hold operators on a stack. Pop higher-precedence operators before pushing a new operator; also pop equal precedence for left-associative operators. Parentheses temporarily override this order.
A+B*C-D/E becomes ABC*+DE/-.

reviews.answer_text: Attempting push when the fixed array is full.
reviews.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 distinguishes full storage from the overflow attempt. Under zero-based top-as-last-occupied convention, full means top=C−1; a count convention uses size=C. A push must check this before writing beyond capacity.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].
Overflow is an attempted insertion into full storage; underflow is an attempted removal from empty storage.

reviews.answer_text: Push, pop, and peek are O(1) for fixed-array or head-linked stacks.
reviews.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 defines push insertion, pop removal/return, and peek observation at top. Fixed-array indexing and linked-head updates take constant work. A resizing append or singly linked tail-pop implementation can change the cost, so the guarantee needs the stated representations.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].

A count-based alternative uses size=0 and A[size++]=x. Do not combine its empty/full tests with the top-index convention. Fixed-array push/pop are constant time. Linked stacks achieve constant time by inserting and deleting at the head; using a singly linked tail for pop would require a predecessor traversal.

reviews.answer_text: Operator position and known arity determine grouping.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA13 places postfix operators after their operands. During stack evaluation, each binary operator consumes the two latest operand values in right-then-left order and pushes their result. The sequence therefore encodes grouping without precedence parentheses.

evidence.quote: Infix places an operator between operands and uses precedence and parentheses. Prefix places it first; postfix places it last. Their fixed operator arity determines grouping. To convert infix to postfix, output operands immediately and hold operators on a stack. Pop higher-precedence operators before pushing a new operator; also pop equal precedence for left-associative operators. Parentheses temporarily override this order.

To evaluate postfix, push operands. At a binary operator, pop right operand first, then left, and push left op right. Build an expression tree for either prefix (preorder) or postfix (postorder); a stack is useful but is not the only possible conversion representation.

reviews.answer_text: Circular wraparound reuses freed front slots; a simple noncircular queue may not.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA15 distinguishes a rear index reaching the array end from circular modulo arithmetic. A circular queue can insert into positions freed at the front, while a simple noncircular version may report overflow despite those gaps. Capacity and empty/full conventions still must be consistent.

evidence.quote: A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.

reviews.answer_text: FIFO among equal priorities: the task that arrived earlier is served first.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: The priority comparison ties, so the specified comparator proceeds to the arrival counter. An increasing counter gives the earlier arrival the smaller secondary key, causing it to be removed first. Equal-priority tasks are therefore served FIFO under this stable policy. That result follows from the explicitly chosen tie rule; an ordinary priority queue without a stability or comparator rule would not inherently guarantee arrival-order service.

evidence.quote: Arrays and lists can also implement priority queues: an unordered sequence gives cheap insertion but linear extremum removal; an ordered sequence reverses that tradeoff. Equal priorities have no inherent FIFO guarantee. If stable service is required, compare (priority, arrival_counter). Choose the priority direction and tie rule before tracing.

question_revision.original_stem: In a priority queue, if two tasks have equal priority, how are they served?
question_revision.stem: A stable priority queue serves smaller numeric priority keys first and compares equal priorities by an increasing arrival counter, also smallest first. If two tasks have equal priority, in what order are they served?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the missing execution or service model.
assumptions: Specify a stable lexicographic (priority, arrival_counter) comparator with increasing counters and ascending selection.

reviews.answer_text: Dequeue on an empty queue causes underflow.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 defines underflow as attempted removal from empty storage; DSA15’s count convention detects empty using size==0. This indicates that no item exists to return, not that the array is full or that an ordinary emptiness test itself failed.

evidence.quote: Overflow is an attempted insertion into full storage; underflow is an attempted removal from empty storage. Merely checking isEmpty does not underflow.

A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.

reviews.answer_text: Runtime call frames, undo/redo history, and string or sequence reversal.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA12 gives nested calls latest-first returns, moving latest actions between undo and redo stacks, and reversing input by pushing then popping. Each example uses the same latest-pending-item discipline. A new edit after undo normally clears redo history.

evidence.quote: Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first. Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top. Reversal pushes input then pops it. Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back. A new edit after undo normally clears redo. DFS and backtracking use the same latest-pending-choice discipline.

reviews.answer_text: Every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key larger, for distinct keys.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA19 imposes this invariant over entire subtrees at every node, not only immediate children. A descendant can satisfy its parent comparison yet violate an ancestor bound. Duplicate keys require an explicit count or placement policy instead of silently weakening the distinct-key rule.

evidence.quote: With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.

reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA20 visits left subtree, node, then right subtree for inorder, and says BST inorder returns sorted keys. The supplied seven distinct keys therefore appear in increasing order even though the internal child shapes are not fully specified. Shape would matter to preorder or postorder.

evidence.quote: Preorder visits node,left,right; inorder left,node,right; postorder left,right,node. Apply recursively; null children do nothing. Inorder returns sorted keys only for a BST. Preorder supports copying, postorder supports deleting children before parents, and level order uses a FIFO queue.

With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.

reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA21 identifies the maximum key in the left subtree and minimum key in the right subtree as valid replacement values. Copy one into the deleted node, then remove that value’s original node, which has at most one child. These preserve the subtree order invariant.

evidence.quote: A leaf can be detached by clearing its parent link. For one child, make the parent bypass the node and point to the child. For two children, copy the inorder predecessor (left-subtree maximum) or successor (right-subtree minimum), then delete that replacement from its original location. That second deletion has at most one child.

reviews.answer_text: Best successful search Θ(1); arbitrary BST worst Θ(n), balanced worst Θ(log n).
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA19 gives a constant root hit and O(height) search. A chain has linear height, producing linear worst work; logarithmic height disciplines in DSA22 improve that worst bound. Calling every BST logarithmic would incorrectly assume balance.

evidence.quote: Search compares at each node and follows one child until equality or null. Insertion uses that same path to attach a new leaf. Operations cost O(height): logarithmic for balanced trees, linear for a chain. Best-case successful search is Theta(1), a root hit. An optimal BST minimizes expected search cost using access probabilities; constructing it is a different problem from searching it.

AVL balance factor is height(left)-height(right); every node must have factor -1,0 or 1. After insertion or deletion, update heights upward and rotate where necessary. LL imbalance needs a right rotation; RR needs left; LR rotates the left child left then the node right; RL is symmetric. Rotations preserve inorder key order.

reviews.answer_text: BFS explores distance layers with FIFO; DFS finishes branches with a stack or recursion.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA41 enqueues discoveries in layer order, while DSA42 resumes the latest unfinished branch before later neighbors. Both can traverse all reachable vertices, but their pending-work discipline and visitation order differ. BFS also has the unweighted minimum-edge guarantee.

evidence.quote: Mark the source when enqueuing it. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it. Store predecessor[v] when discovering v if a path must be reconstructed. FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.

Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours. An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline. Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles.

reviews.answer_text: Directed: following accounts; undirected: a mutual friendship relationship.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA40 gives following as directed because u following v need not imply v following u. It gives mutual friendship as undirected, representing a symmetric connection. The examples concern relation semantics rather than whether lines happen to be drawn with arrows.

evidence.quote: A graph has vertices V and edges E. Directed edges distinguish u→v from v→u; undirected edges represent two-way relationships. Following accounts is directed; a mutual friendship relation is undirected. Weighted edges carry costs; unweighted shortest-path questions count edges. DAG expands to directed acyclic graph. Trees are connected acyclic graphs, although graph data structures may also contain cycles.

reviews.answer_text: Edge-processing algorithms do more work when E is larger.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA40 says dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts and adjacency lists use Θ(V+E) space. Traversals or algorithms inspecting every edge therefore require more work as density increases. This is not universal: a vertex-only operation need not inspect edges.

evidence.quote: A matrix uses Theta(V²) space and constant edge lookup. Adjacency lists use Theta(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours. Dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts. Examining every edge costs more on denser graphs; vertex-only operations need not inspect every edge.

BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths. With adjacency lists it costs O(V+E); scanning a matrix costs O(V²). To traverse a disconnected graph, restart from each unvisited vertex. Neighbour order affects tied traversal order but not minimum distances.

reviews.answer_text: Full restricts each node to zero or two children; complete restricts level filling.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA18 defines full by each node’s child count and complete by filled earlier levels plus left-filled final level. Those are distinct conditions: completeness can allow one child at the boundary, while fullness alone need not keep every level filled.

evidence.quote: Binary means at most two children. Full means each node has zero or two children. Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left. Perfect means all leaves share a level and every internal node has two children. Balanced means height stays logarithmic under a stated rule; it does not require a perfect shape.

reviews.answer_text: Weighted edges carry differing costs; use them when edge costs matter.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA40 assigns costs to weighted edges and says unweighted shortest-path questions count edges. Distances or travel costs can therefore justify weights when fewer edges is not the true objective. DSA43 then distinguishes weighted shortest paths from unweighted BFS.

evidence.quote: A graph has vertices V and edges E. Directed edges distinguish u→v from v→u; undirected edges represent two-way relationships. Following accounts is directed; a mutual friendship relation is undirected. Weighted edges carry costs; unweighted shortest-path questions count edges. DAG expands to directed acyclic graph. Trees are connected acyclic graphs, although graph data structures may also contain cycles.

For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)). A min-priority queue supports the next choice. BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.

reviews.answer_text: An ordinary unbalanced insertion forms a right chain; worst search is Θ(n).
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA19 explicitly traces sorted insertion 1,2,3,4,5 into a right chain. Each new larger key follows right links to the tail, making the height linear. Worst search follows that chain, while a root hit remains constant. Balanced insertion would rotate and is a different assumption.

evidence.quote: Search compares at each node and follows one child until equality or null. Insertion uses that same path to attach a new leaf. Operations cost O(height): logarithmic for balanced trees, linear for a chain. Best-case successful search is Theta(1), a root hit. An optimal BST minimizes expected search cost using access probabilities; constructing it is a different problem from searching it.
Sorted insertions 1,2,3,4,5 instead form a right chain.

reviews.answer_text: Choose links for frequent known-location updates, such as a doubly linked history cursor.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA10 gives browser history with a doubly linked cursor as an application. With references to current insertion or removal positions, link changes avoid shifting an array’s later elements; arbitrary positional lookup can still be linear. This concrete scenario supports the choice without claiming universal superiority.

evidence.quote: Lists suit changing sequences when references to insertion positions are already available. Finding a position is still linear. Lists can hold polynomial terms (coefficient, exponent), directory or block links, child lists in nonbinary trees, and hash chains. Browser history can use a doubly linked cursor. A playlist may be circular; airline seat lookup requires a specified seat-record model, not an automatic linked-list answer.

A fixed array has a chosen capacity; the choice need not occur at compile time. A resizable array allocates a larger block and copies when needed. Inserting in the middle shifts later elements, so it costs linear time. Appending into spare capacity is constant; a resizing append can be linear, though repeated geometric growth gives amortized constant append cost.

reviews.answer_text: Stack: LIFO for undo; queue: FIFO for equal-priority printer jobs.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 gives latest-first stack service and DSA12 applies it to undoing the latest edit. DSA14 gives arrival-order queues for equal-priority printing. Both ADTs may use arrays or nodes; their service order, not that representation, is the distinction.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].

FIFO suits equal-priority printer jobs, shared-resource waiting, asynchronous buffers and level-order exploration. A play sequence can also use a queue. Distinguish airline seat records from waiting requests; an application name alone does not force one representation.
Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back.

reviews.answer_text: Balance prevents linear-height chains and guarantees logarithmic worst search.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA22 maintains AVL balance factors through rotations that preserve inorder. DSA19 shows ordinary sorted insertion producing a chain, where a search can traverse all nodes. Maintaining logarithmic height prevents that worst degradation, though root-hit best time remains constant.

evidence.quote: AVL balance factor is height(left)-height(right); every node must have factor -1,0 or 1. After insertion or deletion, update heights upward and rotate where necessary. LL imbalance needs a right rotation; RR needs left; LR rotates the left child left then the node right; RL is symmetric. Rotations preserve inorder key order.

Search compares at each node and follows one child until equality or null. Insertion uses that same path to attach a new leaf. Operations cost O(height): logarithmic for balanced trees, linear for a chain. Best-case successful search is Theta(1), a root hit. An optimal BST minimizes expected search cost using access probabilities; constructing it is a different problem from searching it.

reviews.answer_text: A collision maps different keys to one home address; compare chaining and open addressing.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA26 stores colliding entries in bucket lists for chaining, whereas open addressing probes other array slots. Chaining uses link or bucket overhead and expected O(1+α) work; probing keeps entries inside the table and requires careful load and deletion policies. Neither prevents all collisions.

evidence.quote: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.

Linear probing tries (h(k)+j)%m. For size 7 and keys 10,17,24, all home addresses are 3 and occupied positions become 3,4,5. Quadratic probing changes the step; double hashing uses h1(k)+j h2(k), modulo m, with a step relatively prime to m to cover all slots. Neither method guarantees no collisions. Deletion needs tombstones or reinsertion so searches do not stop prematurely.

reviews.answer_text: BFS uses FIFO layers and finds shortest unweighted paths; DFS uses branch-first stack order.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA41 guarantees minimum-edge paths for BFS on unweighted graphs. DSA42 says DFS paths are reachability witnesses but need not be shortest. Differing edge weights require an appropriate weighted-path algorithm, such as Dijkstra under nonnegative weights.

evidence.quote: BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths. With adjacency lists it costs O(V+E); scanning a matrix costs O(V²). To traverse a disconnected graph, restart from each unvisited vertex. Neighbour order affects tied traversal order but not minimum distances.

Using the same graph and alphabetical neighbours, recursive DFS can discover A,B,D,C. Its path is a valid reachability witness but not necessarily shortest. Adjacency-list cost is O(V+E), with O(V) visited state and possible stack depth. DFS supports cycle and connectivity analysis; a directed cycle test distinguishes active recursion vertices from already completed ones.
BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.

reviews.answer_text: Use an undo stack, with a second redo stack if needed.
reviews.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
reviews.explanation: DSA12 moves the latest action from undo to redo and reverses that movement for redo. Pushing each new edit and popping for undo naturally matches the most-recent-edit-first requirement. A new edit after undo normally clears redo history.

evidence.quote: Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first. Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top. Reversal pushes input then pops it. Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back. A new edit after undo normally clears redo. DFS and backtracking use the same latest-pending-choice discipline.

reviews.hint: Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule.
reviews.explanation: DAA16 explicitly classifies heap sort as outside standard divide and conquer: it builds a heap and repeatedly extracts its maximum. Quicksort partitions and recursively sorts ranges; merge sort recursively sorts halves; binary search recursively or iteratively reduces to a smaller half. Thus heap sort is the single exclusion among the listed algorithms.

evidence.quote: Divide and conquer solves smaller largely independent instances and combines results. DP reuses a defined set of subproblem states. Greedy commits to a feasible local choice only when a safety argument supports it. Backtracking grows/retracts candidates when constraints fail; branch and bound also rejects candidates whose best possible objective cannot beat an incumbent.

Heap sort builds a max-heap in Θ(n), then extracts/restores in O(log n) per item: O(n log n) total, Θ(1) auxiliary space, ordinarily unstable. It is not standard D&C. Merge sort offers stability/worst-case guarantees; quicksort’s practical advantage depends on implementation/workload.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Quicksort partitions its input and recursively sorts the resulting smaller ranges, a standard divide-and-conquer pattern.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search repeatedly reduces a sorted search interval to one half; the note treats this as divide-and-conquer.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort divides into halves, sorts each recursively, and combines them by merging.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Heap sort builds a heap and repeatedly restores it after extraction, rather than independently sorting and combining subinstances.

reviews.answer_text: B. A single algorithm’s recurrence alone does not prove a class-wide lower bound.
reviews.hint: Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule.
reviews.explanation: A recurrence describes the running time of the particular algorithm it models. An upper or tight bound for that algorithm does not exclude a different comparison algorithm using fewer operations, so B is false. The class-wide decision-tree argument instead distinguishes n! orders of distinct keys and needs height at least log₂(n!), giving Ω(n log n). Ignoring constants and allowing ordinary array access do not defeat that comparison-count argument.

evidence.quote: A comparison decision tree needs at least n! leaves for distinct-key orderings. Height h allows at most 2^h leaves, so h≥log 2(n!)=Ω(n log n); merge sort matches this worst-case bound. Array indexing is not forbidden.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is a true premise of the comparison decision-tree lower-bound argument, so it is not the requested false statement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is false: a recurrence for one algorithm does not lower-bound every other algorithm.

choices.explanation: This is true: asymptotic lower bounds intentionally disregard constant factors.

The P-versus-NP problem asks whether these classes coincide. Option D captures the question of efficient algorithms for this particular class of problems, although its wording is broad. It does not concern parallelism, language comparisons, or timing one program.

evidence.quote: P contains decision problems solvable deterministically in polynomial input-bit time. NP contains decision problems with polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time, equivalently solvable by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine. NP does not mean non-polynomial; P⊆NP. Whether P=NP remains open.

reviews.hint: Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness.

P is a contained class defined using deterministic machines; NP-complete adds hardness, which the stem never requires. Exponential is a time-growth description rather than the requested definition. The alternate set replaces Exponential with NP-hard, which likewise does not change the defining NP answer.

evidence.quote: P contains decision problems solvable deterministically in polynomial input-bit time. NP contains decision problems with polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time, equivalently solvable by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine. NP does not mean non-polynomial; P⊆NP. Whether P=NP remains open.

A polynomial many-one reduction A≤p B transforms each A-instance into a B-instance preserving yes/no. To prove B NP-hard, reduce a known hard A to B, not the reverse. NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP; optimization TSP is normally called NP-hard, while its bounded-tour decision form is NP-complete. A valid proposed tour and its cost are easy to check, but certifying global optimality is another task. Pseudo-polynomial O(nW) knapsack is not polynomial in the bit length of W.

choices.explanation: P is defined through deterministic polynomial time; it is contained in NP but does not name the full defined class.
