reviews.hint: Identify the required operational function, then compare its scope, inputs and constraints with the cited note definitions.
reviews.explanation: NSA01 explicitly identifies least privilege among administration principles: give accounts and processes only the access required for their work. Agile development and object-oriented programming are development approaches; cloud computing is a computing/deployment model. They may occur in administered systems but are not the administration access principle asked for.

evidence.quote: Create named accounts, assign only needed groups/rights, disable departed users and audit privileged activity. Authentication verifies the account; authorization permits operations. A user right such as remote logon differs from a permission on one file. Group-based administration is easier to review than many hidden individual grants.

Least privilege limits an account or process to the rights its task needs. Agile development instead organizes frequent delivery and adaptation of software. Object-oriented programming organizes software around objects with state and behavior. Cloud computing supplies on-demand access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources. A development approach or hosting model does not itself define an access-rights principle.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Least privilege is explicitly named as a system-administration principle in NSA01.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Agile development organizes software work rather than specifying the administration access principle in the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Object-oriented programming structures software; it is not the stated system-administration principle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cloud computing is a delivery/deployment model, not the access-control principle listed in NSA01.

reviews.hint: Identify the required operational function, then compare its scope, inputs and constraints with the cited note definitions.
reviews.explanation: Name-to-address translation is forward DNS resolution. NSA06 specifies A records for IPv4 and AAAA for IPv6. DHCP instead provides host configuration, while FTP and HTTP provide application data-transfer services. Those functions are distinct from resolving a domain name into its address records.

evidence.quote: Forward resolution obtains an address from a name, using A for IPv4 and AAAA for IPv6. Reverse lookup uses a PTR record in the reverse namespace to obtain a name from an address. CNAME aliases a name, MX identifies mail exchangers and NS identifies authoritative name servers. Forward and reverse records need not both exist or be perfect inverses.

DNS resolves names; DHCP supplies host configuration. SMTP sends/relays mail, while IMAP/POP retrieve it. FTP is a named file-transfer protocol; HTTP also transfers files, so “transfers files” is not an exclusive FTP description. HTTP/HTTPS serve web resources. SSH provides encrypted remote login; SFTP transfers files over SSH and differs from FTP or FTPS.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DNS forward resolution maps names to address records, using A or AAAA as appropriate.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: DHCP supplies client addresses and options rather than translating arbitrary domain names.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: FTP transfers files and does not provide the domain-name resolution service.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: HTTP exchanges web resources rather than serving as the name-to-address directory service.

reviews.hint: Identify the required operational function, then compare its scope, inputs and constraints with the cited note definitions.
reviews.explanation: NSA04 assigns host-address configuration to DHCP, including a server-managed scope and time-limited leases. DNS resolves names, while FTP and HTTP transfer application content. Therefore DHCP is the network service responsible for automatically supplying a device’s IP configuration among these options.

evidence.quote: DHCP supplies addresses and configuration options. Typical initial IPv4 allocation is Discover→Offer→Request→ACK. The server manages its scope/pool, allocated leases, exclusions and reservations; options may include mask, gateway and DNS servers. A dynamic lease lasts for a specified interval, not forever.

DNS resolves names; DHCP supplies host configuration. SMTP sends/relays mail, while IMAP/POP retrieve it. FTP is a named file-transfer protocol; HTTP also transfers files, so “transfers files” is not an exclusive FTP description. HTTP/HTTPS serve web resources. SSH provides encrypted remote login; SFTP transfers files over SSH and differs from FTP or FTPS.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DNS resolves names into records; it does not lease the device’s own network address.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: DHCP supplies addresses and configuration options to clients from a managed scope.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: FTP transfers files rather than assigning network addresses to devices.

Make reruns predictable: compute the desired state, compare with current state and change only what differs. Validate a small dry run before mutation. Avoid requiring privilege for read-only reporting. A good script reports failures and has a meaningful exit status rather than printing success unconditionally.

reviews.explanation: The NSA34 example uses try with specific exception handlers to report expected read failures while exposing unexpected programming errors. Exception handling is therefore the language feature directly intended for handling errors and exceptions. Loops repeat work, conditions choose branches and functions package reusable operations; none alone supplies exception interception.

evidence.quote: Exception handling transfers control from a failing operation to a matching handler. A try block contains the attempted work; an except clause handles specified raised exceptions. A loop repeats operations, a conditional chooses an ordinary branch, and a function packages reusable work; these constructs do not by themselves intercept exceptions.

Scripts automate repeatable administration; they are not inherently faster than compiled programs or automatically secure. Python, shells and PowerShell are common choices; HTML is markup. Define inputs and outputs, use variables for state, if/elif/else for decisions, loops for repeated work and functions for reusable operations. Python indentation defines blocks; == compares while = assigns.

choices.label: A

reviews.explanation: Regular expressions describe text patterns and can capture fields from matching log lines. A script can then count events, correlate entries or report anomalies. evidence.quote: Regex recognizes textual patterns; it does not encrypt, compress or rotate logs. search finds a match anywhere, while fullmatch requires the entire string to fit. Use raw Python strings for backslash-heavy patterns, capture only the needed fields and treat unmatched/malformed lines explicitly. Log rotation bounds file size and preserves historical segments; it is complementary to parsing.

Count the event actually requested, use timestamps/hosts to correlate, and separate absence of matches from failure to read the log. Logs support security and performance analysis, so neither purpose is universally exclusive.

reviews.explanation: DHCP can reduce repetitive configuration in small as well as large networks. evidence.quote: A client renews before expiry; it later tries rebinding if renewal fails. A disconnected host does not automatically renew forever. Use a scope matching the subnet, exclude manually assigned server/router addresses, set correct options and provide a relay when client broadcasts must cross a router. Static assignments and DHCP can coexist; avoid address conflicts. DHCP lowers repetitive administration but availability/security depend on deployment and protection from rogue replies. It does not guarantee connectivity whenever a device changes location.

evidence.quote: A client renews before expiry; it later tries rebinding if renewal fails. A disconnected host does not automatically renew forever. On lease expiry the address becomes eligible for reuse, subject to server policy. Reconnection normally triggers validation/renewal/new allocation, so an expired lease alone does not prove persistent failure. reviews.hint: Compare striping granularity, redundancy placement, usable capacity and required disk-failure tolerance.
reviews.explanation: With exactly two equal disks, RAID1 mirrors the data and leaves one disk’s usable capacity while tolerating either disk failing. RAID0 provides no disk-failure tolerance. RAID2 and RAID3 rely on different striping and redundancy layouts rather than the two-disk mirrored arrangement that meets these requirements. The choice follows the stated disk count, capacity and failure goal rather than the institution’s size or industry.

evidence.quote: RAID0 stripes for capacity/throughput with no disk-failure tolerance. RAID1 mirrors; a two-disk mirror has one disk’s usable capacity and survives one disk failure. RAID2 uses bit striping/Hamming-code redundancy, RAID3 byte striping with dedicated parity, RAID4 block striping with dedicated parity and RAID5 block striping with distributed parity. RAID6 distributes dual parity and tolerates two disk failures. RAID10 stripes mirrored pairs; survival depends on which disks fail.

With N equal disks of capacity D, RAID0 usable=ND, paired RAID1/10≈ND/2, RAID5=(N−1)D and RAID6=(N−2)D. Hardware RAID may offload work to controller resources/cache but does not universally outperform software RAID. Rebuilds consume bandwidth; parity writes have overhead. A large university/bank alone does not select a level. Striping plus parity is not uniquely RAID5 unless distributed block parity is specified.

reviews.hint: Identify the platform and permission model; for an rwx string, separate owner/group/other triplets and use the stated bit weights.
reviews.explanation: Each ordinary Unix permission triplet contains read, write and execute bits. There is no fourth delete bit in that model. Deletion generally depends on permissions on the parent directory, with other mechanisms such as sticky bits or ACLs able to add restrictions. Windows can have an explicit delete permission, so naming the Unix rwx model is essential to make the exception accurate.

evidence.quote: The nine ordinary permission bits are owner, group and other triplets. In each triplet read=4,write=2,execute=1; sum enabled bits to get an octal digit. A leading ls -l character denotes file type, not another permission bit. For directories, read lists names, execute permits traversal/search, and write changes entries subject to other checks. File deletion usually depends on parent directory permissions, with sticky-bit/ACL rules also possible.

Deleting can be an explicit permission; therefore an OS-unspecified question claiming Delete is not a permission is false in Windows. Modify and full control are not identical: full control includes changing permission/ownership capabilities. Separate data access from logon rights. A user allowed to read a file is not necessarily allowed to write it or administer its parent folder.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Read is a recognized permission in both Windows and ordinary Unix permission models.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Write is a recognized access permission, not the requested generic exception.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Execute/read-execute permissions exist in the models described in the note.

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: Block every port, including ports required by legitimate services.
reviews.hint: Identify the required operational function, then compare its scope, inputs and constraints with the cited note definitions.
reviews.explanation: Hardening reduces unnecessary exposure while preserving the services the system must provide. Removing unused software, deploying supported patches and restricting accounts or permissions all support that goal. Filtering unused ports can help too, but indiscriminately blocking ports required by legitimate services destroys availability. The repaired port option states that harmful action explicitly rather than treating every form of port filtering as inappropriate.

evidence.quote: Hardening reduces exposure through unnecessary-service removal, supported patches, restricted accounts/permissions and appropriate port filtering. Blocking an unused known port can be hardening; blocking every useful port merely destroys availability. Weak passwords and unpatched exploitable software are vulnerabilities; attacks exploit weaknesses, and risk combines likelihood with impact.

Use documentation, standardization, least privilege, automation and measured change. Record the current state, intended change, rollback and validation. Schedule maintenance according to service impact and urgency, not merely because a calendar date arrived. Fault management restores failures; performance management measures service behavior; configuration management tracks settings; security management controls access; accounting tracks usage.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Removing unnecessary applications/services reduces attack surface and is an explicit hardening action.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Supported patches repair known weaknesses and are part of hardening.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Restricting users and permissions is an explicit hardening measure.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Blocking ports required by legitimate services defeats availability rather than sound hardening.

reviews.hint: Identify the platform and permission model; for an rwx string, separate owner/group/other triplets and use the stated bit weights.
reviews.explanation: The leading hyphen identifies an ordinary file and is not a permission bit. Split the remaining characters as rwx | r-- | r--. The owner has 4+2+1=7, the group has read only (4), and others have read only (4). Writing those three octal digits in order gives 744, so A is correct.

evidence.quote: The nine ordinary permission bits are owner, group and other triplets. In each triplet read=4,write=2,execute=1; sum enabled bits to get an octal digit. A leading ls -l character denotes file type, not another permission bit. For directories, read lists names, execute permits traversal/search, and write changes entries subject to other checks. File deletion usually depends on parent directory permissions, with sticky-bit/ACL rules also possible.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 744 exactly represents owner rwx, group r-- and others r--.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 700 would deny both group and others all permissions, unlike the two read permissions shown.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 755 would give group and others execute permission as well as read permission; those execute bits are absent.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 766 would give group and others write permission; neither triplet contains w.

evidence.quote: Hardening reduces exposure through unnecessary-service removal, supported patches, restricted accounts/permissions and appropriate port filtering. Blocking an unused known port can be hardening; blocking every useful port merely destroys availability. Preventive controls restrict harmful actions, detective controls expose them and recovery controls restore service. A vulnerability scan checks known weakness patterns, not bandwidth. Test/stage patches, prepare rollback, deploy and verify; testing and installation are both legitimate administrator duties.

reviews.explanation: FTP is specifically a file-transfer protocol, while HTTP also transfers file resources through web request and response exchanges. Their service semantics differ, but the broad content-transfer capability applies to both. SMTP is classified here as mail submission and relay, and DNS as name resolution. The revised selection instruction recognizes the two qualifying services without pretending that file transfer is exclusive to one protocol.

evidence.quote: DNS resolves names; DHCP supplies host configuration. SMTP sends/relays mail, while IMAP/POP retrieve it. FTP is a named file-transfer protocol; HTTP also transfers files, so “transfers files” is not an exclusive FTP description. HTTP/HTTPS serve web resources. SSH provides encrypted remote login; SFTP transfers files over SSH and differs from FTP or FTPS.

Forward resolution obtains an address from a name, using A for IPv4 and AAAA for IPv6. Reverse lookup uses a PTR record in the reverse namespace to obtain a name from an address. CNAME aliases a name, MX identifies mail exchangers and NS identifies authoritative name servers. Forward and reverse records need not both exist or be perfect inverses.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SMTP is identified with mail submission/relay rather than the file-transfer service in this comparison.

choices.label: B

reviews.explanation: Security policies can support confidentiality, integrity and availability, with priorities set by organizational objectives. This scenario explicitly prioritizes preventing unauthorized disclosure of confidential records, which is sensitive-data protection. Availability remains a legitimate security goal but addresses continued service rather than disclosure. Network speed and user experience have different primary objectives. The explicit policy objective determines the selection without imposing one universal priority on all policies.

evidence.quote: A security policy states required behavior, scope, accountable roles and enforcement. Begin with assets/service objectives, assess threats and weaknesses, choose controls, define exceptions/incident procedures, approve/communicate, monitor and periodically review. CIA means confidentiality, integrity and availability; neither sensitive-data protection nor availability alone is the universal primary goal.

Encryption provides confidentiality with correct key/nonce use; authenticated encryption adds integrity/authenticity. Unspecified encryption alone does not guarantee both properties. A password hash supports verification without recovering the original password; it is not a reversible credential store. Encryption can protect a recoverable credential only if its key is separately protected.

choices.label: B

reviews.hint: Distinguish the security objective from the control that prevents, detects or recovers from the stated problem.

evidence.quote: A security policy states required behavior, scope, accountable roles and enforcement. Begin with assets/service objectives, assess threats and weaknesses, choose controls, define exceptions/incident procedures, approve/communicate, monitor and periodically review. CIA means confidentiality, integrity and availability; neither sensitive-data protection nor availability alone is the universal primary goal.

A policy can require password controls, approved encryption, restricted administrative access, backups and patch deadlines; firewall rules implement part of it. Open unrestricted wireless access conflicts with controlled internal access unless intentionally isolated as a guest service. “Use the system passively” is not a purpose of security policy. evidence.quote: Preventive controls restrict harmful actions, detective controls expose them and recovery controls restore service. reviews.answer_text: Rebooting the system; Performing a software update; Resetting network configurations; Conducting a network scan
reviews.hint: Identify the required operational function, then compare its scope, inputs and constraints with the cited note definitions.
reviews.explanation: Rebooting, updating software, resetting configuration and scanning can each help with an appropriate diagnosed problem. Their value depends on the hypothesis and operational context: an update may address a known bug, a reset may correct damaged settings, and a scan may gather service evidence. None should be performed blindly. The question asks which actions can belong to troubleshooting, not which one should always be tried first.

evidence.quote: Define the symptom, scope, time and recent changes; gather the configuration, baseline and logs. Form a testable hypothesis, test the least disruptive explanation, isolate the failing component, apply a targeted fix, verify the user service and document the result. Change one relevant factor at a time when possible. A reboot can hide evidence and is not a diagnosis by itself.

Use bottom-up checks from physical link, top-down checks from application errors, or divide-and-conquer by testing a middle layer. Divide-and-conquer narrows the working/failing boundary; it is not random trial-and-error. Rebooting, updates, resetting settings and scanning can all be troubleshooting actions in suitable circumstances; a question without fault evidence cannot rank them uniquely.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Rebooting can be a justified troubleshooting action, although it can hide evidence and is not itself diagnosis.

choices.label: C

reviews.explanation: Logs can reveal suspicious activity that suggests a security breach and can also expose timing, error or workload patterns related to performance. These are complementary uses of recorded observations. Changing firewall rules may follow the analysis, but it is a separate configuration action. Encryption protects communications in transit or storage rather than emerging from analysis of past records. Both analytical purposes therefore qualify.

evidence.quote: Count the event actually requested, use timestamps/hosts to correlate, and separate absence of matches from failure to read the log. Logs support security and performance analysis, so neither purpose is universally exclusive.

Measure a baseline, sample over an interval, compare with workload and correlate symptoms before changing hardware. CPU utilization/run queues identify processing pressure; low free memory alone is weak evidence because cache may be reclaimable. Persistent paging with high latency indicates memory pressure. Storage capacity and I/O latency are separate: a disk can be nearly empty but saturated, or nearly full while lightly loaded.

reviews.hint: Distinguish the security objective from the control that prevents, detects or recovers from the stated problem.
reviews.explanation: An IDS detects suspicious activity and alerts, while traffic analysis can provide additional detective evidence. User authentication establishes identity for subsequent access decisions. Correctly implemented encryption protects data against unauthorized disclosure. These mechanisms address different security needs, so all are examples of controls under the broad question. Their inclusion does not imply that any single mechanism provides complete security by itself.

evidence.quote: An IDS detects/alerts; an IPS can block inline. Scanning identifies potential weaknesses rather than proving successful exploitation. A captured packet, open port or alert needs context. Monitoring network usage is not the same as configuring access control or encrypting communications.

Encryption provides confidentiality with correct key/nonce use; authenticated encryption adds integrity/authenticity. Unspecified encryption alone does not guarantee both properties. A password hash supports verification without recovering the original password; it is not a reversible credential store. Encryption can protect a recoverable credential only if its key is separately protected.

Segmentation separates groups of systems and enforces allowed flows with routing/filtering policies; VLAN membership alone does not establish complete security. NAC assesses device/user admission and can reject or quarantine unauthorized/noncompliant devices. Authentication proves an identity, while access rules decide which resources it may use.

choices.label: B

A recognized NIC makes a missing driver less likely, not proof of a working physical link. Ethernet commonly uses RJ45 connectors; an RJ11 telephone jack is not the expected Ethernet connection.

Use bottom-up checks from physical link, top-down checks from application errors, or divide-and-conquer by testing a middle layer. Divide-and-conquer narrows the working/failing boundary; it is not random trial-and-error. Rebooting, updates, resetting settings and scanning can all be troubleshooting actions in suitable circumstances; a question without fault evidence cannot rank them uniquely.

reviews.explanation: Python’s subprocess module launches child programs and provides interfaces for collecting output, checking status and limiting runtime. Pass an argument list to avoid accidental shell interpretation; quote handling differs from composing a shell string.

Echo prints, grep searches text and ipconfig/ifconfig reports/configures networking; none is the general Python child-process abstraction. Explain the language before choosing subprocess in a generic “which command” question.

Use the format’s parser for structured JSON/INI rather than blindly replacing every matching substring. Open text with an explicit encoding and use with so files close even when processing fails.

Scripts automate repeatable administration; they are not inherently faster than compiled programs or automatically secure. Python, shells and PowerShell are common choices; HTML is markup. reviews.explanation: Loopback lets a host address its own protocol stack and reach local services without an external link. The conventional IPv4 address is 127.0.0.1, within the broader reserved 127/8 block. It is therefore local self-reference rather than an external address. The clarified example wording permits all three true descriptions without incorrectly restricting the entire loopback range to a single address.

evidence.quote: 127.0.0.1 conventionally names the local IPv4 loopback interface; 127/8 is reserved for loopback. Loopback tests local protocol processing, not cable, switch or remote reachability. Programs can use it for local services. Thus several loopback descriptions or several 127/8 addresses may be valid, even when the bank expects one.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Loopback refers to the host itself rather than a remote device.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Programs can reach local services through network protocols using loopback.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Loopback is local and does not require an external network link.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 127.0.0.1 is the conventional IPv4 loopback address, although the reserved block is broader.

reviews.hint: Identify the required operational function, then compare its scope, inputs and constraints with the cited note definitions.
reviews.explanation: Quality of service classifies, queues and prioritizes traffic to meet performance objectives such as low delay or limited loss. It can span layers while supporting applications. Proxies and agents are mediating components, and installing a service or configuring email are administrative activities. The revised question uses those explicit functional categories, so it does not require an unsupported taxonomy that labels every item an application-layer service.

evidence.quote: A proxy acts on behalf of a client or backend service and can cache, filter or mediate application requests. A default IP gateway is a next-hop router; an application gateway may translate protocols. It need not be a modem/router combination. These terms describe functions that can coexist on one machine.

QoS classifies, queues and prioritizes traffic to meet performance objectives such as low delay or limited loss. It can operate across layers and support applications, so it is not exclusively an application-layer service. Installing a new service is an administrative action; email configuration is another action and proxies/agents are components. A question mixing these labels needs a specified service-management taxonomy before a unique exclusion can be chosen.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Proxies and agents mediate requests rather than naming the traffic-prioritization mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Installing a service is an administrative activity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Email configuration is an administrative activity.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: QoS classifies and prioritizes traffic and can operate across layers.

reviews.hint: Compare striping granularity, redundancy placement, usable capacity and required disk-failure tolerance.
reviews.explanation: With exactly two equal disks, RAID1 mirrors the data and leaves one disk’s usable capacity while tolerating either disk failing. RAID0 provides no disk-failure tolerance. RAID2 and RAID3 rely on different striping and redundancy layouts rather than the two-disk mirrored arrangement that meets these requirements. The choice follows the stated disk count, capacity and failure goal rather than the institution’s size or industry.

evidence.quote: RAID0 stripes for capacity/throughput with no disk-failure tolerance. RAID1 mirrors; a two-disk mirror has one disk’s usable capacity and survives one disk failure. RAID2 uses bit striping/Hamming-code redundancy, RAID3 byte striping with dedicated parity, RAID4 block striping with dedicated parity and RAID5 block striping with distributed parity. RAID6 distributes dual parity and tolerates two disk failures. RAID10 stripes mirrored pairs; survival depends on which disks fail.

With N equal disks of capacity D, RAID0 usable=ND, paired RAID1/10≈ND/2, RAID5=(N−1)D and RAID6=(N−2)D. Hardware RAID may offload work to controller resources/cache but does not universally outperform software RAID. Rebuilds consume bandwidth; parity writes have overhead. A large university/bank alone does not select a level. Striping plus parity is not uniquely RAID5 unless distributed block parity is specified.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RAID3 uses byte striping with dedicated parity, not the required two-disk fault-tolerant layout.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A two-disk RAID1 mirror provides one disk’s capacity and survives either disk failing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: RAID2 uses bit striping and Hamming redundancy rather than the required two-disk solution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: RAID0 cannot tolerate a disk failure.

reviews.answer_text: Passive system use is not a security-policy purpose
reviews.hint: Distinguish the security objective from the control that prevents, detects or recovers from the stated problem.
reviews.explanation: NSA26 assigns policies risk reduction, coordinated required behavior and CIA goals. D’s passive-use statement does not describe those governance/protection purposes and is explicitly rejected by the note. B expresses the desired CIA objective, not a guarantee that policy alone prevents every incident. The remaining statements fit legitimate policy aims.

evidence.quote: A security policy states required behavior, scope, accountable roles and enforcement. Begin with assets/service objectives, assess threats and weaknesses, choose controls, define exceptions/incident procedures, approve/communicate, monitor and periodically review. CIA means confidentiality, integrity and availability; neither sensitive-data protection nor availability alone is the universal primary goal.

A policy can require password controls, approved encryption, restricted administrative access, backups and patch deadlines; firewall rules implement part of it. Open unrestricted wireless access conflicts with controlled internal access unless intentionally isolated as a guest service. “Use the system passively” is not a purpose of security policy. Policies coordinate action and reduce risk; they do not guarantee every attack will fail.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reducing risk is a stated security-policy aim, so this is not wrongly stated.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: CIA protection is a legitimate policy objective, with actual success depending on implemented controls.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Coordinating required behavior and enforcement across the organization is a legitimate policy purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Passive use is not the defined purpose of security policy and does not express its governance/protection objectives.

reviews.hint: Respect operator grouping and operand types, then trace each operation in evaluation order.
reviews.explanation: Start with n=6. The subtraction assignment n-=m computes 6-15, leaving n=-9. The multiplication assignment then uses that updated value: -9*3=-27. OOP23 includes this exact trace. The sign cannot become positive because only subtraction followed by multiplication by positive three occurs.

evidence.quote: Java evaluates operands left to right while respecting precedence. With n=6,m=15,p=3, n-=m then n*=p leaves -27.

choices.explanation: 27 discards the negative sign produced when 15 is subtracted from 6.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Three is the unchanged multiplier p, not the updated value of n that is printed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 24 does not follow either the subtraction result -9 or its subsequent multiplication by 3.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The ordered updates yield n=-9 and then n=-27, which System.out.print outputs.

reviews.explanation: The length-four array is visited at indices 0,1,2,3. Assigning i*3 stores 0,3,6,9. Starting sum at zero and adding each element gives 18, exactly the example in OOP27. The loop processes four elements, not merely the first one or an uninitialized default array.

evidence.quote: For int[] a=new int[4], setting a[i]=i*3 and accumulating yields 0+3+6+9=18.
Valid indices are 0..a.length-1; an invalid access throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Three is the element assigned at index 1, rather than the full accumulator result.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 36 doubles the actual total; each of the four elements is added only once.

D supplies exactly those rows with comma-separated nested initializers. B is syntactically valid but adds an unwanted middle-row zero. Java two-dimensional arrays are arrays of arrays and may be ragged: {{12,-9,8},{7,14},{-32,-1,0}} has row lengths 3,2,3. Java does not expose a portable physical contiguity guarantee, so a language-level answer should not rely on raw addresses.

reviews.answer_text: Compilation fails because the subtype catch is unreachable.
reviews.hint: Check the thrown type and catch order before tracing propagation or handler output.
reviews.explanation: Exception is caught before its subclass ArithmeticException. OOP30 says that a general catch before a subtype catch makes the latter unreachable and prevents compilation. The program therefore never executes the division or either print statement. Reasoning about which handler would run cannot bypass this compile-time restriction.

evidence.quote: Catch blocks are considered in source order. Place FileNotFoundException before IOException and IOException before Exception; a general catch before a subtype catch makes that later handler unreachable and prevents compilation.

Throwable is the root of throwable values, with Exception and Error branches. RuntimeException and Error subclasses are unchecked; other throwable classes are checked. IOException, FileNotFoundException and SQLException are standard checked examples. ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ClassCastException and array bounds exceptions are unchecked.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The ArithmeticException handler is unreachable at compile time, so it cannot print its message.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Compilation fails before execution; the statement following the catches never prints finished.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Although Exception could catch this runtime type, the illegal later catch prevents any execution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The earlier Exception catch subsumes ArithmeticException, making the later handler unreachable and the program uncompilable.

Modern Java also supports source-file launch with a .java argument, but the revised question explicitly asks for the already compiled class. The compiler invocation without the source extension is not the requested launch either.

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: double is not an integer primitive type.
reviews.hint: Identify the primitive category, width and conversion rule before evaluating a declaration or expression.
reviews.explanation: OOP06 lists byte, short, int and long as the signed integer types with widths 8,16,32,64 bits. Of the supplied options, long, byte and short belong to that group. double represents floating-point values rather than an integer primitive, so it is the exception requested by the question.

reviews.hint: Identify the primitive category, width and conversion rule before evaluating a declaration or expression.
reviews.explanation: OOP06 states that byte ranges from -128 to 127. These inclusive endpoints provide 256 values for an 8-bit signed type. Options that include positive 128 exceed the upper endpoint, and those starting at -127 omit the lowest permitted value. Only D preserves both limits correctly.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The lower endpoint -127 omits the valid minimum byte value -128.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both endpoints are wrong: -128 is omitted and the invalid positive value 128 is included.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The inclusive limits -128 and 127 exactly match the byte range stated in OOP06.

reviews.hint: Identify the primitive category, width and conversion rule before evaluating a declaration or expression.

reviews.hint: Identify the primitive category, width and conversion rule before evaluating a declaration or expression.

This differs from postfix increment, which would supply the old value to the multiplication. Only one increment occurs in this expression.

reviews.hint: Read the cited conceptual rules, state the model, and apply them before comparing the alternatives.
reviews.explanation: Java groups pi * r * r as (pi * r) * r and rounds each double multiplication using binary64 arithmetic. The resulting value has hexadecimal representation 0x1.2d90cb295e9e2p+8. Java 17’s standard conversion prints that value as 301.5656, followed by println’s line terminator. The supplementary Oracle rules establish the precise arithmetic and text conversion; no separate decimal-place formatting is applied.

evidence.quote: Java 17 float uses IEEE 754 binary32, and double uses binary64. Successive multiplications group from left to right. Each floating-point operation rounds to its representable result, using nearest-value rounding with ties to even; regrouping a product can change its result.

PrintStream.print(double) converts the stored value through String.valueOf and Double.toString. For finite nonzero magnitudes from 0.001 inclusive to 10000000 exclusive, the standard decimal form uses at least one fractional digit and only the further digits needed to distinguish the value from adjacent doubles. println(double) also adds a line terminator. This is not fixed-decimal-place formatting.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 301.5656 is the standard Java 17 printed representation of the computed double.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: There is no integer conversion that discards the fractional part.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The program does not truncate or format the result to two decimal places.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The program does not round its displayed output to two decimal places.

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified Java 17 for the original console-output question.
assumptions: The program runs on Java 17 with its standard double arithmetic and println(double) conversion.
Options compare the visible output line; println also appends a line terminator.

external_evidence.statement: For a finite double of this magnitude the decimal representation uses only the fractional digits needed to distinguish the value from adjacent doubles. The computed value is the same binary64 value as literal 301.5656, and this decimal is its distinguishing representation.

reviews.hint: Read the cited conceptual rules, state the model, and apply them before comparing the alternatives.
reviews.explanation: The prefix decrement reduces g from 6 to 5 before multiplication uses it. The resulting integer expression is 5*8, which equals 40. The updated value is used immediately; it is not the old 6 and no later increment occurs. Thus the integer printed is 40.

evidence.quote: Prefix ++ and -- update a variable before supplying its value; postfix forms supply the old value before the update. Multiplication, division and remainder bind before addition and subtraction; same-level binary arithmetic groups left to right. Integer division truncates toward zero.
Java evaluates operands left to right while respecting precedence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 48 uses the old value 6, which would not reflect the prefix decrement before multiplication.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Prefix decrement supplies 5 to the multiplication, producing 5*8=40.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 56 uses 7, but decrement reduces the initial 6 instead of increasing it.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 44 is not 5 multiplied by 8 and does not follow the stated prefix update.

reviews.hint: Locate the declaration scope and check default initialization versus definite assignment.
reviews.explanation: OOP05 illustrates a declaration with int a=10,b=10, separating the declarators with a comma. The shared type applies to each name in that declaration. Colons and brackets serve other syntactic purposes and do not separate ordinary variable declarators in the example. The comma-separated option states the required list form.

evidence.quote: Initializers such as int a=10,b=10; assign initial values.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A colon does not separate the ordinary variable declarators shown in the note’s shared-type declaration.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Brackets describe array types or indexing rather than separating names in a declarator list.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The example int a=10,b=10 uses a comma between variable declarators sharing the type int.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Comma-separated is an offered and supported list form, so none of the above is false.

reviews.answer_text: Both numeric values and characters can participate in arithmetic.
reviews.hint: Identify the primitive category, width and conversion rule before evaluating a declaration or expression.
reviews.explanation: OOP06 states that arithmetic promotes char, byte and short to int in many expressions. Characters are therefore allowed alongside numeric operands. boolean does not convert to numeric truth values and is not an arithmetic operand. D gives the complete supported pair; A and C each mention only part of that operand domain.

evidence.quote: Arithmetic promotes char, byte and short to int in many expressions. boolean does not convert to or from numeric truth values; if(0) and for(...;0;...) are invalid.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Characters are permitted through promotion, but this option alone omits the also-permitted numeric operand category.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Java boolean does not convert to numeric values for arithmetic, as OOP06 explicitly states.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Numeric operands are permitted, but this option alone omits the also-permitted character category.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Both numeric and char operands are permitted; chars undergo numeric promotion for arithmetic.

reviews.answer_text: Both integers and floating-point numbers in Java.
reviews.hint: Respect operator grouping and operand types, then trace each operation in evaluation order.
reviews.explanation: OOP23 explicitly contrasts Java with C++: Java % accepts floating-point operands as well as integers. This course’s Java context therefore makes A the complete domain among the offered choices. B and C each name only one supported category. Importing C++’s integral-only restriction would give the wrong answer for Java.

evidence.quote: Unlike C++, Java % also accepts floating-point operands.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Both integer and floating-point operands are accepted by Java’s remainder operator according to OOP23.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Integers are allowed, but this option alone omits Java’s also-supported floating-point operands.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Floating-point values are allowed, but this option alone omits the also-supported integer operands.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note explicitly supports both supplied operand categories, so none of the mentioned is false.

reviews.hint: Respect operator grouping and operand types, then trace each operation in evaluation order.
reviews.explanation: The remainder operation is evaluated first: 10%4 is 2. The remaining additions and subtraction group left to right, yielding 6-2+2+7 = 4+2+7 = 13. OOP23 includes the same expression and result. No floating conversion or increment operation appears in this calculation.

evidence.quote: Java evaluates operands left to right while respecting precedence.

Prefix ++ and -- update a variable before supplying its value; postfix forms supply the old value before the update. Multiplication, division and remainder bind before addition and subtraction; same-level binary arithmetic groups left to right. Integer division truncates toward zero.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 14 does not follow the remainder 10%4=2 and the resulting sum 6-2+2+7.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 12 is one below the computed total and does not respect the stated remainder result.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Evaluating 10%4 first gives 2; then 6-2+2+7 equals 13.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 10 omits or miscalculates part of the expression; the full integer evaluation gives 13.

reviews.hint: Respect operator grouping and operand types, then trace each operation in evaluation order.
reviews.explanation: Both additions initially produce 6. Assigning one to double makes var1=6.0, so var1/4 gives 1.5. var3 remains int, so var3/4 truncates to integer 1. The string containing a space then concatenates their representations, producing 1.5 1 rather than giving the integer result a decimal suffix.

evidence.quote: Integer 6/4 is 1; double 6.0/4 is 1.5.
Once a String operand is encountered, + concatenates in left-to-right groups: 1+2+"x" gives "3x", while "x"+1+2 gives "x12".

A while header is while(condition). A basic for header is for(initialization; condition; update). A do-while statement places its condition after the body. An if selects its true branch or, when present, its else branch; only the selected branch executes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The double division of 6.0 by 4 yields 1.5, not zero.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The first quotient is floating point and retains .5 rather than becoming integer 1.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The double quotient prints 1.5, followed by the space and integer quotient 1.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: var4 is int, so its string representation is 1 rather than 1.0.

reviews.hint: Respect operator grouping and operand types, then trace each operation in evaluation order.
reviews.explanation: The AND produces 11&9 = 1011&1001 = 1001, or 9. XOR with 3 gives 1001^0011 = 1010, or 10. OR with 12 then gives 1010|1100 = 1110, or 14. OOP23 explicitly provides this chain; these are integer bitwise operations, not Boolean short-circuit operations.

evidence.quote: For bitwise values, write binary columns: 11&9=9; 9^3=10; 10|12=14.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Seven has binary 0111, whereas the final OR produces 1110.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The final OR includes the set bits of 12, so it cannot produce zero.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The chain produces x=9, y=10 and final y|12=14.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Eight omits bits set by the final OR of binary 1010 and 1100.

reviews.hint: Read the cited conceptual rules, state the model, and apply them before comparing the alternatives.
reviews.explanation: Relational expressions test a relation rather than return one of their numeric operands. In Java that truth result is Boolean, consistent with OOP06’s prohibition on treating boolean as numeric truth values and OOP23’s Boolean output discussion. Integer, character and double values can be compared in suitable expressions, but are not the comparison result type.

evidence.quote: Java relational comparisons (<, <=, >, >=) and equality tests (==, !=) produce primitive boolean truth values. Their result is not an integer truth code or a value of the numeric operand type.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Java comparison results are logical values rather than integer truth codes such as zero and one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A relational test yields the Boolean truth value true or false.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Characters can be compared, but a comparison does not return a character result.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Double operands may participate in comparisons, but their relation yields a Boolean rather than a double.

reviews.hint: Read the cited conceptual rules, state the model, and apply them before comparing the alternatives.
reviews.explanation: Greater-than, less-than and equality operators express truth tests. Java represents their results as Boolean values, not integers or floating-point numbers. OOP06 distinguishes boolean from numeric values, and OOP23 describes printing Boolean true as lowercase true. The operand type therefore does not become the result type of the test.

evidence.quote: Java relational comparisons (<, <=, >, >=) and equality tests (==, !=) produce primitive boolean truth values. Their result is not an integer truth code or a value of the numeric operand type.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Java uses Boolean truth values for comparisons rather than returning integer zero or one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Comparing floating operands still yields a truth value, not a floating-point numerical result.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Greater-than, less-than and equality comparisons return Boolean true or false.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Boolean is explicitly offered and is the appropriate logical result type, so none is false.

reviews.answer_text: Java requires boolean or Boolean for the first operand of ?: .
reviews.hint: Read the cited conceptual rules, state the model, and apply them before comparing the alternatives.
reviews.explanation: Java’s conditional operator requires its first operand to have primitive boolean or boxed Boolean type. That condition chooses which of the other two expressions is evaluated; the unselected alternative is not evaluated. Integer and floating-point values are not accepted as numeric truth codes. The Boolean option therefore names the required logical category, and None is false because that category is offered.

evidence.quote: The conditional expression condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse requires a boolean or Boolean condition. It evaluates only the selected alternative. An integer or floating-point first operand is a compile-time error.
boolean does not convert to or from numeric truth values; if(0) and for(...;0;...) are invalid.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Java integer values do not satisfy the JLS first-operand requirement of boolean or Boolean.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Floating-point values do not satisfy Java’s Boolean conditional-operand requirement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Boolean names the required logical category; Java accepts primitive boolean or boxed Boolean.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The Boolean category is offered and satisfies the JLS requirement, so none is false.

external_evidence.title: Java Language Specification SE17 §15.25: Conditional Operator
external_evidence.statement: Java conditional expressions require a first operand of type boolean or Boolean.
