reviews.hint: Compare the stated historical clues and distinguish origin, characteristic era and technical capability.
reviews.explanation: The first four generations in NYU’s historical taxonomy associates second-generation transistor machines with uniprogrammed batch systems whose OS remains resident between jobs. The first era has no separate resident OS; the third emphasizes ICs and multiprogramming, and the fourth personal computers. OS02 explains batch operation, while the generation mapping is supplied by the supplementary university notes. This is a scoped teaching convention rather than a universal first-OS claim.

evidence.quote: In the first four generations of the cited NYU teaching taxonomy, the first generation uses vacuum tubes and manual single-user operation without a separate resident OS. The second generation pairs transistors with uniprogrammed batch systems; the resident OS starts successive jobs without being reloaded for every job.

The third generation pairs integrated circuits with multiprogramming. The fourth emphasizes personal computers. These are characteristic-era associations, not claims that each feature existed exclusively in one era.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The first era is the manual/no-separate-resident-OS era in this taxonomy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The second era pairs transistor machines with resident uniprogrammed batch systems.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The third era emphasizes ICs and multiprogramming rather than the initial resident batch stage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The fourth era emphasizes personal computers and follows the batch-monitor era.

question_revision.original_stem: Which generation of computers introduced the use of operating systems?
question_revision.stem: Using the first four generations described in NYU’s OS-history notes (vacuum tubes; transistors; integrated circuits; personal computers), which generation is associated with resident uniprogrammed batch operating systems, following the manual/no-resident-OS era?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the historical teaching taxonomy and the resident-batch milestone.
assumptions: Use the first four generations in NYU’s cited history taxonomy rather than an absolute first invention date.

external_evidence.title: NYU OS 2250 — History of Operating Systems
external_evidence.statement: The teaching taxonomy places no separate OS in the first era, resident uniprogrammed batch systems in the second, ICs/multiprogramming in the third and personal computers in the fourth.

reviews.hint: Distinguish command interfaces, privileged core services and the stages of booting.
reviews.explanation: Antivirus and disk-management products can combine ordinary user processes with privileged helper components. Their user-space components count as user programs even though some work requires kernel services. The stem explicitly confines the driver and interrupt-handler options to kernel-resident components, avoiding architectures with user-space drivers. Thus antivirus software and the partition-manager utility are both valid examples under the stated component-level interpretation.

evidence.quote: Utilities such as antivirus and disk tools can combine user processes with privileged components.

Being scheduled or managed by the kernel does not give application thread code kernel privilege. Ordinary applications and supporting utilities execute in restricted user mode and request protected services through libraries and system calls. Kernel component code executes in privileged kernel mode and performs permitted low-level hardware operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The driver is explicitly kernel-resident in this question.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Antivirus software can have a user-process component alongside privileged helpers.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A disk partition manager can have a user-process component invoking privileged services.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The interrupt handler is explicitly kernel-resident in this question.

question_revision.original_stem: Which of the following is an example of a user program?
question_revision.stem: In a conventional monolithic OS, which listed utilities can have user-space program components that invoke privileged OS services, even if the complete product also includes privileged helpers? Treat “device driver” and “interrupt handler” here as kernel-resident components. Select all that apply.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Defined the component-level scope and allowed both user-space utility examples.
assumptions: Driver and interrupt-handler options denote kernel-resident components.
A product qualifies if it can contain a user-space program component.

reviews.hint: Separate handling before allocation from actions taken after detection, and consider the cost of checking.
reviews.explanation: The ostrich or ignoring policy accepts the risk of a sufficiently rare, insignificant deadlock problem when systematic handling is not worthwhile. That is the intended meaning of Ignorance. Prevention instead constrains requests to break a necessary deadlock condition, and recovery acts after detection. Merely waiting is not the same as deliberately choosing to tolerate the rare problem.

evidence.quote: Ignoring a sufficiently rare problem is sometimes called the ostrich policy, but real systems still prevent or detect selected deadlocks. “Deadlock acceptance” can mean intentional ignoring, not necessarily an invalid approach.

Prevention constrains how requests are made. Share a resource where safe to remove mutual exclusion; request all needed resources before holding any to remove hold-and-wait; permit safe resource withdrawal/restart to attack no-preemption; impose a global acquisition order to remove circular wait.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Prevention constrains resource requests to remove a necessary deadlock condition; it does not deliberately ignore the problem.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Waiting describes a process behavior, not the deliberate policy of accepting rare deadlocks.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Recovery takes action after deadlock detection rather than choosing to ignore the rare problem.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ignorance names the intentional ignoring or ostrich policy in this context.

question_revision.original_stem: One of the following deadlock handling methods is used if it occurs rarely and is insignificant.
question_revision.stem: One of the following deadlock handling methods is used if it occurs rarely and is insignificant.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: one distractor uses a standard deadlock-handling policy term.
assumptions: Ignorance means the intentional ignoring/ostrich policy.
Prevention is a deliberate practice-option repair of presentation, not a claimed source-image transcription.

reviews.hint: Compare per-thread execution context with shared process resources and the stated thread mapping.
reviews.explanation: Multithreading means that one process contains multiple threads of execution. The described spreadsheet and browser processes each have several threads sharing their process resources. The specified server implementation has only its main thread and therefore is not multithreaded. This conclusion follows from the supplied designs, not from a universal claim about every version of Excel, every browser, or every server.

evidence.quote: A thread has its own PC, registers and stack. Threads in a process share code, address space and usually open-file resources. A process can contain many threads; a thread belongs to one process at a time. Threads are not a group of processes and need not execute sequentially.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The specified Excel process has several worker threads and is multithreaded.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The specified browser process has multiple threads and is multithreaded.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The specified server has only one thread and is not multithreaded.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: C is a valid non-multithreaded implementation, so none is incorrect.

question_revision.original_stem: One of the following processes is not based on multithreading.

original_options.label: D
original_options.text: None of the choices is correct

question_revision.stem: Consider three specified implementations: an Excel application process with several worker threads, a client-browser process with multiple threads sharing its address space, and a server process using only its single main thread. Which listed process does not use multithreading?

options.label: D
options.text: None of the choices is correct

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Supplied hypothetical process designs instead of assuming threading from product names.
assumptions: Only the described hypothetical implementations are classified.
The server creates no additional threads.

reviews.answer_text: None: modern OS families can support all three techniques.
reviews.hint: Distinguish identity checks, permission checks and the particular security property at issue.
reviews.explanation: OS39 states that modern OS families can support cryptography, authentication and firewalls, while support/configuration depends on product. Therefore none of the three is categorically unsupported by modern operating systems. The answer is a capability-category statement, not a guarantee that every installation includes every feature or enables it by default. Each technique has a distinct security role.

evidence.quote: Password hashing verifies secrets without storing plaintext; one-time passwords expire after use. Encryption protects confidentiality under correct key use but does not automatically provide integrity. Trojans masquerade as useful software, worms propagate independently and viruses attach to hosts; denial of service harms availability. Modern OS families can support cryptography, authentication and firewalls, but support/configuration depends on product.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Cryptography is explicitly a capability that modern OS families can support, though configuration varies.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Authentication is explicitly supported as a modern OS capability for verifying identity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Firewalls are explicitly within modern OS support capabilities, even though product and configuration matter.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All three techniques can be supported; none is categorically outside modern operating-system security capabilities.

reviews.hint: Follow namespace structure and distinguish names, underlying files and mounted filesystems.
reviews.explanation: A multilevel or tree namespace supports nested directories and paths that can be absolute or relative. That is the structure the notes identify as commonly presented by modern general-purpose systems. A two-level structure separates users but does not express arbitrary nesting, and a single-level structure has only one namespace level. The aggregate therefore includes structures that do not match the requested hierarchical category.

evidence.quote: A single-level directory requires unique names in one namespace. Two-level directories separate users. A tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths; links can create shared graphs. Modern general-purpose systems commonly present hierarchical namespaces, but a feature name alone does not prove that every system excludes simpler arrangements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multilevel describes the hierarchical nested namespace.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Single-level and two-level arrangements do not both describe the requested nested tree, so all is incorrect.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two-level separates users without providing the general nested hierarchy asked for.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Single-level has no nested directory hierarchy.

question_revision.original_stem: Which of the following directory structure used in modern operating systems.
question_revision.stem: Which directory structure describes the commonly presented namespace of modern general-purpose operating systems, with nested directories and absolute or relative paths? Choose the structural category, not every simpler arrangement that might also be implemented.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Asked for the common nested namespace category rather than any structure ever used.
assumptions: Multilevel means a tree/hierarchical namespace.

reviews.answer_text: Second generation -> multiprogramming; Fourth generation -> real time systems; Third generation → uniprogrammed batch systems
reviews.hint: Compare the stated historical clues and distinguish origin, characteristic era and technical capability.
reviews.explanation: The first four generations in NYU’s teaching taxonomy associates the first era with one user and no separate OS, the second with uniprogrammed batch systems, the third with IC-based multiprogramming, and the fourth with personal computers. Thus A, B and D mismatch the characteristic eras, while C fits. OS02 supplies the operating-mode background; the generation associations come from the supplementary university history notes rather than the unchanged master note.

evidence.quote: In the first four generations of the cited NYU teaching taxonomy, the first generation uses vacuum tubes and manual single-user operation without a separate resident OS. The second generation pairs transistors with uniprogrammed batch systems; the resident OS starts successive jobs without being reloaded for every job.

The third generation pairs integrated circuits with multiprogramming. The fourth emphasizes personal computers. These are characteristic-era associations, not claims that each feature existed exclusively in one era.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multiprogramming characterizes the third era, so pairing it with the second is wrong.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The fourth-era heading is personal computers, not the introduction of real-time systems.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Manual single-user operation without a separate OS matches the first era.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Uniprogrammed batch characterizes the second era, not the defining third-era advance.

question_revision.original_stem:
Advancement of operating systems is closely tied to computer architectures; therefore, it has
passed through different generations. Which one of the following generation and advancement pairings is
WRONGLY coupled?
question_revision.stem: For the first four generations described in NYU’s OS-history notes, which pairings incorrectly identify the defining historical characteristic of the named generation? Judge characteristic era, not whether a feature could also exist later. Select all that apply.

options.label: C
options.text: First generation → manual single-user operation without a separate resident OS

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified a cited historical taxonomy, clarified two pairings and selected every mismatch.
assumptions: Use the cited NYU characteristic-era taxonomy.
A pairing concerns the characteristic historical advance rather than every feature present during an era.

external_evidence.title: NYU OS 2250 — History of Operating Systems
external_evidence.statement: The headings and descriptions associate first-generation manual operation with no separate OS, second-generation machines with uniprogrammed batch, third-generation machines with multiprogramming and fourth-generation machines with personal computers.

reviews.hint: Identify how data moves, which participant waits and what event allows the operation to continue.
reviews.explanation: OS09 defines nonblocking operations as returning promptly with data, progress or a would-block result. Among the options, nonblocking receive therefore supplies the asynchronous/non-waiting behavior being contrasted. Blocking receive waits for a message, blocking send waits for its defined completion condition, and direct message concerns how endpoints are addressed rather than whether the call blocks.

evidence.quote: Blocking send waits for the required handoff/buffering/receipt condition defined by its API. Blocking receive waits for a message. Nonblocking operations return promptly with data, progress or a would-block result. “Sender blocked until received” identifies blocking send under rendezvous semantics.

Direct message communication names the receiving process explicitly. Indirect communication uses a mailbox or port. This naming distinction is independent of whether a send or receive blocks: naming a destination does not determine synchronization semantics.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Nonblocking receive returns promptly instead of waiting until a message arrives, matching this asynchronous contrast.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Blocking receive waits for a message rather than providing the non-waiting behavior requested.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Blocking send waits for its defined handoff or receipt condition rather than returning promptly.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Direct messaging describes endpoint addressing, not whether sending or receiving blocks.

reviews.hint: Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures.
reviews.explanation: OS13 defines throughput as completed jobs divided by elapsed time. Counting process completions per hour is exactly that rate. Waiting, turnaround and response are delays associated with an individual process or an average of such delays; they are not completion counts per hour. The stated measurement therefore identifies system throughput without any scheduling trace.

evidence.quote: For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B. With I/O, subtract all CPU and blocked time to isolate ready-queue waiting. Throughput=completed jobs/elapsed time; CPU utilization=busy time/elapsed time. Minimize response/turnaround/waiting under the selected goal and maximize useful throughput/utilization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Waiting time measures ready-queue delay, not the number of processes completed in an hour.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Completed processes divided by hours elapsed is system throughput by the note’s definition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Turnaround measures arrival-to-completion duration for a process rather than a system completion rate.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Response measures arrival-to-first-start delay, not the number of jobs finished per unit time.

reviews.hint: Separate creation, image replacement and termination; classify termination by its cause.
reviews.explanation: OS07 explicitly identifies a reference to nonexistent/protected memory as a fatal fault. Here the OS terminates the process because of that fault, so this is involuntary fatal termination. It is not the program’s voluntary error exit, normal completion or a kill request by another ordinary process. The cause in the stem resolves the otherwise loose exit terminology.

evidence.quote: Normal completion and a program-detected error exit are voluntary; an unrecoverable fault or being killed is involuntary. exit() terminates normally through the runtime; abort() requests abnormal termination. A reference to nonexistent/protected memory is a fatal fault, unlike an application deciding to exit after bad input.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Normal exit is voluntary completion, unlike OS-enforced termination for an invalid memory reference.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A program-detected error exit is voluntary; the stem specifies an unrecoverable memory-access fault.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The stated cause is a fault handled by the OS, not a kill request from another process.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note explicitly classifies nonexistent-memory access as a fatal fault causing involuntary termination.

reviews.answer_text: Maximizing response time is the wrong optimization direction.
reviews.hint: Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures.
reviews.explanation: OS13 says to minimize response, turnaround and waiting while maximizing useful throughput/utilization under the chosen objective. Thus maximum response time is the mismatched criterion: making first response later worsens responsiveness. The other alternatives name a standard metric or its conventional optimization direction. The question is about preferred direction, not whether response time itself is measurable.

evidence.quote: For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B. With I/O, subtract all CPU and blocked time to isolate ready-queue waiting. Throughput=completed jobs/elapsed time; CPU utilization=busy time/elapsed time. Minimize response/turnaround/waiting under the selected goal and maximize useful throughput/utilization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU utilization is a standard scheduling metric measuring the fraction of elapsed time the CPU is busy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Minimizing turnaround is the conventional goal for reducing arrival-to-completion delay.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Maximizing useful throughput is a conventional goal for increasing completed work per unit time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Response delay should ordinarily be minimized; maximizing it reverses the responsiveness objective.

reviews.hint: Check priority direction, preemption and whether waiting can change effective rank.
reviews.explanation: OS17 describes aging as increasing waiting jobs’ effective priority to reduce indefinite postponement. That is a direct adjustment within a priority scheme and matches the stem exactly. RR rotates turns, SJN selects the shortest next burst, and SRTF selects the shortest remaining work. Those policies may be modified, but they are not the named priority-aging mechanism requested.

evidence.quote: Aging increases waiting jobs’ effective priority according to a rule, reducing indefinite postponement when the priority scheme and workload permit.
RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn.
Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs. SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR cycles ready jobs by quantum rather than defining aging through increasing priority.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SJN chooses shortest next bursts; aging refers specifically to adjusting the effective priority of waiting work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Priority scheduling can raise a waiting task’s effective priority through aging to reduce starvation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SRTF compares remaining bursts rather than increasing priority solely because a task has waited longer.

reviews.answer_text: Allocated resources cannot be forcibly withdrawn.
reviews.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines no resource preemption as requiring voluntary release by the holder. C states that resources cannot be preempted while in use and therefore matches. A reverses the condition. B and D describe policies attacking hold-and-wait by limiting requests or requiring release; they are different from the no-preemption property itself.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.
“If waiting, release all held resources and try again” removes simultaneous holding while waiting.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Permitting withdrawal and reassignment is resource preemption, directly reversing the condition requested.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Forbidding additional requests while holding resources attacks hold-and-wait rather than defining no-preemption.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The holder retains the resource until voluntary release, so it cannot simply be forcibly withdrawn.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Requiring release when blocked removes holding-while-waiting; it is not the no-preemption definition.

reviews.answer_text: Multiple execution is not itself a process-creation event.
reviews.hint: Separate creation, image replacement and termination; classify termination by its cause.
reviews.explanation: OS07 lists initialization, user requests, service requests and a running process’s creation call as creation causes. B, C and D match that list. Multiple execution of processes describes work being run, not an explicit request or initialization event creating a new process. Existing processes can execute repeatedly without creating a child, so A is the unsupported creation trigger.

evidence.quote: Processes arise during initialization, user requests, service requests or a running process’s creation call.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Executing existing processes multiple times is not itself the explicit creation trigger identified by the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A running process’s creation system call is explicitly one of the listed process-creation causes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: System initialization is explicitly listed as a time when processes are created.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A user request to create a process is explicitly a valid process-creation cause.

reviews.answer_text: It is a CPU scheduling algorithm
reviews.hint: Compute remaining needs and simulate feasible completions before deciding whether an allocation is safe.
reviews.explanation: Banker’s algorithm is a deadlock-avoidance technique, not a CPU scheduling policy. It requires maximum resource claims, computes remaining needs, and simulates possible completions to check for a safe sequence. A request is evaluated after receipt and before being granted, including checks against need and availability. The clarified factual alternatives therefore describe the supported safety procedure, leaving only the CPU-scheduling classification false.

evidence.quote: Avoidance allows requests only if the resulting state remains safe. Banker requires maximum claims. Compute Need=Max−Allocation. Set Work=Available and repeatedly find an unfinished process with Need≤Work componentwise; simulate completion by adding its Allocation to Work. Finishing all gives a safe sequence. Tentatively grant a request only if it is within Need and Available and the safety test succeeds. Unsafe does not mean already deadlocked. Banker is avoidance, not CPU scheduling, detection or prevention by breaking a condition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Banker is deadlock avoidance rather than CPU scheduling, so this statement is false.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Maximum resource claims are required input, so this statement is true.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The safety test repeatedly simulates feasible completions, so this statement is true.

choices.label: D

A process being terminated, multiple processes executing, or an OS crash describes a different condition. The revised definition also distinguishes deadlock from starvation caused by unfair repeated bypass.

evidence.quote: A set is deadlocked when each member waits for an event/resource that only another blocked member can provide. Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies.

reviews.answer_text: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no-preemption and circular wait.
reviews.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.
reviews.explanation: OS22 lists the four necessary conditions in the standard reusable-resource model. A preserves the exact set: exclusion, holding while requesting more, no forced resource withdrawal, and a wait cycle. B introduces preemption in place of no-preemption; C and D replace exclusion with inclusion. These are not harmless wording changes because they remove or reverse the relevant restrictions.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.
All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. Their availability as general system policies does not prove a deadlock exists at this instant; inspect actual allocations/requests.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This option states all four standard necessary conditions with their correct meanings and polarity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It substitutes preemption for no-preemption, reversing the required resource-withdrawal restriction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: It substitutes mutual inclusion for mutual exclusion, losing the nonshareable-resource condition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It reverses both exclusion and no-preemption, so it is not the required condition set.

reviews.answer_text: At most one process holds the nonshareable resource at a time.
reviews.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines mutual exclusion as allowing at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. B states that one-at-a-time condition. A describes concurrent sharing, C describes holding while requesting another resource, and D describes indefinite waiting without establishing exclusivity. The definition concerns access safety, not a guarantee that every waiting process eventually obtains the resource.

evidence.quote: Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies. Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Simultaneous access by several processes contradicts the exclusive-holder condition for a nonshareable resource.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Only one process at a time may hold or use the nonshareable resource.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Retaining one resource while requesting another defines hold-and-wait rather than mutual exclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Indefinite waiting describes a possible failure outcome and does not define exclusive resource possession.

reviews.answer_text: Retain a resource while waiting for another.
reviews.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.
reviews.explanation: OS22 directly defines hold-and-wait as retaining a resource while requesting another. A contains both parts of that definition. Merely waiting indefinitely does not establish a retained allocation, simultaneous sharing contradicts exclusion, and one-at-a-time access describes mutual exclusion rather than a process holding one resource while requesting more.

evidence.quote: Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies. Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The process simultaneously retains an allocated resource and waits to acquire a further one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Indefinite waiting does not establish that the process still holds another resource.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Simultaneous shared access is not the retained-allocation-plus-request condition defining hold-and-wait.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: One process accessing a resource at a time defines mutual exclusion, not hold-and-wait.

reviews.answer_text: A resource may be forcibly taken from its holder.
reviews.hint: Identify the resource-request restriction and which necessary condition it removes.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines no-preemption as voluntary release only, while OS24 permits safe withdrawal/restart as a way to attack that restriction. Preemption is the opposite permission: a resource can be forcibly reclaimed. D directly states it. The answer concerns resources that can safely be withdrawn, not a claim that every device or lock can be preempted without corruption.

evidence.quote: Prevention constrains how requests are made. Share a resource where safe to remove mutual exclusion; request all needed resources before holding any to remove hold-and-wait; permit safe resource withdrawal/restart to attack no-preemption; impose a global acquisition order to remove circular wait. Not every physical resource is shareable or safely preemptable.

Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies. Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Holding one resource while waiting for another describes hold-and-wait rather than forced resource withdrawal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Indefinite waiting is a possible outcome, not the permission to reclaim a held resource.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrent sharing concerns resource shareability rather than withdrawing an existing allocation from its holder.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Forcibly taking a held resource is resource preemption, subject to safe withdrawal/restart support.

reviews.answer_text: A closed chain of resource waits.
reviews.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines circular wait as a closed chain of waits. D specifies that each process holds a resource requested by the next in a circular chain, which returns the dependency to the starting participant. C describes only one hold-and-wait relationship, which need not be cyclic. Indefinite waiting and simultaneous sharing likewise fail to establish a closed chain.

evidence.quote: Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies. Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Indefinite waiting does not identify a closed cycle of dependencies among resource holders.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Simultaneous resource sharing is not a chain of blocked requests and does not define circular wait.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One process holding while requesting another establishes hold-and-wait but not necessarily a cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The circular chain of holdings and requests explicitly forms the required closed wait dependency.

reviews.explanation: Prevention constrains requests to break a necessary condition; avoidance keeps tentative allocations safe; detection and recovery identifies and resolves an existing deadlock. It is still a possible policy choice, but is the only listed one outside the active-control category specified by the revised stem.

evidence.quote: Detection asks whether the current state is deadlocked. Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint. Termination and rollback are both possible tools, so a question offering both as recovery methods needs a criterion.
Ignoring a sufficiently rare problem is sometimes called the ostrich policy, but real systems still prevent or detect selected deadlocks.
Prevention constrains how requests are made.
Avoidance allows requests only if the resulting state remains safe.

evidence.quote: In a resource-allocation graph, P→R is a request and an instance R→P is an assignment. Follow these directions to form waits. No cycle implies no deadlock; with one instance of every resource type, a cycle implies deadlock. With multiple instances a cycle alone is insufficient: another instance may permit completion. A wait-for graph replaces single-instance resource nodes with P→Q when P waits for Q.

reviews.answer_text: Banker’s algorithm, technically an avoidance policy.
reviews.hint: Compute remaining needs and simulate feasible completions before deciding whether an allocation is safe.
reviews.explanation: OS25 states that Banker grants requests only while preserving a safe state. That can prevent entry into a deadlocked state in the broad everyday sense used by can help prevent, although its technical category is avoidance rather than condition-breaking prevention. FCFS, RR and SJN are CPU scheduling policies and do not themselves test resource-allocation safety.

evidence.quote: Avoidance allows requests only if the resulting state remains safe. Banker requires maximum claims. Compute Need=Max−Allocation.

Non-preemptive scheduling keeps a running CPU burst until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding. Preemptive scheduling can return running work to ready, usually after a timer quantum or a more urgent arrival. FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive. Priority can be either, so its name alone cannot decide. Cooperative describes relying on voluntary release.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS orders CPU bursts by arrival rather than testing maximum resource claims and safe allocations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: RR schedules CPU turns; time slicing does not establish safe allocation of locks or other resources.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN selects shortest next CPU bursts rather than performing a resource-state safety test.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Banker admits resource requests only when the resulting state is safe; its strict classification is avoidance.

reviews.answer_text: Ensure each granted request preserves a safe state.
reviews.hint: Compute remaining needs and simulate feasible completions before deciding whether an allocation is safe.
reviews.explanation: Banker’s algorithm checks whether a tentative resource grant preserves a safe state. It computes remaining needs and simulates an order in which all processes can finish, granting only requests within the declared need and available resources that pass this safety test. It is an avoidance policy, not a fairness guarantee, an already-deadlocked-state detector, or prevention by eliminating hold-and-wait.

evidence.quote: Avoidance allows requests only if the resulting state remains safe. Banker requires maximum claims. Compute Need=Max−Allocation. Set Work=Available and repeatedly find an unfinished process with Need≤Work componentwise; simulate completion by adding its Allocation to Work. Finishing all gives a safe sequence. Tentatively grant a request only if it is within Need and Available and the safety test succeeds. Unsafe does not mean already deadlocked. Banker is avoidance, not CPU scheduling, detection or prevention by breaking a condition.
Prevention constrains how requests are made.
Detection asks whether the current state is deadlocked. Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Banker does not require removing hold-and-wait; it checks whether tentative allocation remains safe.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Its safety criterion is not a guarantee of fair or equal allocation among processes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Detection and recovery address actual deadlock, whereas Banker checks safety before granting a request.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Preserving a safe state after each grant is the purpose of the Banker avoidance test.

reviews.hint: Compare the ready jobs using the stated burst or remaining-time rule.
reviews.explanation: OS16 says SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work. This matches the estimated remaining-time criterion in the stem. SJN chooses the shortest next burst non-preemptively, while RR uses cyclic quanta and FCFS arrival order. The distinction matters after execution has begun: the originally shortest burst need not be the currently shortest remaining job.

evidence.quote: Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs. SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt. Future burst lengths normally need estimates.
Repeated short arrivals can starve a long job. The shortest total original burst is not necessarily the shortest remaining burst after execution has begun.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR rotates bounded turns rather than selecting the job with the smallest estimated remaining execution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS follows arrival order rather than comparing estimated remaining CPU work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Non-preemptive SJN compares next burst lengths when selecting, not continuously reconsidered remaining work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SRTF explicitly selects the shortest remaining work and can preempt on a shorter arrival.

reviews.hint: Identify the allocation entity, entitlement weights and whether the guarantee is probabilistic.
reviews.explanation: Fair-share scheduling allocates service according to stated weights, which may apply to users or groups rather than individual processes. That directly implements proportional entitlement. FCFS respects arrival order, SJN chooses shorter bursts, and priority chooses a ranking; those rules do not themselves specify weighted user/group shares. The revised fairness criterion therefore identifies fair-share without implying every fair policy must use equal shares.

evidence.quote: Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process. Equal per-process RR can let a user obtain more aggregate CPU by launching more processes. Proportional shares address that policy choice; fair need not mean equal.
FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.
Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs.
Priority scheduling chooses the highest-priority ready job.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Priority ranking does not itself implement proportional user/group shares.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Fair-share scheduling allocates according to declared weights and participant scope.

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Defined fairness as proportional user/group entitlement.
assumptions: Fairness means allocation according to declared weights, not merely arrival-order fairness.

reviews.hint: Identify the allocation entity, entitlement weights and whether the guarantee is probabilistic.
reviews.explanation: A fair-share policy allocates CPU according to declared weights and participant scope. Weights of 3:1 give intended group shares of 75 and 25 percent. Plain RR supplies equal turns to processes and does not implement those unequal group entitlements independently of task count. FCFS and SJN also lack that share rule. The question asks for the policy design rather than a universal finite-time deadline.

evidence.quote: Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process. Equal per-process RR can let a user obtain more aggregate CPU by launching more processes. Proportional shares address that policy choice; fair need not mean equal.
RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn. Unfinished jobs return to the tail; completed/blocked jobs leave.
FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.
Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS orders bursts by arrival rather than enforcing weighted group service.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Plain per-task RR does not enforce unequal group weights independent of task count.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN selects short bursts rather than proportional group entitlements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Configured fair-share scheduling implements the declared group-weight allocation.

question_revision.original_stem:
Which scheduling algorithm guarantees that each task will get its fair share of CPU time
over a longer period?
question_revision.stem: Two continuously ready user groups have declared CPU entitlements of 3:1, independent of how many tasks each launches. Which listed policy is designed to enforce those unequal per-group shares over time?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified unequal group weights and removed an undefined blanket guarantee.
assumptions: Both groups stay ready.
RR is ordinary equal per-task RR.
Fair-share is configured for the stated group entitlements; no finite deadline is claimed.

reviews.answer_text: Error exit, when the program detects an error and chooses to terminate.
reviews.hint: Separate creation, image replacement and termination; classify termination by its cause.
reviews.explanation: OS07 explicitly classifies program-detected error exits as voluntary. Being killed or terminated by another process is imposed, and a fatal unrecoverable fault is involuntary. The distinction is the termination decision’s origin, not whether the run succeeded: a program can voluntarily exit because its input is invalid or it detects another handled error.

evidence.quote: Normal completion and a program-detected error exit are voluntary; an unrecoverable fault or being killed is involuntary. exit() terminates normally through the runtime; abort() requests abnormal termination.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A program-detected error exit is a deliberate voluntary termination path, even though execution was unsuccessful.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Being killed by another process is imposed externally and is therefore involuntary.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Termination by another process is external rather than a voluntary exit chosen by the program.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A fatal unrecoverable fault causes involuntary termination rather than a deliberate program error exit.

reviews.hint: Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required.
reviews.explanation: OS10 defines a critical section as code accessing shared state that needs protection. The stem describes execution that may change shared data and therefore requires mutual exclusion, directly matching that definition. Deadlock and blocking are waiting states or failures, while termination means execution has ended. None identifies the protected shared-state code currently being executed.

evidence.quote: A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses. A critical section is code accessing shared state that needs protection, not the resource itself. A correct exclusion solution requires mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under stated assumptions.

New processes are created/admitted; ready means eligible for CPU but not currently running. Running uses a CPU. Waiting/blocked means unable to proceed until an event; terminated means execution has ended.
A set is deadlocked when each member waits for an event/resource that only another blocked member can provide.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Deadlock involves blocked dependencies, whereas the stem describes protected code actively accessing shared data.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A terminated process has ended execution, contradicting the stem’s currently executing shared-data operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Code that accesses shared data and requires mutual exclusion is a critical section.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A blocked process cannot proceed pending an event; the stem instead identifies the code requiring protection.

reviews.hint: Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation.
reviews.explanation: The MMU performs execution-time translation from a process’s logical or virtual address to a physical RAM address. A relocation register can supply a base used in a simple translation, but it is a register rather than the complete translating unit. IRQ concerns interrupts, DMA moves data, and a cache stores reusable information. The corrected direction therefore identifies the MMU uniquely.

evidence.quote: Logical/virtual addresses are generated for a process; physical addresses select RAM. An MMU translates logical to physical, not the reverse as one malformed bank stem says.
In the standard base/limit model, base is that process’s physical starting address and limit is its permitted length. Check 0≤logical_offset<limit, then physical=base+offset.
Polling checks readiness repeatedly; interrupts request CPU attention; DMA transfers blocks after setup without CPU work for every byte.
Caching retains copies to accelerate reuse.
IRQ means interrupt request.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The MMU is the hardware unit performing logical-to-physical translation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An IRQ signals an interrupt rather than translating process addresses.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DMA transfers data between devices and memory after setup.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A cache retains reusable contents; it is not the general address-translating unit.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: A relocation register holds a base parameter used by translation hardware.

question_revision.stem: Which hardware unit translates a process’s logical/virtual addresses to physical memory addresses during execution?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Corrected the direction of address translation.

reviews.hint: Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures.
reviews.explanation: The closed workload and explicit policy parameters determine each scheduling timeline. SJF orders known bursts, SRTF uses remaining bursts, priority uses the supplied fixed order, and RR uses its quantum and ready queue. Completion minus arrival minus burst then gives waiting time. Each named algorithm is individually computable, so the aggregate option is the most complete answer under these assumptions.

evidence.quote: For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B.
Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs. SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt.
Priority scheduling chooses the highest-priority ready job. Check whether a smaller or larger numeric value means higher priority. State whether a high-priority arrival preempts.
RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn. Unfinished jobs return to the tail; completed/blocked jobs leave.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SJF waiting is computable, but this option omits the other computable policies.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SRTF waiting is computable for the known closed workload, but this is incomplete.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fixed-priority waiting is computable with the supplied priorities and tie rule, but this is incomplete.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: RR waiting is computable with the known quantum and queue order, but this is incomplete.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: All four schedules and their total waiting times can be computed from the fully specified finite workload.

question_revision.original_stem:
Assuming process execution time is known in advance, for which of the following algorithm(s)
can the maximum wait time for a given process be computed at the time the job is submitted?
question_revision.stem: All jobs arrive together at submission, have known finite CPU bursts, perform no I/O, and no further jobs arrive. Assume one CPU, zero switching overhead, known fixed priorities (smaller value is higher; non-preemptive priority), a known positive RR quantum, and listed order for ties. For which listed algorithms can each job’s total waiting time be computed at submission? Choose the most complete answer.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified a closed known workload and all scheduling parameters; requested the complete set.
assumptions: All bursts, priorities, quantum and initial tie order are inputs known at submission.
There are no later arrivals, I/O, policy changes or switching costs.

reviews.hint: Identify the abstraction layer and separate a protected service request from an application task.
reviews.explanation: A system call requests a protected kernel service, such as process creation or file access. An application may call an API implemented by a library, but that wrapper is distinct from the direct user/kernel service boundary. Assembly can encode the machine instructions used to enter that boundary without being its general interface name. The requested abstraction is therefore system calls.

evidence.quote: A system call requests a protected kernel service, such as creating a process, reading a file or opening a socket. A user-facing API/library may wrap that request; not every library function enters the kernel. Therefore a stem asking merely for the interface to OS services must distinguish the application API from the direct user/kernel boundary.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A library can wrap system calls but is not itself the direct kernel-service boundary.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: System calls directly request protected kernel services.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Assembly instructions are a programming representation, not the named service-interface abstraction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An API is the application-facing interface and may wrap the direct system-call request.

question_revision.original_stem: To access the services of operating system, the interface is provided by the:
question_revision.stem: Which named interface directly requests protected operating-system services across the user/kernel boundary, rather than merely providing application-facing wrappers?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the direct user/kernel protection boundary.
assumptions: The named service interface, rather than its machine-level instruction encoding, is requested.

reviews.answer_text: To execute a program instance with its own address space and resources
reviews.hint: Distinguish stored instructions, an executing instance and its saved execution state.
reviews.explanation: A process is an executing instance of a program, accompanied by an address space and resources. Its application may administer accounts, interact with hardware through services, or display a user interface, but none of those specialized jobs defines every process. The repaired execution option expresses the general role. It also distinguishes a running instance from a program stored as instructions.

evidence.quote: A program is stored instructions; a process is an executing instance with address space and resources. A process does not universally “manage applications” or “provide a user interface.” The PCB records identity, state, PC/registers, scheduling information, memory/accounting details and I/O/open-resource state.
An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Account administration is only one possible application responsibility.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hardware management is an OS responsibility rather than the general role of every process.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Executing a program instance with an address space and resources is the process abstraction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Many processes run without providing a user interface.

question_revision.original_stem: What is the main purpose of a process in an operating system?
question_revision.stem: What is the general execution role of a process in an operating system, regardless of the application it runs?

options.label: C
options.text: To execute a program instance with its own address space and resources

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Replaced the application-management distractor with the missing general execution role.
assumptions: General process semantics, rather than a particular program’s business purpose, are requested.

reviews.answer_text: To request a protected kernel service
reviews.hint: Identify the abstraction layer and separate a protected service request from an application task.
reviews.explanation: A system call is the mechanism through which executing code requests a protected kernel service. Process creation, file reads and socket operations are examples. A program that manages accounts, applications or a user interface may use system calls, but those tasks are not the mechanism’s general purpose. The repaired option captures the common role without restricting it to one kind of resource.

evidence.quote: A system call requests a protected kernel service, such as creating a process, reading a file or opening a socket. A user-facing API/library may wrap that request; not every library function enters the kernel.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Account management can use system calls but does not define their general purpose.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Requesting a protected kernel service states the general purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Managing applications is a possible use rather than the system-call mechanism’s definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A UI may issue calls, but providing a UI is not the general system-call role.

question_revision.original_stem: What is the purpose of a system call in an operating system?
question_revision.stem: What is the general purpose of a system call in an operating system?

options.label: B
options.text: To request a protected kernel service

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Inserted the missing protected-service purpose into the resource-management option.
assumptions: The general mechanism is asked about, rather than a specific service category.

reviews.hint: Separate broad resource-management goals from individual services or applications.
reviews.explanation: CPU time, memory and input devices such as a keyboard are hardware resources allocated or controlled by the OS. A user account is an identity used in administration and protection, rather than a hardware device. The OS may manage accounts too, but that does not put them in the hardware-resource category. Completing the stem and replacing one option gives a unique exclusion.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs.
Input/output/storage/NIC devices are OS-managed hardware; user accounts are identities.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The CPU is a managed processing resource.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Memory is a managed storage resource used during execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A keyboard is a managed input device.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A user account is an identity rather than a hardware resource.

question_revision.original_stem: Which of the following is not a type of system resource managed by an
question_revision.stem: Which listed item is not a hardware resource managed by an operating system?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Completed the truncated stem and replaced one hardware option with an identity.
assumptions: The requested category is hardware resources rather than every entity administered by an OS.

reviews.hint: Distinguish command interfaces, privileged core services and the stages of booting.
reviews.explanation: The note states that kernel mode permits privileged operations and that supervisor mode commonly denotes the same privileged mode. The stated model makes those names explicitly synonymous. User mode is restricted. Protected mode is defined here as a broader processor mode that can still run user code, so its name alone does not identify the privileged execution level. Both kernel and supervisor are selected.

evidence.quote: Kernel mode has privileged operations; supervisor mode often means the same privileged mode, so offering both as exclusive answers is ambiguous.

Being scheduled or managed by the kernel does not give application thread code kernel privilege. Ordinary applications and supporting utilities execute in restricted user mode and request protected services through libraries and system calls. Kernel component code executes in privileged kernel mode and performs permitted low-level hardware operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Kernel mode denotes the privileged execution level.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: User mode is the restricted level.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Supervisor mode is explicitly synonymous with kernel mode in this model.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Protected mode is not a privilege level under the supplied definition.

question_revision.original_stem: Which mode provides higher privileges and access to system resources in an operating system?
question_revision.stem: In a two-level privilege model where “kernel mode” and “supervisor mode” are synonymous names for the privileged execution level, which listed names denote that level? “Protected mode” denotes a processor operating mode that can include restricted user execution. Select all that apply.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Fixed the privilege model and made its synonymous privileged names selectable.
assumptions: Kernel and supervisor are synonymous privilege-level names.
Protected mode may include restricted user execution and is not itself the privileged level.

reviews.answer_text: Arrival of a higher-priority ready process that preempts it
reviews.hint: Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role.
reviews.explanation: Preemption removes the CPU from a running process that can still execute, returning it to ready. In the stated priority policy, arrival of a higher-priority ready process triggers that handoff. Final completion ends execution, while a blocking I/O request makes the process wait for an event. Suspension while waiting also does not describe ordinary readiness, so only the explicit preemption event fits.

evidence.quote: New processes are created/admitted; ready means eligible for CPU but not currently running. Running uses a CPU. Waiting/blocked means unable to proceed until an event; terminated means execution has ended. Running→ready follows time-slice expiry or another preemption. Running→waiting follows blocking I/O. I/O completion normally gives waiting→ready, not a guaranteed immediate running state.
Priority scheduling chooses the highest-priority ready job. Check whether a smaller or larger numeric value means higher priority. State whether a high-priority arrival preempts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The higher-priority arrival preempts the runnable process and returns it to ready.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Final completion transitions to terminated, not ready.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Suspended waiting work is not eligible for the ordinary ready queue.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Blocking I/O transitions running to waiting.

question_revision.original_stem: One of the following conditions is happened to transit a process from running to ready state.
question_revision.stem: Under preemptive priority scheduling, which event sends a currently running, unfinished process back to the ready state?

options.label: A
options.text: Arrival of a higher-priority ready process that preempts it

options.label: B
options.text: Completion of its final CPU burst

options.label: C
options.text: Suspension while waiting for an event

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Expanded the incomplete event labels and specified preemptive priority scheduling.
assumptions: A higher-priority arrival immediately preempts.
I/O requests block and completed work has no remaining execution.

reviews.answer_text: Paging leads to internal fragmentation whereas segmentation leads external fragmentation; The size of block is fixed in the case of paging but variable in the case of segmentation; Paging use page table whereas segmentation use segmentation table
reviews.hint: Check the logical region and offset bound before computing its physical location.
reviews.explanation: Basic paging uses fixed-size pages and page tables, and its final allocated page can contain unused space. Basic segmentation uses variable-length logical units and segment tables, so free holes can cause external fragmentation. Those properties make A, B and C valid contrasts. D reverses the usual abstraction relationship: segments reflect program structure, while ordinary page placement is largely transparent to the application.

evidence.quote: Under the basic models, paging uses fixed units/page tables and can waste space internally; segmentation uses variable logical units/segment tables and can fragment externally. Segments reflect program structure whereas ordinary pages are largely transparent to applications. Consequently an old item offering all three true contrasts A/B/C cannot have a unique correct choice.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Paging can waste space internally; variable-length segmentation can fragment externally.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Pages have a fixed size while segments have variable lengths.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Paging uses page tables and segmentation uses segment tables.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Segments reflect program structure; ordinary pages are largely transparent, reversing this option.

reviews.hint: Separate broad resource-management goals from individual services or applications.
reviews.explanation: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources. The umbrella term for coordinating these allocations is resource management. File, process and security management cover narrower responsibilities, so none alone names the full scope of the question. Replacing device management with the umbrella category preserves the combined CPU/memory/I/O concept and gives the item one complete answer.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs.
Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.

A file has content and metadata such as name, size, owner, permissions and timestamps. open obtains an open-file reference, read/write transfer bytes, seek changes an offset, close releases a reference, truncate changes size and unlink removes a name.
Authentication verifies identity; authorization checks permitted operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: File management concerns files and storage abstractions rather than all named resources.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Resource management spans CPU time, memory and I/O devices.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Process management covers execution and CPU scheduling but is narrower than the combined scope.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Security management controls protection and permissions rather than naming all allocation functions.

question_revision.original_stem:
Which function of modern operating systems involves managing hardware resources such as
CPU, memory, and I/O devices?
question_revision.stem: Which umbrella function of modern operating systems allocates and coordinates hardware resources such as CPU time, memory and I/O devices?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Replaced device management with the missing umbrella function.
assumptions: The full combined resource scope is requested, not one contributing subsystem.

reviews.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.
reviews.explanation: The specified set has a closed dependency: every member is waiting for something only another blocked member can provide. None can reach the release operation needed by another, so the state is deadlock. Queuing can occur during ordinary waits that eventually finish; preemption withdraws or reallocates a resource; overload concerns excessive demand. The added dependency condition makes the deadlock interpretation definite.

evidence.quote: A set is deadlocked when each member waits for an event/resource that only another blocked member can provide. Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies.

Prevention constrains how requests are made. Share a resource where safe to remove mutual exclusion; request all needed resources before holding any to remove hold-and-wait; permit safe resource withdrawal/restart to attack no-preemption; impose a global acquisition order to remove circular wait.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The closed dependency among blocked members defines deadlock.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary queuing does not require a dependency that prevents every member from progressing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Preemption is resource withdrawal or reassignment rather than this blocked state.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Overload does not by itself create the specified closed dependency.

question_revision.original_stem: A set of processes management which is waiting for a resource that is owned by another process refers to:
question_revision.stem: A set of processes is blocked: each holds a resource and waits for another resource that only another blocked member of the set can release. No member can proceed without intervention. This state is called:
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Added the missing closed dependency and removed OCR noise in option names.
assumptions: Resources are not forcibly reclaimed and blocked members cannot release the required holdings.

reviews.answer_text: To manage and allocate system resources efficiently
reviews.hint: Separate broad resource-management goals from individual services or applications.
reviews.explanation: Resource management allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communications to programs. That directly matches efficient management and allocation in B. User interfaces support convenience, protection controls permitted access, and execution speed is a performance concern. Those are related goals, but the clarified question asks specifically for the allocation objective rather than ranking every legitimate OS goal as universally most important.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs. Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions. Efficiency means using resources effectively; it is not synonymous with the fastest response for every process. Application development tools use OS services but application development itself is not a core resource-management function.
Authentication verifies identity; authorization checks permitted operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Providing an interface concerns convenience rather than the specific allocation objective.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Efficient management and allocation directly names the requested resource objective.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Security and protection concern access control rather than allocation efficiency itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Program speed is a performance concern and is not equivalent to efficient allocation of all resources.

reviews.hint: Separate device hardware, device-specific software and general event or transfer mechanisms.
reviews.explanation: A device driver translates OS I/O requests into the particular operations a device requires. The kernel provides broader resource management and can contain drivers, but the question asks for that specific hardware-facing component. The scheduler selects runnable work and the filesystem organizes file abstractions. Neither performs the general per-device request translation described, making device drivers the precise answer.

evidence.quote: A controller is device hardware exposing status, control and data registers. A driver converts OS requests into device-specific operations. Device independence and uniform naming hide brand-specific details; error handling reports/retries supported failures.
The kernel implements core resource management, protection and system-call handling.
Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The kernel is the larger system containing or coordinating the specific component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The scheduler chooses runnable CPU work rather than translating device commands.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The filesystem organizes files rather than translating requests for every device type.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Drivers convert OS requests into device-specific operations.

Which component of an operating system is responsible for managing input and output
operations?

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the device-specific I/O translation layer.
assumptions: The requested component is narrower than the kernel as a whole.

reviews.answer_text: Provide translated, protected per-process address spaces.
reviews.hint: Separate a permitted nonresident access from an illegal access and trace the required handling steps.
reviews.explanation: OS32 defines virtual memory as translated/protected address spaces with nonresident portions backed by storage. D is the option matching separate process memory spaces. A describes machine virtualization; B falsely adds physical RAM and C falsely removes all memory constraints. Isolation and translation are the supported purpose, with backing storage providing flexibility within finite resource limits.

evidence.quote: Virtual memory provides translated, protected address spaces and allows nonresident portions of a program to be backed by storage. It does not add physical RAM or remove all capacity constraints.
Virtualization presents a virtual machine environment, often allowing guest operating systems on one host through a hypervisor. It differs from virtual memory, which translates a process’s addresses.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Running multiple guest OSs describes machine virtualization, explicitly distinguished from process virtual memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Virtual memory does not physically add RAM; it maps address spaces using existing RAM and backing storage.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly retains capacity constraints; virtual memory does not make execution memory-unlimited.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Separate translated/protected process address spaces match the virtual-memory purpose described by the note.

reviews.answer_text: To coordinate shared-state access and required operation ordering safely
reviews.hint: Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required.
reviews.explanation: Conflicting accesses need coordination so interleaving does not corrupt shared state or violate required operation order. Critical-section protection provides mutual exclusion, with progress and bounded waiting required under the stated solution assumptions. Synchronization does not automatically eliminate deadlock; inconsistent lock acquisition can introduce it. It may also serialize work rather than create parallelism, so safe shared-access coordination is the precise primary purpose.

evidence.quote: A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses. A critical section is code accessing shared state that needs protection, not the resource itself. A correct exclusion solution requires mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under stated assumptions. Mutual exclusion is a desired safety property; races, starvation and deadlock are possible failures.

Keep critical regions small and ensure every conflicting access uses the same protection. A barrier waits until a defined set of participants reaches a point; a monitor encapsulates protected operations with condition synchronization. Locking can itself introduce deadlock if acquisition order is inconsistent.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Locking can itself deadlock, so universal deadlock prevention is not the primary definition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: General resource-allocation fairness is broader than coordinating shared-state operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Synchronization can serialize conflicting operations and does not itself create parallel execution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Coordinating shared accesses and required ordering safely captures the primary purpose.
