reviews.answer_text: An easy-to-use interface is the convenience example.
reviews.hint: Separate broad resource-management goals from individual services or applications.
reviews.explanation: OS01 defines convenience as making tasks easy through consistent interfaces and abstractions. A directly exemplifies that user-facing goal, although a GUI is one possible interface rather than a universal requirement. B and C concern speed/resource efficiency, and D protection. Those are worthwhile OS objectives but do not match the convenience dimension specifically named in the stem.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs. Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions. Efficiency means using resources effectively; it is not synonymous with the fastest response for every process. Application development tools use OS services but application development itself is not a core resource-management function.

choices.label: B

choices.label: D

reviews.hint: Check whether the running burst can be interrupted before completion or blocking.
reviews.explanation: FCFS ordinarily serves each ready burst in arrival order without forcibly taking the CPU away. SJN, as explicitly defined, chooses the shortest ready burst and then lets it continue non-preemptively. RR can interrupt a burst at its quantum boundary, while the stated priority variant interrupts for a higher-priority arrival. Thus FCFS and SJN are the two non-preemptive policies in this list.

evidence.quote: Non-preemptive scheduling keeps a running CPU burst until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding. Preemptive scheduling can return running work to ready, usually after a timer quantum or a more urgent arrival. FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive. Priority can be either, so its name alone cannot decide. Cooperative describes relying on voluntary release.
Priority scheduling chooses the highest-priority ready job. Check whether a smaller or larger numeric value means higher priority. State whether a high-priority arrival preempts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR uses quantum expiry to preempt unfinished work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS ordinarily lets the selected burst continue without forced preemption.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN is explicitly the non-preemptive shortest-next-burst policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This option explicitly preempts for a higher-priority arrival.

question_revision.original_stem: Which scheduling algorithm is typically used for non-preemptive scheduling?

reviews.hint: Identify the allocation entity, entitlement weights and whether the guarantee is probabilistic.
reviews.explanation: Equal-turn RR gives each of the five tasks roughly one fifth of CPU service, so user A receives about 80 percent and B about 20 percent. Equal per-user fair-share instead gives each user half, dividing A’s half among its four tasks. FCFS and SJN do not enforce that user entitlement. The explicitly defined participant scope makes fair-share the unique matching policy.

evidence.quote: Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process. Equal per-process RR can let a user obtain more aggregate CPU by launching more processes. Proportional shares address that policy choice; fair need not mean equal.
If user A runs four ready tasks and B runs one, plain RR gives A about 80% overall. A policy granting each user half the CPU instead gives A’s tasks about 12.5% each and B’s task 50%.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Per-task RR gives A four fifths of service rather than equal per-user shares.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS orders bursts by arrival and does not enforce per-user entitlements.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN favors short bursts and does not allocate equal user shares.

choices.label: D

assumptions: All five tasks remain ready.
RR is ordinary equal per-task RR.
Fair-share is configured with equal per-user weights.

reviews.hint: Follow arrival order, include idle periods and distinguish waiting from completion time.
reviews.explanation: RR gives the target a turn after the finite work ahead has received bounded turns. FCFS serves the finite earlier bursts before later arrivals, so the target eventually starts. SJN can repeatedly prefer later short jobs, and fixed priority can repeatedly prefer later high-priority jobs. The assumptions distinguish guaranteed eventual service from policies that permit an endless stream to bypass the target.

evidence.quote: FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt. If the CPU is idle, jump to the next arrival. Long CPU-bound work can make many short jobs wait: the convoy effect. A finite burst with finitely many jobs ahead eventually starts, but waiting can still be large.
RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn. Unfinished jobs return to the tail; completed/blocked jobs leave.

Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs under continued high-priority load. SJF can also starve long jobs, so a single-choice question offering both as starvation-prone has multiple answers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR’s finite cyclic turns reach the target without later-arrival bypass.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS drains the finite predecessor work before serving later arrivals.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An endless sequence of short arrivals can keep a long target waiting under SJN.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An endless sequence of higher-priority arrivals can starve a low-priority target without aging.

question_revision.original_stem:
Which scheduling algorithm provides a guarantee that no task will suffer indefinite
postponement?
question_revision.stem: A ready target has finitely many jobs ahead, all CPU bursts and RR quanta are finite and positive, context overhead is finite, and later arrivals join the tail without bypassing existing peers. Infinitely many later short or high-priority jobs may arrive over time. Which policies prevent that target from being postponed forever by later arrivals? D uses fixed priorities without aging. Select all that apply.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Replaced an undefined guarantee label with an explicit fixed-priority policy and stated eventual-service assumptions.
assumptions: Arrivals are locally finite so only finitely many exist at each finite time.
All work ahead uses finite bursts/turns with finite overhead.
New RR and FCFS arrivals join the tail.
SJN and fixed-priority may continually prefer later arrivals.

reviews.hint: Check priority direction, preemption and whether waiting can change effective rank.
reviews.explanation: SJN can continually choose newly arrived short bursts while an older long job remains ready. Fixed priority without aging can likewise keep choosing high-priority arrivals over a low-priority target. Ordinary RR cycles peers, and FCFS does not let later arrivals overtake a finite set of predecessors. Thus the preference rules of SJN and fixed priority create the two stated starvation risks.

evidence.quote: Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs under continued high-priority load. SJF can also starve long jobs, so a single-choice question offering both as starvation-prone has multiple answers.

FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt. If the CPU is idle, jump to the next arrival. Long CPU-bound work can make many short jobs wait: the convoy effect. A finite burst with finitely many jobs ahead eventually starts, but waiting can still be large.
RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn. Unfinished jobs return to the tail; completed/blocked jobs leave.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary RR returns ready jobs to recurring turns rather than repeatedly bypassing a peer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS preserves arrival order, so later arrivals do not overtake the target.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Repeated short arrivals can starve an older long SJN job.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Continued high-priority arrivals can starve a low-priority job without aging.

question_revision.original_stem: Which scheduling algorithm is prone to starvation?
question_revision.stem: Which policies can starve a ready job through repeated preference for later arrivals? Assume correct implementations, finite bursts, ordinary RR with a positive quantum, FCFS without bypass, non-preemptive SJN, and fixed-priority scheduling without aging. Select all that apply.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Made both starvation-prone policies selectable and specified standard variants.
assumptions: SJN is non-preemptive SJF.
Priority is fixed and has no aging.
Finite work ahead and locally finite arrivals are assumed for FCFS/RR eventual turns.

reviews.hint: Compare the ready jobs using the stated burst or remaining-time rule.
reviews.explanation: For the simultaneous known-burst workload, shortest-job order minimizes total waiting. Consider adjacent bursts L>S after an elapsed prefix T. Long then short gives waits T and T+L; short then long gives T and T+S, reducing their sum by L−S. Jobs outside the pair are unaffected. Repeatedly removing inversions gives SJN order. FCFS does not enforce it, while RR and SRTF are preemptive policies.

evidence.quote: Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs. SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt. Future burst lengths normally need estimates. SJF minimizes average waiting for the usual fixed simultaneous ready set with known bursts and no preemption/switch cost; that theorem is not a workload-independent comparison against every preemptive policy.
For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B.
FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR is preemptive and is outside the requested non-preemptive policy class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS can tie on favorable orders but does not minimize waiting for arbitrary burst orders.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN selects the shortest ready bursts and gives the standard minimum-average-waiting order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SRTF is the preemptive remaining-time policy rather than the requested non-preemptive one.

question_revision.original_stem: Which scheduling algorithm is optimal in terms of average waiting time?
question_revision.stem: For a fixed finite set of simultaneous ready jobs with known CPU bursts, no I/O and zero switch cost, which listed non-preemptive policy minimizes average waiting over all possible execution orders for arbitrary burst lengths?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the standard simultaneous-burst non-preemptive optimality theorem.
assumptions: All jobs arrive together, have known finite bursts and perform no I/O.
Only non-preemptive execution orders are compared; switch cost is zero.

reviews.hint: Check whether the running burst can be interrupted before completion or blocking.
reviews.explanation: RR limits a turn to a quantum and can return an unfinished runnable job to the ready queue. That is preemption. FCFS and the stated SJN variant keep a selected burst until it ends or blocks. The priority option is explicitly non-preemptive, so a higher-priority arrival does not interrupt its current burst. RR is therefore the unique preemptive policy in this clarified list.

evidence.quote: Non-preemptive scheduling keeps a running CPU burst until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding. Preemptive scheduling can return running work to ready, usually after a timer quantum or a more urgent arrival. FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive. Priority can be either, so its name alone cannot decide. Cooperative describes relying on voluntary release.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS ordinarily does not forcibly interrupt the selected burst.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: RR preempts unfinished work at quantum expiry.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN is explicitly the non-preemptive shortest-job policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The stated priority variant is explicitly non-preemptive.

question_revision.original_stem: Which of the following scheduling algorithms is preemptive?
question_revision.stem: Which listed policy is preemptive? SJN denotes non-preemptive shortest-job-next, and D specifically keeps the running burst until completion, blocking or voluntary release.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the non-preemptive priority variant.
assumptions: SJN is non-preemptive SJF.
Priority is non-preemptive.

reviews.hint: Check priority direction, preemption and whether waiting can change effective rank.
reviews.explanation: Starvation can arise from the policy even when its implementation is correct. SJN repeatedly favors short arrivals over an older long burst, while fixed priority can repeatedly favor high-priority arrivals over low-priority work. FCFS preserves arrival order, and RR provides recurring turns under the stated finite-work assumptions. Thus SJN and fixed priority are the two policies with the specified inherent bypass risk.

evidence.quote: Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs under continued high-priority load. SJF can also starve long jobs, so a single-choice question offering both as starvation-prone has multiple answers.

FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt. If the CPU is idle, jump to the next arrival. Long CPU-bound work can make many short jobs wait: the convoy effect. A finite burst with finitely many jobs ahead eventually starts, but waiting can still be large.
RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn. Unfinished jobs return to the tail; completed/blocked jobs leave.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS later arrivals cannot bypass a target with finite predecessor work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary RR returns peers to recurring turns rather than favoring newcomers indefinitely.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Repeated shorter arrivals can indefinitely postpone a long SJN job.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Continued higher-priority arrivals can indefinitely postpone low-priority work without aging.

question_revision.original_stem: Which scheduling algorithm can result in starvation if not implemented properly?
question_revision.stem: Which correctly implemented policies can still cause starvation under an ongoing stream of preferred arrivals? Assume finite bursts, ordinary RR with tail insertion, FCFS without bypass, non-preemptive SJN, and fixed priority without aging. Select all that apply.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Removed the implementation-error ambiguity and specified the starvation-prone variants.
assumptions: Implementations follow their stated policies correctly.
A target has finite predecessor work; arrivals are locally finite.
Priority has no aging.

reviews.hint: Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures.
reviews.explanation: FCFS completes P1, P2, P3 at 24, 27 and 30, giving average turnaround 27. RR completes them at 30, 7 and 10, averaging 47/3. SJN completes short jobs at 3 and 6, then P1 at 30, averaging 13. Priority runs P2, P1, P3 and averages 20. FCFS is uniquely highest for this specified workload, without a universal worst-policy claim.

evidence.quote: For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B.
FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.
Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs.
Priority scheduling chooses the highest-priority ready job. Check whether a smaller or larger numeric value means higher priority. State whether a high-priority arrival preempts.
RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn. Unfinished jobs return to the tail; completed/blocked jobs leave.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS average turnaround is (24+27+30)/3=27, the largest.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: RR average turnaround is (30+7+10)/3=47/3, below 27.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN average turnaround is (3+6+30)/3=13.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Priority average turnaround is (3+27+30)/3=20.

question_revision.original_stem: Which scheduling algorithm provides the highest average turnaround time?
question_revision.stem: Three jobs all arrive at time 0 in listed order P1, P2, P3, with CPU bursts 24, 3, 3 and priorities 2, 1, 3 (smaller number is higher). There is no I/O or overhead. Compare FCFS, RR with quantum 4, non-preemptive SJN, and non-preemptive priority; use listed order for ties. Which has the highest average turnaround for this workload?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Supplied a complete workload, quantum, priorities and policy variants for the comparison.
assumptions: All jobs arrive at zero and have one CPU burst each.
SJN and priority are non-preemptive; priority 1 is highest.
RR quantum is 4; ties use listed order; overhead is zero.

reviews.answer_text: Threads within a process execute sequentially; Processes are not independent of one another
reviews.hint: Compare per-thread execution context with shared process resources and the stated thread mapping.
reviews.explanation: Threads within one process need not finish sequentially; their execution may interleave or run on multiple CPUs. Independent processes can also exist, so C’s universal dependence claim is false. The defined creation operations make A true without imposing a thread-parent hierarchy. Under one-to-one mapping, one blocked thread need not block every other thread, making D a valid possibility rather than a false statement.

evidence.quote: A thread has its own PC, registers and stack. Threads in a process share code, address space and usually open-file resources. A process can contain many threads; a thread belongs to one process at a time. Threads are not a group of processes and need not execute sequentially. Independent processes can exist; cooperating ones communicate/share data.
One-to-one permits another kernel thread to run when one blocks.
Processes arise during initialization, user requests, service requests or a running process’s creation call.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The defined process and thread creation operations are allowed, so A is true.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Mandatory finish-before-next sequential execution is false; threads can interleave or run in parallel.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Universal process dependence is false because independent processes can exist.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: One-to-one mapping permits another runnable thread to execute when one blocks, so D is true.

In B, “execute sequentially” means threads are required to finish one after another without interleaving. Select all that apply.

Threads use one-to-one kernel mapping.
B claims compulsory noninterleaved completion, and C claims universal dependence.

reviews.answer_text: In single user systems many users can login simultaneously; Multiuser system can allow at most one user at a time
reviews.hint: Compare interaction, CPU sharing and deadline requirements under the stated system model.
reviews.explanation: Single-user and multiuser describe concurrent user access rather than application count. A therefore contradicts single-user status, and C contradicts the supported multiple-user capacity. One user may still run several applications accessing a database concurrently, which is the explicit meaning of B here. D states the multiuser capability correctly. The selected false statements are A and C.

evidence.quote: Single-user and multiuser describe concurrent user access, not the number of applications.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Many simultaneous logged-in users contradict the single-user definition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Concurrent applications belonging to one user do not violate single-user status, so B is true.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A capacity of at most one user contradicts the multiuser definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Supporting concurrent access by many users is the multiuser capability, so D is true.

reviews.answer_text: Allocate the CPU to a process.
reviews.hint: Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role.
reviews.explanation: Allocating the CPU to a ready process is the scheduling role within process management. Device allocation belongs to device management. Allocating requested memory and reclaiming memory that has been released belong to memory management. Specifying the resource in the deallocation option removes its former overlap with several managers and leaves processor allocation as the distinct process-management function.

evidence.quote: Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work. The dispatcher performs the handoff/context restore after selection.

Memory management tracks which primary-memory regions are free or in use, assigns memory to processes and data, and deallocates it when no longer needed or when a process terminates. Allocation and deallocation concern memory ownership; CPU selection belongs to scheduling.
An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Allocating a device is a device-management responsibility.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Reclaiming released memory is a memory-management responsibility under the stated resource classification.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Allocating requested memory belongs to memory management.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Selecting a ready process to receive the CPU is the process-scheduling responsibility.

reviews.answer_text: Act as the service/resource intermediary between users/programs and hardware.
reviews.hint: Separate broad resource-management goals from individual services or applications.
reviews.explanation: OS01 describes the OS allocating hardware resources and providing program services, with convenient interfaces and abstractions. D captures that intermediary role. Internet connectivity and document creation are narrower tasks, and hardware design is not a runtime OS service. The answer combines convenience and resource control rather than reducing the OS to one application or device function.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs. Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions. Efficiency means using resources effectively; it is not synonymous with the fastest response for every process. Application development tools use OS services but application development itself is not a core resource-management function.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Internet access is one supported communication activity rather than the general purpose of an operating system.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Document and spreadsheet creation are application tasks that use OS services rather than define the OS.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Designing hardware is not the runtime resource/service function described for an operating system.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The OS provides interfaces and controlled resource services linking users/programs to the underlying hardware.

reviews.hint: Separate device hardware, device-specific software and general event or transfer mechanisms.
reviews.explanation: OS34 defines plug-and-play as discovering/configuring compatible new hardware, which directly matches automatic printer setup. A driver may still be needed, so automatic configuration does not imply driver-free operation. Manual driver installation and hardware management contradict the scenario’s automatic action. Resource allocation may occur during setup but is broader than the specific feature named.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The stem specifies automatic setup, not user-performed manual installation of a driver.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Allocation can be part of setup, but it does not specifically name automatic device discovery/configuration.

reviews.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines no resource preemption as voluntary release by the current holder. The stem repeats that resources cannot be forcibly taken, giving a direct match. Holding while requesting another resource, one-at-a-time ownership and a closed chain of waits are separate conditions and do not by themselves express the withdrawal restriction.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The holder must release voluntarily, so the system cannot forcibly preempt the resource.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hold-and-wait concerns retaining one resource while requesting another rather than whether withdrawal is allowed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion limits simultaneous ownership, not whether allocated resources can be forcibly reclaimed.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circular wait concerns a closed dependency chain, not the resource-release rule specified here.

reviews.answer_text: Time-sharing and scheduling distribute CPU service among users/processes.
reviews.hint: Compare interaction, CPU sharing and deadline requirements under the stated system model.
reviews.explanation: OS02 describes time-sharing as rapid scheduling/preemption supporting interactive users. OS20 explains that fair allocation needs a share policy and may operate per user/group. C describes those relevant mechanisms rather than disabling services or requiring manual intervention. Its fairly should be understood under a specified policy, not as an automatic equality guarantee from time-sharing alone.

evidence.quote: Multiprogramming keeps several jobs available so another can use the CPU while one waits; it does not require fixed time slices. Time-sharing uses rapid scheduling/preemption to support interactive users. A single CPU interleaves execution; multiple CPUs can execute work truly in parallel.

Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process. Equal per-process RR can let a user obtain more aggregate CPU by launching more processes. Proportional shares address that policy choice; fair need not mean equal.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Restricting access to one user contradicts the multiuser setting rather than explaining its efficient sharing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Disabling every background service is neither required nor the time-sharing/resource-allocation mechanism described.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Scheduling/time-sharing interleave useful work and can allocate service according to the system’s fairness policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Manual intervention for each task adds administration rather than explaining efficient automatic CPU allocation.

reviews.hint: Separate broad resource-management goals from individual services or applications.
reviews.explanation: OS01 defines both allocation of CPU/memory/storage/devices/communications and services to programs, while describing convenient interfaces. B combines those core responsibilities. Running applications only, providing connectivity only or permanently storing files each captures a narrower task and omits the overall system-management role. The primary role is therefore the resource/interface combination, not a single service.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs. Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions. Efficiency means using resources effectively; it is not synonymous with the fastest response for every process. Application development tools use OS services but application development itself is not a core resource-management function.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Application execution is supported, but only excludes the OS’s other essential resource and service duties.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Resource management plus user/program interfaces matches the combined OS role defined by the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Internet connectivity is one communication service rather than the complete primary OS role.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Permanent file storage is a storage-device/filesystem service and not the complete operating-system purpose.

reviews.hint: Compare interaction, CPU sharing and deadline requirements under the stated system model.
reviews.explanation: OS02 defines batch jobs as running with little interaction after submission. That matches processing submitted similar jobs without user interaction during execution. Time-sharing targets interactive users, real-time targets timing correctness, and single-user classifies concurrent access rather than job interaction. The job-processing clue therefore selects batch rather than a user-count or deadline category.

evidence.quote: Batch jobs run with little interaction after submission. Multiprogramming keeps several jobs available so another can use the CPU while one waits; it does not require fixed time slices. Time-sharing uses rapid scheduling/preemption to support interactive users.

Single-user and multiuser describe concurrent user access, not the number of applications. Network systems expose remote services; distributed systems coordinate work across machines, sometimes hiding location. Real-time correctness includes timing: hard deadlines must be met, while soft deadline misses degrade service.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Real-time classification concerns meeting deadlines rather than the absence of user interaction during submitted job processing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Time-sharing supports interactive users through rapid scheduling, unlike the noninteractive batch description.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Batch processing runs submitted jobs with little interaction, directly matching the scenario.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Single-user describes concurrent user access, not whether a workload is submitted and processed as batches.

reviews.answer_text: The saved next-instruction position for resuming the process.
reviews.hint: Distinguish stored instructions, an executing instance and its saved execution state.
reviews.explanation: OS05 says the PCB records PC/registers alongside scheduling, memory/accounting and I/O information, and a saved PC identifies where execution resumes. Thus B describes its specific field role. Priority, CPU usage and open files can be other PCB information, but they are not the program-counter value. The question requires distinguishing fields within one record rather than excluding them from the PCB entirely.

evidence.quote: A saved PC identifies where execution resumes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Priority is scheduling information in the PCB, not the saved next-instruction position held by PC.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The saved PC records the instruction position at which the process will resume execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CPU time consumed is accounting information rather than the program-counter address.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Open files belong to I/O/open-resource state, not to the saved instruction-pointer field.

reviews.hint: Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role.
reviews.explanation: OS06 defines waiting/blocked as unable to proceed until an event and maps blocking I/O from running to waiting. Therefore a process waiting for I/O completion is in Waiting. It is not ready while the event prevents progress, not running during the wait, and not terminated merely because its request is outstanding. Completion normally makes it ready afterward.

evidence.quote: New processes are created/admitted; ready means eligible for CPU but not currently running. Running uses a CPU. Waiting/blocked means unable to proceed until an event; terminated means execution has ended. Running→ready follows time-slice expiry or another preemption. Running→waiting follows blocking I/O. I/O completion normally gives waiting→ready, not a guaranteed immediate running state.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ready means eligible for CPU immediately; the outstanding blocking I/O prevents that eligibility.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Running means currently using a CPU, unlike the blocked interval awaiting I/O completion.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Waiting/blocked is the state for a process that cannot proceed until its I/O event completes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Terminated means execution has ended, not temporarily paused pending completion of an I/O request.

reviews.answer_text: Save one execution context and restore another.
reviews.hint: Distinguish stored instructions, an executing instance and its saved execution state.
reviews.explanation: OS05 directly defines a context switch as saving one execution context and restoring another, with overhead interrupting useful application work. B matches. A process may later resume, so switching does not permanently stop or kill it. Allocating memory is another management operation, and a privilege transition alone need not switch processes.

evidence.quote: A context switch saves one execution context and restores another; useful application work is interrupted by this overhead. An interrupt or system call can switch privilege without switching process.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The outgoing process can resume later; permanent stopping is termination rather than context switching.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Saving current state and restoring the selected execution context is the defined context-switch purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Memory allocation changes resource assignment, not the saved/restored execution context defining a switch.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A context switch need not terminate any process, regardless of priority.

reviews.hint: Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role.
reviews.explanation: OS06 assigns admission to the long-term scheduler, suspension/swapping to the medium-term scheduler and ready-work selection to the short-term scheduler. The question specifically asks which ready process receives the CPU next, so C is exact. The dispatcher then performs the handoff; that is distinct from selecting the ready process. Device request ordering is not CPU ready-queue selection.

evidence.quote: The ready queue contains eligible work; device queues hold blocked requests. The broad textbook job queue contains processes in the system, while an admission queue more narrowly holds jobs awaiting memory/admission. Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work. The dispatcher performs the handoff/context restore after selection.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The long-term scheduler admits jobs rather than making each immediate ready-queue CPU selection.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The medium-term scheduler suspends/swaps work rather than choosing the next CPU-ready process.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The short-term CPU scheduler selects the next eligible process from ready work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An I/O scheduler orders device work rather than selecting the next process for the CPU.

reviews.answer_text: Suspend/swap processes between resident and backing-store states.
reviews.hint: Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role.
reviews.explanation: OS06 explicitly assigns suspension/swapping to the medium-term scheduler. OS27 distinguishes traditional whole-process swapping to backing storage from page movement. Thus C is the matching memory/load-control role. Admitting jobs belongs to long-term scheduling, picking the next ready process to short-term scheduling, and servicing drivers to device-management paths.

evidence.quote: Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.
Swapping traditionally moves a whole process to backing store; paging moves individual pages.
A driver converts OS requests into device-specific operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Deciding admission into the system is the long-term scheduler’s role in the supplied model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selecting the next CPU process belongs to the short-term scheduler, not the medium-term one.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps processes to control resident load and memory use.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Device-driver requests concern I/O service rather than the scheduler’s suspension/swapping function.

reviews.answer_text: Uncoordinated conflicting shared accesses make results depend on interleaving.
reviews.hint: Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required.
reviews.explanation: OS10 defines a race by results depending on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses. B is the intended match, with shared access understood to include a conflict such as an update; simultaneous read-only access alone is insufficient. Coincident completion, ordinary priority selection and preemption do not by themselves establish a shared-state race.

evidence.quote: A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses.
Two threads read counter=0, each computes 1 and each stores 1. Two increments produce 1 instead of 2. Protecting the entire read-modify-write with one lock prevents that lost update.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two completions at the same time need not involve conflicting shared accesses or interleaving-dependent results.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Unsynchronized conflicting shared accesses can make results depend on execution interleaving, which is the race condition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Priority order alone is a scheduling choice and does not establish a conflicting shared-data race.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Preemption can expose a race but is not itself sufficient without conflicting unprotected accesses.

reviews.answer_text: Preemption is not a necessary condition; no-preemption is.
reviews.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.
reviews.explanation: OS22 names mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no resource preemption and circular wait as the necessary set. The option Preemption reverses one of those conditions. Therefore C is the exception, while the other three are genuine members. This resource-preemption rule is separate from whether CPU scheduling uses timer preemption.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.
All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion is explicitly one of the four necessary conditions in the standard resource model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hold-and-wait is explicitly necessary: a process retains a resource while requesting another.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The required condition is no-preemption; permitting preemption is not one of the necessary conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circular wait is explicitly a required closed dependency chain in the standard model.

reviews.hint: Follow arrival order, include idle periods and distinguish waiting from completion time.
reviews.explanation: FCFS runs P1 from 0 to 24 ms, P2 from 24 to 27 ms, and P3 from 27 to 30 ms. Because every process arrives at 0, their waiting times are 0, 24 and 27 ms. The average is (0+24+27)/3 = 51/3 = 17 ms, so C is correct. The average turnaround is a different quantity: (24+27+30)/3 = 27 ms.

evidence.quote: FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.

All ready at time 0, tie order P1=24,P2=3,P3=3: schedule 0–24 P1,24–27 P2,27–30 P3. Waiting times 0,24,27 average to 17. Turnarounds 24,27,30 average to 27. If arrivals are not simultaneous, recompute using their actual times.
For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 3 ms is the burst time of P2 or P3, not the average ready-queue wait.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The three waits total 51 ms, so dividing by three cannot give 9 ms.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The waits 0, 24 and 27 ms average to 17 ms.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 27 ms is the average turnaround time in this example, not the average waiting time.

question_revision.original_stem: In the FCFS scheduling algorithm, if processes P1(24ms), P2(3ms), P3(3ms) arrive in order P1, P2, P3, what is the average waiting time?
question_revision.stem: All three processes arrive at time 0 and are ready immediately. Their CPU burst times are P1 = 24 ms, P2 = 3 ms and P3 = 3 ms. Using non-preemptive FCFS with tie order P1, P2, P3, and ignoring context-switch overhead, what is the average waiting time?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: all arrivals are at time 0, with FCFS tie order P1, P2, P3.
assumptions: All processes arrive at time 0.
FCFS resolves the simultaneous-arrival tie as P1, P2, P3.
Each process has one CPU burst and context-switch overhead is ignored.

reviews.hint: Check priority direction, preemption and whether waiting can change effective rank.
reviews.explanation: OS17 defines aging as increasing waiting jobs’ effective priority to reduce indefinite postponement under suitable rules/workloads. Thus B names the problem it addresses. It does not remove a deadlock dependency cycle, coordinate conflicting memory updates or consolidate fragmented memory. The result still depends on the priority/aging policy; naming aging alone does not provide an unconditional deadline guarantee.

evidence.quote: Aging increases waiting jobs’ effective priority according to a rule, reducing indefinite postponement when the priority scheme and workload permit. It is not a deadlock cure.
A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses.
Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Aging changes priority rather than breaking the blocked resource dependencies of a deadlock.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Increasing effective priority of waiting low-priority jobs addresses their starvation under sustained higher-priority load.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Races require shared-access synchronization; priority aging is not a mutual-exclusion mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory fragmentation concerns allocation layout rather than the priority of waiting CPU jobs.

reviews.hint: Compare the ready jobs using the stated burst or remaining-time rule.
reviews.explanation: OS16 distinguishes non-preemptive SJF/SJN from SRTF, which reconsiders at arrivals and can preempt for shorter remaining work. Therefore SRTF is the preemptive SJF variant. RR uses fixed cyclic turns, FCFS arrival order and generic priority an independently defined ranking. The original burst length and the remaining length must not be confused after a job has executed.

evidence.quote: Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs. SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt. Future burst lengths normally need estimates.
RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn.
FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR selects cyclic quantum turns rather than the shortest remaining CPU work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS follows arrival order and is ordinarily non-preemptive rather than preemptive shortest-job scheduling.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SRTF chooses minimum remaining work and can interrupt a running job for a shorter arrival.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Generic priority scheduling does not specifically rank by remaining burst length and can be either variant.

reviews.hint: Trace bounded turns in ready-queue order and include the stated overhead and arrivals.
reviews.explanation: OS18 says a large RR quantum approaches FCFS, while tiny quanta increase context-switch overhead. Selecting q therefore trades responsiveness against overhead, matching B. Priority management, deadlock policy and memory allocation are separate concerns rather than the defining parameter-selection challenge of ordinary Round Robin. The useful quantum depends on workloads and switching cost.

evidence.quote: A large quantum approaches FCFS; tiny quanta increase switch overhead.

With n continuously ready jobs, no priority bypass and zero overhead, a just-requeued job waits at most (n−1)q for its next turn. This bounds one interval, not total lifetime waiting when arrivals or blocking are unrestricted. Include context-switch costs if given.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Basic RR uses cyclic ready-queue turns rather than requiring a hierarchy of priority levels.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quantum length controls responsiveness and switching overhead, creating RR’s characteristic tuning tradeoff.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deadlock avoidance concerns resources and dependencies, not the defining RR quantum parameter.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory allocation is a separate management problem rather than the Round Robin selection rule’s main parameter.

reviews.answer_text: A synchronization variable with atomic wait and signal operations.
reviews.hint: Track available permits and blocked operations using the stated semaphore model.
reviews.explanation: OS11 defines a semaphore through atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations. Tokens control whether participants can proceed with shared resource work, with binary or counting forms. C identifies that synchronization role. Scheduling, memory-management and file-allocation policies solve different resource-selection/layout problems and do not define semaphore semantics.

evidence.quote: A semaphore provides atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations. Under the nonnegative-token model, wait consumes one available token or blocks when none is available; signal supplies a token and may wake a waiter. Implementations using negative internal counts encode waiters differently, so state the model. A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several. A mutex normally has ownership rules that a general semaphore lacks.
FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.
A contiguous allocation gives a process one continuous region.
Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A semaphore synchronizes participants; it is not itself a CPU-selection scheduling algorithm.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It controls coordination through permits, rather than choosing memory locations or translation layouts.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Atomic wait/signal on a synchronization variable controls permits for concurrent shared-resource operations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: File allocation chooses storage-block layout; that is separate from semaphore synchronization semantics.

reviews.answer_text: Binary tracks one permit; counting tracks several.
reviews.hint: Track available permits and blocked operations using the stated semaphore model.
reviews.explanation: OS11 defines a binary semaphore as one permit and a counting semaphore as several, under the nonnegative-token model. Thus binary availability is 0/1 while a resource pool can have a larger count. B states this logical distinction. Internal negative-waiter encodings are implementation details, not a reason to claim speed guarantees, deadlock-only usage or no difference.

evidence.quote: A semaphore provides atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations. Under the nonnegative-token model, wait consumes one available token or blocks when none is available; signal supplies a token and may wake a waiter. Implementations using negative internal counts encode waiters differently, so state the model. A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several. A mutex normally has ownership rules that a general semaphore lacks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The note gives no universal relative-speed guarantee; permit capacity is the defining distinction.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: In the nonnegative-token model, binary availability is zero/one while counting semaphores track several available permits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Counting semaphores coordinate resource pools and are not limited to preventing deadlock.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The allowed permit count is a substantive difference explicitly stated by the note.

reviews.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.
reviews.explanation: OS22 says all four conditions are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. C names that full set. Any two or a cycle alone does not state the complete conjunction. This is a necessary-condition answer, not an assertion that merely allowing all four policies proves a deadlock already exists in a particular allocation state.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.
All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. Their availability as general system policies does not prove a deadlock exists at this instant; inspect actual allocations/requests.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It omits hold-and-wait and no-preemption, both necessary in the stated standard resource model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An arbitrary pair does not supply all four necessary restrictions for the standard deadlock model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This option lists mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no-preemption and circular wait together.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A cycle alone omits other necessary restrictions; it is not the complete standard condition set.

reviews.answer_text: Definite deadlock under single-instance resource assumptions.
reviews.hint: Follow request and assignment arrows and check how many instances each resource has.
reviews.explanation: OS23 says a cycle implies deadlock when every resource type has one instance. The stem supplies that decisive assumption, so C follows. With multiple instances a cycle would indicate only a possibility, but importing that different model would ignore the literal question. A graph cycle also says nothing by itself about high CPU utilization.

evidence.quote: In a resource-allocation graph, P→R is a request and an instance R→P is an assignment. Follow these directions to form waits. No cycle implies no deadlock; with one instance of every resource type, a cycle implies deadlock. With multiple instances a cycle alone is insufficient: another instance may permit completion. A wait-for graph replaces single-instance resource nodes with P→Q when P waits for Q.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Potential-only applies to the more general multiple-instance caveat, not the supplied single-instance case.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A cycle in the stated single-instance model establishes deadlock rather than excluding it.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly gives cycle implies deadlock for a graph with one instance per resource type.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Resource dependency cycles do not measure CPU busy time or establish high processor utilization.

reviews.hint: Separate handling before allocation from actions taken after detection, and consider the cost of checking.
reviews.explanation: OS26 describes recovery through terminating selected processes or safely reclaiming resources and rolling work back after deadlock is detected. That matches allowing occurrence and then resolving it. Prevention removes a necessary condition, avoidance preserves safety before granting, and ignoring accepts risk without committing to recovery. The complete handling strategy is detection plus recovery; C is the offered recovery component.

evidence.quote: Detection asks whether the current state is deadlocked. Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint. Termination and rollback are both possible tools, so a question offering both as recovery methods needs a criterion.
Prevention constrains how requests are made.
Avoidance allows requests only if the resulting state remains safe.
Ignoring a sufficiently rare problem is sometimes called the ostrich policy, but real systems still prevent or detect selected deadlocks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Prevention constrains requests so the targeted deadlock class cannot arise rather than accepting occurrence first.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ignoring rare deadlock does not define active detection and subsequent recovery.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Recovery acts on an actual detected deadlock using termination, reclamation or rollback as appropriate.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Avoidance checks safe states before grants rather than deliberately permitting deadlock and then repairing it.

reviews.answer_text: Relocate addresses when the program is loaded.
reviews.hint: Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation.
reviews.explanation: OS27 defines load-time binding as relocation when placed into memory. That matches C’s final-address assignment at load when placement was unknown at compile time. Fixing absolute addresses during compilation is compile-time binding; translating while running is execution-time binding. Merely storing address bytes on a disk describes neither the placement decision nor its timing.

evidence.quote: Compile-time binding uses absolute addresses if placement is known. Load-time binding relocates when placed into memory. Execution-time binding translates while running and permits movement with hardware support.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fixing absolute addresses in the compiler is compile-time binding, not relocation on loading.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Translation during execution is execution-time binding rather than assignment during loading.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The loader resolves placement-dependent addresses when placing the program into memory.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Storing address information on disk does not define when placement-dependent address binding occurs.

reviews.answer_text: Fixed-size paging avoids external page-frame fragmentation; variable segments can fragment externally.
reviews.hint: Check the logical region and offset bound before computing its physical location.
reviews.explanation: Paging maps fixed-size pages into equal-size frames, avoiding external fragmentation of frame allocation, although internal waste can remain. Segmentation uses variable-length logical regions and can leave external holes. This is the unit-size and fragmentation contrast in B. A reverses the sizes. C does not supply that contrast, and D substitutes a hardware-support claim for it; page translation still requires mappings and checks.

evidence.quote: Under the basic models, paging uses fixed units/page tables and can waste space internally; segmentation uses variable logical units/segment tables and can fragment externally. Segments reflect program structure whereas ordinary pages are largely transparent to applications.

Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags. Physical address=frame×P+offset.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The sizes are reversed: pages are fixed-size units and segments are variable-length regions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This gives the required fixed-page versus variable-segment size and external-fragmentation contrast.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An exclusive-use statement does not compare allocation-unit sizes or external fragmentation as requested.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This does not give the requested size/fragmentation contrast; paging also uses translation mappings and checks.

question_revision.original_stem: What is the key difference between Paging and Segmentation?

original_options.label: A
original_options.text: Paging uses variable-sized blocks; segmentation uses fixed-sized blocks

original_options.label: B
original_options.text: Paging divides memory into fixed-sized pages eliminating external fragmentation; segmentation uses variable-sized logical segments but can cause external fragmentation

original_options.label: C
original_options.text: Segmentation is used only in virtual memory

question_revision.stem: Under basic page-frame allocation and variable-segment allocation, which statement correctly contrasts allocation-unit size and external fragmentation?

options.label: A
options.text: Paging uses variable-sized blocks; segmentation uses fixed-sized blocks

options.label: B
options.text: Paging divides memory into fixed-sized pages eliminating external fragmentation; segmentation uses variable-sized logical segments but can cause external fragmentation

options.label: C
options.text: Segmentation is used only in virtual memory

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: the requested comparison dimensions and basic allocation models are explicit.
assumptions: External-fragmentation claims concern page-frame allocation, not every allocator inside an OS.

reviews.answer_text: Free capacity is split across holes too small for a required contiguous allocation.
reviews.hint: Locate unused space relative to an allocated unit and distinguish total free space from contiguous free space.
reviews.explanation: OS29 defines external fragmentation as sufficient total free space split into holes unable to satisfy a contiguous allocation. B matches that definition, with large requests understood to require one continuous region. A instead describes internal fragmentation. CPU time and open-file counts may create other pressures but do not define the spatial fragmentation of free memory.

evidence.quote: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unused space within an oversized allocated block is internal fragmentation, not external free-hole fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Noncontiguous small holes can have enough total capacity yet fail to satisfy one contiguous request.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CPU execution time does not define the spatial layout of free memory holes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Open-file count is a resource-use limit rather than the definition of external memory fragmentation.

reviews.answer_text: Map virtual/logical pages to physical frames.
reviews.hint: Split the address into page and offset, then apply the mapping and access checks.
reviews.explanation: OS30 says the page table maps each virtual page to a frame with protection/status flags. B directly states the primary translation role. CPU time allocation belongs to scheduling; file permissions belong to filesystem metadata, despite page tables also having memory-protection bits. Disk I/O may service nonresident pages but does not define the page table’s mapping purpose.

evidence.quote: Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags.

A file has content and metadata such as name, size, owner, permissions and timestamps. open obtains an open-file reference, read/write transfer bytes, seek changes an offset, close releases a reference, truncate changes size and unlink removes a name.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU time allocation is scheduling, not the page-to-frame translation recorded by a page table.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The table identifies the physical frame corresponding to each virtual page and records relevant flags.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Memory access-protection flags differ from filesystem file-access permissions; file permissions are not the page table’s purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Page faults may cause I/O, but general disk-operation management is not the table’s translation role.

reviews.answer_text: Physical address = segment base + valid offset.
reviews.hint: Check the logical region and offset bound before computing its physical location.
reviews.explanation: OS31 gives segment-table base, limit and permissions, then validates (segment,offset) and adds base+offset. B matches, conditional on the offset passing the bound/protection checks. A and D mix in paging components and omit required scaling or displacement, while subtracting a limit is not the segment translation formula. An invalid offset traps rather than spilling into another segment.

evidence.quote: Segmentation uses logical variable-length units such as code, stack and arrays. A segment-table entry provides base, limit and permissions. For (segment,offset), validate the segment and check the bound, then add base+offset. An out-of-range offset traps; it must not spill into the next segment.

Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags. Physical address=frame×P+offset.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Page number times frame size is not the segment base-plus-offset translation and omits required mapping.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: After segment and bound checks, add the selected segment’s physical base to the offset.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The limit is a bound for validation, not a number subtracted to form the physical address.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Frame terminology belongs to paging, and adding an unscaled frame number is not the segmentation formula.

reviews.answer_text: Translated protected address spaces can use backing storage for nonresident portions.
reviews.hint: Separate a permitted nonresident access from an illegal access and trace the required handling steps.
reviews.explanation: OS32 describes virtual memory as protected translated address spaces with nonresident program portions backed by storage. B gives the disk-backed extension aspect and can allow programs exceeding resident physical memory to execute. It is not a complete definition of virtual memory, nor does it eliminate finite capacity constraints. The other alternatives confuse RAM installation, cache or an OS-only restriction.

evidence.quote: Virtual memory provides translated, protected address spaces and allows nonresident portions of a program to be backed by storage. It does not add physical RAM or remove all capacity constraints.
Caching retains copies to accelerate reuse.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Installing RAM chips adds physical capacity; virtual-memory translation is a different mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Backing storage holds nonresident portions, permitting a program’s address space to exceed its currently resident physical memory.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CPU cache retains copied memory blocks and is not the virtual-address/backing-store mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Processes receive virtual address spaces; virtual memory is not restricted to storage used only by the OS.

reviews.answer_text: When the CPU tries to access a page not currently in physical memory, requiring the OS to load it from disk
reviews.hint: Separate a permitted nonresident access from an illegal access and trace the required handling steps.
reviews.explanation: A valid nonresident access traps so the OS can obtain the page contents, update the mapping and restart the access. The specified page is disk-backed and requires a read, making B accurate for this scenario. Page faults in general need not read disk; zero-fill and shared mappings are other cases. Nothing here requires hardware failure, table corruption or exceeding the permitted address range.

evidence.quote: Demand paging brings a page in when accessed. On a nonresident access: trap, validate mapping/permissions, find a frame or choose a victim, save a dirty victim if needed, obtain contents, update mapping and restart.
Not every fault reads a disk: some allocate zero-filled pages or establish shared mappings. An illegal access is rejected, not automatically loaded.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The trap does not imply damaged memory hardware.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The valid disk-backed page is nonresident, so this access requires the stated page-in.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A correct table may intentionally mark a valid page nonresident.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The page is explicitly within the valid permitted mapping, so no allocation violation is implied.

question_revision.original_stem: What is a Page Fault?

original_options.label: B
original_options.text: When the CPU tries to access a page not currently in physical memory, requiring the OS to load it from disk

original_options.label: C
original_options.text: An error in the page table

original_options.label: D
original_options.text: When a process exceeds its allocated memory

question_revision.stem: In demand paging, assume the accessed virtual page is valid, permitted and backed by disk, but its contents are not resident and must be read from disk. What event is the page fault in this scenario?

options.label: B
options.text: When the CPU tries to access a page not currently in physical memory, requiring the OS to load it from disk

options.label: C
options.text: An error in the page table

options.label: D
options.text: When a process exceeds its allocated memory

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Restricted the definition question to a valid disk-backed demand-paging case.
assumptions: The page is valid, permitted and disk-backed.
Obtaining its nonresident contents requires a disk read in this scenario.

reviews.answer_text: Bring a page into memory when it is needed/accessed.
reviews.hint: Separate a permitted nonresident access from an illegal access and trace the required handling steps.
reviews.explanation: OS32 defines demand paging as bringing a page in when accessed. B matches loading only the pages demanded during execution, with disk backing for the described stored portions. Not all pages must literally originate on disk because zero-fill/shared cases exist. Whole-program loading, fixed contiguous partitions and whole-process swapping do not name this per-page demand policy.

evidence.quote: Demand paging brings a page in when accessed. On a nonresident access: trap, validate mapping/permissions, find a frame or choose a victim, save a dirty victim if needed, obtain contents, update mapping and restart.
Swapping traditionally moves a whole process to backing store; paging moves individual pages.
A contiguous allocation gives a process one continuous region.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Loading the entire program before execution is eager loading rather than fetching pages on demand.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Pages are brought in as execution needs them; disk backing is the described common stored-page case.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fixed partitions are a contiguous-allocation arrangement rather than the page-access-triggered loading policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Moving an entire process is traditional swapping, not the individual-page demand mechanism.

reviews.answer_text: Internal waste is inside allocations; external holes are between them.
reviews.hint: Locate unused space relative to an allocated unit and distinguish total free space from contiguous free space.
reviews.explanation: OS29 defines internal fragmentation as unused space inside an allocated unit and external fragmentation as free holes unable to serve a required contiguous request. B states the location distinction. C is not the general definition and needs allocator scope; D adds an unsupported virtual-memory-only restriction. These wastes can arise from allocation geometry rather than the program’s CPU behavior.

evidence.quote: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.
Basic fixed-frame paging avoids external fragmentation of page-frame allocation but can waste the final page internally.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The note explicitly distinguishes internal unused allocation space from external free-hole fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Internal space is wasted within an allocation; external waste is free space split between allocations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This does not define the contrast; basic page-frame allocation avoids external fragmentation, though other allocators may differ.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Unused space within an allocated unit is not limited by definition to virtual-memory systems.

reviews.hint: Apply the stated hole-selection or base-and-bound rule with its explicit convention.
reviews.explanation: OS28 defines first-fit as selecting the first adequate hole. This is exactly the stem’s first hole large enough. Best-fit searches for the smallest adequate hole, worst-fit for the largest, and next-fit resumes from a prior search position. The explicit first-hole condition selects first-fit without any numeric hole trace.

evidence.quote: First-fit selects the first adequate hole; next-fit continues from the previous search position; best-fit selects the smallest adequate hole; worst-fit selects the largest.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Best-fit minimizes adequate hole size rather than stopping at the first adequate hole.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Worst-fit selects the largest available hole rather than the first adequate one encountered.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: First-fit stops at the first hole that can accommodate the requested allocation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Next-fit continues from the previous search position; the stem gives the ordinary first-fit criterion.

reviews.answer_text: Temporarily move a whole process to backing store.
reviews.hint: Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation.
reviews.explanation: OS27 explicitly distinguishes traditional swapping of a whole process to backing store from paging individual pages and context switching execution state. B describes the whole-process memory-management operation. Saving registers is a context-switch task, file copying is a filesystem operation, and replacing instruction contents does not define swapping’s residence change.

evidence.quote: Swapping traditionally moves a whole process to backing store; paging moves individual pages. These differ from a context switch, which primarily changes execution state.
A context switch saves one execution context and restores another; useful application work is interrupted by this overhead.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Saving/restoring CPU register contexts is context switching rather than moving a whole process out of RAM.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Traditional swapping moves a process image to backing storage to free resident memory.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Copying files changes directory/storage contents rather than a process image’s memory residence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Replacing instruction contents is not the defined transfer of a whole process between RAM and backing store.

reviews.answer_text: Load a routine only when needed.
reviews.hint: Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation.
reviews.explanation: OS27 directly defines dynamic loading as bringing a routine in when needed. B states the routine-on-call form of that rule. Eager startup loading is the opposite, priority changes are scheduling, and automatic page movement is a virtual-memory mechanism at a different granularity. Dynamic loading concerns when code routines become resident, not which process gets CPU priority.

evidence.quote: Dynamic loading brings a routine in when needed.
Demand paging brings a page in when accessed.
Priority scheduling chooses the highest-priority ready job.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Loading all routines at startup is eager loading rather than bringing them in only on demand.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A routine is loaded when execution actually calls or needs it, matching dynamic loading.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Changing priority affects scheduling and does not load a routine’s code into memory.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Paging moves pages by virtual-memory demand, whereas dynamic loading names demand-driven routine loading.

reviews.answer_text: User-level threads are managed by a user-space library; kernel-level threads are known to and managed by the OS
reviews.hint: Compare per-thread execution context with shared process resources and the stated thread mapping.
reviews.explanation: User-level threads are managed by a library, while kernel threads are execution contexts known to the OS. Their mapping affects blocking behavior and use of multiple CPUs. The management layer alone does not guarantee faster creation, faster execution or greater stability; those depend on implementation. It also does not grant user code privileged hardware access. The repaired option keeps the supported management distinction.

evidence.quote: User-level threads are managed by a library; kernel threads are known to the OS. In many-to-one mapping, a blocking kernel call can block all user threads and one kernel execution context cannot use multiple CPUs simultaneously. One-to-one permits another kernel thread to run when one blocks. Many-to-many multiplexes user threads over several kernel threads. Speed and reliability depend on implementation; the management layer alone guarantees neither. Application names such as browser or Excel do not prove a particular version’s threading model.

Being scheduled or managed by the kernel does not give application thread code kernel privilege. Ordinary applications and supporting utilities execute in restricted user mode and request protected services through libraries and system calls. Kernel component code executes in privileged kernel mode and performs permitted low-level hardware operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This states library management versus OS-known kernel threads.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No management layer guarantees that kernel threads are always faster.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: User-level thread management does not grant direct privileged hardware access.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Blocking and CPU-use differences show that the distinction has practical effects.

question_revision.original_stem: What is the key difference between User-Level Threads and Kernel-Level Threads?

original_options.label: A
original_options.text: User-level threads are faster to create but managed entirely in user space without OS knowledge; kernel-level threads are managed by the OS providing more control and stability

original_options.label: C
original_options.text: User-level threads can access hardware directly

original_options.label: D
original_options.text: There is no practical difference between them

question_revision.stem: What is the key management-layer distinction between user-level threads and kernel-level threads, without assuming universal speed or reliability advantages?

options.label: A
options.text: User-level threads are managed by a user-space library; kernel-level threads are known to and managed by the OS

options.label: C
options.text: User-level threads can access hardware directly

options.label: D
options.text: There is no practical difference between them

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Removed unsupported speed and stability guarantees from the management distinction.
assumptions: The question compares management layers rather than a specific implementation’s measured speed.

reviews.answer_text: Mechanisms for exchanging information and coordinating processes.
reviews.hint: Identify how data moves, which participant waits and what event allows the operation to continue.
reviews.explanation: OS09 describes shared-memory communication, send/receive, pipes, queues, sockets and RPC, including synchronization for conflicting updates. B summarizes the exchange and coordination role.
