IPC is not a CPU selection algorithm or a particular memory-allocation/file operation, even though shared memory and file-based mechanisms may be used to implement it.

evidence.quote: Shared memory lets processes access a common region and requires synchronization for conflicting updates. Message passing exchanges data through send/receive operations. Pipes provide streams; message queues preserve messages; sockets connect endpoints; RPC requests a remote operation. HTTP is an application protocol over a communication mechanism and can carry interprocess communication, so it is not universally “not IPC.”
File locks coordinate access rather than transfer arbitrary payloads, though locking is synchronization within IPC.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU scheduling selects execution opportunities, rather than defining communication and coordination among processes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Exchanging information with appropriate synchronization/coordination captures the IPC mechanisms described by the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shared memory can implement IPC, but memory allocation alone does not define interprocess communication.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Files can participate in communication, but IPC is not restricted to one filesystem operation.

reviews.hint: Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required.
reviews.explanation: OS10 defines a critical section as code accessing shared state needing protection and lists mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting as requirements. B states the exclusion aspect for critical sections protecting the same conflicting resource. The problem also includes progress/fair-waiting requirements, so exclusion is not its entire specification. CPU quotas, disk management and real-time scheduling are different topics.

evidence.quote: A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses. A critical section is code accessing shared state that needs protection, not the resource itself. A correct exclusion solution requires mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under stated assumptions. Mutual exclusion is a desired safety property; races, starvation and deadlock are possible failures.

Keep critical regions small and ensure every conflicting access uses the same protection. A barrier waits until a defined set of participants reaches a point; a monitor encapsulates protected operations with condition synchronization. Locking can itself introduce deadlock if acquisition order is inconsistent.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU consumption limits are not the shared-access exclusion problem defining critical sections.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Conflicting critical regions must not execute simultaneously; this is the mutual-exclusion part of the correctness requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Disk I/O can involve shared state, but managing it generally is not the critical-section problem definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Real-time selection addresses timing/scheduling, not the core shared-state exclusion requirement requested.

reviews.hint: Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures.
reviews.explanation: Turnaround is completion time minus arrival time, including CPU execution, ready-queue waiting and blocked intervals. Ready waiting plus CPU service omits blocked time when I/O occurs. Start plus burst may resemble a completion timestamp for uninterrupted work, but it is not elapsed turnaround and does not subtract arrival. Burst minus waiting has no general elapsed-time interpretation. Only B remains valid in the full stated model.

evidence.quote: For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B. With I/O, subtract all CPU and blocked time to isolate ready-queue waiting.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Subtracting ready waiting from CPU service is not turnaround.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Completion minus arrival includes the entire elapsed lifetime.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Start plus burst is not generally completion with I/O and does not subtract arrival.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ready waiting plus CPU service omits blocked intervals.

question_revision.original_stem: In a Turnaround Time formula: Turnaround Time = ?
question_revision.stem: For a general process that may perform I/O, which formula defines turnaround time from event timestamps? Waiting means time in the ready queue; burst means total CPU service. The formula must remain valid for nonzero arrival times and blocked intervals.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the general I/O-capable model and timestamp definition.
assumptions: Waiting is ready-queue time only.
Blocked/I/O intervals and nonzero arrivals are permitted.
The selected identity must hold generally, not only for a special no-I/O trace.

reviews.answer_text: Short jobs wait behind a long FCFS burst.
reviews.hint: Follow arrival order, include idle periods and distinguish waiting from completion time.
reviews.explanation: OS15 describes the convoy effect as long CPU-bound work making many short jobs wait under non-preemptive FCFS. C directly states that queueing effect and its high waiting-time consequence. FCFS does not use priority order or grant equal total CPU, and shared address space is unrelated to the arrival-order delay. The effect depends on a long burst preceding shorter ones.

evidence.quote: FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt. If the CPU is idle, jump to the next arrival. Long CPU-bound work can make many short jobs wait: the convoy effect.
RR gives recurring opportunities, not identical total CPU consumption for jobs of different lengths.
A thread has its own PC, registers and stack. Threads in a process share code, address space and usually open-file resources.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Priority order does not define FCFS, which follows arrival order rather than high-priority completion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS serves entire bursts of possibly different lengths rather than enforcing equal CPU shares.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Short jobs are delayed behind the long non-preempted burst, producing the FCFS convoy effect.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shared memory concerns address-space organization rather than the scheduling delay called a convoy.

reviews.answer_text: Voluntary release versus possible forced CPU preemption.
reviews.hint: Check whether the running burst can be interrupted before completion or blocking.
reviews.explanation: OS14 says non-preemptive scheduling retains the CPU until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding, while preemptive scheduling may return running work to ready. B captures the voluntary-versus-forced distinction, with completion/blocking included among natural release events. C contradicts preemption, D claims an unsupported universal performance ranking, and A erases the defining difference.

evidence.quote: Non-preemptive scheduling keeps a running CPU burst until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding. Preemptive scheduling can return running work to ready, usually after a timer quantum or a more urgent arrival. FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive. Priority can be either, so its name alone cannot decide. Cooperative describes relying on voluntary release.
There is no universally best policy for response, waiting, fairness and throughput simultaneously.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The policies differ in whether a running CPU burst can be forcibly interrupted for another process.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Non-preemptive work releases naturally/voluntarily; preemptive policy may forcibly reassign CPU execution time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Forcibly interrupting running work is exactly what preemptive scheduling permits.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No policy universally performs better for all workloads and objectives, so the absolute performance claim fails.

reviews.hint: Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures.
reviews.explanation: OS13 defines throughput as completed jobs divided by elapsed time. That exactly matches the stem’s process-completion rate. CPU utilization is busy-time fraction; response measures delay to first start, and turnaround delay to completion. The units therefore distinguish throughput from the other criteria without requiring a scheduling example.

evidence.quote: For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B. With I/O, subtract all CPU and blocked time to isolate ready-queue waiting. Throughput=completed jobs/elapsed time; CPU utilization=busy time/elapsed time. Minimize response/turnaround/waiting under the selected goal and maximize useful throughput/utilization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU utilization measures busy-time fraction, not how many processes finish per unit time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Response measures first-service delay for a process rather than a completion-count rate.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Throughput is explicitly the number of completed jobs divided by elapsed time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Turnaround measures arrival-to-completion elapsed duration rather than completed jobs per time.

reviews.answer_text: All processes in the broad textbook system/job-queue sense.
reviews.hint: Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role.
reviews.explanation: OS06 explicitly defines the broad textbook job queue as processes in the system and distinguishes a narrower admission queue awaiting memory. B matches that broad usage, including not-yet-admitted jobs. Ready/running or I/O-blocked work are subsets, not the whole category; already-ended processes are not the intended current job population. The answer retains the note’s terminology qualification.

evidence.quote: The ready queue contains eligible work; device queues hold blocked requests. The broad textbook job queue contains processes in the system, while an admission queue more narrowly holds jobs awaiting memory/admission. Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.

New processes are created/admitted; ready means eligible for CPU but not currently running. Running uses a CPU. Waiting/blocked means unable to proceed until an event; terminated means execution has ended. Running→ready follows time-slice expiry or another preemption. Running→waiting follows blocking I/O. I/O completion normally gives waiting→ready, not a guaranteed immediate running state.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Currently running work is only a subset, not the broad population represented by the textbook job queue.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The broad textbook usage includes system processes/jobs, including those awaiting memory admission.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: I/O waiting belongs to device queues and does not exhaust the broad job-queue population.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Already-terminated work is not the current job population intended by the note’s broad system queue.

reviews.answer_text: The current position within an open file for the next read or write operation
reviews.hint: Distinguish a file operation, a resource handle, an offset and file metadata.
reviews.explanation: The current offset records the logical position used for the next read or write on a seekable open file. A descriptor is instead a process-local integer handle referring to open-file state. Physical disk-block locations, permissions and creation timestamps describe other mapping or metadata information. By asking specifically about the position field, the revised stem makes B precise without conflating a descriptor with an offset.

evidence.quote: A file has content and metadata such as name, size, owner, permissions and timestamps. open obtains an open-file reference, read/write transfer bytes, seek changes an offset, close releases a reference, truncate changes size and unlink removes a name. A file descriptor is a process-local integer handle; the associated open-file state contains the current offset and access mode. Descriptor and offset are not synonyms.
Read advances the offset on seekable files and may return fewer bytes than requested; zero normally indicates end-of-file.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Physical disk location is separate from the current logical I/O offset.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The file-offset field records the position for the next read or write.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Owner permissions are access-control metadata rather than the current position.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Creation time is metadata rather than the current I/O offset.

question_revision.original_stem: In file systems, what does a File Descriptor / File Pointer track?

original_options.label: A
original_options.text: The physical location of the file on disk

original_options.label: B
original_options.text: The current position within an open file for the next read or write operation

question_revision.stem: In an open seekable file’s state, what does its current file-offset field (the file-position pointer, rather than the descriptor handle) track?

options.label: A
options.text: The physical location of the file on disk

options.label: B
options.text: The current position within an open file for the next read or write operation

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Selected the file-offset concept instead of conflating it with a descriptor.
assumptions: The file is seekable.
File pointer means the current offset field, not a language stream object or descriptor handle.

reviews.answer_text: Specify principals and permitted access rights.
reviews.hint: Distinguish identity checks, permission checks and the particular security property at issue.
reviews.explanation: OS39 defines an ACL as listing principals and rights. B states that users/groups can receive different read/write/execute permissions for a file. Authentication verifies identity first; authorization uses these permitted operations. Space accounting, fragmentation and I/O ordering do not define an access-control list. The answer does not assume universal default rights or that every filesystem uses exactly the same permission model.

evidence.quote: Authentication verifies identity; authorization checks permitted operations. An ACL lists principals and rights; owner/group/other bits are a simpler policy model, not universal defaults granting all owners full access or everyone read. Read, write, execute, append and delete are different rights, with filesystem-specific rules.
Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.
The ready queue contains eligible work; device queues hold blocked requests.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Disk-space usage is storage accounting, not the list of principals and allowed operations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ACL associates users/groups or other principals with specified access rights on the resource.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fragmentation concerns block placement and free-space layout rather than authorization entries.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Scheduling I/O requests controls service order, not which principal is authorized to access a file.

reviews.answer_text: A file occupies consecutive disk blocks.
reviews.hint: Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata.
reviews.explanation: OS38 defines contiguous allocation through consecutive blocks, with logical block i at start+i. This permits sequential and direct access without following a chain. B matches. Scattered pointers describe linked allocation, a separate index describes indexed allocation, and fixed physical memory frames belong to paging rather than file-contiguity organization. Growth and external fragmentation remain drawbacks.

evidence.quote: Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems. Extents allow several contiguous runs. Linked allocation chains blocks and supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file; locating block i requires traversing preceding links. FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping.
Indexed allocation uses a per-file array/tree of block pointers and supports direct lookup with metadata overhead.
Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Scattered blocks linked by pointers describe linked allocation rather than one consecutive run.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A consecutive block run supports start-plus-index lookup and sequential/direct file access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A separate block-pointer index describes indexed allocation, not contiguous placement itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Physical memory frames are paging units rather than the disk-block contiguity rule for a file.

reviews.answer_text: Linked blocks permit growth without reserving a full contiguous run.
reviews.hint: Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata.
reviews.explanation: OS38 says linked allocation supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file. Since successive blocks can occupy separate free locations, it removes the external-contiguity problem and the need to reserve the final length beforehand. B captures that advantage. Random access still requires traversing earlier links, internal last-block waste may remain, and no universal smaller-metadata claim follows.

evidence.quote: Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems. Extents allow several contiguous runs. Linked allocation chains blocks and supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file; locating block i requires traversing preceding links. FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping.
Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Locating a later linked block requires traversal, so faster random access is not its general advantage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Separate linked blocks allow incremental growth without a single reserved contiguous region or preknown final length.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A partially used final block can still waste space internally; linking does not specifically remove that waste.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Pointers add metadata, and the note gives no universal less-memory guarantee over contiguous allocation.

reviews.answer_text: A per-file block of data-block pointers in the simple indexed model.
reviews.hint: Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata.
reviews.explanation: OS38 defines indexed allocation through a per-file array/tree of block pointers and gives an index-block capacity example. B describes the simple single-index-block form. Large files may need multiple index levels, so all addresses in one block is model-dependent rather than universal. A is linked allocation, C a global-table description, and D ordinary metadata without the defining data-block pointers.

evidence.quote: Indexed allocation uses a per-file array/tree of block pointers and supports direct lookup with metadata overhead. A Unix inode can combine direct pointers with indirect levels. Check pointer size, block size, index capacity and whether metadata reads are cached.
A 1024-byte index block with 4-byte pointers holds 256 block addresses. With 1024-byte data blocks, one such index level addresses 256 KiB of file data, excluding metadata and any reserved entries.
FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A next pointer in each data block describes linked allocation rather than a separate per-file index.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: In the simple indexed model, a dedicated per-file index contains pointers to the file’s data blocks.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A global table for all files is not the per-file index block described by indexed allocation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Size/timestamps alone do not provide the data-block address index that defines this allocation structure.

reviews.answer_text: Sequential access proceeds in order; direct access selects a position.
reviews.hint: Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata.
reviews.explanation: OS38 contrasts linked traversal of preceding blocks with contiguous start+i and indexed direct lookup. These illustrate the access distinction in B: sequential progression versus selecting a numbered position without reading every preceding record. Nothing restricts direct access to text or requires sequential files to occupy more disk space merely because of their access method.

evidence.quote: Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems. Extents allow several contiguous runs. Linked allocation chains blocks and supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file; locating block i requires traversing preceding links. FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping.
Indexed allocation uses a per-file array/tree of block pointers and supports direct lookup with metadata overhead.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Order-dependent traversal and direct selection are different access behaviors, not identical methods.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sequential access advances through records; direct access identifies a chosen block/position for access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The direct block-lookup rule does not impose a text-file-only restriction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Access order alone does not determine a greater storage-space requirement for sequential files.

reviews.answer_text: A rooted hierarchy of nested directories and files.
reviews.hint: Follow namespace structure and distinguish names, underlying files and mounted filesystems.
reviews.explanation: OS37 says a tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths. In the pure tree model, each entry has a path from the root, matching B. Flat lists instead describe single-level organization; sharing among users and deletion at reboot do not define tree structure. Links can add graph relationships, but that is an extension beyond the pure tree premise.

evidence.quote: A single-level directory requires unique names in one namespace. Two-level directories separate users. A tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths; links can create shared graphs. Modern general-purpose systems commonly present hierarchical namespaces, but a feature name alone does not prove that every system excludes simpler arrangements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One flat file list is single-level organization rather than nested branches from a root.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A root with nested subdirectories and paths is the tree hierarchy described by the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple users sharing a directory does not by itself define its structural hierarchy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Deletion on reboot is a lifetime policy rather than the rooted directory-tree organization.

reviews.answer_text: Hard links name one file object; symbolic links store a pathname.
reviews.hint: Follow namespace structure and distinguish names, underlying files and mounted filesystems.
reviews.explanation: A hard link supplies another name for the same underlying file object; a symbolic link stores a pathname. Symbolic links can cross filesystems and may dangle, whereas ordinary hard links stay within a filesystem. Linux’s link operation supplies a direct counterexample to the Windows-only claim. unlink can remove a symbolic-link name, so the link is not undeletable. B states the correct distinction.

evidence.quote: A hard link is another name for the same underlying file object, usually within one filesystem; a symbolic link stores a pathname and can point across filesystems or become dangling. Removing one hard link does not erase content while other names/open references retain it.

Linux provides link() to create another hard-link name for an existing file. The old and new names identify the same file, so hard links are not a Windows-only facility. unlink() removes a filesystem name; when that name is a symbolic link, it removes the link itself. Removing a name and erasing the target’s contents are different operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The boundary is reversed: symbolic links may cross filesystems, while ordinary hard links remain within one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Both hard-link names identify the same underlying file; a symbolic link contains a pathname to resolve.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A symbolic-link name can be removed with unlink; removing it does not erase the target’s contents.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Linux provides hard links through link(), so they are not supported only in Windows.

reviews.answer_text: Attach a filesystem at a mount point.
reviews.hint: Follow namespace structure and distinguish names, underlying files and mounted filesystems.
reviews.explanation: OS37 explicitly defines mounting as attaching a filesystem at a mount point and distinguishes it from formatting. B states that integration into the existing namespace. Creation/formatting establish a filesystem’s on-device structure; deleting files frees content space. None of those is the namespace attachment operation requested by mounting.

evidence.quote: NFS provides remote filesystem access; FTP transfers files rather than itself mounting a local filesystem.
Disk initialization/filesystem creation is OS/tool work, firmware begins boot, and drive firmware may remap bad sectors.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Creating a new filesystem establishes storage structure rather than attaching it to an existing namespace.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Mounting makes a filesystem accessible at a chosen point in the directory hierarchy.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deleting files changes contents/free space rather than attaching a filesystem to the namespace.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Formatting is explicitly distinguished from mounting in the supplied note.

reviews.answer_text: Restore an affected process to a prior checkpoint after reclaiming resources.
reviews.hint: Separate handling before allocation from actions taken after detection, and consider the cost of checking.
reviews.explanation: OS26 describes reclaiming safely preemptable resources and rolling affected work back to a checkpoint. B states that restoration to a safe prior state after resources are withdrawn. Restarting the entire OS/computer and killing all involved processes are different coarse recovery actions, not the meaning of rollback. Safe checkpoints/restart semantics are required to make withdrawal and restoration coherent.

evidence.quote: Detection asks whether the current state is deadlocked. Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint. Termination and rollback are both possible tools, so a question offering both as recovery methods needs a criterion.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Restarting the whole OS is not the checkpoint restoration of affected work that defines rollback.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rollback restores an affected process to a previous recoverable state after safe resource reclamation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Terminating processes is a separate recovery tool rather than restoring their earlier execution state.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Rebooting frees broad machine state but is not the process-checkpoint restoration definition of rollback.

reviews.answer_text: The relocation register stores the process’s physical base and the limit its permitted length; hardware checks the logical offset before adding the base
reviews.hint: Apply the stated hole-selection or base-and-bound rule with its explicit convention.
reviews.explanation: In the standard base/limit model, the base identifies the process’s physical starting address and the limit gives its permitted length. Hardware checks that the logical offset is nonnegative and smaller than the limit, then computes base plus offset. This protects accesses to the assigned region. The registers do not describe the OS base and size, schedule CPU work, track disk files or manage page tables.

evidence.quote: A contiguous allocation gives a process one continuous region. In the standard base/limit model, base is that process’s physical starting address and limit is its permitted length. Check 0≤logical_offset<limit, then physical=base+offset. The relocation register does not normally hold the OS base.
Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: These registers check memory accesses rather than schedule CPU work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The repaired option states the process base, length bound and checked translation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Disk-block locations are not the purpose of RAM base/limit registers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Simple contiguous base/limit translation does not manage page-table mappings.

question_revision.original_stem: What is the purpose of the Relocation Register and Limit Register in Single Partition Memory Allocation?

original_options.label: A
original_options.text: They speed up CPU scheduling decisions

original_options.label: B
original_options.text: The relocation register stores the OS base address; the limit register defines the OS size — together they protect OS memory from user process access

original_options.label: C
original_options.text: They track file system locations on disk

original_options.label: D
original_options.text: They manage virtual memory page tables

question_revision.stem: What is the purpose of relocation/base and limit registers in the standard contiguous single-process-region memory model? The limit denotes the permitted region length.

options.label: A
options.text: They speed up CPU scheduling decisions

options.label: B
options.text: The relocation register stores the process’s physical base and the limit its permitted length; hardware checks the logical offset before adding the base

options.label: C
options.text: They track file system locations on disk

options.label: D
options.text: They manage virtual memory page tables

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Corrected the register description to process base and length and stated the limit convention.
assumptions: Limit means permitted length, not last valid offset.
The standard contiguous process-region model is intended.

reviews.answer_text: Share suitable library code pages across programs.
reviews.hint: Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation.
reviews.explanation: OS27 says dynamic linking resolves external-library references at load/runtime and allows suitable library code pages to be shared, whereas static linking copies selected code into the executable. B captures the potential memory saving. It is not an unconditional speed guarantee, does not remove address translation/page tables and cannot eliminate programming bugs. Only shareable code/pages are implied, not arbitrary writable library state.

evidence.quote: Dynamic linking resolves references to external libraries at load/runtime, allowing suitable library code pages to be shared; static linking copies selected code into the executable.
Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Dynamic resolution/sharing does not guarantee faster execution for every program or workload.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Several processes can share suitable library code pages rather than each embedding a separate static copy.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Library linking does not remove virtual-address translation or its page-table requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Choosing dynamic rather than static linking cannot guarantee the absence of programming errors.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: Spiral organizes each cycle around objectives, alternatives, risk assessment and reduction before further commitment. That directly addresses the specified major feasibility risks and supported risk-analysis capability. Iterative enhancement can aid learning but does not make risk assessment its defining organizer; RAD needs rapid construction and skilled support. Classical waterfall fits stable requirements and familiar technology, which the scenario does not supply.

evidence.quote: Select a process using requirement stability, technical risk, delivery urgency, stakeholder availability, team skills and assurance needs. “Team has little experience” alone does not uniquely identify a process. A risk-driven cycle, prototype or carefully planned staged process may each help, depending on the actual uncertainty. No process eliminates the need for testing or documentation.

Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment. A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment. The amount and type of work depend on the risks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Iteration supports feedback but is not defined by risk-driven commitments.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: RAD emphasizes rapid construction rather than the specified risk cycle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Spiral explicitly organizes commitment around major risk reduction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Unfamiliar technology and unresolved risks do not fit the stated classical waterfall rationale.

question_revision.original_stem: _________ is a software development life cycle model that is chosen if the development team has less experience on similar projects.
question_revision.stem: A team has little experience with a project’s unfamiliar technology. Major feasibility risks must be evaluated before each further commitment, and experienced risk-analysis support is available. Which lifecycle is selected specifically by that risk-driven criterion?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: scope, project conditions and modeling conventions are made explicit.
assumptions: Add explicit major technical risks and available risk-analysis expertise.
Choose by risk-driven commitment rather than inexperience alone.

reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE08 distinguishes the business reason and objectives of a project from user needs and detailed system obligations. The question asks why the project is needed and what objectives it serves, so business requirements match directly. Functional requirements describe behavior, while nonfunctional requirements describe qualities or constraints; neither primarily states the project's business justification.

evidence.quote: Business requirements explain why the project exists and its goals. User requirements describe stakeholder needs at a useful high level; system requirements specify detailed services and constraints. The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) organizes the agreed requirements. In the module, a natural-language specification communicates with clients while analysis models formalize it for technical discussion; real specifications can also contain diagrams.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Business requirements state the project's purpose, justification and intended organizational goals.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Functional requirements specify observable system services rather than the overall business reason for the project.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Nonfunctional requirements specify qualities or constraints rather than why the project exists.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: User requirements describe stakeholder needs at a high level rather than the project's business justification.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE23 explicitly separates logical abstraction from deployment separation. A layer organizes responsibilities logically, whereas a tier describes their deployment separation or platform arrangement. A use case models an actor goal, and a component is a software building block. Neither is the term for the deployment distinction asked for here.

evidence.quote: A layer is a logical abstraction level; a tier is a deployment separation. A closed layered architecture permits calls only to the immediately lower layer; an open one permits approved skipping. For top-to-bottom A,B,C,D, A→B obeys closed layering, A→C skips, and lower-to-upper calls violate the simple dependency rule unless explicitly mediated by a defined mechanism.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A use case models a goal or interaction rather than the deployment platform separation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A tier identifies deployment separation, contrasting with logical layering.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A layer is a logical abstraction level and need not occupy a distinct deployment platform.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A component is a software element and does not itself denote a deployment tier.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: The runtime interaction of software elements is the subject of component-and-connector structures in SE23. Module structures instead organize the code, while allocation structures relate software to hardware, teams or environments. These are different architectural views, so the inclusive choice fails: only the C&C option specifically answers the runtime-interaction focus.

evidence.quote: A structure is the elements/relations themselves; a view represents selected aspects. Module structures show code organization, component-and-connector structures runtime interaction, and allocation structures map software to hardware, teams or environment. Processes/threads belong in concurrency views. Evaluate architectures against quality attributes and scenarios; processor allocation, decomposition and style selection can all be architectural concerns.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The alternatives address different architectural concerns, so not every choice focuses on runtime interaction.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: C&C structures show runtime elements and the connectors through which they interact.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Allocation structures map software to hardware, teams or environments rather than primarily describing runtime exchanges.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Module decomposition shows code organization rather than the runtime interactions emphasized by the stem.

reviews.answer_text: Omission or inclusion of elements; Extension point
reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: Omitting or including selected elements permits configured architectural variation, and extension points define places where additional behavior can be supplied. Overloading by itself supplies alternate code signatures and does not establish either architectural mechanism. Thus B and C meet the specified architectural scope. The all-of-the-above choice includes that insufficient code-level case and therefore cannot be selected as a correct aggregate.

evidence.quote: Variability can use selectable features, omission/inclusion and extension points; overloading supplies alternate signatures in code but is not every variability mechanism. Testability improves with controllable inputs, observable outputs, replaceable dependencies and limited structural complexity. A sandbox can isolate execution. Self-referential combination choices such as “A and B” in option B cannot establish a unique correct answer.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Alternate signatures alone do not define the specified architectural variability.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selectable omission or inclusion changes architectural configuration.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Extension points explicitly support variation at defined boundaries.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It incorrectly includes overloading alone as an architectural mechanism.

question_revision.original_stem: Which among the following introduces architectural mechanisms of variability?
question_revision.stem: Which choices explicitly provide architectural variability through selectable elements or defined extension interfaces? Select all that apply. Treat overloading as alternate code signatures only.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: scope, project conditions and modeling conventions are made explicit.
assumptions: Distinguish architectural variation from code-level overloading alone.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE27 describes Factory Method as letting subclasses choose a concrete product through a creation operation, reducing dependence on concrete constructors. Those are exactly the two benefits in A and B, so C is the inclusive answer. The reference is to Factory Method; a simple factory is related but does not necessarily delegate product choice to subclasses.

evidence.quote: Factory Method lets subclasses choose a concrete product through a creation operation, reducing coupling to concrete constructors. A simple factory centralizes creation but is not identical to Factory Method. Singleton controls access to one instance; Observer notifies subscribers; Memento stores/restores state while hiding representation; Iterator traverses; Decorator adds behavior through wrapping. “Momento” in the bank means Memento.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Factory Method lets subclasses select the concrete product through the creation operation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Depending on the creation abstraction reduces coupling to concrete product constructors.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both listed benefits hold for Factory Method, making this the inclusive answer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note explicitly supports both benefits, so none is false.

question_revision.original_stem: Which among the following is an advantage of the factory design pattern?

original_options.label: A
original_options.text: Allows the sub-classes to choose the type of objects to create

question_revision.stem: Which choice most completely describes the stated advantages of the Factory Method pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Allows the sub-classes to choose the type of objects to create

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: the comparison and stated conditions are explicit.
assumptions: The aggregate refers to the substantive listed alternatives; choose the most complete selection.

reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE11 identifies scope, understanding and volatility as distinct elicitation difficulties. Scope concerns agreeing what belongs in the system; understanding concerns discovering and interpreting actual needs; volatility concerns needs changing as the project progresses. Since all three listed problems are valid, the inclusive answer is appropriate rather than choosing just one source of difficulty.

evidence.quote: Correct requirements reflect actual stakeholder needs. Complete requirements address the agreed scope, normal and exceptional behavior. Consistency excludes contradictions. Clarity/unambiguity gives one intended interpretation; feasibility/realism means achievable within constraints. Verifiability means objective evidence can check fulfillment. Replace “fast for most users” with a defined metric, workload and threshold.

Trace each requirement backward to its source/rationale and forward to design, code and tests. Record dependencies among requirements. A traceability matrix links these artifacts and helps impact analysis; it is not just a cost/schedule ledger. Stakeholders must negotiate conflicting requirements rather than independently approving incompatible demands. Scope, understanding and volatility are distinct elicitation difficulties.

Elicitation difficulties have several distinct sources. Scope problems concern agreeing on system boundaries and the appropriate level of detail. Understanding problems arise when stakeholders and analysts have different domain knowledge, omit tacit needs or communicate conflicting interpretations. Volatility means that requirements change as circumstances and understanding develop.
These difficulties call for repeated communication, explicit boundaries, negotiated meanings and controlled revision. They can occur together; resolving one does not automatically remove the others.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: All three listed difficulties are explicitly recognized in the complete note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Unclear system boundaries make agreeing on included and excluded requirements difficult.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Different interpretations and tacit stakeholder needs complicate accurate understanding.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Changing needs make elicitation an ongoing activity rather than a one-time capture.

question_revision.original_stem: Why is Requirements Elicitation a difficult task?
question_revision.stem: Which choice most completely identifies the listed reasons requirements elicitation can be difficult?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: the comparison and stated conditions are explicit.
assumptions: The aggregate refers to the substantive listed alternatives; choose the most complete selection.

reviews.hint: Classify the motive for the change before its implementation: repair, environment, useful capability or reduced future risk.
reviews.explanation: Repeated changes without coherent boundaries can accumulate dependencies and make the evolving system harder to understand. Refactoring and good subsystem design help control that structural complexity while maintenance still requires impact analysis and regression checks. User engagement is a product-use outcome rather than the structural risk asked for. Automation is an execution technique, not itself structural deterioration, and ongoing evolution does not eliminate maintenance costs.

evidence.quote: Software engineering applies systematic methods to development, operation and maintenance. A software product includes executable code and relevant requirements, designs, test assets, configuration and user documentation. A process defines activities, ordering, roles, products and entry/exit conditions. Its four broad activities are specification, design/implementation, validation and evolution.

Corrective maintenance fixes faults; adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes; perfective maintenance improves useful capability/performance; preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as restructuring fragile code. Motive determines category; refactoring can support preventive or perfective work. Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost.

Cohesion measures how well elements inside a module serve a related purpose; coupling measures dependency between modules. Seek high cohesion and low coupling. Shared mutable data and knowledge of another module’s internal representation increase coupling. Information hiding exposes stable operations while concealing changeable decisions.
poor object design can still be complex.
Refactor to preserve behavior while improving structure; optimize only against measured needs; record rationale and update traceability and regression evidence after change.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Engagement concerns user behavior rather than the internal structural deterioration asked for.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Accumulated poorly coordinated changes can increase structural complexity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Automation does not itself describe deterioration of responsibilities or dependency structure.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Changing software still requires maintenance and regression work.

question_revision.original_stem: What is a common problem with evolving software?
question_revision.stem: Which structural risk can arise when repeated software changes are made without coherent design or refactoring?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: the comparison and stated conditions are explicit.
assumptions: Use the explicit scope and standard definitions stated in the clarified prompt.

reviews.answer_text: PERT models uncertain durations; traditional CPM uses point durations.
reviews.hint: Write out the supplied quantities and dependency constraints. Compute and compare values under the stated metric, finish condition and assumptions.
reviews.explanation: SE30 gives traditional CPM point estimates and PERT optimistic, most-likely and pessimistic duration estimates. PERT therefore represents duration uncertainty, whereas the traditional CPM calculation uses known or fixed activity durations. The cost-versus-time contrast is not the defining distinction here, and the other two choices reverse the described treatment of uncertainty.

evidence.quote: Traditional CPM uses point durations; PERT models uncertainty with optimistic a, most-likely m and pessimistic b. The classic estimate is TE=(a+4m+b)/6 and variance=((b-a)/6)^2. For 3,6,15 days, TE=42/6=7 days and variance=4 days². Do not replace the weighted estimate by a simple average. These formulas are approximations, not guaranteed actual completion times.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The note's defining contrast concerns duration uncertainty rather than assigning cost exclusively to CPM.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This reverses the models: PERT explicitly represents uncertain activity durations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: PERT uses uncertain three-point estimates, while traditional CPM uses fixed point durations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The probabilistic/deterministic characterization is reversed relative to the note.

reviews.hint: Distinguish the planning or organization goal from the tool or structure used to support it. Apply the stated project conditions.
reviews.explanation: SE28 says planning tools coordinate ownership, dependencies and progress while leaving judgment to people. That coordination supports communication and collaboration. The tool does not automatically detect and repair code faults, replace project managers or directly guarantee faster coding. Those benefits would require other capabilities and evidence beyond project-management tooling itself.

evidence.quote: Planning is continuous: identify scope/deliverables, decompose work, estimate effort/duration/cost, assign resources, sequence dependencies and revise as evidence changes. A WBS is hierarchical and covers project scope without adding unrelated work. Tools help coordinate ownership, dependencies and progress; they do not replace judgment or automatically fix bugs.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Project-management tools do not automatically detect and repair software defects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: They support planning and coordination while human managers still supply judgment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shared ownership, dependency and progress information helps the team communicate and collaborate.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A direct increase in coding efficiency is not the general coordination benefit established by the note.

reviews.answer_text: Ordinary browsers used by the team are usually tools, not product configuration items.
reviews.hint: Separate artifact history and controlled changes from scheduling, collaboration benefits and automated execution.
reviews.explanation: SE33 includes source files, requirements, manuals and test plans among controlled configuration items. A team's ordinary browser is normally just a tool. A particular browser version can become an environment CI if the project deliberately controls it for reproducible testing, but the word typically makes A the appropriate exception in the stated scenario.

evidence.quote: Configuration management identifies controlled items, versions/baselines, change procedures, status and audits. Items may include source code, requirements, manuals, test plans, environments and build configurations. A team’s ordinary browser is usually a tool rather than product CI, but a controlled test-browser version may be an environment CI.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An ordinary team browser is usually a tool; a deliberately controlled test-browser version would be an exception.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Source code files are standard controlled product configuration items.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: User manuals can be versioned and baselined alongside the software product.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Test plans are controlled project artifacts whose versions must match the tested configuration.

reviews.answer_text: Independent distributed development followed by merging.
reviews.hint: Separate artifact history and controlled changes from scheduling, collaboration benefits and automated execution.
reviews.explanation: SE33 says a distributed Git clone contains local history and allows independent branches that can later be merged. B matches that working arrangement directly. Git does not require everyone to lock files, use one local branch or obtain central permission before every local commit. Additional review policies can be imposed, but they do not define distributed version control.

evidence.quote: Change management handles request, impact assessment, decision/prioritization, implementation and validation; configuration management keeps all affected versions consistent. Distributed Git gives each clone local history and supports independent branches followed by merging; it does not eliminate merge conflicts or approvals. Plan test configuration management early and apply it throughout testing, not at just one exclusive phase.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Exclusive file locking is not the defining distributed Git collaboration model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Local histories and independent branches support geographically distributed work followed by merging.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A colocated team can use Git, but this scenario does not express its independent distributed-work benefit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Central approval policies can exist, but they do not define or require distributed local commits.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: Coding can be part of building an executable prototype even if the process diagram labels that work construction. It is therefore the offered activity that is not a separately named stage in the stated convention. Quick design, refinement and production engineering are named stages there. This answer concerns the diagram’s labels and does not claim that prototyping excludes coding or always follows one universal phase taxonomy.

evidence.quote: A prototype explores requirements, usability or technical feasibility. A throwaway prototype is discarded after learning; an evolutionary prototype is deliberately refined toward production. A quick prototype may omit robustness, security or architecture, so do not deploy it unchanged without evaluation. Coding may occur during prototyping even if a diagram labels that activity construction rather than coding.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Coding can occur inside construction without a separate stage label.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Prototype refinement is a named stage.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Engineering the production product is a named stage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Quick design is a named stage.

question_revision.original_stem: Which one of the following is not a phase of the Prototyping Model?
question_revision.stem: Use a process diagram whose named stages are requirements gathering, quick design, prototype construction, prototype refinement and engineering the production product. Which offered activity is not a separately named stage, although it can occur within prototype construction?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: scope, project conditions and modeling conventions are made explicit.
assumptions: Fix the process-diagram naming convention.
Distinguish a missing stage label from an excluded activity.

reviews.answer_text: The need for highly skilled developers and designers.
reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE07 describes RAD as rapid construction using timeboxes, user participation and often reusable components, but requiring skilled designers and developers. That staffing prerequisite is the listed drawback. Reuse and customer feedback are useful features. A combines the genuine prerequisite with a benefit, so C states the drawback accurately without misclassifying reuse.

evidence.quote: RAD uses rapid construction, timeboxing, user participation and often reusable components; it requires available users and skilled designers/developers. Reuse-oriented development searches components, evaluates fit, may adjust requirements, designs around interfaces and builds missing parts. Product-line assets may include requirements, architecture, components and tests; all are potentially reusable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It bundles a genuine staffing drawback with component reuse, which is generally a benefit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Component reuse helps rapid construction and is not the drawback asked for.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: RAD depends on skilled designers and developers, which can constrain staffing and feasibility.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Customer feedback supports learning and fit rather than being the stated RAD disadvantage.

reviews.answer_text: Amount of general technical development work.
reviews.hint: Distinguish process assurance from product evaluation, and compare specified obligations with actual stakeholder needs.
reviews.explanation: SE34 identifies assurance responsibilities, evaluations, reviews, audits and assurance records as SQA-plan contents. The documents produced by SQA are assurance records; evaluations, audits and reviews are assurance activities. The amount of general technical development work belongs primarily to project scope and effort planning rather than defining the SQA activities listed here.

evidence.quote: Quality assurance establishes and checks processes/standards; quality control evaluates work products. An SQA plan identifies standards, responsibilities, evaluations, reviews, audits and assurance records. Quality of conformance means following the design/specification; a product can conform to a poor specification. Verification asks whether specified obligations are implemented correctly; validation asks whether the product meets intended stakeholder needs. Both can use reviews, analysis or execution, so “human-only versus computer-only” is false.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Assurance documents and records are legitimate SQA-plan deliverables.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Planned evaluations are explicitly part of an SQA plan.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Reviews and audits are explicitly listed assurance-plan activities.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: General technical-work quantity is a project scope/effort concern rather than the listed assurance-plan content.

reviews.answer_text: Incident reports are execution outputs, rather than the test plan itself.
reviews.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
reviews.explanation: SE39 places objectives, scope, resources, schedule, risks and entry/exit criteria in test planning. Incident reports document observed problems during execution and are normally outputs of that work. They may be referenced by later plans, but that does not make actual incident reports an intrinsic part of the prospective test plan.

evidence.quote: A test plan describes intended work; incident/defect reports are normally execution outputs. A defect report should identify build/environment, steps, expected versus actual behavior, evidence and severity. Anyone finding a fault should record it; testers often coordinate reporting, but it is not their exclusive permission. Configuration control makes the tested version reproducible.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The test schedule is planned work and belongs in a test plan.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Incident reports normally record execution findings rather than describing the planned testing work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Entry and exit criteria define when testing can start or finish and belong in planning.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Testing risks influence scope and priorities and are legitimate test-plan content.

reviews.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
reviews.explanation: SE36 explicitly classifies exploratory testing as experience based because learning, test design and execution occur together. It may use knowledge of specifications or internals, but black-box, white-box and grey-box describe different bases of test derivation. None of them replaces the defining experience-based classification asked for in this question.

evidence.quote: Black-box techniques derive cases from specified behavior; white-box techniques derive them from internal structure; grey-box uses partial internal knowledge. Regression testing checks for unintended effects after change; confirmation testing checks the particular defect repair. Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution and is experience based. Manual/automated describe execution support, not a compulsory black-/white-box classification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Exploratory testing uses experience while learning, designing and executing tests together.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It may use external behavior, but black-box alone is not its defining classification.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Exploratory testing does not require test cases to be derived from internal code structure.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Partial internal knowledge can help exploration, but it does not define the technique.

reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE13 defines entity objects as domain information and gives ReportForm as a boundary mediating interaction. Thus forms normally suggest boundary objects rather than entity objects. Real-world things, domain activities represented as information and relevant stored data can suggest entity candidates; those are heuristics, not mechanical rules guaranteeing a class for every noun or activity.

evidence.quote: Use nouns as candidate objects, possessive descriptions as candidate attributes, and verbs such as manages/reports-to as candidate associations. These are heuristics, not automatic parsing rules. CRC means Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators. A control per use case or participating actor can be a useful starting point, not a mandatory UML rule or fixed object lifetime.
A UI form is normally boundary, not entity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Real-world domain entities are natural candidates for entity objects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A domain activity represented as persistent domain information can suggest an entity candidate.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A user-interface form normally mediates interaction and is modeled as a boundary object.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Relevant domain data sources can suggest information-holding entities, subject to analysis rather than automatic conversion.

reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: The stem describes observing people's actual daily tasks and recording what they do. SE12 names that observation-based elicitation approach ethnography. Interviews ask stakeholders questions, while scenarios and use cases describe executions or goals; those can complement observation but do not name the day-to-day fieldwork technique itself.

evidence.quote: Interviews ask stakeholders about needs; document analysis examines manuals, contracts and current records; observation/ethnography studies actual daily work. Prototypes reveal tacit expectations. Workshops/JAD bring users, managers and developers together with a facilitator and recorder to build consensus. Use several sources and check assumptions against observed work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A use case describes goal-oriented interactions rather than naming observational fieldwork.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ethnography gathers understanding by observing actual day-to-day work and recording it.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A scenario is one concrete execution, not the observation-based elicitation technique itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An interview asks people questions rather than primarily observing their daily tasks.

reviews.hint: Distinguish the planning or organization goal from the tool or structure used to support it. Apply the stated project conditions.
reviews.explanation: Democratic teams share decisions, whereas chief-programmer teams centralize technical coordination. Functional and project organizations classify how people are grouped, not how authority is distributed. Asking about shared decision-making therefore makes democratic the unique answer. It does not require every individual to perform every lifecycle task; a democratic team can still divide work by expertise and responsibilities.

evidence.quote: Functional organizations group specialists by discipline; project organizations group people around projects. Functional specialization helps staffing and knowledge continuity but may create handoff barriers. Democratic teams share decisions; chief-programmer teams centralize technical coordination. These are different classification dimensions. Tuckman’s sequence is forming→storming→norming→performing→adjourning: orientation, conflict, norms, effective work and closure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Functional organization groups specialists by discipline.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Project organization groups people by project rather than defining shared authority.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Democratic teams share decisions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Chief-programmer teams centralize technical coordination.

reviews.hint: Distinguish the planning or organization goal from the tool or structure used to support it. Apply the stated project conditions.
reviews.explanation: SE32 explicitly assigns requirements management, software project planning, quality assurance and configuration management to historical Software CMM Level 2. Its name is Repeatable, rather than the later CMMI label Managed. The other named choices correspond to levels 1, 3 and 4 in this historical model, so A matches both practices and terminology.

evidence.quote: Historical Software CMM levels are 1 Initial, 2 Repeatable, 3 Defined, 4 Managed, 5 Optimizing. Level2 establishes basic project discipline including requirements management, project planning, quality assurance and configuration management. These historical labels must not be silently replaced by modern CMMI terminology. A maturity model concerns process capability, not a guarantee that every product is defect free.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Repeatable is historical Software CMM Level 2, which establishes the listed basic project practices.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Initial is historical Level 1, before the repeatable project discipline specified here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Defined is historical Level 3, not the level associated with this basic practice list.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Managed is historical Software CMM Level 4; modern CMMI terminology must not be substituted.

reviews.answer_text: No need for job specialization is false of a functional organization.
reviews.hint: Distinguish the planning or organization goal from the tool or structure used to support it. Apply the stated project conditions.
reviews.explanation: SE32 defines functional organizations as grouping specialists by discipline. Claiming that specialization is unnecessary contradicts that organizing principle. Ease of staffing and knowledge continuity are benefits of specialization; continuity can help with turnover. Specialist expertise can also support documentation quality, although no organizational form guarantees good documents. C is the clear exception.

evidence.quote: Functional organizations group specialists by discipline; project organizations group people around projects. Functional specialization helps staffing and knowledge continuity but may create handoff barriers. Democratic teams share decisions; chief-programmer teams centralize technical coordination. These are different classification dimensions. Tuckman’s sequence is forming→storming→norming→performing→adjourning: orientation, conflict, norms, effective work and closure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Grouping specialists supports staffing within established disciplines, so this is a plausible benefit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Specialist expertise can support good documentation; this is not the direct contradiction of functional grouping.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This contradicts the defining use of specialist disciplines in a functional organization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Knowledge continuity within a functional group can help absorb staff turnover.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE06 makes risk the organizing principle of spiral development. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops an appropriate next result and plans further commitment. Time, efficiency and quality still matter, but they do not distinguish spiral from other processes as directly as its explicit risk-driven cycles.

evidence.quote: Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment. A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment. The amount and type of work depend on the risks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Efficiency is useful, but it is not the defining organizing feature of spiral cycles.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Time management matters in many processes and does not distinguish spiral.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Quality management is important generally, but the defining spiral emphasis is risk.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Each spiral cycle explicitly evaluates and reduces the most important risks.

reviews.hint: Classify the motive for the change before its implementation: repair, environment, useful capability or reduced future risk.
reviews.explanation: The purpose of the change determines the maintenance category. Corrective maintenance repairs faults observed during use. Adaptive maintenance handles environmental changes, perfective maintenance improves useful capability or performance, and preventive maintenance reduces future risk before a corresponding failure occurs. Because the scenario starts with observed bugs that need repair, corrective maintenance is the direct category rather than one of the other three motives.

evidence.quote: Corrective maintenance fixes faults; adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes; perfective maintenance improves useful capability/performance; preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as restructuring fragile code. Motive determines category; refactoring can support preventive or perfective work. Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Adaptive maintenance responds to a changed environment.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Corrective maintenance repairs observed defects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Perfective maintenance improves useful capability or performance.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Preventive maintenance reduces future risk rather than primarily fixing the stated observed bugs.

reviews.answer_text: Engine is part of Car and cannot exist independently under the stated lifetime policy.
reviews.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.
reviews.explanation: The filled diamond at Car denotes composition: Car is the whole and Engine is its strongly owned part. Composition destroys parts that remain owned when the whole is destroyed. Because this model forbids detachment or transfer, the Engine’s lifetime cannot continue independently of its Car. Temporary use would be a dependency, and inheritance would use a hollow generalization triangle instead.

evidence.quote: Composition uses a filled diamond at the whole end and strong ownership: a part is in at most one composite at a time, and parts still owned are destroyed with that composite. Parts may be detached/transferred under a defined model. Thus “cannot ever exist independently” is an oversimplification. For Car composing Engine, the diamond belongs beside Car; saying it points to Engine is imprecise. The intended bank relationship is composition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Temporary use is a dependency, not composition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The stipulated permanent ownership excludes an independent Engine lifetime.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Engine is the owned part and cannot outlive Car under the stated policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inheritance uses a hollow triangle rather than a filled diamond.
