reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE21 recommends grouping related functionality, minimizing cross-subsystem associations and isolating communication infrastructure where useful. Grouping objects serving one use case can be a starting heuristic, though workflows do not dictate every boundary. B and C directly support isolation and low coupling. Since the question asks what can be a heuristic, the inclusive option is appropriate.

evidence.quote: System design turns the analysis model into architecture: design goals, subsystem responsibilities, dependencies, hardware mapping, data management, access control, control flow and startup/shutdown/error policies. Detail/object design refines APIs, parameter/return types, exceptions, component choices and algorithms. A subsystem is a manageable logical collection with services and an interface; it need not be a physical replaceable artifact.
Group closely related objects and functionality, minimize associations crossing boundaries, and isolate communication infrastructure where useful.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Objects collaborating on one use case can be grouped as a starting heuristic, subject to other design constraints.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Communication infrastructure can be isolated in a dedicated subsystem when useful.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Reducing cross-boundary associations reduces coupling between subsystems.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All three can guide decomposition, provided use-case grouping is not treated as an absolute rule.

None of A–C is inherently excluded by its asset type. The repaired D expresses this conclusion directly rather than contradicting the negative stem with an undefined all-choices assertion.

evidence.quote: RAD uses rapid construction, timeboxing, user participation and often reusable components; it requires available users and skilled designers/developers. Reuse-oriented development searches components, evaluates fit, may adjust requirements, designs around interfaces and builds missing parts. Product-line assets may include requirements, architecture, components and tests; all are potentially reusable.

choices.explanation: Test cases can be reusable product-line assets.

choices.label: B

reviews.answer_text: This software model is less precise than the specified mathematical sketch.
reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: The software model states exact preconditions and balance equations, whereas the informal mathematical sketch omits those constraints. It is therefore not less precise in the stated comparison, making A false. Omitting implementation detail makes it more abstract than the specified detailed engine drawing, and representing design ideas remains a legitimate purpose. These are scenario-specific judgments rather than universal rankings of all software and mathematical models.

evidence.quote: Choose designs by their effect on stated goals. Fine-grained self-contained components, separation of producers/consumers and limited shared mutable data often improve maintainability. Trade-offs remain: interfaces can add latency, isolation can complicate transactions, and global state can simplify one operation while coupling many others. Prefer measurable quality scenarios to counting components alone.

A contract states preconditions, postconditions and invariants. For withdraw(amount): require amount>0 and amount<=balance; ensure balance=oldBalance-amount; preserve balance>=0. Validation checks inputs; implementation enforces the transition. A complete feature needs both UI/API and persisted behavior, not only a diagram.

A layer is a logical abstraction level; a tier is a deployment separation. A closed layered architecture permits calls only to the immediately lower layer; an open one permits approved skipping. For top-to-bottom A,B,C,D, A→B obeys closed layering, A→C skips, and lower-to-upper calls violate the simple dependency rule unless explicitly mediated by a defined mechanism.
A structure is the elements/relations themselves; a view represents selected aspects.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Its exact constraints make the stated less-precise comparison false.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The software model omits implementation detail retained in the detailed drawing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A design model can represent the designer’s ideas and decisions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A is false, so the no-false-statements alternative is wrong.

reviews.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.
reviews.explanation: SE20 defines a DFD through data flows, stores and transformations from inputs to outputs. That matches the functional-transformation focus in the stem. An ER diagram focuses on domain data relationships, while a component diagram describes software components and dependencies. A DFD need not show detailed control timing merely because it depicts connected transformations.

evidence.quote: Choose a sequence diagram for message order between participants, a state machine for event-dependent state changes, and activity for workflow. Both sequence and state diagrams describe behavior over time. State machines are useful for objects with significant states, whether entity or control. A DFD shows data stores/flows and transformations from inputs to outputs; it is not a UML diagram.

An entity–relationship diagram models entity types, their attributes and the relationships between them, commonly for data design. Its focus differs from a use-case diagram of external roles and goals, a class diagram of classes and their features, or a deployment diagram mapping artifacts to execution nodes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: ER diagrams describe entities and relationships rather than transformations of input data into outputs.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: DFDs depict data flows and the processes that transform inputs into outputs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Component diagrams describe component interfaces and dependencies rather than this data-transformation view.

reviews.hint: Classify the motive for the change before its implementation: repair, environment, useful capability or reduced future risk.
reviews.explanation: A typical evolution sequence is change request, impact analysis, release planning, implementation/testing and release. Once the request has arrived, impact analysis is the earliest listed technical step, assessing consequences before scheduling and implementation. Change management names the broader handling process rather than that next step. Release planning and testing occur later, so neither starts the specified post-request technical sequence.

evidence.quote: A typical evolution sequence is change request→impact analysis→release planning→implementation/testing→release. Among a list lacking the request step, impact analysis may be the earliest listed technical activity. Major restructuring is reengineering; if the architecture itself changes, architectural transformation is the more specific description. Markets, technology, stakeholders and funding can all change scope or priorities.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Release planning follows impact analysis.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Change management is the overarching process.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Impact analysis is the first listed technical activity after the request.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Testing follows analysis, planning and implementation.

reviews.hint: Write out the supplied quantities and dependency constraints. Compute and compare values under the stated metric, finish condition and assumptions.
reviews.explanation: Each complete path takes 9 days: A→B is 4+5 and C→D is 3+6. Working backward from day 9, D must start by day 3. Therefore C must finish by day 3 and start by day 0. C has LS=0 and ES=0, so total slack = LS−ES = 0 days (equivalently LF−EF = 3−3). A is correct. Delaying C would delay its successor D and the required project finish.

evidence.quote: Early start/finish values alone do not determine slack without successor relationships and the project completion constraint. If C3→D6 is a complete path parallel to A4→B5 and both finish at day9, C has zero float. That network cannot be silently inferred from four unrelated ES/EF rows.

Traditional CPM uses point durations; PERT models uncertainty with optimistic a, most-likely m and pessimistic b. The classic estimate is TE=(a+4m+b)/6 and variance=((b-a)/6)^2. For 3,6,15 days, TE=42/6=7 days and variance=4 days². Do not replace the weighted estimate by a simple average. These formulas are approximations, not guaranteed actual completion times.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: C has latest start 0 and earliest start 0, giving zero total slack.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A one-day delay would make the C→D path finish on day 10, beyond the day-9 finish.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: C’s three-day duration is not its slack; a three-day delay would finish this path on day 12.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: D’s six-day duration is not C’s slack; a six-day delay to C would finish the path on day 15.

question_revision.original_stem: Given the following activities in a project: Activity A: Duration = 4 days, ES = 0, EF = 4, Activity B: Duration = 5 days, ES = 4, EF = 9, Activity C: Duration = 3 days, ES = 0, EF = 3, Activity D: Duration = 6 days, ES = 3, EF = 9. What is the slack time for Activity C?
question_revision.stem: A project starts at day 0 and must finish at day 9. It consists of exactly two parallel paths, A → B and C → D. A and C have no predecessors, B depends only on A, D depends only on C, and the project finishes when both B and D are complete. Activity durations and early times are: A: duration 4 days, ES=0, EF=4; B: duration 5 days, ES=4, EF=9; C: duration 3 days, ES=0, EF=3; D: duration 6 days, ES=3, EF=9. What is the total slack (float) of Activity C?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: A → B and C → D are the complete parallel paths, both ending at day 9.
assumptions: The complete dependency network is A → B and C → D, with a common start at day 0 and common finish at day 9.
There are no additional activities, dependencies or resource constraints.

evidence.quote: Traditional CPM uses point durations; PERT models uncertainty with optimistic a, most-likely m and pessimistic b. The classic estimate is TE=(a+4m+b)/6 and variance=((b-a)/6)^2. For 3,6,15 days, TE=42/6=7 days and variance=4 days². Do not replace the weighted estimate by a simple average. These formulas are approximations, not guaranteed actual completion times.

reviews.explanation: A throwaway prototype is built to learn about requirements, usability or feasibility and is discarded after serving that purpose. An evolutionary prototype is deliberately refined toward production. Either may involve successive steps, multiple tasks and varying development time, so those features do not define the difference. The artifact’s intended future, rather than how quickly it was built, distinguishes the approaches.

evidence.quote: A prototype explores requirements, usability or technical feasibility. A throwaway prototype is discarded after learning; an evolutionary prototype is deliberately refined toward production. A quick prototype may omit robustness, security or architecture, so do not deploy it unchanged without evaluation. Coding may occur during prototyping even if a diagram labels that activity construction rather than coding.

choices.label: C

reviews.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
reviews.explanation: The concern is that small changes may disturb other previously working parts of the software. SE36 defines regression testing as checking unintended effects after change, rather than only confirming the repaired defect. Such testing can span multiple levels and a large scope; the question describes its purpose, not the size of a unit or an acceptance decision.

evidence.quote: Black-box techniques derive cases from specified behavior; white-box techniques derive them from internal structure; grey-box uses partial internal knowledge. Regression testing checks for unintended effects after change; confirmation testing checks the particular defect repair. Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution and is experience based. Manual/automated describe execution support, not a compulsory black-/white-box classification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Preventive testing is not the defined technique for detecting unintended effects of a specific software change.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Unit testing isolates a small component and does not by itself define the cross-system change-impact purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Regression tests check whether changes unintentionally damage previously working behavior elsewhere.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Acceptance testing supports a user acceptance decision rather than specifically checking unintended change effects.

reviews.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
reviews.explanation: SE37 derives decision-table cases from combinations of specified conditions and resulting actions. This is specification-based rather than code-structure-based testing. It therefore belongs to black-box techniques. Experience or partial internal knowledge may help a tester, but they do not define the decision-table method or change its condition/action test basis.

evidence.quote: A decision table lists condition combinations and resulting actions. For validCard and enoughFunds, enumerate TT,TF,FT,FF; specify dispense only for TT and the proper rejection for others. Cover feasible rules rather than blindly using every impossible combination. These are specification-based techniques. Test requirements can also define state-transition cases, such as rejecting dispatch from an already closed incident.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: White-box techniques derive tests from internal implementation structure rather than specified condition/action rules.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Decision tables derive cases from specified conditions and expected actions, making them black-box.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The technique has an explicit specification-based structure rather than being defined by tester experience.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Partial knowledge of internals is not required to derive decision-table test cases.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: Bottom-up design begins with existing components and assembles them into a larger solution. Top-down design instead starts with high-level structure and refines it, although it can still reuse components later. A hybrid combines the two directions, but the question asks which approach characteristically begins with the parts. Reuse by itself would not distinguish them; the explicit starting direction does.

evidence.quote: Use abstraction and decomposition to manage complexity; preserve consistency, traceability and clear responsibilities. Top-down design refines high-level structure; bottom-up design assembles existing components. A hybrid combines both. SOLID includes Single Responsibility, Open–Closed, Liskov substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion. Depend on abstractions; add compatible extensions; avoid forcing unused operations. DRY limits duplicated knowledge, KISS avoids unnecessary complexity, and YAGNI avoids speculative work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A hybrid may use both directions but does not name the specifically described starting approach.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Top-down begins with high-level structure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Bottom-up assembles existing components into the larger system.

choices.label: D

Layer structure instead describes logical abstraction levels, while uses and service relations describe different dependencies or interfaces. Thus the concurrent structure is the offered category that directly matches these runtime execution elements.

evidence.quote: A structure is the elements/relations themselves; a view represents selected aspects. Module structures show code organization, component-and-connector structures runtime interaction, and allocation structures map software to hardware, teams or environment. Processes/threads belong in concurrency views. Evaluate architectures against quality attributes and scenarios; processor allocation, decomposition and style selection can all be architectural concerns.

choices.explanation: Service structure emphasizes provided behavior or interfaces rather than processes and threads as execution elements.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

A simple average would give 8, but that discards the fourfold weighting of the most-likely estimate. The expected duration is an estimate, not a guaranteed actual completion time.

evidence.quote: Traditional CPM uses point durations; PERT models uncertainty with optimistic a, most-likely m and pessimistic b. The classic estimate is TE=(a+4m+b)/6 and variance=((b-a)/6)^2. For 3,6,15 days, TE=42/6=7 days and variance=4 days². Do not replace the weighted estimate by a simple average. These formulas are approximations, not guaranteed actual completion times.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Eight is the simple mean of 3, 6 and 15, not the weighted PERT estimate.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: Trace each requirement back to its source and rationale.
reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE11 directs requirements backward to their source or rationale and forward to design, code and tests. Backward traceability therefore establishes why a requirement exists and where it came from. It can assist reviews, but redundancy detection is not its definition. Design mappings and future phases primarily describe the forward direction.

evidence.quote: Trace each requirement backward to its source/rationale and forward to design, code and tests. Record dependencies among requirements. A traceability matrix links these artifacts and helps impact analysis; it is not just a cost/schedule ledger. Stakeholders must negotiate conflicting requirements rather than independently approving incompatible demands. Scope, understanding and volatility are distinct elicitation difficulties.

choices.explanation: Redundancy detection can benefit from traceability, but it is not the definition of backward tracing.

choices.label: B

Trace each requirement backward to its source/rationale and forward to design, code and tests. Record dependencies among requirements. A traceability matrix links these artifacts and helps impact analysis; it is not just a cost/schedule ledger.
Planning is continuous: identify scope/deliverables, decompose work, estimate effort/duration/cost, assign resources, sequence dependencies and revise as evidence changes.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

Quality of conformance means following the design/specification; a product can conform to a poor specification. reviews.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
reviews.explanation: SE36 defines regression testing as checking for unintended effects after a software change. That matches the stated goal of finding newly introduced errors. Static and dynamic describe execution-related approaches rather than this change-focused purpose; beta describes an external-user test setting. Although the stem says level, regression is more accurately a testing purpose/type.

evidence.quote: Black-box techniques derive cases from specified behavior; white-box techniques derive them from internal structure; grey-box uses partial internal knowledge. evidence.quote: A typical evolution sequence is change request→impact analysis→release planning→implementation/testing→release. Among a list lacking the request step, impact analysis may be the earliest listed technical activity. Major restructuring is reengineering; if the architecture itself changes, architectural transformation is the more specific description. Markets, technology, stakeholders and funding can all change scope or priorities.

reviews.answer_text: When major risks make one-block development unsafe.
reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE06 uses explicit risk assessment and reduction to distinguish spiral development from other iterative approaches. B directly states that risk makes a single overall commitment inappropriate. Changing or unstable requirements can occur in several processes and do not alone identify spiral; clear business modeling likewise does not supply the distinctive risk-based reason.

evidence.quote: Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment. A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment. The amount and type of work depend on the risks.
Use risk emphasis to distinguish spiral from a generic changing-requirements scenario.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE22 defines logical cohesion as grouping operations in a similar category, often selected through a flag. D matches that shared logical category. A instead describes temporal cohesion, where operations occur at the same time. Interface complexity concerns dependencies, and a loose collection of unrelated tasks does not state the defining category-based relationship.

evidence.quote: Logical cohesion groups similar-category operations, often selected by a flag; temporal cohesion groups operations done at the same time; functional cohesion focuses on one task. Splitting an unrelated three-purpose component improves modularity. If behavior is preserved, the restructuring is refactoring; the words are not mutually exclusive answers. Smaller modules can aid understanding, independent work, reuse and maintenance, but too many interfaces also create complexity.

choices.explanation: Grouping operations because they occur at the same time is temporal cohesion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Interface complexity concerns dependencies and does not define logical cohesion inside a module.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Loose task relatedness alone does not establish the shared operation category defining logical cohesion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Grouping similar-category operations is the defining feature of logical cohesion.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: Spiral development repeatedly identifies objectives, assesses and reduces risks, develops an appropriate result and plans further commitment. Its cycles can incorporate prototyping, incremental work or sequential activities according to the risks. The other listed models name particular exploratory or staged organizations rather than this risk-driven choice framework. This explains the conventional general-model reading without claiming that every process is formally a specialization of spiral.

evidence.quote: Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.

Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment. A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment. The amount and type of work depend on the risks.

choices.explanation: Spiral selects cycle work through risk assessment.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Prototyping is one learning activity that a spiral cycle may use.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Classical waterfall is a planned sequential organization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Iterative waterfall adds feedback without defining the risk-driven cycle.

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: scope, project conditions and modeling conventions are made explicit.
assumptions: Responsibility applies to the discoverer rather than being exclusive to testers.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: The saved image confirms the options. SE24 defines an API gateway as one entry point that routes or combines service calls and hides service boundaries from clients. That directly matches the stated role. Logging records activity and a layered system describes broader organization; a generic proxy label alone does not establish the multi-service routing and composition role given in the note.

evidence.quote: An API gateway presents one entry point and routes/combines calls to services, hiding service boundaries from clients. It can centralize policies but also become a bottleneck. A component diagram shows components/interfaces/dependencies; a deployment diagram places software artifacts on nodes. Choose the style for the required interactions and qualities rather than selecting a universally best architecture.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Layering organizes abstraction levels rather than naming this single microservice-facing entry component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An API gateway hides service boundaries behind a unified entry point and routes or combines requests.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: API logging records activity rather than routing clients across hidden service boundaries.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A generic proxy forwards requests; the note names the broader multi-service entry-point role an API gateway.

reviews.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
reviews.explanation: There are three decisions: width>length and one separate height comparison inside each outer branch. Covering both inner outcomes requires two tests with outer true and two with outer false. For example (w,l,h)=(3,2,4),(3,2,1),(2,3,4),(2,3,1) covers all outcomes. One execution cannot visit both outer branches, so two or three tests cannot suffice; six are unnecessary.

evidence.quote: Statement coverage is the number of distinct executable statements exercised divided by the total executable statements in the declared test scope. Unreachable statements can prevent100%; any justified exclusions must be documented with the adjusted scope. Decision coverage counts decision outcomes; branch coverage counts control-flow edges, including unconditional edges under the stated convention. Testing both true and false of each decision may need more than two overall test cases when branches nest. Coverage is evidence of exercised structure, not proof of all behavior.

In the width/length/height bank program, the outer if has separate inner decisions in each branch. Need outer true with inner true and false, and outer false with its inner true and false: four tests, for example (w,l,h)=(3,2,4),(3,2,1),(2,3,4),(2,3,1). One run cannot exercise both outer branches. All paths may be infeasible or infinite with loops; specify the chosen coverage target.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Four tests cover true/false of the inner decision on each of the two outer branches.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Six can cover the decisions, but four suffice; it is not the required minimum.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two cover the outer decision but cannot cover both outcomes of both separate inner decisions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Three leave at least one inner decision outcome uncovered because each outer branch needs two tests.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE27 explicitly identifies Memento as storing and restoring state while hiding representation, and notes that Momento in this question bank is a spelling error for Memento. That makes C the intended pattern name. Iterator traverses a collection and Observer notifies subscribers; neither supplies the state-snapshot restoration responsibility asked for here.

evidence.quote: Factory Method lets subclasses choose a concrete product through a creation operation, reducing coupling to concrete constructors. A simple factory centralizes creation but is not identical to Factory Method. Singleton controls access to one instance; Observer notifies subscribers; Memento stores/restores state while hiding representation; Iterator traverses; Decorator adds behavior through wrapping. “Momento” in the bank means Memento.

Variability can use selectable features, omission/inclusion and extension points; overloading supplies alternate signatures in code but is not every variability mechanism. Testability improves with controllable inputs, observable outputs, replaceable dependencies and limited structural complexity. A sandbox can isolate execution. Self-referential combination choices such as “A and B” in option B cannot establish a unique correct answer.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Iterator traverses elements rather than storing a restorable snapshot of object state.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Observer notifies subscribers about changes rather than restoring an earlier object state.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Momento is the bank's misspelling of Memento, the state capture-and-restoration pattern.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Visitor is not the state-snapshot restoration pattern; the note assigns that role to Memento.

reviews.hint: Distinguish the planning or organization goal from the tool or structure used to support it. Apply the stated project conditions.
reviews.explanation: SE32 lists orientation first, then conflict, development of norms, effective performance and closure. Their stage names are forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. D preserves that order. The other alternatives either put performance before norms or move orientation after later stages, contradicting the taught sequence.

evidence.quote: Functional organizations group specialists by discipline; project organizations group people around projects. Functional specialization helps staffing and knowledge continuity but may create handoff barriers. Democratic teams share decisions; chief-programmer teams centralize technical coordination. These are different classification dimensions. Tuckman’s sequence is forming→storming→norming→performing→adjourning: orientation, conflict, norms, effective work and closure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It places performing before norming, reversing the stated development sequence.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It starts with norming before the initial forming and storming stages.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: It places storming before the initial forming stage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It matches the taught progression from orientation through conflict, norms, performance and closure.

reviews.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
reviews.explanation: Test planning specifies intended work, objectives, resources and schedule; configuration-management procedures should be defined early as part of that preparation. They then apply throughout testing to preserve reproducible builds, data and environments. Execution and closing use those procedures rather than being their exclusive establishment point. Initiation may set context, but the question specifically asks for the activity that defines them in the test plan.

evidence.quote: Configuration management identifies controlled items, versions/baselines, change procedures, status and audits. Items may include source code, requirements, manuals, test plans, environments and build configurations. A team’s ordinary browser is usually a tool rather than product CI, but a controlled test-browser version may be an environment CI.

A test plan describes intended work; incident/defect reports are normally execution outputs. A defect report should identify build/environment, steps, expected versus actual behavior, evidence and severity. Anyone finding a fault should record it; testers often coordinate reporting, but it is not their exclusive permission. Configuration control makes the tested version reproducible.
Plan test configuration management early and apply it throughout testing, not at just one exclusive phase.
Analysis asks what to test and assesses testability; design asks how.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Execution applies the planned procedures to tested versions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Test planning defines procedures with the other planned work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Closing preserves final artifacts under established control.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Initiation sets context rather than the specified test-plan definition activity.

question_revision.original_stem: As a software tester, when do you implement configuration management procedures?
question_revision.stem: During which listed activity should the test plan define configuration-management procedures alongside objectives, resources and schedule, before those procedures are applied during execution?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: scope, project conditions and modeling conventions are made explicit.
assumptions: Ask about establishing procedures in the test plan, not every phase where configuration control applies.

reviews.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
reviews.explanation: The stem explicitly defines branches as outgoing control-flow edges. SE38 identifies branch coverage as counting exercised control-flow edges under the declared convention. This differs from merely counting executed statements or evaluating decision outcomes. Branch boundary, branch control and branch expansion are not the coverage criterion described by selecting paths that exercise graph edges.

evidence.quote: Statement coverage is the number of distinct executable statements exercised divided by the total executable statements in the declared test scope. Unreachable statements can prevent100%; any justified exclusions must be documented with the adjusted scope. Decision coverage counts decision outcomes; branch coverage counts control-flow edges, including unconditional edges under the stated convention. Testing both true and false of each decision may need more than two overall test cases when branches nest. Coverage is evidence of exercised structure, not proof of all behavior.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Branch boundary is not the defined edge-coverage criterion in the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Branch coverage measures whether control-flow edges are exercised by the selected test paths.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Branch control is not the name of the specified structural coverage measure.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Branch expansion does not name the outgoing-edge coverage criterion described.

reviews.answer_text: Change request → impact analysis → release planning → implementation → release.
reviews.hint: Classify the motive for the change before its implementation: repair, environment, useful capability or reduced future risk.
reviews.explanation: SE40 gives the sequence directly. A requested change is analyzed before commitment to a release, then planned, implemented and tested, and finally released. B preserves those dependencies. The alternatives analyze consequences too late, begin analysis before a request exists, or implement before release planning. Implementation here includes the testing work omitted from the abbreviated options.

evidence.quote: A typical evolution sequence is change request→impact analysis→release planning→implementation/testing→release. Among a list lacking the request step, impact analysis may be the earliest listed technical activity. Major restructuring is reengineering; if the architecture itself changes, architectural transformation is the more specific description. Markets, technology, stakeholders and funding can all change scope or priorities.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It postpones impact analysis until after implementation, too late to guide planning and commitment.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It preserves request, analysis, planning, implementation/testing and release in the taught order.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: It begins impact analysis before identifying a change request and implements before release planning.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It places implementation before release planning instead of planning the analyzed change first.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: Pareto’s 80/20 idea is a prioritization heuristic: a relatively small set of causes may account for a large share of observed impact. It encourages examining evidence to focus improvement effort. It does not promise that exactly one fifth of the effort fixes exactly four fifths of all defects. The revised question asks for this named heuristic, so the other principle names do not identify the rule described.

evidence.quote: Pareto’s 80/20 rule is a prioritization heuristic: a small subset of causes may account for much of the observed impact. It does not guarantee 80% of defects can be fixed with exactly 20% effort. Refactor to preserve behavior while improving structure; optimize only against measured needs; record rationale and update traceability and regression evidence after change.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Pareto names the small-subset/large-impact heuristic often expressed as 80/20.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is not the name of the described 80/20 prioritization heuristic.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Partitioning does not name the described concentration-of-impact heuristic.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Parametric reasoning does not name the described concentration-of-impact heuristic.

question_revision.original_stem: Which principle states that 80% of the problems can be fixed with 20% of the entire effort?
question_revision.stem: Which named prioritization heuristic suggests that a small subset of causes may account for much of the observed impact, often summarized as 80/20?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: the comparison and stated conditions are explicit.
assumptions: Use the explicit scope and standard definitions stated in the clarified prompt.

reviews.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
reviews.explanation: Test analysis examines the test basis, identifies what can be tested and evaluates testability. Test design then specifies how to test it through cases and expected results. The analysis-and-design pair therefore covers both responsibilities. Requirements work, planning and implementation are relevant elsewhere, but do not replace case design: planning addresses resources and scope, while implementation prepares data, scripts and the environment.

evidence.quote: A test plan describes intended work; incident/defect reports are normally execution outputs. A defect report should identify build/environment, steps, expected versus actual behavior, evidence and severity. Anyone finding a fault should record it; testers often coordinate reporting, but it is not their exclusive permission. Configuration control makes the tested version reproducible.
Analysis asks what to test and assesses testability; design asks how.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Requirements work does not supply the requested case-design half.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Analysis assesses testability and design specifies cases and expected results.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Planning addresses intended work, resources and schedule rather than case design.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Implementation prepares scripts, data and environment rather than being the design half.

question_revision.original_stem: Select an activity that suits in the fundamental test process which includes evaluation of the testability of the requirements and system?
question_revision.stem: Which paired activity assesses requirements/system testability and then designs test cases and expected results?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: scope, project conditions and modeling conventions are made explicit.
assumptions: Ask for both testability assessment and case design in the offered pair.

reviews.hint: Write out the supplied quantities and dependency constraints. Compute and compare values under the stated metric, finish condition and assumptions.
reviews.explanation: SE31 distinguishes removing a risk, reducing it, transferring consequences and retaining or accepting it. It explicitly says passive acceptance may take no action. The stem describes recognizing the risk and allowing it to remain without action, so retention matches. The other responses all involve a deliberate change to the risk or its consequences.

evidence.quote: Avoidance changes the plan to remove a risk, mitigation reduces likelihood/impact, transfer assigns consequences contractually, and retention/acceptance keeps the risk; passive acceptance may take no action. Resource leveling adjusts dates to respect resource availability and can change project finish; smoothing uses available float within schedule constraints. Neither magically creates extra staff.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transfer assigns consequences contractually rather than simply keeping the risk without action.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Retention or passive acceptance keeps the risk and may involve no immediate action.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Reduction actively lowers likelihood or impact instead of merely accepting exposure.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Avoidance changes the plan to remove the risk rather than allowing it to remain.

reviews.hint: Write out the supplied quantities and dependency constraints. Compute and compare values under the stated metric, finish condition and assumptions.
reviews.explanation: SE31 defines resource leveling as adjusting dates to respect resource availability, potentially changing the project finish. That matches balancing resource demand against supply by moving starts and finishes. Smoothing instead works within available float and schedule constraints. A responsibility matrix assigns ownership, and resource grouping is not the defined date-adjustment technique.

evidence.quote: Avoidance changes the plan to remove a risk, mitigation reduces likelihood/impact, transfer assigns consequences contractually, and retention/acceptance keeps the risk; passive acceptance may take no action. Resource leveling adjusts dates to respect resource availability and can change project finish; smoothing uses available float within schedule constraints. Neither magically creates extra staff.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Smoothing uses available float while retaining schedule constraints rather than generally leveling against availability.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A responsibility assignment matrix maps work to owners rather than adjusting task dates for resource capacity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Resource leveling changes dates to balance required resources against available supply.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Resource grouping is not the defined schedule-adjustment method described by the stem.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE25 includes Single Responsibility among the SOLID principles. That principle assigns a component one well-defined responsibility. DRY limits duplicated knowledge, KISS avoids unnecessary complexity and YAGNI avoids speculative work. Those can complement focused responsibilities, but none is the named principle directly described by the question.

evidence.quote: Use abstraction and decomposition to manage complexity; preserve consistency, traceability and clear responsibilities. Top-down design refines high-level structure; bottom-up design assembles existing components. A hybrid combines both. SOLID includes Single Responsibility, Open–Closed, Liskov substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion. Depend on abstractions; add compatible extensions; avoid forcing unused operations. DRY limits duplicated knowledge, KISS avoids unnecessary complexity, and YAGNI avoids speculative work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DRY limits duplication of knowledge rather than specifically assigning one responsibility per component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SOLID includes the Single Responsibility principle that the stem describes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: KISS favors simplicity, a different design concern from the specific single-responsibility rule.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: YAGNI avoids speculative work rather than defining responsibility boundaries.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE05 presents Scrum through timeboxed Sprints, a Sprint Goal and a usable Increment, in the Agile context. Waterfall and the V-model organize planned stages and corresponding tests, while spiral is defined by risk-driven cycles. Therefore Scrum is the specifically Agile approach among the listed alternatives; iteration alone does not make every process Scrum.

evidence.quote: Scrum uses timeboxed Sprints of at most one month, with a Sprint Goal, selected work and a usable Increment meeting a Definition of Done. Scope is discussed before and during planning; it is not forbidden to agree scope. Timeboxes tend to stay fixed while content is adapted without endangering the goal. Agile can be combined with required assurance/documentation; safety-critical context alone cannot prove it is unsuitable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Classical waterfall organizes planned phases rather than the Agile Scrum approach described.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Scrum is the Agile framework using Sprints and usable Increments.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The V-model pairs development stages with test levels rather than being the listed Agile framework.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Spiral is risk driven and is not the specifically Agile methodology named among these choices.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE25 lists Dependency Inversion within SOLID and explicitly directs designs to depend on abstractions. That reduces dependence on concrete implementation details and matches the stem. DRY, KISS and YAGNI address duplication, simplicity and speculative functionality respectively; none is the principle defining the abstraction-based dependency relationship.

evidence.quote: Use abstraction and decomposition to manage complexity; preserve consistency, traceability and clear responsibilities. Top-down design refines high-level structure; bottom-up design assembles existing components. A hybrid combines both. SOLID includes Single Responsibility, Open–Closed, Liskov substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion. Depend on abstractions; add compatible extensions; avoid forcing unused operations. DRY limits duplicated knowledge, KISS avoids unnecessary complexity, and YAGNI avoids speculative work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DRY addresses duplicated knowledge rather than the direction and target of dependencies.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SOLID includes Dependency Inversion, which directs dependencies toward abstractions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: KISS addresses unnecessary complexity rather than specifying abstraction-based dependencies.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: YAGNI limits speculative work rather than defining dependency direction.

reviews.hint: Distinguish the planning or organization goal from the tool or structure used to support it. Apply the stated project conditions.
reviews.explanation: SE28 distinguishes version tracking, issue tracking, automated checks and container packaging. It names Jira as an issue tracker for work and defects, matching bugs and tasks across development. Git records versions, Jenkins automates checks and Docker packages runtime dependencies; those tools may integrate with issue tracking but have different primary roles.

evidence.quote: Function points estimate functional size using inputs, outputs, inquiries, internal logical files and external interface files, weighted under the chosen method. They are not just lines of code and are not a direct exact measure of complexity. Git tracks versions; issue trackers such as Jira track work/defects; CI tools such as Jenkins automate checks; Docker packages application/runtime dependencies into containers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Git tracks source versions and history rather than serving as the named issue/task tracker.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Jira tracks work items, defects and tasks through their development workflow.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Jenkins automates checks and integration work rather than primarily managing issue records.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Docker packages runtime dependencies into containers rather than tracking bugs and tasks.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE25 lists Open–Closed within SOLID and recommends adding compatible extensions. The stem quotes that principle's central idea: support extension while keeping established code stable. DRY, KISS and YAGNI address other concerns. Open–Closed is a design goal achieved through suitable abstractions, rather than a claim that software can never need modification.

evidence.quote: Use abstraction and decomposition to manage complexity; preserve consistency, traceability and clear responsibilities. Top-down design refines high-level structure; bottom-up design assembles existing components. A hybrid combines both. SOLID includes Single Responsibility, Open–Closed, Liskov substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion. Depend on abstractions; add compatible extensions; avoid forcing unused operations. DRY limits duplicated knowledge, KISS avoids unnecessary complexity, and YAGNI avoids speculative work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DRY limits duplicated knowledge rather than defining openness for extension.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SOLID includes the Open–Closed principle explicitly described by the stem.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: KISS favors simple solutions rather than the specific extension-versus-modification relationship.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: YAGNI avoids speculative functionality rather than defining the Open–Closed design goal.

reviews.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
reviews.explanation: SE36 defines regression testing by the purpose of detecting unintended effects after change. That includes retesting changed and affected areas to find newly introduced faults. Unit, integration and system testing describe levels or scope; regression tests can be run at any of them, so the change-driven purpose uniquely identifies C.

evidence.quote: Black-box techniques derive cases from specified behavior; white-box techniques derive them from internal structure; grey-box uses partial internal knowledge. Regression testing checks for unintended effects after change; confirmation testing checks the particular defect repair. Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution and is experience based. Manual/automated describe execution support, not a compulsory black-/white-box classification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unit testing defines a small-component scope rather than the purpose of checking change-induced defects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Integration testing focuses on interfaces and interactions, which may be regression-tested but do not define regression.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Regression testing retests previously working behavior to detect unintended effects of modifications.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: System testing addresses the complete integrated system rather than specifically the after-change purpose.

reviews.hint: Distinguish the planning or organization goal from the tool or structure used to support it. Apply the stated project conditions.
reviews.explanation: SE28 explicitly says Docker packages an application and its runtime dependencies into containers. That matches the deployment packaging task in the question. Git tracks versions, Jira tracks issues and Jenkins automates checks; they can participate in a deployment pipeline, but none replaces Docker's specified container packaging responsibility.

evidence.quote: Function points estimate functional size using inputs, outputs, inquiries, internal logical files and external interface files, weighted under the chosen method. They are not just lines of code and are not a direct exact measure of complexity. Git tracks versions; issue trackers such as Jira track work/defects; CI tools such as Jenkins automate checks; Docker packages application/runtime dependencies into containers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Git manages version history rather than packaging the runtime into a container.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Jira manages work and defects rather than building application containers.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Jenkins automates checks and pipelines but is not the named container-packaging tool.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Docker packages the application and runtime dependencies into a deployable container.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE25 identifies Single Responsibility among the core design principles. The question asks directly for one responsibility per component, so D is the exact named rule. Encapsulation protects internal decisions, inheritance creates subtype relations, and polymorphism supports varying implementations through a common interface. Those can help a design but do not themselves define a single responsibility.

evidence.quote: SOLID includes Single Responsibility, Open–Closed, Liskov substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion.

Generalization places common concepts in a more general superclass and specialized concepts in subclasses. Available inherited attributes and operations are shared by subclasses, which may extend or override behavior.

Encapsulation groups state with operations and hides representation behind an interface. Polymorphism permits different object types to respond differently through a common operation or interface. Abstraction exposes the relevant contract while omitting unnecessary detail. Reusability means using suitable existing classes or components in new contexts rather than writing them again. These ideas support each other but name different properties.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encapsulation hides implementation details rather than requiring one responsibility per component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Inheritance establishes superclass/subclass reuse rather than the focused-responsibility rule.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Polymorphism supports compatible varying implementations rather than defining responsibility count.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Single Responsibility explicitly calls for one focused responsibility in a software component.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE27 describes Singleton as controlling access to one instance. That is the pattern requested by the one-instance condition. Factory patterns address how concrete objects are created, Observer notifies subscribers and Decorator adds behavior by wrapping. None of those other pattern responsibilities guarantees a single shared instance by itself.

evidence.quote: Factory Method lets subclasses choose a concrete product through a creation operation, reducing coupling to concrete constructors. A simple factory centralizes creation but is not identical to Factory Method. Singleton controls access to one instance; Observer notifies subscribers; Memento stores/restores state while hiding representation; Iterator traverses; Decorator adds behavior through wrapping. “Momento” in the bank means Memento.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Singleton controls creation and access so that the intended class has one shared instance.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A factory selects or constructs products rather than inherently limiting a class to one instance.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Observer distributes notifications to subscribers rather than restricting object instance count.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Decorator adds behavior through wrapping rather than enforcing a single instance.

reviews.answer_text: Functional programming, for the side-effect emphasis.
reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: The phrase promotes the use of data is not distinctive because all these paradigms use data. The discriminating part is avoiding or controlling side effects. SE01 explicitly assigns function evaluation and controlled side effects to functional programming. Procedural, object-oriented and event-driven styles organize behavior differently and do not inherently impose that emphasis.

evidence.quote: Procedural decomposition organizes functions; object oriented decomposition organizes objects with state and behavior. Either can use iterative or sequential development. OOP does not automatically shorten every project. Reuse, encapsulation and consistent models can reduce duplication and ease change; poor object design can still be complex. Functional programming emphasizes function evaluation and controlled side effects; event-driven programs react to events.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Functional programming emphasizes evaluating functions and controlling side effects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Procedural decomposition organizes functions or procedures without inherently avoiding state-changing effects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Object-oriented decomposition combines state and behavior and does not inherently exclude side effects.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Event-driven programs react to events; that does not itself require avoiding side effects.

reviews.hint: Classify the motive for the change before its implementation: repair, environment, useful capability or reduced future risk.
reviews.explanation: SE40 defines adaptive maintenance as responding to changes in the environment. New platforms or technologies therefore create an adaptive-maintenance need even when the original software is not faulty. Corrective maintenance fixes faults, perfective work improves useful capability or performance, and preventive work reduces future risk. The stated environmental motive makes B the appropriate category.

evidence.quote: Corrective maintenance fixes faults; adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes; perfective maintenance improves useful capability/performance; preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as restructuring fragile code. Motive determines category; refactoring can support preventive or perfective work. Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Corrective work fixes faults rather than primarily accommodating changed environments or technology.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Adaptive maintenance changes software so it continues working in a new environment or technology context.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Perfective work improves capability or performance rather than specifically responding to an environmental change.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Preventive work reduces future maintenance risk rather than defining adaptation to a new environment.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.

It therefore represents optional additional behavior and extends the base with added steps, making both B and C true. Factoring required reused behavior is the include relationship. Associations between actors and use cases are separate from the extend relationship linking use cases to one another.

reviews.answer_text: To represent an error or exceptional situation in the use case
reviews.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.
reviews.explanation: An exception flow handles an error or failure encountered in the use case. Such a path is also an alternative to the main success flow in a broad sense, but B alone does not distinguish exceptional handling from normal conditional variations. An exception may allow correction and recovery instead of terminating the use case. Actor relationships do not define its failure-handling purpose.

evidence.quote: Example: Submit Incident. Precondition: officer authenticated. 1 Officer supplies location and description. 2 System validates details. 3 System records the incident. 4 System returns its ID. Alternative 2a: location missing → report the problem and request correction; save nothing. Success postcondition: incident and ID persist; failure guarantee: no partial record. An alternate flow is a conditional variation; an exception flow handles a failure. Preconditions hold before entry, while a trigger starts the use case.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Error or exceptional handling is the specific defining purpose.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Alternative path is broader and does not identify the exceptional nature.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Exceptions need not terminate the entire use case.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Actor relationships do not describe failure handling.

reviews.answer_text: Engine is part of Car and cannot exist independently under the stated lifetime policy.

Since this model does not permit Engine to detach or transfer, it cannot continue an independent lifetime without Car. Parts may be detached/transferred under a defined model. Thus “cannot ever exist independently” is an oversimplification. For Car composing Engine, the diamond belongs beside Car; saying it points to Engine is imprecise. The intended bank relationship is composition.

reviews.answer_text: Poor suitability when requirements have substantial change risk.
reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE03 says waterfall fits stable understood requirements and familiar technology. Late feedback can make changes costly, so moderate-to-high requirement-change risk is a direct disadvantage. Simplicity and milestone visibility are advantages. Sequential phase organization characterizes the classical model; it can contribute to rigidity, but C explicitly identifies the adverse scenario asked for.

evidence.quote: Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Simplicity and ease of understanding are presented as advantages rather than the adverse scenario.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Manageable milestones can be an advantage of planned rigidity, despite its trade-offs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Likely requirement changes make late feedback and rigid commitments costly.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sequential phases describe the model; C more directly states the requested disadvantage.

reviews.answer_text: The system respond to user’s request within 2 second under normal load
reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: The two-second response obligation bounds the speed of a service under the stated load, so it is a performance requirement. Generating a PDF and submitting an emergency report describe services the system provides. The database clause describes storage behavior together with an implementation choice; it does not impose a response-time threshold. The explicit performance scope removes the broader taxonomy overlap between nonfunctional requirements and technology constraints.

evidence.quote: Nonfunctional requirements include quality attributes and constraints. Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use; reliability concerns failure-free service; availability concerns being ready for use; usability concerns task success and ease of learning. Security concerns protection; compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments; maintainability/supportability concern change, diagnosis and evolution.

“Search responds within two seconds under 100 concurrent users” is measurable performance. “New users finish checkout within one minute without help” is usability. “Use Java” is a technology/pseudo-requirement, often separately classified as a system constraint. Dependability includes reliability, safety and robustness; portability is not its usual central category. Performance degradation at peak load primarily concerns performance, not automatically reliability.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Report generation specifies a service, not its response-time limit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A two-second response bound under normal load is a quantitative speed target.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This specifies storage behavior and a database technology, without a timing bound.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Submitting an emergency report specifies a function rather than its speed.

reviews.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.
reviews.explanation: SE17 explicitly describes structural things as conceptual or physical structural elements. They make up the static model in contrast with behavior over time. Behavioral things cover dynamic aspects, grouping organizes elements and annotations add explanatory information rather than being the static elements themselves. Thus A directly matches both parts of the definition.

evidence.quote: A class box lists name, attributes and operations; + public, - private, # protected and ~ package indicate visibility. A class diagram shows static types and relationships, while an object diagram shows particular instances/links. UML is maintained and standardized by OMG; it is a modeling language, not a lifecycle process. Structural things describe conceptual or physical structural elements.

In the course’s UML building-block terminology, structural things describe static conceptual or physical elements. Behavioral things describe dynamic interactions and state behavior. Grouping things organize model elements into packages. Annotational things attach explanatory remarks or constraints, usually as notes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Structural things are the static conceptual or physical building blocks described.

choices.label: B
