reviews.answer_text: Functional requirements specify observable behavior; nonfunctional requirements specify qualities or constraints. Example: generate a PDF report versus respond within two seconds under a stated load.
reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE09 includes required and prohibited services, so generating a PDF report is functional. SE10 specifies qualities such as performance, usability and availability; a response-time threshold under defined load is nonfunctional. Security mechanisms can implement functional behavior as well as support quality goals, so a negative or security-related statement is not automatically nonfunctional.

evidence.quote: A functional requirement states an observable service or behavior, including reactions to inputs, errors and forbidden actions. “When the sensor detects intrusion, send an alert” is functional.

“The system shall generate a PDF report” is functional. “The system shall not reveal another customer’s balance” can be a security-related functional rule. Security as a broad quality goal and the functions implementing it must be distinguished.

Nonfunctional requirements include quality attributes and constraints. Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use; reliability concerns failure-free service; availability concerns being ready for use; usability concerns task success and ease of learning.
“Search responds within two seconds under 100 concurrent users” is measurable performance. “New users finish checkout within one minute without help” is usability.

reviews.answer_text: Low coupling limits dependencies, so changes remain local and modules are easier to understand, replace, test and maintain.
reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: SE22 measures coupling through dependencies between modules and recommends low coupling with high cohesion. Shared mutable data and knowledge of another module’s representation increase the chance that one change affects others. Stable interfaces and information hiding constrain that impact. More interfaces can add complexity, so minimizing harmful dependencies matters more than simply maximizing the number of modules.

evidence.quote: Cohesion measures how well elements inside a module serve a related purpose; coupling measures dependency between modules. Seek high cohesion and low coupling. Shared mutable data and knowledge of another module’s internal representation increase coupling. Information hiding exposes stable operations while concealing changeable decisions.

reviews.answer_text: Waterfall uses planned, reviewed stages and suits stable requirements; Agile emphasizes collaboration, working results, feedback and adaptation.
reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE03 describes planned phases with costly late feedback, useful for stable requirements and familiar technology. SE05 values customer participation and adaptation with useful working increments. Agile still plans and documents; waterfall can revisit work under control. The practical difference is feedback and commitment organization, not a claim that one process forbids change or the other forbids documentation.

evidence.quote: Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.

Agile favors people collaborating, useful working results, customer participation and adaptation over rigid adherence to procedures, exhaustive documents, contracts or fixed plans. The latter still have value. Agile does not mean no planning or no documentation. A user story states a small user need and value, supported by acceptance criteria; an epic groups broader work.

reviews.answer_text: Include factors required reused behavior, with base→included; extend adds conditional behavior, with extension→base.
reviews.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.
reviews.explanation: SE16 uses include for reused required behavior incorporated when the inclusion point is reached. Extend adds behavior at extension points under a condition, and the base remains meaningful independently. The dashed arrows have different directions: including use case toward included, and extending use case toward base. Neither relation should be confused with actor association or specialization generalization.

evidence.quote: Include factors required reused behavior: Submit Order includes Validate Order, with the dashed arrow from the including/base use case to the included one. Extend adds conditional behavior at extension points: Apply Discount extends Checkout, with the arrow from the extension to the base. The base is meaningful independently. The short note’s receipt example reverses this direction if it says Withdrawal extends Print Receipt.

Generalization relates a specialized actor/use case to a more general one, with a hollow triangle toward the general element. An abstract use case specifies behavior for specialization and is not directly instantiated as a complete use case. It is not defined merely by reuse or lack of a direct actor line. Included behavior is incorporated where the inclusion is reached; do not infer every conditional branch in the base always executes.

reviews.answer_text: Maintenance can dominate cost because it lasts years and repeatedly requires legacy understanding, changes, regression testing and release work.
reviews.hint: Classify the motive for the change before its implementation: repair, environment, useful capability or reduced future risk.
reviews.explanation: SE40 says maintenance often spans years and includes understanding existing code plus regression effort. Work is not limited to bug fixes: environments, useful capabilities and future risks also change. Repeated impact analysis, implementation and testing accumulate across the operational lifetime, so maintenance may dominate lifecycle cost. This is a common outcome, not a guarantee for every project.

evidence.quote: Corrective maintenance fixes faults; adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes; perfective maintenance improves useful capability/performance; preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as restructuring fragile code. Motive determines category; refactoring can support preventive or perfective work. Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost.

A typical evolution sequence is change request→impact analysis→release planning→implementation/testing→release. Among a list lacking the request step, impact analysis may be the earliest listed technical activity. Major restructuring is reengineering; if the architecture itself changes, architectural transformation is the more specific description. Markets, technology, stakeholders and funding can all change scope or priorities.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE01 contrasts procedural decomposition organized around functions with object-oriented decomposition organized around objects combining state and behavior. B is the available traditional/procedural label for functions operating on data. Agile and iterative describe lifecycle organization rather than this decomposition paradigm, and either can be used with procedural or object-oriented programming.

evidence.quote: Procedural decomposition organizes functions; object oriented decomposition organizes objects with state and behavior. Either can use iterative or sequential development. OOP does not automatically shorten every project. Reuse, encapsulation and consistent models can reduce duplication and ease change; poor object design can still be complex. Functional programming emphasizes function evaluation and controlled side effects; event-driven programs react to events.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Object orientation combines state and behavior in objects rather than organizing primarily around separate procedures.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Traditional/procedural decomposition organizes functions and procedures acting on data.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Agile concerns process adaptation rather than requiring function-based decomposition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Iteration describes revisiting development work and does not determine procedural versus object decomposition.

reviews.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
reviews.explanation: The stem explicitly asks about using existing classes elsewhere without rewriting them, which is reuse. SE01 lists reuse alongside encapsulation and consistent models as ways to reduce duplication and ease change. Encapsulation and abstraction can make reuse safer, while polymorphism supports compatible varying implementations, but those are enabling concepts rather than the name of the capability described.

evidence.quote: Encapsulation groups state with operations and hides representation behind an interface. Polymorphism permits different object types to respond differently through a common operation or interface. Abstraction exposes the relevant contract while omitting unnecessary detail. Reusability means using suitable existing classes or components in new contexts rather than writing them again. These ideas support each other but name different properties.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encapsulation hides implementation and can enable reuse, but it is not the capability's name.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Polymorphism supports differing implementations through compatible interfaces rather than directly naming reuse.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Reusability means using suitable existing classes or components in other contexts without rewriting them.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Abstraction exposes relevant contracts and can assist reuse, but the requested property is reusability.

reviews.hint: Classify the motive for the change before its implementation: repair, environment, useful capability or reduced future risk.
reviews.explanation: SE40 describes maintenance and evolution through change requests, impact analysis, planning, implementation/testing and release. Updating a deployed product to meet changing customer needs belongs to evolution among the four broad process activities. Specification, implementation and validation still occur within that work, but D names the lifecycle-wide change activity asked for rather than one constituent task.

evidence.quote: Corrective maintenance fixes faults; adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes; perfective maintenance improves useful capability/performance; preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as restructuring fragile code. Motive determines category; refactoring can support preventive or perfective work. Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost.
A typical evolution sequence is change request→impact analysis→release planning→implementation/testing→release.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Specification captures needs but does not name the overall postdeployment change activity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Design/implementation is part of making a change rather than the broad evolution activity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Validation checks the changed product against needs rather than naming ongoing adaptation itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Evolution updates existing software as stakeholder needs and operating conditions change.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: The stem defines up-front planning and measurement against that plan. B names the plan-driven organization, illustrated by SE03’s planned phases and reviewed deliverables. Incremental delivery and evolution describe how results grow or change and can coexist with planning. Agile also plans, but it emphasizes adaptation rather than defining all activity commitments in advance as stated here.

evidence.quote: In a plan-driven process, activities are planned in advance and progress is assessed against that plan. Agile planning is incremental and adapts to changing needs. This distinction concerns planning strategy; a process can combine advance planning with staged deliveries and feedback.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Agile uses planning but adapts content as feedback arrives rather than defining this fixed up-front emphasis.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Plan-driven explicitly organizes activities and progress measurement around an advance plan.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incremental describes staged capability delivery and does not alone specify up-front planning commitments.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Evolutionary describes progressive change rather than necessarily advance planning of all activities.

reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE08 states that the Software Requirements Specification organizes agreed requirements. That is the artifact describing what the system should do for client/developer agreement. Analysis models support technical discussion, a use-case diagram captures only selected goals/relationships and a design document describes solution decisions. None replaces the overall agreed requirements specification.

evidence.quote: Business requirements explain why the project exists and its goals. User requirements describe stakeholder needs at a useful high level; system requirements specify detailed services and constraints. The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) organizes the agreed requirements. In the module, a natural-language specification communicates with clients while analysis models formalize it for technical discussion; real specifications can also contain diagrams.

choices.explanation: Analysis models formalize selected aspects for discussion rather than replacing the full agreed requirements document.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A use-case diagram shows goals and roles but not the complete requirements specification.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The requirements specification organizes the agreed services and constraints the system must satisfy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A design document describes how the solution is organized rather than the complete statement of required behavior.

reviews.answer_text: In the taught convention, natural-language client specification versus symbolic/diagrammatic analysis models.
reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE08 explicitly describes natural-language specification for clients and analysis models that formalize it for technical discussion. B matches that teaching convention. This is not a universal ban on diagrams in an SRS: the note immediately allows them in real specifications. The other choices reverse the convention or impose unsupported exclusive audiences and purposes.

evidence.quote: Business requirements explain why the project exists and its goals. The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) organizes the agreed requirements. In the module, a natural-language specification communicates with clients while analysis models formalize it for technical discussion; real specifications can also contain diagrams.

reviews.answer_text: External interacting roles played by people, devices or other systems.

Actors are not restricted to primary users or humans, and internal components are inside the chosen system boundary rather than external roles. One person may play several actors, so actor instances should not be confused with individual people.

Being an internal component is different from being an external actor; the chosen boundary determines which role applies.
An actor is an external role interacting with the system; it can be a person, device or another system.

A one-second threshold constrains how well a service responds rather than naming the service itself, so C is the appropriate category. A complete measurable requirement should also define the operation, load and timing conditions. evidence.quote: Nonfunctional requirements include quality attributes and constraints. Security concerns protection; compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments; maintainability/supportability concern change, diagnosis and evolution.

reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: The statement prescribes an implementation technology rather than an externally observable service or a measurable product quality. In the course’s explicit separation of quality attributes from technology constraints, the specific category is a system or constraint requirement. A broad requirements taxonomy can place constraints under nonfunctional requirements, but the question asks for the more specific category. No performance, reliability or usability threshold is supplied by merely naming Java.

evidence.quote: “Search responds within two seconds under 100 concurrent users” is measurable performance. “New users finish checkout within one minute without help” is usability. “Use Java” is a technology/pseudo-requirement, often separately classified as a system constraint. Dependability includes reliability, safety and robustness; portability is not its usual central category. Performance degradation at peak load primarily concerns performance, not automatically reliability.

question_revision.original_stem: A constraint that states 'the system must be built using Java' is best classified as:
question_revision.stem: When technology constraints are separated from quality attributes, what is the most specific category for “the system must be built using Java”?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: the intended comparison and scope are explicit.
assumptions: Use the explicit scope and standard definitions stated in the clarified prompt.

reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE10 distinguishes compatibility, which concerns cooperating environments, from portability, which concerns moving environments. Supporting different browsers and devices in the question is the offered compatibility category. Reliability concerns failure-free service, scalability concerns growth and usability concerns task success/ease of learning. None of those names the stated cross-environment cooperation requirement as directly.

evidence.quote: Nonfunctional requirements include quality attributes and constraints. Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use; reliability concerns failure-free service; availability concerns being ready for use; usability concerns task success and ease of learning. Security concerns protection; compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments; maintainability/supportability concern change, diagnosis and evolution.

Scalability is the ability to accommodate additional workload while maintaining the required service, often by increasing available resources. It concerns growth in demand. Compatibility concerns supported cooperating environments, such as browsers and devices; usability concerns successful and learnable user tasks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reliability concerns failure-free service rather than which browsers and devices can cooperate with the system.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Scalability concerns handling increased workload rather than cross-browser/device compatibility.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Usability concerns ease of learning and successful tasks, not the supported environment set itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Compatibility addresses operating/cooperating across the specified browsers and device environments.

reviews.answer_text: Portability is the exception to the usual central dependability categories.
reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE10 explicitly includes reliability, safety and robustness in dependability and says portability is not its usual central category. Portability instead concerns moving environments. Thus D is the listed exception. The distinction does not imply portability never affects practical service outcomes, only that it is a different quality category from the taught dependability grouping.

evidence.quote: Dependability includes reliability, safety and robustness; portability is not its usual central category.
Security concerns protection; compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments; maintainability/supportability concern change, diagnosis and evolution.
Robustness concerns reliable operation across varied or difficult operating conditions and controlled failure outside the supported range.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reliability is explicitly included in the taught dependability grouping.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Robustness is explicitly included in the broader dependability concept.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Safety is explicitly included among dependability concerns.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Portability concerns moving environments rather than the usual central dependability categories.

reviews.answer_text: Identifying use cases by abstracting concrete scenarios.
reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE13 calls a scenario one concrete execution and a use case an abstraction of related success and alternative scenarios. Formalizing those interactions into the more general use-case description therefore identifies use cases. Identifying actors establishes external roles, identifying scenarios captures individual executions and later refinement adds detail to an already identified use case.

evidence.quote: A scenario is one concrete execution; a use case abstracts the related successful and alternative scenarios. Analysis integrates functional (use cases/scenarios), structural/object (classes) and dynamic (states/interactions) models. Entity objects represent domain information such as Incident; boundary objects mediate interaction, such as ReportForm; control objects coordinate a use case. A UI form is normally boundary, not entity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Actor identification establishes external roles rather than generalizing scenario executions into interaction descriptions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Use cases abstract related concrete scenarios into structured goal-oriented interaction descriptions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Scenario identification captures concrete executions rather than their use-case abstraction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Refinement elaborates an existing use case; the scenario-to-use-case abstraction is the identification step asked here.

reviews.answer_text: Document exceptions separately from the main success flow.
reviews.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.
reviews.explanation: SE15 instructs writers to use active subject–verb steps and separate errors from normal flow. C follows that rule directly. Passive voice hides responsibility, detailed UI design distracts from goal-level behavior, and combining unrelated tasks does not produce a clear use case. The distinction concerns organizing scenarios rather than omitting exception handling.

evidence.quote: Example: Submit Incident. Precondition: officer authenticated. 1 Officer supplies location and description. 2 System validates details. 3 System records the incident. 4 System returns its ID. Alternative 2a: location missing → report the problem and request correction; save nothing. Success postcondition: incident and ID persist; failure guarantee: no partial record. An alternate flow is a conditional variation; an exception flow handles a failure. Preconditions hold before entry, while a trigger starts the use case.
Use active subject–verb steps at one abstraction level; separate errors from the normal flow.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Passive voice makes responsibility less clear, contrary to the active subject–verb guideline.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Detailed UI elements are not the goal-level behavior and flow structure emphasized by the guide.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Separating exception behavior keeps the main success flow clear while still documenting failures.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Combining multiple unrelated tasks sacrifices a coherent goal and consistent abstraction level.

reviews.answer_text: Technical risks and constraints are not one of the three initial FAST lists.
reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE12 explicitly lists environment elements, outputs and inputs as the initial participant categories. A, B and D match them. Technical risks and constraints can matter elsewhere in engineering, but they are not one of those three named initial FAST lists. The negative question asks about that procedure, not whether risk information is ever useful.

evidence.quote: In the taught FAST technique, participants list environment elements, outputs and inputs, consolidate lists and develop smaller specifications. QFD prioritizes customer value: normal needs are explicitly stated, expected needs are assumed, and exciting needs provide unanticipated benefit. Brainstorm first to generate ideas, then evaluate and prioritize; do not confuse that with letting every idea become a committed requirement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Environment elements are explicitly one of the initial FAST categories.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: System outputs are explicitly included in the three initial lists.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Risks and constraints are not one of the specified environment/output/input categories.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inputs and things the system uses are part of the stated initial categories.

reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE12 distinguishes explicitly stated normal needs, assumed expected needs and exciting needs that bring unanticipated benefit. Features exceeding expectations and producing additional satisfaction match the exciting category. Calling them merely implicit would confuse customer assumptions with unexpected added value rather than identify the QFD term.

evidence.quote: In the taught FAST technique, participants list environment elements, outputs and inputs, consolidate lists and develop smaller specifications. QFD prioritizes customer value: normal needs are explicitly stated, expected needs are assumed, and exciting needs provide unanticipated benefit. Brainstorm first to generate ideas, then evaluate and prioritize; do not confuse that with letting every idea become a committed requirement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Normal requirements are explicitly stated needs rather than unexpected extra benefits.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Expected requirements are assumed by customers and do not denote surprising added satisfaction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Exciting requirements deliver unanticipated benefit beyond the customer’s expectations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Implicit describes assumed needs more generally, not the QFD category for unanticipated benefits.

reviews.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.
reviews.explanation: SE11 directly defines consistency as excluding contradictions. Completeness covers agreed scope, clarity gives one intended interpretation, and correctness reflects stakeholder needs. A specification can be complete yet inconsistent, or clear yet wrong, so these properties cannot substitute for the precise no-contradictions condition.

evidence.quote: Correct requirements reflect actual stakeholder needs. Complete requirements address the agreed scope, normal and exceptional behavior. Consistency excludes contradictions. Clarity/unambiguity gives one intended interpretation; feasibility/realism means achievable within constraints. Verifiability means objective evidence can check fulfillment. Replace “fast for most users” with a defined metric, workload and threshold.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Completeness concerns covering scope and behavior, not whether requirements contradict each other.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistency requires the specification’s statements to coexist without contradiction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Clarity addresses interpretive ambiguity rather than logical compatibility between requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Correctness concerns actual stakeholder needs, a different validation property.

reviews.answer_text: Stable requirements and familiar, stable technology.
reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE03 says classical waterfall fits well-understood stable requirements and familiar technology, directly supporting C among these alternatives. Frequent change, evolving needs and early small deliveries call for feedback or incremental capability rather than waterfall’s late feedback. Short duration alone is not a proof, but C also supplies the decisive stability conditions stated in the note.

evidence.quote: Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Frequent requirement changes make late-feedback sequential planning a poor fit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Large evolving needs do not establish the stable requirements that favor classical waterfall.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Constant requirements and stable technology match the note’s stated waterfall selection conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Prioritized usable small deliveries are the rationale for incremental delivery rather than a single sequential release.

reviews.answer_text: Late feedback can make requirement changes costly through rework of earlier phase deliverables.
reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: Classical waterfall separates planned phases and may receive important feedback late. Correcting earlier assumptions can then require costly rework across completed deliverables, which is its characteristic drawback here. Changes are still possible under control. Skilled developers are needed across approaches, and waterfall provides milestone visibility and documentation, so the other alternatives do not identify the stated comparative disadvantage.

evidence.quote: Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Skill requirements are not unique to waterfall.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Late feedback can make requirement changes costly after earlier phases.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Waterfall provides clear reviewed milestones.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Waterfall supports planned documentation.

reviews.answer_text: Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality.
reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: Iteration revisits and improves a solution, while an increment adds usable functionality. A process can refine existing capability and add new capability in the same cycle, so the concepts are compatible but not identical. Neither requires rebuilding the entire system or making every increment completely independent. Risk analysis is a separate concern rather than the structural distinction defining these two terms.

evidence.quote: Choose incremental delivery when prioritized partial capability must reach users early. Smaller changes can be easier to debug and permit feedback, though architecture and integration still require planning. Iteration need not rebuild the whole system every time, and increments need not be perfectly independent modules. Broad descriptions of early working software can fit prototypes, iterative or Agile processes; identify the purpose of that early version.
Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality. A process may do both.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Iteration refines; increments add usable capability.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The terms differ even when combined in one process.

choices.label: D

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: The stated emphasis is iterative: revisiting and improving an existing solution in response to feedback. Incremental development names the addition of usable functionality, which is not the primary goal specified, although both can coexist. Classical waterfall’s stable staged planning and the V-model’s paired assurance structure do not directly name this refinement emphasis. Large size and anticipated change alone would not have selected a unique model.

evidence.quote: Choose incremental delivery when prioritized partial capability must reach users early. Smaller changes can be easier to debug and permit feedback, though architecture and integration still require planning. Iteration need not rebuild the whole system every time, and increments need not be perfectly independent modules. Broad descriptions of early working software can fit prototypes, iterative or Agile processes; identify the purpose of that early version.

A common lifecycle names requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance. Analysis clarifies the problem; system design chooses architecture; object/detail design specifies interfaces and algorithms; implementation writes code; testing evaluates behavior; deployment puts it into service. These activities may overlap and repeat.
Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality. A process may do both.

question_revision.original_stem: Which SDLC model is MOST suitable when 'the software application is large and changes are expected in the future'?
question_revision.stem: A large application already has its core capabilities. The main development goal is to revisit and improve that existing solution repeatedly as feedback and future changes arrive, rather than primarily add new capability in each delivery. Which concept most directly names that emphasis?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: scope, project conditions and modeling conventions are made explicit.
assumptions: Specify refinement of existing capability as the primary goal.
The question names an emphasis; a real process may also use increments.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE05 defines a user story as a small user need and value supported by acceptance criteria. Sprints and iterations name cycles or timeboxes, not the need itself. An epic groups broader work. C therefore names the small functional work unit intended here, without claiming that Agile requirements consist only of story text.

evidence.quote: Scrum uses timeboxed Sprints of at most one month, with a Sprint Goal, selected work and a usable Increment meeting a Definition of Done. Scope is discussed before and during planning; it is not forbidden to agree scope. Timeboxes tend to stay fixed while content is adapted without endangering the goal. Agile can be combined with required assurance/documentation; safety-critical context alone cannot prove it is unsuitable.
A user story states a small user need and value, supported by acceptance criteria; an epic groups broader work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A Sprint is a timeboxed development interval rather than the individual user need.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An iteration is a cycle of work or refinement, not a small functional requirement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A user story states a small user need and its value with acceptance criteria.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An epic groups broader work rather than naming the smaller story-sized need.

reviews.answer_text: Risk analysis and reduction in every spiral cycle.
reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE06 defines spiral development as risk driven, with each cycle identifying objectives and alternatives, assessing and reducing risks, producing a result and planning commitment. That emphasis distinguishes it from merely repeating phases or delivering only at the end. It can adapt requirements and combine other activities rather than enforcing an unchangeable initial specification.

evidence.quote: Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment. A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment. The amount and type of work depend on the risks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A spiral can contain staged work, but sequential completion is not its defining driver.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Risk assessment and reduction guide each cycle’s work and further commitment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Only delivering at the end is not the distinguishing spiral principle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A risk-driven cycle can revise plans and requirements rather than rigidly freeze them.

reviews.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
reviews.explanation: SE03 explicitly places coding at the bottom of the V while specification and design stages correspond to later testing levels. Requirements therefore begin the development side rather than occupy the bottom; deployment and maintenance are not that connecting implementation activity. This is a model-diagram convention, not a claim that all real work follows a perfect geometric sequence.

evidence.quote: The V-model pairs specification/design stages with later test levels. Requirements inform acceptance tests; system design informs system tests; component/detail design informs integration/unit tests. Coding lies at the bottom. Test planning starts early. Stable requirements and strong assurance may favor this organization, but neither a V shape nor waterfall guarantees safety or correctness.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Requirements occur on the specification side, not at the coding bottom of the V.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Deployment is not the implementation activity joining the V-model’s sides.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly identifies coding as the bottom of the V.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Maintenance occurs in lifecycle evolution rather than at this implementation point.

reviews.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.
reviews.explanation: The note identifies the Object Management Group as UML’s standardizing and maintaining organization. UML is a modeling language rather than a software lifecycle process. This stewardship question does not claim that the organization originally invented every contributing notation. IEEE, ISO and W3C are not the organization to which the supplied note attributes this particular standardization and maintenance role.

evidence.quote: A class box lists name, attributes and operations; + public, - private, # protected and ~ package indicate visibility. A class diagram shows static types and relationships, while an object diagram shows particular instances/links. UML is maintained and standardized by OMG; it is a modeling language, not a lifecycle process. Structural things describe conceptual or physical structural elements.

A context may be communicated by the diagram, but it is not the specific box name requested; packages and modules serve different grouping roles rather than defining this external actor boundary.

evidence.quote: Draw actors outside the system boundary rectangle and use-case ovals inside. Name a goal with a verb and noun. The diagram shows roles, goals and relationships, not the full detailed algorithm or UI layout. Being an internal component is different from being an external actor; the chosen boundary determines which role applies.

choices.label: B

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: The included behavior is required whenever execution reaches the inclusion point.
reviews.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.
reviews.explanation: Include factors required reused behavior into another use case. When the base reaches the inclusion point, the included behavior is incorporated and performed as specified. This does not imply that every possible conditional branch of the base reaches that point. Optional conditional additions correspond to extend, specialization to generalization, and timing constraints are separate from the inclusion relationship.

evidence.quote: Generalization relates a specialized actor/use case to a more general one, with a hollow triangle toward the general element. An abstract use case specifies behavior for specialization and is not directly instantiated as a complete use case. It is not defined merely by reuse or lack of a direct actor line. Included behavior is incorporated where the inclusion is reached; do not infer every conditional branch in the base always executes.
Include factors required reused behavior: Submit Order includes Validate Order, with the dashed arrow from the including/base use case to the included one.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Conditional optional added behavior describes extend.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The included behavior is required when its inclusion point is reached.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Specialization is generalization rather than include.

choices.label: D

reviews.explanation: SE18 defines shared aggregation with a hollow diamond at the whole end. Composition instead uses a filled diamond; dependency is a dashed arrow and generalization uses a hollow triangle. The question’s whole-end description is consistent with the notation, so the hollow shape uniquely identifies aggregation among these alternatives.

evidence.quote: Composition uses a filled diamond at the whole end and strong ownership: a part is in at most one composite at a time, and parts still owned are destroyed with that composite. Parts may be detached/transferred under a defined model. Thus “cannot ever exist independently” is an oversimplification. For Car composing Engine, the diamond belongs beside Car; saying it points to Engine is imprecise. The intended bank relationship is composition.
Shared aggregation uses a hollow diamond at the whole end and weak whole-part meaning;

reviews.answer_text: Composition has exclusive composite ownership at a time and destroys still-owned parts with the whole; shared aggregation gives weaker whole-part meaning.
reviews.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.
reviews.explanation: Composition gives strong ownership: a part is in at most one composite at a time, and still-owned parts are destroyed with that composite. Shared aggregation indicates weaker whole-part meaning without that detailed lifecycle policy. A model can permit detachment or transfer, so permanent inability to exist independently is too strong. Neither relationship is inheritance, and composition is not restricted to interfaces.

evidence.quote: Composition uses a filled diamond at the whole end and strong ownership: a part is in at most one composite at a time, and parts still owned are destroyed with that composite. Parts may be detached/transferred under a defined model. Thus “cannot ever exist independently” is an oversimplification. For Car composing Engine, the diamond belongs beside Car; saying it points to Engine is imprecise. The intended bank relationship is composition.

choices.explanation: Composition is not restricted to interfaces.
