options.text: A function invoked by the browser runtime or API when the response becomes available

options.label: B
options.text: A function that is called by the client to request a specific operation from the server

options.label: C
options.text: A function that is called by the server to handle concurrent client requests

options.label: D
options.text: A function that is called by the client to synchronize with the server

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified browser response handling and corrected who invokes the function.
assumptions: The callback is the browser’s response handler for an asynchronous request.

reviews.hint: Identify the execution side and communication pattern, keeping runtime, transport, data format and callback roles distinct.
reviews.explanation: WebSocket establishes a persistent bidirectional channel on which either endpoint can exchange messages after the handshake. HTTP requests can also be issued asynchronously, but asynchronous programming alone does not supply this specific channel model. FTP has a different transfer role, and TCP/IP names lower-level networking foundations rather than the requested application protocol. The revised interaction requirement therefore distinguishes WebSocket without claiming it is the only way to avoid blocking a client.

evidence.quote: WebSocket establishes a persistent bidirectional message channel after its handshake.
Either HTTP-based AJAX or WebSockets can support nonblocking user interaction and carry JSON, so generic questions may be nonexclusive.
HTTP defines web application requests, response status codes and representations.
An HTTP exchange can use underlying TCP connections and IP addresses; naming that network stack does not identify the application-level method or status semantics.
FTP is a file-transfer application protocol.
SMTP transports electronic mail.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Asynchronous HTTP requests do not by themselves define this persistent bidirectional message channel.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FTP is not the specified WebSocket-style application messaging protocol.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: TCP/IP refers to lower-level networking rather than this application-level channel protocol.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: WebSocket supplies the described persistent bidirectional channel.

question_revision.original_stem:
Which protocol is commonly used for asynchronous communication between a client and
server?
question_revision.stem: Which application-level protocol provides a persistent bidirectional message channel after its handshake?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Replaced the nonexclusive asynchronous requirement with the channel model.
assumptions: The requirement is the persistent bidirectional application-level channel after a handshake.

reviews.answer_text: write is a property; write is a method; document is a property; write is an object
reviews.hint: Track the value and type at each operation, applying the stated conversion, indexing or mathematical rule.
reviews.explanation: document.write is a method and also a function-valued property of document. In a normal browser page, document is exposed as a property of window. Functions are objects in JavaScript, so the write function value is also an object. These descriptions are compatible views of the same expression rather than mutually exclusive categories. All four statements are therefore true under the explicit inclusive-classification convention.

evidence.quote: In a normal browser page, window exposes the browsing context and document is its document property.
document.write is a method/function property; writing after document load can replace the document.
JavaScript primitives are undefined, null, Boolean, Number, BigInt, String and Symbol; objects include arrays, functions and dates.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: write is a function-valued property of document.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Calling that function through document is a method invocation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: document is the browsing context’s document property.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The write function value is an object because JavaScript functions are objects.

question_revision.original_stem: Which one is true about the following JavaScript statement? document.write("Hello World");
question_revision.stem: In an ordinary browser page, which statements about document.write("Hello World") are true? Classify properties and values inclusively: a method is also a function-valued property. Select all that apply.
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified inclusive classification and allowed every true description.
assumptions: Normal browser window; method, property and object-value descriptions are inclusive.

reviews.answer_text: Remove list bullets and default margin/padding.
reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB08 explicitly evaluates this navigation reset. list-style-type:none removes markers, and zero margin/padding removes default list spacing. None of those declarations specifies alignment, hover styling, or dropdown behavior. Thus A describes the actual effect, leaving layout and interaction to additional rules. This version has intact options unlike original-wave Q00888.

evidence.quote: Resetting nav ul with list-style-type:none; margin:0; padding:0 removes bullets and default spacing only; it does not itself arrange links horizontally or create a dropdown.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: These declarations remove markers and default spacing so later layout rules can start from a clean list.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No text alignment, flex justification, or positioning rule aligns the navbar right.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No :hover selector or hover-specific declaration is present.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A dropdown needs additional layout and interaction rules, not just this reset.

reviews.hint: Identify the data source or security responsibility precisely, and check whether a combined source or a different control could also qualify.
reviews.explanation: $_GET is the dedicated query-parameter source. $_REQUEST can also contain GET values depending on configuration, but it is a combined-source array and is explicitly excluded by this question. $_POST represents supported form POST data, while isset tests existence and non-null rather than acting as an input-data container. Removing placeholder brackets makes the array names clear without inventing a particular field name or request value.

evidence.quote: $_GET contains query parameters; $_POST contains supported form POST data; $_FILES upload metadata; $_SERVER request/environment details; $_COOKIE cookie values; $_SESSION session data after startup.
$_REQUEST may combine GET/POST/cookie data according to configuration; it is not a database interface and has ambiguous precedence, so prefer the intended source.
isset tests existence and non-null, not truth or valid syntax.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This combines configured request sources rather than being dedicated to query parameters.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the supported form POST source.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the dedicated URL-query source.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This tests whether a variable or entry exists and is non-null.

question_revision.original_stem:
Which one of the following php method is used to retrieve the information from the form 
control through the parameters sent in the URL?
question_revision.stem: Which PHP superglobal is dedicated to URL query parameters, excluding configurable combined-source arrays?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the dedicated source and removed placeholder brackets.
assumptions: Array names are requested, not complete element-read expressions.

reviews.hint: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages.
reviews.explanation: WEB02 defines hosting as supplying the environment where a website is served. This is the service enabling an organization’s site or page to be made available online. An ISP supplies connectivity, domain registration reserves a name, and a web client requests resources. Those supporting roles are not the hosting service described.

evidence.quote: Hosting supplies an environment where a site is served; domain registration reserves a name, and DNS maps names to network records.
An ISP provides connectivity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Hosting supplies an environment in which the site is served to users.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ISP provides connectivity rather than necessarily the environment serving the website.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A web client requests resources instead of providing the publishing environment.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Domain registration reserves a name rather than serving the site’s content.

reviews.hint: Identify the protocol layer and the intended request, response or channel semantics.
reviews.explanation: WEB01 describes the Web as a resource system commonly using HTTP, and WEB03 details its request/response exchange. HTTPS adds TLS protection to HTTP but does not make one of the other offered protocols the ordinary web exchange. Among these choices, HTTP is the application protocol used to request and return web resources.

evidence.quote: The Internet connects networks; the Web is a resource system commonly using HTTP.
An HTTP/1.1 request begins with method, request-target and version, followed by header fields, a blank line, and an optional body.
HTTP defines web application requests, response status codes and representations.
An HTTP exchange can use underlying TCP connections and IP addresses; naming that network stack does not identify the application-level method or status semantics.
FTP is a file-transfer application protocol.
SMTP transports electronic mail.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FTP is not the HTTP request/response web protocol described in the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SMTP is not the webpage request/response protocol developed in WEB03.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: HTTP carries the web resource requests and responses described in the complete note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SSH is not the ordinary webpage request/response protocol identified here.

reviews.answer_text: .js is the conventional JavaScript source extension.
reviews.hint: Check exact language syntax, declaration rules and execution context before reasoning about the result.
reviews.explanation: WEB15 uses an external app.js script and explicitly calls it a .js file. B identifies that extension family despite its uppercase printed letters. Actual filename case must match the deployed resource where paths are case-sensitive; the conventional spelling is lowercase .js. The other choices name different or invented file extensions rather than JavaScript source.

evidence.quote: Use <script src="app.js"></script> for an external .js file; script content has no HTML closing-tag syntax inside its JavaScript source.
JavaScript originated at Netscape; it is distinct from Java and supports sophisticated applications through prototype-based objects and first-class functions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The invented .javaS suffix is not the conventional .js extension specified by WEB15.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This identifies the JS extension; use conventional lowercase .js and preserve actual filename case in paths.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: .java is not the .js source-file extension used for JavaScript in the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: CSS identifies stylesheet source rather than the JavaScript file extension.

reviews.answer_text: The cookie edit can bypass the transfer endpoint, but does not grant access to the profile endpoint
reviews.hint: Follow the identifier and server-side state through the stated lifecycle or access check; distinguish client-controlled claims from server decisions.
reviews.explanation: The two endpoints use different trust paths. The transfer endpoint trusts an attacker-controlled flag, so the forged value satisfies its stated access check without a valid session. The profile endpoint requires authenticated server-side state, which the attacker lacks, so the unrelated cookie does not grant access there. HTTPS protects transport rather than validating the truth of a client-generated login claim. The bypass therefore affects the transfer endpoint only.

evidence.quote: A client cookie logged_in=1 is attacker-controlled.
If the server trusts it alone, authorization can be bypassed.
If the server checks a valid session ID and its server-side user/role on every protected action, editing that unrelated flag does not grant rights.
HTTPS does not make client-generated claims trustworthy.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Only the transfer endpoint relies solely on the forgeable flag; the profile endpoint still requires a valid session.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Receiving the same cookie does not make the endpoints apply the same authorization rule.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The transfer check requires no genuine session identifier, so stealing one is unnecessary for that bypass.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: HTTPS does not prevent a client from submitting a false authorization flag.

question_revision.original_stem:
A developer stores user login status in both 
$_SESSION['user_id'] on the server 
document.cookie = "logged_in=1" on the client 
An attacker tampers with cookies to set logged_in=1 without authenticating. Which 
statement is the most accurate?

original_options.label: A
original_options.text: The system is vulnerable — cookie-only checks bypass server session validation

original_options.label: B
original_options.text: The system is secure — session data cannot be forged without the server-side secret

original_options.label: C
original_options.text: The system is vulnerable only if session_id is exposed

original_options.label: D
original_options.text: The system is secure if HTTPS is used,

question_revision.stem: A web application has two protected endpoints. The profile endpoint checks a valid session identifier and its server-side user record on every request. The transfer endpoint grants access whenever the editable logged_in cookie equals 1 and ignores session validation. An unauthenticated attacker has no valid session and sets logged_in=1. Which result follows from these access checks?

options.label: A
options.text: The cookie edit can bypass the transfer endpoint, but does not grant access to the profile endpoint

options.label: B
options.text: The cookie edit grants access to both endpoints because both receive the same cookie

options.label: C
options.text: Neither endpoint can be bypassed unless the attacker first obtains a genuine session identifier

options.label: D
options.text: HTTPS alone prevents either endpoint from accepting a forged logged_in value

question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: A distinct application scenario makes the execution or interface assumptions explicit.
assumptions: The stated endpoint checks are enforced exactly; the attacker has no valid session or server-side user record.

reviews.answer_text: Provide an accessible label associated with the input.
reviews.hint: Separate the control role, displayed content, submitted value and form destination.
reviews.explanation: WEB09 links a label’s for to the control id, and WEB07 requires programmatic control labels. That association lets assistive technology identify the input and announce its label. It does not alter storage, encryption, or network submission speed. D states the accessibility purpose directly, rather than confusing it with unrelated browser or transport features.

evidence.quote: A label’s for matches the control’s id; name identifies its submitted field.
Give controls programmatic labels, clear link text and keyboard access; visual styling alone does not establish accessibility.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Label association does not create offline storage for form values.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Labels do not encrypt data or replace HTTPS transport protection.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Associating a label does not accelerate form submission over the network.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The programmatic label identifies the focused input for screen readers and other assistive technology.

reviews.answer_text: GET retrieves safely and usually places form values in the query; POST asks the target to process body content.
reviews.hint: Identify the protocol layer and the intended request, response or channel semantics.
reviews.explanation: WEB04 recommends GET for reading representations rather than intentional state changes. POST suits submitted processing or actions such as enrollment with proper authorization and CSRF controls. Neither method encrypts data; use HTTPS for channel protection. POST body values remain visible to tools and subject to configured size limits rather than becoming secret or unlimited.

evidence.quote: GET retrieves a representation with safe semantics; do not implement an intentional state-changing action as a GET link.
POST asks the target to process supplied content.
GET forms usually put name/value pairs in the URL query; POST forms put them in the body.
For an enrollment action use POST with CSRF controls, server authorization, capacity checks and a transaction; show success only after commit.

reviews.answer_text: Clients can bypass or alter browser checks, so the server must validate and authorize again.
reviews.hint: Separate event dispatch, handler registration and cancellation of the browser default action.
reviews.explanation: WEB27 requires server checks for required fields, type, length, and range, plus authentication and authorization before processing. Browser validation improves feedback but arbitrary clients can submit different requests. Bind SQL values and encode output for its context as well; encryption or merely connecting to a database does not replace these application controls.

evidence.quote: Read input, check required fields/type/length/range, authenticate and authorize, then process.
Bind SQL parameters to keep values separate from commands.
Encode output for HTML/attribute/JS context; textContent handles plain browser text.
Browser checks improve feedback; repeat validation and authorization on the server.

reviews.answer_text: The DOM is the document’s node hierarchy, enabling scripts to inspect and update page content and behavior.
reviews.hint: Track which node is selected or created, and distinguish changing content from attaching a node.
reviews.explanation: WEB20 selects nodes, creates elements, and attaches them to that hierarchy. Creating a node does not itself insert it, and missing lookups must be guarded. textContent safely inserts untrusted plain text, whereas innerHTML reparses markup and can replace descendant state. The DOM connects document structure to interactive browser updates.

evidence.quote: The DOM is a hierarchy of nodes representing the document.
Creation alone does not insert it.
innerHTML parses/replaces descendants, so += reparses/replaces the prior descendant content too and can destroy listeners/state.
Use textContent for untrusted plain text.

reviews.answer_text: A persistent remember/session token or browser restoration can preserve the login flow.
reviews.hint: Follow the identifier and server-side state through the stated lifecycle or access check; distinguish client-controlled claims from server decisions.
reviews.explanation: WEB28 says reopening while logged in may use persistent session or remember tokens or browser restoration. The browser can retain an identifier, but the server still has to accept and validate it against its authorization state. Local persistence alone is not proof of authenticated access, and the observation does not identify one unique storage mechanism.

evidence.quote: Being logged in after reopening may use a persistent session/remember token or browser restoration; storage alone does not prove server acceptance.
If the server checks a valid session ID and its server-side user/role on every protected action, editing that unrelated flag does not grant rights.

reviews.answer_text: localStorage persists origin data without automatically attaching it to every matching request.
reviews.hint: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages.
reviews.explanation: WEB28 contrasts localStorage’s persistent strings with cookies’ automatic request transmission. It can avoid transmitting data needed only by the client. JavaScript can still send stored tokens explicitly, so localStorage is not inherently incapable of session designs. Script-access risks and persistence policies must be considered; neither mechanism is universally preferable for sensitive authentication data.

evidence.quote: localStorage persists origin-specific string values across sessions until removed/cleared; sessionStorage is scoped to a page session/tab.
Neither is automatically transmitted like matching cookies, but JavaScript can send stored data explicitly.
Thus all four are client storage techniques, and localStorage can participate in token-based session designs, with script-access risks.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB06 directly expands HTML as HyperText Markup Language. The name identifies markup used for document structure and meaning rather than a general programming or transfer protocol. The other phrases substitute different words and are not the expansion in the note. This vocabulary answer does not depend on a browser version or an implementation choice.

evidence.quote: HTML means HyperText Markup Language.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Hyper Text Markup Language matches the note’s expansion, with only spacing variation in HyperText.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: High Tech Modern Language is not the expansion given in WEB06.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transfer replaces the required word Text and gives the wrong expansion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Home Tool Markup Language is not the HTML expansion in the note.

reviews.hint: Identify which elements a rule targets and distinguish selector syntax from declaration syntax.
reviews.explanation: WEB07 gives Read as the link pattern. The anchor element creates the user-facing hyperlink; href is its destination attribute, not a standalone tag. link is used for relationships such as external stylesheets, and url is not the anchor element. Thus C names the correct element among the supplied choices.

evidence.quote: Use Read for a link; href is the destination, not url/link.
An external sheet uses <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css"> in head; an internal sheet uses style; an inline declaration uses an element’s style attribute.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: link is used for resource relationships such as external stylesheets rather than the shown user-facing anchor.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: href is an attribute on an anchor, not the hyperlink element itself.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The anchor element with href creates the hyperlink described in WEB07.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: url is not the supported HTML anchor tag.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation:
WEB06 explicitly distinguishes
as a line break from

paragraphs and

thematic breaks. C is the defined break element; the other options invent element names not used by the note. A line break is an HTML structure operation rather than a requirement to insert a physical newline into the source file.

evidence.quote:
marks paragraphs;
is a line break and

a thematic break.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: break is not the HTML line-break element defined in WEB06.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: lb is not the supported line-break element spelling.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: br is explicitly the HTML line-break element.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: newline is not the HTML line-break element defined in the note.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB06 gives <pre> the whitespace-preservation role. It is therefore the appropriate element for text whose source spaces and line breaks should be retained. code marks code semantics but does not itself guarantee preformatted whitespace, while paragraph and emphasis elements have other meanings. Custom CSS can alter defaults, but the question concerns the native tag role.

evidence.quote: <pre> preserves source whitespace; <code> marks code.
<strong> indicates importance and <em> stress; <b>/<i> have other text semantics and are not identical to importance/emphasis.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A paragraph does not itself preserve all source spacing and line breaks.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: pre is the element explicitly defined to preserve source whitespace.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: code marks code semantics; preformatted whitespace preservation is a separate role.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: em expresses stress emphasis rather than preformatted source layout.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB06 defines heading levels h1 through h6 as a hierarchy. h1 is the highest level and h6 the lowest, regardless of CSS choices that can change their visual size. heading and h0 are not the defined heading-level tags. The answer is semantic rank, not whichever text happens to be styled largest.

evidence.quote: Heading levels h1–h6 express hierarchy, with h6 conventionally smallest in default styling, not a mandatory CSS size.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: h6 is the lowest of the defined heading levels, not the highest.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: heading is not one of the defined h1–h6 heading-level tags.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: h0 is outside the defined heading levels in WEB06.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: h1 is the highest semantic heading level in the h1–h6 hierarchy.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB06 explicitly identifies html as the document root, with head holding metadata and body containing document content. Those two elements are inside the document rather than replacing its root. root is not the HTML tag used for this role. Thus the root-element question directly selects C.

evidence.quote: <!DOCTYPE html> selects modern standards mode; <html> is the document root, <head> holds metadata, and <body> contains document content.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: head holds metadata and is not the document root.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: body holds document content but is not the document’s root element.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: html is explicitly defined as the document root in WEB06.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: root is not the HTML root tag given by the note.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB07 gives img a src for its resource and alt for alternative text. Informative images need meaningful alternatives; decorative ones use empty alt. A title is not a replacement for alt, and a caption is separate visible context rather than the requested attribute. Therefore C names the accessibility text attribute.

evidence.quote: supplies source and alternative text.
Use empty alt for purely decorative images; informative images need meaningful alternatives.
Width/height reserve dimensions; title is not a replacement for alt.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: title is not a replacement for the image’s alternative-text attribute.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: src identifies the image resource rather than its alternative text.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: alt supplies the image’s alternative text, or an empty value for purely decorative images.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: caption is not the requested image alternative-text attribute.

reviews.answer_text: Open a new browsing context, commonly a new tab or window.
reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB07 maps _blank to a new context, _self to current, and _parent to parent. Browser preferences decide tab versus window, so B correctly allows either. The target does not close the current window or select the parent frame. This is a browsing-context request rather than a guaranteed window-management UI behavior.

evidence.quote: target="_self" uses the current context, _blank a new context, _parent its parent and _top the top-level context.
Browser preferences determine tab versus window.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The current context is selected by _self rather than _blank.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: _blank requests a new context, with tab versus window determined by browser behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The target does not request that the current window be closed.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The parent context is selected by _parent rather than _blank.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB08 defines ul as unordered and ol as ordered, with li items inside either. C therefore supplies the requested container. li is only an item, and list is not the defined HTML list-container name. Presentation of markers can be changed with CSS without changing whether the element is the unordered-list structure.

evidence.quote: Unordered <ul> and ordered <ol> contain <li> items.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: ol is an ordered-list container, not the unordered-list container requested.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: li marks an item inside a list rather than the list container itself.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: ul is explicitly the unordered-list container in WEB08.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: list is not the unordered-list element spelling defined by the note.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB08 distinguishes the table element, row elements, and header/data cells. tr defines one row, while th and td are cells placed within rows. table contains the complete tabular structure. Therefore D is the row tag, independent of how many columns or spans the cells in that row occupy.

evidence.quote: <table> contains rows <tr>, header cells <th> and data cells <td>; a td is not the table itself.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: td defines a data cell, not the containing row.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: th defines a header cell, not the containing row.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: table defines the whole table rather than one row.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: tr is the table-row element explicitly identified in WEB08.

reviews.answer_text: Make one cell span multiple columns.
reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB08 explicitly distinguishes colspan from rowspan. colspan allocates a cell across columns, often described informally as merging cells horizontally; it does not change a column’s color or width rule. rowspan is the vertical counterpart across rows. B therefore matches, while actual placement must still account for positions already occupied by spans.

evidence.quote: colspan spans columns; rowspan spans rows.
Account for occupied cells before placing the next cell, and use header associations for accessible data.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Column color is a styling concern rather than the colspan structural span.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: colspan makes one cell occupy positions across multiple columns.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Column width is not the meaning of the colspan count.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Spanning rows is rowspan, not colspan.

reviews.hint: Identify the requested presentation effect and layout context before matching the property or rule.
reviews.explanation: WEB06 gives viewport metadata control over mobile viewport behavior, and WEB14 includes it alongside flexible layout and media queries for responsive design. Keywords and description concern metadata for content/discoverability, while robots concerns crawler directives. The viewport entry is the relevant mobile-layout metadata; it does not replace responsive CSS by itself.

evidence.quote: Meta charset declares encoding; description summarizes the page; viewport controls mobile viewport behavior.
Responsive design combines flexible layout, images, viewport metadata and media queries, for example @media(max-width:600px){.cards{grid-template-columns:1fr}}.
The keywords metadata name supplies terms relevant to the page, while description supplies a page summary.
Robots metadata supplies crawler indexing or search-presentation instructions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Keywords metadata does not configure the mobile viewport used for responsive layout.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Robots metadata concerns crawler handling rather than the mobile viewport.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Description summarizes the page rather than controlling mobile viewport behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Viewport metadata configures mobile viewport behavior as part of responsive design.

reviews.hint: Identify which elements a rule targets and distinguish selector syntax from declaration syntax.
reviews.explanation: WEB11 explicitly uses #logo as an ID selector and .notice as a class selector. Thus an element whose id is logo is targeted with #logo. A bare logo would be a type selector for an element named logo, while the starred concatenation is not the stated ID syntax. D is the correct selector.

evidence.quote: Type p selects paragraph elements, .notice selects a class, #logo an ID, h1,h2 groups selectors, nav ul selects descendants and nav>ul direct children.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: .logo targets a class named logo rather than id="logo".

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Bare logo is a type selector, not the ID selector requested.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: *logo is not the defined CSS ID-selector syntax.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: #logo is the explicit ID-selector pattern supplied in WEB11.

reviews.hint: Identify which elements a rule targets and distinguish selector syntax from declaration syntax.
reviews.explanation: WEB11 gives a dot-prefixed name as a class selector and a hash-prefixed name as an ID selector. Applying that rule to highlight yields .highlight. A bare word selects element type, and *highlight is not the supported class syntax. The class rule can match every element carrying that class, rather than only one unique ID.

evidence.quote: Type p selects paragraph elements, .notice selects a class, #logo an ID, h1,h2 groups selectors, nav ul selects descendants and nav>ul direct children.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: #highlight selects an ID rather than elements with the highlight class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: .highlight is the dot-prefixed class selector matching the requested class.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: *highlight is not the defined class-selector syntax.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Bare highlight is an element-type selector rather than a class selector.

reviews.hint: Identify which elements a rule targets and distinguish selector syntax from declaration syntax.
reviews.explanation: WEB11 says external CSS promotes reuse and consistent design through a linked stylesheet. Multiple documents can link the same styles.css file, so one shared source applies across pages. Inline declarations belong to one element and internal/embedded style blocks belong to their document. They can be copied, but copying is not the shared-source attachment method requested.

evidence.quote: An external sheet uses <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css"> in head; an internal sheet uses style; an inline declaration uses an element’s style attribute.
External CSS promotes reuse, consistent design and caching; it does not guarantee that every page becomes smaller or accessible.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Inline declarations belong to an element rather than one shared stylesheet linked by multiple pages.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An internal style block belongs to its document rather than a separately shared resource.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple pages can link the same external stylesheet for shared rules and maintenance.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Embedded styles are document-local rather than the shared external attachment method.

reviews.hint: Identify which elements a rule targets and distinguish selector syntax from declaration syntax.
reviews.explanation: WEB11 groups selectors using h1,h2. The comma separates alternative selectors that receive the same declaration block. Semicolons separate declarations, colons separate a property from its value or occur in pseudo syntax, and dots introduce classes. Thus C is the selector-list grouping separator, not a declaration delimiter.

evidence.quote: Type p selects paragraph elements, .notice selects a class, #logo an ID, h1,h2 groups selectors, nav ul selects descendants and nav>ul direct children.
A rule is selector { property: value; }.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Semicolons separate declarations rather than selectors in a selector list.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A colon is not the separator for grouped alternative selectors.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A comma groups selector alternatives, as in the note’s h1,h2 example.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A dot introduces a class selector rather than grouping multiple selectors.

reviews.hint: Identify the requested presentation effect and layout context before matching the property or rule.
reviews.explanation: WEB13 assigns text-decoration effects such as underline. The specific value underline therefore adds an underline decoration. Bold uses font-weight and italic uses font-style; a strike-through is a different decoration value. The declaration changes presentation rather than the semantic importance or stress of the underlying HTML text.

evidence.quote: color sets text color; background-color sets background; font-size size, font-family face, font-style italic, font-weight weight, text-align inline-content alignment, and text-decoration effects such as underline.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Boldness is controlled by font-weight rather than the underline decoration.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Italic styling uses font-style rather than text-decoration:underline.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The underline value requests an underline text decoration.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A strike-through is a different decoration, not the underline value shown.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB06 says strong expresses importance while em expresses stress, and warns that b/i are not identical to those meanings. Thus the semantic-importance requirement selects strong rather than merely a bold-looking b. Default styling is commonly bold but CSS can change appearance; the semantic distinction remains the reason for the answer.

evidence.quote: <strong> indicates importance and <em> stress; <b>/<i> have other text semantics and are not identical to importance/emphasis.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: b has different text semantics and is not the element for importance specified in WEB06.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: bold is not the semantic importance element defined in the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: strong explicitly indicates importance and is the requested semantic choice.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: em marks stress emphasis rather than the stated importance role.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB06 pairs sub and sup with subscript and superscript. The raised exponent in E=mc² is a superscript, so sup is the matching element. sub would lower text, and small or em have other meanings rather than expressing the exponent’s raised placement. The answer identifies the markup role rather than a CSS font-size choice.

evidence.quote: <sub>/<sup> mark sub/superscripts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: sub marks subscript, the opposite vertical placement from the raised exponent.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: sup marks superscript such as the raised two in E=mc².

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: small does not identify the superscript placement required by the example.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: em marks stress emphasis rather than superscript position.

reviews.answer_text: Comments add source notes without appearing as ordinary page content.
reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB06 states that <!-- comment --> is not displayed but remains visible in source. Thus C’s ignored wording should mean ignored for ordinary visual rendering, not removed from the DOM or hidden from source inspection. Comments do not themselves style content or link an external file, so the other purposes do not match.

evidence.quote: <!-- comment --> is not displayed but remains visible in source.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: HTML comments are not displayed as ordinary document content.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Comments do not supply CSS declarations or style the content by themselves.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Comments hold source notes and are not normally rendered; they remain visible in source.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A comment is not the markup mechanism for linking external resources.

reviews.hint: Check exact language syntax, declaration rules and execution context before reasoning about the result.
reviews.explanation: WEB15 explicitly distinguishes function/global var from block-scoped let and const. Of the offered names, let declares a block-scoped variable. const would additionally prevent rebinding but is not offered here. def and dim are not JavaScript declaration keywords in the supplied syntax. Therefore B matches the requested scope behavior.

evidence.quote: var has function/global scope; let/const are block-scoped.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: var has function/global scope rather than the block scope requested.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: let declares a block-scoped JavaScript variable.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: def is not the JavaScript variable-declaration keyword defined in the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: dim is not the JavaScript variable-declaration keyword defined in the note.

reviews.hint: Check exact language syntax, declaration rules and execution context before reasoning about the result.
reviews.explanation: WEB15 says const prevents rebinding but does not prevent mutation of an object’s contents. That is the precise constant-binding property in the stem. var permits reassignment, while static and final are not the declaration form described here. D therefore answers the binding question without claiming that every object assigned to const becomes deeply immutable.

evidence.quote: var has function/global scope; let/const are block-scoped.
const prevents rebinding but not mutation of an object’s contents.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: static is not the const variable-declaration form for preventing rebinding.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: final is not the JavaScript binding declaration defined in WEB15.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: var permits reassignment and does not provide a constant binding.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: const prevents rebinding, though object contents can still be mutated.

reviews.hint: Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name.
reviews.explanation: WEB15 defines // comments as ending at the line end and /* */ as block comments. Therefore C is the single-line comment syntax. A block comment may be physically written on one line, but it remains a different delimiter form and can span lines. HTML and hash-style markers are not the single-line syntax requested in the note.

evidence.quote: // comments end at line end; /* */ span a block.
<!-- comment --> is not displayed but remains visible in source.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The shown marker is an HTML comment form rather than the standard JavaScript single-line form.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is block-comment syntax, even when physically written on one line.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Double slash starts a JavaScript comment that ends at the line end.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A hash is not the ordinary JavaScript single-line comment delimiter given in WEB15.

reviews.hint: Separate event dispatch, handler registration and cancellation of the browser default action.
reviews.explanation: The inline onsubmit convention consumes the value returned by validate. Returning false therefore cancels the form’s default submission in this stated setup. It does not clear fields or explicitly refresh the page. The caller matters: returning false from a callback installed through addEventListener would not by itself cancel submission and would require preventDefault instead. The revised question includes the handler convention needed for the definite result.

evidence.quote: Returning false from an addEventListener callback does not cancel it; return false works in an appropriate inline/onsubmit property handler whose caller uses that return.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The consumed false result cancels rather than initiates default submission.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No page-refresh action is requested by returning false.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The inline onsubmit return convention cancels the default submission.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Returning a Boolean does not clear control values.

question_revision.original_stem: What does return false do in a JavaScript form validation function?
question_revision.stem: A form uses onsubmit="return validate()". If validate() returns false, what happens to the cancelable default submission?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Specified the caller and handler convention.
assumptions: Inline onsubmit returns the validation result; the submission default is cancelable.

reviews.answer_text: window.onload is the handler property for the page load event.
reviews.hint: Separate event dispatch, handler registration and cancellation of the browser default action.
reviews.explanation: WEB22 says window.onload handles load, typically after dependent resources finish. D therefore names the relevant handler property, although the actual event name is load rather than window.onload. Click, submit, and input refer to other interactions. This distinction avoids confusing a property used to register a handler with the event object or event name itself.

evidence.quote: window.onload is a handler property for the load event, typically after dependent resources finish.
An event handler runs when an event occurs: click, input, keydown, mouseover, submit and load are examples.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: onclick handles clicks, not completion of page resource loading.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: onsubmit handles form submission, not the page load completion event.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: oninput handles control input changes, not the page load completion event.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: window.onload registers the handler for load, normally after dependent resources finish.

reviews.hint: Check exact language syntax, declaration rules and execution context before reasoning about the result.
reviews.explanation: WEB23 requires a dollar-prefixed PHP variable name and permits dynamic typing without a preceding type declaration. C correctly assigns the single-quoted string to $name. var name and let mix other declaration syntax with PHP, while bare name lacks the required sigil. No separate JavaScript-style declaration keyword is needed for this ordinary PHP assignment.

evidence.quote: Variables begin with $, then a letter/underscore and subsequent letters/digits/underscores; $AGE18 works but $18AGE does not.
Dynamic typing permits values of different types without a preceding type declaration, though optional declarations can constrain them.
A complete ordinary PHP assignment statement ends with a semicolon.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is not the ordinary PHP assignment syntax and lacks the dollar-prefixed variable name.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: let is not the PHP declaration syntax for this assignment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The dollar-prefixed variable and quoted string assignment are valid PHP syntax.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Bare name lacks the required dollar sigil for a PHP variable.

reviews.hint: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages.
reviews.explanation: WEB24 says strlen counts bytes, so it is the matching length function. For ordinary ASCII strings byte count also equals character count; multibyte Unicode can differ. strrev reverses, strpos locates a substring, and a word-count operation does not measure the string’s byte length. The qualification prevents treating strlen as a universal user-perceived-character counter.

evidence.quote: strlen counts bytes; strpos can return integer0 or false, requiring ===false for failure.
strrev reverses bytes and str_replace replaces matching content.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Word counting does not measure the string’s byte length.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: strrev reverses the byte sequence rather than returning its length.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: strlen returns byte length, matching the requested function with the Unicode caveat.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: strpos returns a substring position or false rather than a length.

reviews.hint: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages.
reviews.explanation: WEB24 defines strrev as reversing bytes. Hello is ASCII, so reversing its five bytes gives o,l,l,e,H in that order, retaining the original uppercase H at the final position. The function does not perform lowercase or uppercase conversion and does not leave the sequence unchanged. D is the exact returned string.

evidence.quote: strrev reverses bytes and str_replace replaces matching content.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Hello is unchanged, whereas strrev reverses the byte order.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Lowercasing is not the operation performed by strrev.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Uppercasing is not the operation performed by strrev.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Reversing the ASCII bytes H,e,l,l,o yields o,l,l,e,H.

reviews.hint: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages.
reviews.explanation: WEB24 identifies strpos as the substring-position function and warns that a successful position zero differs from false. Use strict ===false when checking failure so an initial-position match is not mistaken for absence. Replacement, length, and reversal functions perform different operations. Thus B names the lookup API rather than a transformation function.

evidence.quote: strlen counts bytes; strpos can return integer0 or false, requiring ===false for failure.
strrev reverses bytes and str_replace replaces matching content.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: str_replace changes matching content rather than reporting the match position.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: strpos finds a substring position, returning zero legitimately or false for failure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: strlen measures byte length rather than locating a substring.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: strrev reverses bytes instead of reporting a match location.

reviews.answer_text: include warns; failed require raises Error in PHP8 and stops normal execution if uncaught.
reviews.hint: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages.
reviews.explanation: WEB33 distinguishes include’s warning from require’s critical failure. B captures the conventional contrast when require’s failure is uncaught, but PHP8 raises a catchable Error rather than the older E_COMPILE_ERROR description. The distinction is failure behavior, not an inherent speed ranking. C reverses the behaviors and D denies the explicit difference.

evidence.quote: include evaluates another file in the current scope and warns on failure; require fails critically.
In PHP8 a failed require raises Error, which can be caught; uncaught it stops normal execution.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: No inherent speed advantage is the failure-handling distinction defined by WEB33.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the conventional contrast for an uncaught failure; PHP8 require raises a catchable Error.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This reverses include’s warning and require’s critical failure behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note explicitly distinguishes their behavior when the target file cannot be included.

reviews.hint: Identify the data source or security responsibility precisely, and check whether a combined source or a different control could also qualify.
reviews.explanation: $_POST directly represents supported form POST values. $_REQUEST can include POST values under some configurations, but it combines sources and is not dedicated to the form POST channel. $_GET represents URL query values and $_SESSION contains application session state. The source-specific wording makes C unique while preserving the fact that a configurable combined array may also expose some of the same submitted values.

evidence.quote: $_GET contains query parameters; $_POST contains supported form POST data; $_FILES upload metadata; $_SERVER request/environment details; $_COOKIE cookie values; $_SESSION session data after startup.
$_REQUEST may combine GET/POST/cookie data according to configuration; it is not a database interface and has ambiguous precedence, so prefer the intended source.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: $_GET supplies URL query values.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: $_SESSION supplies stored session state rather than the current form POST source.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: $_POST is dedicated to supported form POST data.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: $_REQUEST may combine POST with other configured sources.

question_revision.original_stem: Which PHP superglobal accesses form data sent via the POST method?
question_revision.stem: Which PHP superglobal is dedicated specifically to supported form data submitted through POST, rather than a configurable mixture of request sources?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Restricted the question to the dedicated form POST source.
assumptions: Supported form POST encoding; the dedicated source is requested.

reviews.hint: Identify the API and operation first, then distinguish connection setup, statement execution and result processing.
reviews.explanation: WEB32 directly assigns retrieval to SELECT, adding to INSERT, changing values to UPDATE, and removal to DELETE. Therefore D is the SQL statement role requested. This identifies the operation’s semantics; the actual query still needs appropriate columns, filters, authorization, and safe parameter handling when incorporating submitted values.

evidence.quote: SELECT retrieves rows; INSERT adds; UPDATE ...

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: INSERT INTO adds rows rather than naming the ordinary retrieval statement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: UPDATE changes stored values rather than the retrieval operation requested.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DELETE removes rows rather than retrieving them.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SELECT is explicitly the SQL operation that retrieves rows.

reviews.hint: Identify the API and operation first, then distinguish connection setup, statement execution and result processing.
reviews.explanation: WEB32 gives UPDATE ... SET as the form that changes values. SET introduces the target-column assignments, while WHERE limits which rows are affected. VALUES and INTO occur in other statement roles and do not replace SET’s assignment function. C therefore identifies the keyword requested, distinct from selecting the affected rows.

evidence.quote: SELECT retrieves rows; INSERT adds; UPDATE ...
WHERE limits affected/matching records; omitting it from DELETE ordinarily targets every row, subject to constraints, permissions and errors.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: VALUES does not introduce assignments in the UPDATE ... SET form given by the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: WHERE selects matching rows rather than assigning the new column values.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SET introduces the value assignments in an UPDATE statement.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: INTO does not replace SET for assignments in the stated UPDATE form.

reviews.answer_text: It ordinarily targets all rows for deletion, subject to constraints, permissions, and execution success.
reviews.hint: Identify the API and operation first, then distinguish connection setup, statement execution and result processing.
reviews.explanation: WEB32 says WHERE limits affected rows and omitting it from DELETE ordinarily targets every row. Thus D is the intended effect of a successful unrestricted DELETE. No first-row-only rule exists, and omission is not inherently a syntax error. Permissions, constraints, or other errors can still prevent the operation, so the outcome is not an unconditional execution guarantee.

evidence.quote: WHERE limits affected/matching records; omitting it from DELETE ordinarily targets every row, subject to constraints, permissions and errors.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Without a filter, the statement ordinarily targets rows rather than doing nothing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: There is no implicit first-row-only restriction when WHERE is omitted.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Omitting WHERE is not by itself the stated syntax error.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A successful unrestricted DELETE ordinarily deletes all targeted table rows, subject to database controls.

reviews.hint: Identify the API and operation first, then distinguish connection setup, statement execution and result processing.
reviews.explanation: WEB31 explicitly gives mysqli_connect(host,user,password,database,port,socket) as the MySQLi connection function. The other offered names are not the API identified by the note. Argument defaults and actual credentials affect connection success, so knowing the function name does not remove the need for configuration and failure handling. C is the valid connection entry point.

evidence.quote: mysqli_connect(host,user,password,database,port,socket) opens a connection; selecting a database can be deferred, and defaults make several arguments technically optional.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: mysql_open() is not the MySQLi connection function given in WEB31.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: db_connect() is not the standard MySQLi connection function identified here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: mysqli_connect() is explicitly the MySQLi connection-opening function in the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: connect_mysql() is not the offered standard API name described by WEB31.

reviews.answer_text: mysqli_insert_id($conn), for a generated AUTO_INCREMENT value on that connection.
reviews.hint: Identify the API and operation first, then distinguish connection setup, statement execution and result processing.
reviews.explanation: WEB32 identifies mysqli_insert_id($conn) as reporting the connection’s generated AUTO_INCREMENT value. It is not a universal lookup of an arbitrary last row or a promise of gapless IDs. B names the correct function; the others invent different names. A connection argument and appropriate successful insertion context are needed in actual procedural code.

evidence.quote: mysqli_num_rows counts a result’s rows; mysqli_affected_rows($conn) counts changed/inserted/deleted rows under its options; mysqli_insert_id($conn) reports a generated AUTO_INCREMENT value from the connection.
AUTO_INCREMENT generates numeric values but gaps and explicit values are possible; do not promise gapless consecutive business numbering.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: mysqli_last_id() is not the generated-value function named in WEB32.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: mysqli_insert_id($conn) reports the connection’s generated AUTO_INCREMENT value.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: mysqli_get_id() is not the API identified for the generated insert value.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: mysqli_row_id() is not the API named for a generated insert identifier.

reviews.hint: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages.
reviews.explanation: A variable declared outside functions has global scope. A function normally has separate local bindings, so it can explicitly import such a binding with global or access it through $GLOBALS. The keyword is therefore one mechanism, not a mandatory exclusive spelling. A static local remains a function-local binding whose value persists across calls; session state belongs to a superglobal available across scopes.

evidence.quote: A variable outside a function has global scope.
A function’s locals and by-value parameters are separate bindings; use global $x or $GLOBALS["x"] to refer to a global explicitly.
A static local retains its value across calls during the execution lifecycle; static storage is not simply another visibility scope.
Superglobals are available across scopes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary local bindings already belong to that function; this is not importing an outside binding.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A static local retains its value across calls but remains local to the function.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Global bindings are the outside-function bindings accessed by these two mechanisms.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Session state uses a superglobal available across scopes, rather than this ordinary binding import.

question_revision.original_stem: Which variable scope requires the global keyword to access inside a function?
question_revision.stem: Which ordinary PHP variable scope can be accessed inside a function using a global declaration or, alternatively, the $GLOBALS array?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: Both supported ways to access an outside binding are allowed.
assumptions: Use the explicit scope and standard definitions stated in the clarified prompt.

reviews.answer_text: A local variable that retains its value between calls during the execution lifecycle.
reviews.hint: Check exact language syntax, declaration rules and execution context before reasoning about the result.
reviews.explanation: WEB25 defines a static local by persistence across function calls. It remains a local binding and can change value; static is not the same as constant, global visibility, or server session storage. Thus C supplies both the local-scope and retained-state aspects, without treating static duration as an independent universal visibility scope.

evidence.quote: A static local retains its value across calls during the execution lifecycle; static storage is not simply another visibility scope.
Constants cannot normally be redefined during execution.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Static locals can change value; static does not mean immutable.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Static persistence does not make the variable a global visible everywhere.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A static local retains its value across calls during the execution lifecycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A static local is not the same as data stored in $_SESSION.

reviews.answer_text: Display the variable’s type and value.
reviews.hint: Check exact language syntax, declaration rules and execution context before reasoning about the result.
reviews.explanation: WEB23 explicitly states that var_dump displays type and value. It is diagnostic output, not a deletion, validation, or conversion guarantee. Observing a value can assist debugging, but it does not prove that the input satisfies application constraints. B is therefore the direct API purpose, while the alternatives describe unrelated operations.

evidence.quote: var_dump displays type and value.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: var_dump does not delete the variable whose diagnostic information it displays.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note explicitly defines var_dump as displaying type and value.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Diagnostic display is not a conversion of the original variable binding to a string.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Displaying a value does not establish application-specific validation.

reviews.hint: Check exact language syntax, declaration rules and execution context before reasoning about the result.
reviews.explanation: WEB23 says null means no value. Boolean represents true or false, String text, and integer numeric values; none is the same absence marker. In particular zero, false, and an empty string can be legitimate present values rather than null. D therefore matches the requested absence-of-value representation.

evidence.quote: Scalars include int,float,string,bool; arrays/objects are structured values and null means no value.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A Boolean is a true/false value rather than the absence marker.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A string, including an empty one, is not the null absence marker.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An integer such as zero is still a value rather than null.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NULL is explicitly the no-value representation identified in WEB23.

reviews.answer_text: POST form data normally goes in the request body rather than the URL query, subject to configured size limits
reviews.hint: Identify the protocol layer and the intended request, response or channel semantics.
reviews.explanation: Ordinary GET forms place name/value pairs in the URL query, whereas POST forms place them in the request body. This is a placement distinction, not encryption: tools can inspect the body, and servers impose configured limits. The other claims either put POST fields in the wrong location or assert universal speed/ease advantages that do not follow from the method semantics.

evidence.quote: GET forms usually put name/value pairs in the URL query; POST forms put them in the body.
Neither method encrypts data.
POST bodies are visible to developer tools and subject to server/configured size limits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Method choice does not guarantee that a POST operation is faster; this is not the placement contrast asked for.

choices.label: B
